How to Read This Book

This is a chapter-wise Question Bank: every MTP, RTP, and PYQ descriptive/scenario question that has tested a chapter, collected in one place with the official answer. MCQs are deliberately not included — practise those on the dedicated MCQ platform; this book is for descriptive/scenario practice with full worked solutions.

Colour key

Answer / Solution Case Scenario Examiner’s Comment Author’s Note Flagged / Unverified

  • Examiner’s Comment (tan/orange) is a real quote from ICAI’s own published "Examiner’s Comments on the Performance of the Examinees" — when you see this colour, it is ICAI’s own words.
  • Author’s Note (pale pink) is the author’s own identification of a likely pitfall where no real ICAI comment exists for that question — informed guidance, not an official finding, and may not apply in every case.
  • A flagged card (reddish border) means one detail on that question has not been independently re-verified with full confidence — still usable for practice, just read the answer a little more critically.

What's on every question card, and why

  • Source line — paper, question number, marks, and Approx Time (marks × 1.8 minutes, rounded up; RTP questions with no stated marks show a 10–20 minute range) — pace your practice the way you'd have to on the real exam.
  • Topic tag — just the topic number and its specific name (e.g. Topic 2.7: Revaluation model for subsequent measurement). You're already inside that chapter's own book, so the chapter name itself isn't repeated on every card — only the exact sub-topic, so you know precisely where to go back and re-read.
  • Student Self Notes — a small blank box for your own two lines on this specific question.
  • My NB Page No / My Tag / Revision Phase — one compact line under each answer. My NB Page No records the page in your own practice notebook where you worked this question by hand. My Tag is a freeform label of your own — try things like "Last-day Revision", "Not Important", "Easy", or "Must Practice" to triage your own revision; the box is intentionally blank so you choose the word. Revision Phase is three tick-boxes to mark off as you revisit a question in later revision passes.

"Sanjeevani Booti 2" — the Error Register (back of the book, not per chapter)

Six blank, dotted-line pages (three double-sided sheets) at the back of the book — alternating Concepts I Forgot and Mistakes I Repeated More Than Twice, with a "Chapter / Topic" column so one shared register can hold entries from any chapter. Revision in the final weeks should mean re-reading your own recorded mistakes, not every question again. If six pages isn't enough, keep a separate notebook for the rest — the point is the habit, not fitting everything in this book.

Coming in a future edition

Two ideas are locked in but not yet built, named here honestly rather than pretended to exist: OP/PP tags (marking which sitting is the original version of a recurring question vs. a later practice repeat) and short chapter names in the topic tag for the handful of very long chapter titles.

A few honest notes on these numbers

  • Each MTP/PYQ sitting's questions sum to 114 marks, not the paper's nominal 100 — Part II offers “answer any N of the remaining M”, and this book deliberately includes every optional question shown so you can practise all of them, not only the subset one particular sitting required.
  • RTP sittings contribute 0 marks to the total above — ICAI's own RTP documents are published without a marks-weighted answer key, not a gap in this book's tagging.
  • 763 of this edition's Common-Student-Mistakes notes are the author's own synthesized guidance (clearly labelled “Author's Note” wherever they appear), because a real ICAI Examiner's Comment document doesn't exist for every sitting yet.

I. Descriptive & Scenario-Based Questions (pure Intro to AS)

Full descriptive/scenario questions where this chapter is the sole topic tested (after independent-question splitting).

MTP January 2025 Set 2 · Q6(a) [OR-alt 2] · Marks: 4 · Approx Time: 8 minutes (approx.) · Topic 9: What are Carve Outs/Ins in Ind AS?
Question:

What do you mean by Carve outs/ins in Ind AS? Explain.

Answer / Solution:

Certain changes have been made in Ind AS considering the economic environment of the country, which is different as compared to the economic environment presumed to be in existence by IFRS. These differences are due to differences in economic conditions prevailing in India. These differences which are in deviation to the accounting principles and practices stated in IFRS, are commonly known as 'Carve-outs'. Additional guidance given in Ind AS over and above what is given in IFRS, is termed as 'Carve in'.

Author’s Note: A common error is treating every difference between Ind AS and IFRS as a "carve-out", without recognising that removal of an option available under IFRS is explicitly not treated as a carve-out under the Ind AS framework.

MTP May 2023 Set 2 · Q6(a) [OR-alt 1] · Marks: 5 · Approx Time: 9 minutes (approx.) · Topic 1: Introduction
Question:

"Accounting Standards standardize diverse accounting policies with a view to eliminate the non-comparability of financial statements and improve the reliability of financial statements." Discuss and explain the benefits of Accounting Standards.

Answer / Solution:

Accounting Standards standardize diverse accounting policies with a view to eliminate the non-comparability of financial statements and improve the reliability of financial statements. Accounting Standards provide a set of standard accounting policies, valuation norms and disclosure requirements. Accounting standards aim at improving the quality of financial reporting by promoting comparability, consistency and transparency, in the interests of users of financial statements.

The following are the benefits of Accounting Standards:

(i) Standardization of alternative accounting treatments: Accounting Standards reduce to a reasonable extent confusing variations in the accounting treatment followed for the purpose of preparation of financial statements.

(ii) Requirements for additional disclosures: There are certain areas where important information is not statutorily required to be disclosed. Standards may call for disclosure beyond that required by law.

(iii) Comparability of financial statements: The application of accounting standards would facilitate comparison of financial statements of different companies situated in India and facilitate comparison, to a limited extent, of financial statements of companies situated in different parts of the world. However, it should be noted in this respect that differences in the institutions, traditions and legal systems from one country to another give rise to differences in Accounting Standards adopted in different countries.

Author’s Note: A common error is listing the benefits of Accounting Standards as a generic definition of what AS is, rather than specifically explaining how they reduce comparability problems, mandate additional disclosure, and aid cross-company/cross-border comparison.

MTP May 2024 Set 1 · Q6(a) [OR-alt 2] · Marks: 4 · Approx Time: 8 minutes (approx.) · Topic 1: Introduction
Question:

What are the issues, with which Accounting Standards deal?

Answer / Solution:

Accounting Standards deal with the issues of (i) Recognition of events and transactions in the financial statements, (ii) Measurement of these transactions and events, (iii) Presentation of these transactions and events in the financial statements in a manner that is meaningful and understandable to the reader, and (iv) Disclosure requirements.

Author’s Note: A common error is listing only two or three of the four issues (recognition, measurement, presentation, disclosure), or substituting a generic description of "what Accounting Standards are" for this specific four-part enumeration the question asks for.

MTP September 2024 Set 2 · Q6(a) [OR-alt 1] · Marks: 4 · Approx Time: 8 minutes (approx.) · Topic 1: Introduction
Question:

“Accounting Standards standardize diverse accounting policies with a view to eliminate the non-comparability of financial statements and improve the reliability of financial statements.” Discuss and explain the benefits of Accounting Standards.

Answer / Solution:

Accounting Standards standardize diverse accounting policies with a view to eliminating non-comparability of financial statements and improving the reliability of financial statements. They provide a set of standard accounting policies, valuation norms, and disclosure requirements, aiming at improving the quality of financial reporting by promoting comparability, consistency, and transparency in the interests of users of financial statements.

Benefits of Accounting Standards:

(i) Standardization of alternative accounting treatments: Accounting Standards reduce, to a reasonable extent, confusing variations in the accounting treatment used to prepare financial statements.

(ii) Requirements for additional disclosures: there are certain areas where important information is not statutorily required to be disclosed; Standards may call for disclosure beyond that required by law.

(iii) Comparability of financial statements: applying accounting standards facilitates comparison of financial statements of different companies situated in India, and to a limited extent, of companies situated in different parts of the world — though differences in institutions, traditions, and legal systems from one country to another still give rise to differences in the Accounting Standards adopted in different countries.

Author’s Note: A common error here is listing only one or two benefits instead of covering the full range (standardisation, additional disclosure, comparability), or omitting the caveat that cross-country comparability remains limited by differing legal/institutional environments.

PYQ May 2025 · Q6(a) [OR-alt 1] · Marks: 4 · Approx Time: 8 minutes (approx.) · Topic 1: Introduction
Question:

What are Accounting Standards? Explain the objectives of "Accounting Standards" in brief, also state the advantages of setting Accounting Standards. (4 Marks)

Answer / Solution:

Accounting Standards are the written policy documents issued by Government relating to various aspects of measurement, treatment, presentation and disclosure of accounting transactions and events.

Objectives of Accounting Standards: (a) Accounting Standards harmonize the diverse accounting policies and practices followed by different companies in India. (b) Accounting Standards facilitate the preparation of financial statements and make them comparable. (c) Accounting Standards give a sense of faith and reliability to the users.

Advantages of setting Accounting Standards: (a) Accounting Standards make the financial statements of different companies comparable, which helps investors in decision making. (b) Accounting Standards prevent any misleading accounting treatment. (c) Accounting Standards prevent manipulation of data by the management.

Examiner’s Comment: A few examinees could not clearly explain objectives of "Accounting Standards" and advantages of setting the Accounting Standards.

PYQ May 2026 · Q6(a) [OR-alt 1] · Marks: 4 · Approx Time: 8 minutes (approx.) · Topic 5: Need Conv. towa. Global Stds
Question:

Explain the key aspects which required the need for convergence towards global standards of financial reporting. (4 Marks)

Answer / Solution:

A few key aspects which required the need for convergence are as under:

1. Raising funds from international markets: Each country has its own set of rules and regulations for accounting and financial reporting. Therefore, when an enterprise decides to raise capital from markets other than the country in which it is located, the rules and regulations of that other country will apply, requiring the enterprise to understand the differences between the rules governing financial reporting in the foreign country as compared to its own.

2. Comparability of Financial Statements: International analysts and investors would like to compare financial statements based on similar ASs, leading to a growing need for an internationally accepted set of ASs for cross-border filings, raising investor confidence generally.

3. Uniformity, Comparability, Transparency etc.: A strong need was felt to bring about uniformity, rationalisation, comparability, transparency and adaptability in financial statements. A multiplicity of AS systems worldwide produces different reported numbers for the same events, creating confusion and encouraging error or fraud. The cure is a single set of global standards, of the highest quality, set in the public interest.

4. Global Investment: Convergence contributes to the free flow of global investment, improves investors' ability to compare investments globally (lowering risk of errors of judgment), facilitates accounting/reporting for companies with global operations, eliminates costly requirements like reinstatement of financial statements, creates a new standard of accountability and transparency, and reduces operational challenges for accounting firms.

Author’s Note: Several examinees listed only one or two convergence drivers instead of the full range (fund-raising, comparability, uniformity, global investment), losing marks for an incomplete answer to a theory question that explicitly asks for "key aspects" in the plural.

Certain changes have been made in Ind AS considering the economic environment of the country, which is different as compared to the economic environment presumed to be in existence by IFRS. RTP May 2026 · Q5 · Marks: Not stated in source · Approx Time: 10–20 minutes (approx.) · Topic 6: International Acct Std Board
Question:

Write a short note on International Accounting Standard Board (IASB).

Answer / Solution:

With a view of achieving the objective of setting global standards, the London based group namely the International Accounting Standards Committee (IASC), responsible for developing International Accounting Standards (IAS), was established in June, 1973.

  • It is presently known as International Accounting Standards Board (IASB).
  • Between 1973 and 2001, the IASC released IASs. Between 1997 and 1999, the IASC restructured their organisation, which resulted in formation of IASB. These changes came into effect on 1st April, 2001. Subsequently, IASB issued statements about current and future standards.
  • IASB publishes its Standards in a series of pronouncements called International Financial Reporting Standards (IFRS).
  • The standards issued by IASC till 31.03.2001 are known as IASs and the standards issued by IASB since 01.04.2001 are known as IFRSs.
Author’s Note: Some examinees conflated the IASC and IASB timelines, or reversed which body issued IASs versus IFRSs, resulting in imprecise historical sequencing in their responses.

RTP May 2024 · Q5 · Marks: Not stated in source · Approx Time: 10–20 minutes (approx.) · Topic 1: Status of Accounting Standards
Question:

Based upon criteria for rating of non-corporate entity, categorize the following as Level I, Level II, Level III and Level IV entities for the purpose of compliance of Accounting Standards in India.

  1. Rama Textiles whose turnover (excluding other income) exceeds ten crore but does not exceed rupees fifty crore in the immediately preceding accounting year.
  2. Star Industries is having borrowings (including public deposits) in excess of rupees two crore but not in excess of rupees ten crore at any time during the immediately preceding accounting year.
  3. Newman Industries is having borrowings (including public deposits) less than rupees fifty lakh at any time during the immediately preceding accounting year.
  4. SS Finance is a financial institution carrying its business in India since last 10 years.
  5. DD Finance, holding company of SS Finance. (Entity mentioned at Point (v) above)
  6. Reliable Co-op Bank, a co-operative bank, carrying banking operations since last 15 years.
Answer / Solution:
  1. Level III Entity – Rama textiles, whose turnover (excluding other income) exceeds rupees ten crore but does not exceed rupees fifty crore in the immediately preceding accounting year.
  2. Level III Entity – Star industries is having borrowings (including public deposits) in excess of rupees two crore but not in excess of rupees ten crore at any time during the immediately preceding accounting year.
  3. Level IV Entity – Newman Industries is having borrowings (including public deposits) of less than rupees fifty lakhs at any time during the immediately preceding accounting year.
  4. Level I Entity – SS is a financial institution carrying its business in India since last 10 years.
  5. Level I Entity – DD finance, holding company of SS finance (Entity mentioned in point (d) above).
  6. Level I Entity – Reliable co-operative banks carrying on banking business for the last 15 years.
Author’s Note: A common error here is missing that a holding company of a Level I entity is itself automatically Level I regardless of its own size, and that banks/financial institutions/co-operative banks are Level I entities by their nature, not by a turnover or borrowings threshold.

RTP May 2026 · Q7 · Marks: Not stated in source · Approx Time: 10–20 minutes (approx.) · Topic 2.1: Revised MSME classification criteria - turnover/borrowings thresholds
Question:

Virat Traders, an unlisted partnership firm, had a turnover of ₹249.99 crore and borrowings of ₹25.01 crore during the financial year 2023-24. It is not a bank, financial institution, or insurance company, and also not a subsidiary of any other entity. The firm wishes to avail MSME exemptions for FY 2024-25. Is it eligible?

Answer / Solution:

Company qualifies as an MSME if following conditions are satisfied:

  1. whose equity or debt securities are not listed or are not in the process of listing on any stock exchange, whether in India or outside India;
  2. which is not a bank, financial institution or an insurance company;
  3. whose turnover (excluding other income) does not exceed 250 crore rupees in the immediately preceding accounting year;
  4. which does not have borrowings in excess of 50 crore rupees at any time during the immediately preceding accounting year; and
  5. which is not a holding or subsidiary of an entity which is not a MSME entity.

Yes, Virat Traders qualifies as an MSME since it meets all five criteria.

Further, it has been assumed that Virat Traders is not newly qualifying as an MSME in FY 2024-25 because a non-company entity that newly qualifies as an MSME can avail exemptions only after it remains as MSME for two consecutive years.

Until then, full AS compliance is required.

Author’s Note: Some examinees applied the five MSME tests mechanically and concluded eligibility without addressing the two-consecutive-year assumption for newly-qualifying entities, missing part of what the question was testing.

RTP September 2025 · Q4 · Marks: Not stated in source · Approx Time: 10–20 minutes (approx.) · Topic 1: Status of Accounting Standards
Question:

As per the revised scheme effective from accounting periods commencing on or after 1st April, 2024, classify non-company entities for the purpose of applicability of Accounting Standards. Briefly explain the criteria for each category.

Answer / Solution:

Non-company entities are classified into two categories: Micro, Small and Medium Sized Entities (MSMEs) and Large entities.

A non-company entity qualifies as an MSME if it satisfies all of: (i) its equity/debt securities are not listed or in the process of listing on any stock exchange (in India or abroad); (ii) it is not a bank, financial institution, or insurance company; (iii) turnover (excluding other income) does not exceed ₹250 crore in the immediately preceding accounting year; (iv) it does not have borrowings exceeding ₹50 crore at any time during the immediately preceding accounting year; and (v) it is not a holding or subsidiary of an entity that is not itself an MSME. These conditions are assessed as at the end of the relevant accounting period. A Large entity is any non-company entity that does not meet the MSME definition, and must comply in full with all Accounting Standards; MSMEs receive certain exemptions/relaxations.

Author’s Note: A direct recall question from the announcement text; common gaps include omitting one of the five MSME conditions, especially the holding/subsidiary condition.

MTP January 2025 Set 1 · Q6(a) [OR-alt 1] · Marks: 4 · Approx Time: 8 minutes (approx.) · Topic 9: Elements of Financial Statements
Question:

Briefly explain the elements of financial statements.

Answer / Solution:
ElementDefinition
AssetResource controlled by the enterprise as a result of past events from which future economic benefits are expected to flow to the enterprise.
LiabilityPresent obligation of the enterprise arising from past events, the settlement of which is expected to result in an outflow of a resource embodying economic benefits.
EquityResidual interest in the assets of an enterprise after deducting all its liabilities.
Income/gainIncrease in economic benefits during the accounting period in the form of inflows or enhancement of assets or decreases in liabilities that result in increase in equity other than those relating to contributions from equity participants.
Expense/lossDecrease in economic benefits during the accounting period in the form of outflows or depletions of assets or incurrence of liabilities that result in decrease in equity other than those relating to distributions to equity participants.
Author’s Note: A common gap is omitting income and expense from the list of financial statement elements, discussing only assets, liabilities and equity.

MTP January 2025 Set 2 · Q6(a) [OR-alt 1] · Marks: 4 · Approx Time: 8 minutes (approx.) · Topic 7: Qual. Char. Fin Stmts
Question:

"One of the characteristics of financial statements is neutrality"— Do you agree with this statement?

Answer / Solution:

Yes, one of the characteristics of financial statements is neutrality. To be reliable, the information contained in financial statement must be neutral, that is free from bias. Financial Statements are not neutral if by the selection or presentation of information, the focus of analysis could shift from one area of business to another thereby arriving at a totally different conclusion on the business results.

Author’s Note: A common error is confusing neutrality with conservatism/prudence, treating a deliberately cautious understatement of results as still "neutral" when it is in fact a form of bias in the opposite direction.

MTP May 2023 Set 1 · Q6(d) · Marks: 5 · Approx Time: 9 minutes (approx.) · Topic 5: Objectives & Users of Fin Stmts  +  Topic 6: Fundamental Accounting Assumptions  +  Topic 7: Qual. Char. Fin Stmts  +  Topic 9: Elements of Financial Statements
Question:

(i) With regard to financial statements name any four: (1) Users; (2) Qualitative characteristics; (3) Elements.
(ii) What are fundamental accounting assumptions? (5 Marks)

Answer / Solution:

(i) (1) Users of financial statements: Investors, Employees, Lenders, Suppliers/Creditors, Customers, Government & Public.
(2) Qualitative Characteristics of Financial Statements: Understandability, Relevance, Comparability, Reliability & Faithful Representation.
(3) Elements of Financial Statements: Asset, Liability, Equity, Income/Gain and Expense/Loss.

(ii) Fundamental Accounting Assumptions: Accrual, Going Concern and Consistency.

Author’s Note: A common error is confusing the four qualitative characteristics (Understandability, Relevance, Reliability, Comparability) with the three fundamental accounting assumptions (Going Concern, Accrual, Consistency), or listing "Materiality"/"Prudence" as standalone qualitative characteristics rather than as components nested within Relevance and Reliability respectively.

MTP May 2024 Set 1 · Q6(a) [OR-alt 1] · Marks: 4 · Approx Time: 8 minutes (approx.) · Topic 7: Qual. Char. Fin Stmts
Question:

What are the qualitative characteristics of the financial statements which improve the usefulness of the information furnished therein?

Answer / Solution:

The qualitative characteristics are attributes that improve the usefulness of information provided in financial statements. Understandability; Relevance; Reliability; Comparability are the qualitative characteristics of financial statements.

Understandability – Information presented in financial statements should be readily understandable by the users with reasonable knowledge of business and economic activities.

Relevance – Financial statements should contain relevant information only. Information, which is likely to influence the economic decisions of the users is called relevant.

Reliability – Information must be reliable; that is to say, they must be free from material error and bias.

Comparability – Financial statements should provide both inter-firm and intra-firm comparison.

Author’s Note: A common error is naming only two or three of the four characteristics, or confusing "Reliability" (freedom from material error/bias) with "Relevance" (capacity to influence economic decisions) – the two are frequently swapped in a rushed answer.

MTP May 2024 Set 2 · Q6(a) [OR-alt 2] · Marks: 4 · Approx Time: 8 minutes (approx.) · Topic 9: Elements of Financial Statements
Question:

Opening Balance Sheet of Mr. Amit is showing the aggregate value of assets, liabilities and equity ₹16 lakh, ₹6 lakh and ₹10 lakh respectively. During accounting period, Mr. Amit has the following transactions: (1) Earned 10% dividend on 4,000 equity shares held of ₹100 each. (2) Paid ₹1,00,000 to creditors for settlement of ₹1,40,000. (3) Rent of the premises is outstanding ₹20,000. (4) Mr. A withdrew ₹18,000 for his personal use. You are required to show the effect of above transactions on Balance Sheet in the form of Assets – Liabilities = Equity after each transaction.

Answer / Solution:

Effect of each transaction on the Balance Sheet:

TransactionsAssets (₹ lakh)Liabilities (₹ lakh)Equity (₹ lakh)
Opening16.00−6.00=10.00
(1) Dividend earned16.40−6.00=10.80
(2) Settlement of Creditors15.40−4.60=10.80
(3) Rent Outstanding15.40−4.80=10.60
(4) Drawings15.22−4.80=10.42
Author’s Note: A common error here is recording the ₹40,000 gain on settling ₹1,40,000 of creditors for ₹1,00,000 cash as if only the cash paid affects the position, instead of recognising that the ₹40,000 difference is a gain that increases equity while the full liability is extinguished.

MTP May 2025 Set 1 · Q6(a) [OR-alt 1] · Marks: 4 · Approx Time: 8 minutes (approx.) · Topic 7/9/11: Qual. Char. Fin Stmts / Elements of Financial Statements / Capital Maintenance
Question:

(i) With regard to financial statements, name any five qualitative characteristics and elements.

(ii) Aman started a business on 1st April 2023 with ₹24,00,000 represented by 1,20,000 units of ₹20 each. During the financial year ending on 31st March, 2024, he sold the entire stock for ₹30 each. In order to maintain the capital intact, calculate the maximum amount, which can be withdrawn by Aman in the year 2023-24 if Financial Capital is maintained at historical cost.

Answer / Solution:

(i) Qualitative Characteristics of Financial Statements: Understandability, Relevance, Comparability, Reliability & Faithful Representation.

Elements of Financial Statements: Asset, Liability, Equity, Income/Gain and Expense/Loss.

(ii)

ParticularsFinancial Capital Maintenance at Historical Cost (₹)
Closing equity (₹30 × 1,20,000 units)36,00,000, represented by cash
Opening equity1,20,000 units × ₹20 = 24,00,000
Permissible drawings to keep Capital intact12,00,000 (36,00,000 − 24,00,000)
Author’s Note: A common error in the capital-maintenance calculation is treating the ₹36,00,000 closing sale proceeds entirely as profit available for withdrawal, without first setting aside the ₹24,00,000 needed to restore the opening capital before any surplus can be withdrawn.

(ii)

ParticularsFinancial Capital Maintenance at Historical Cost (₹)
Closing equity (₹30 x 1,20,000 units)36,00,000 represented by cash
Opening equity1,20,000 units x ₹20 = 24,00,000
Permissible drawings to keep Capital intact12,00,000 (36,00,000−24,00,000)

MTP November 2023 Set 1 · Q6(c) · Marks: 5 · Approx Time: 9 minutes (approx.) · Topic 11: Capital Maintenance
Question:

A trader commenced business on April 1, 2022 with ₹1,20,000 represented by 6,000 units of a certain product at ₹20 per unit. During the year 2022-23 he sold these units at ₹30/- per unit and had withdrawn ₹60,000. The price of the product at the end of financial year was ₹25/- per unit. Compute retained profit of the trader under the concept of physical capital maintenance at current cost. Also state, whether answer would be different if the trader had not withdrawn any amount.

Answer / Solution:

In the given case, the specific price index applicable to the product is 125 (25/20 × 100).

Current cost of opening stock = (₹1,20,000/100) × 125 Or 6,000 units × ₹25 = ₹1,50,000

Current cost of closing cash = ₹1,20,000 (₹1,80,000 − ₹60,000)

Opening equity at closing current costs = ₹1,50,000

Closing equity at closing current costs = ₹1,20,000

Retained Profit = ₹1,20,000 − ₹1,50,000 = (−) ₹30,000

The negative retained profit indicates that the trader has failed to maintain his capital. The available fund of ₹1,20,000 is not sufficient to buy 6,000 units again at increased price of ₹25 per unit. The drawings should have been restricted to ₹30,000 (₹60,000 − ₹30,000).

If the trader had not withdrawn any amount, then the answer would have been as below:

Current cost of opening stock = ₹1,80,000

Opening equity at closing current costs = ₹1,50,000

Retained Profit = ₹1,80,000 − ₹1,50,000 = ₹30,000

If the trader had not withdrawn any amount, then the retained profit would have been ₹30,000.

Author’s Note: A common error is computing retained profit as historical sale proceeds less historical cost of goods sold (a financial-capital-maintenance answer) instead of restating the opening stock to its current replacement cost and comparing that against the closing cash balance, which is what the physical-capital-maintenance concept specifically requires.

MTP November 2023 Set 2 · Q6(d) · Marks: 4 · Approx Time: 8 minutes (approx.) · Topic 10: Meas of Elements of Fin Stmts
Question:

Explain in brief, the alternative measurement bases, for determining the value at which an element can be recognized in the Balance Sheet or Statement of Profit and Loss.

Answer / Solution:

The Framework for Recognition and Presentation of Financial statements recognizes four alternative measurement bases for the purpose of determining the value at which an element can be recognized in the balance sheet or statement of profit and loss. These bases are: (i) Historical Cost; (ii) Current cost (iii) Realizable (Settlement) Value and (iv) Present Value.

A brief explanation of each measurement basis is as follows:

  1. Historical Cost: Historical cost means acquisition price. According to this, assets are recorded at an amount of cash or cash equivalent paid or the fair value of the asset at the time of acquisition. Liabilities are generally recorded at the amount of proceeds received in exchange for the obligation.
  2. Current Cost: Current cost gives an alternative measurement basis. Assets are carried out at the amount of cash or cash equivalent that would have to be paid if the same or an equivalent asset was acquired currently. Liabilities are carried at the undiscounted amount of cash or cash equivalents that would be required to settle the obligation currently.
  3. Realisable (Settlement) Value: As per realizable value, assets are carried at the amount of cash or cash equivalents that could currently be obtained by selling the assets in an orderly disposal. Liabilities are carried at their settlement values; i.e. the undiscounted amount of cash or cash equivalents paid to satisfy the liabilities in the normal course of business.
  4. Present Value: Under present value convention, assets are carried at present value of future net cash flows generated by the concerned assets in the normal course of business. Liabilities under this convention are carried at present value of future net cash flows that are expected to be required to settle the liability in the normal course of business.
Author’s Note: A common error is confusing Current Cost with Realisable Value – both involve a “current” amount, but Current Cost is the cost to acquire an equivalent asset today while Realisable Value is the amount obtainable by selling the existing asset today, a distinction the Framework treats as two genuinely separate bases.

MTP September 2024 Set 1 · Q6(a) [OR-alt 2] · Marks: 4 · Approx Time: 8 minutes (approx.) · Topic 6: Fundamental Accounting Assumptions
Question:

Summarised Balance Sheet of Cloth Trader as on 31.03.2023: Liabilities – Proprietor's Capital 3,00,000; Profit & Loss Account 1,25,000; 10% Loan Account 2,10,000; Sundry Creditors 50,000; Total 6,85,000. Assets – Fixed Assets 3,60,000; Closing Stock 1,50,000; Sundry Debtors 1,00,000; Deferred Expenses 50,000; Cash & Bank 25,000; Total 6,85,000. Additional Information: (1) The remaining life of fixed assets is 8 years, pattern of use even; net realisable value of fixed assets on 31.03.2024 was ₹3,25,000. (2) Purchases and Sales in 2023-24 amounted to ₹22,50,000 and ₹27,50,000 respectively. (3) Cost and net realizable value of stock on 31.03.2024 were ₹2,00,000 and ₹2,50,000 respectively. (4) Expenses for the year amounted to ₹78,000. (5) Deferred Expenses are amortized equally over 5 years. (6) Sundry Debtors on 31.03.2024 are ₹1,50,000 of which ₹5,000 is doubtful; collection of another ₹25,000 depends on successful re-installation of certain product supplied. (7) Closing Sundry Creditors are ₹75,000, likely to be settled at 10% discount. (8) Cash balance as on 31.03.2024 is ₹4,22,000. (9) There is an early repayment penalty for the loan of ₹25,000. Required: Prepare Profit & Loss Account for the year 2023-24 (not assuming going concern).

Answer / Solution:

Profit and Loss Account for the year ended 2023-24 (not assuming going concern):

Particulars₹Particulars₹
To Opening Stock1,50,000By Sales27,50,000
To Purchases22,50,000By Closing Stock2,50,000
To Expenses78,000By Trade payables (discount on settlement)7,500
To Depreciation35,000
To Provision for doubtful debts30,000
To Deferred cost (written off, not assuming going concern)50,000
To Loan penalty25,000
To Net Profit (balancing figure)3,89,500
Total30,07,500Total30,07,500
Author’s Note: A common error is continuing to amortise the deferred expenses over their normal 5-year period and depreciate fixed assets on the usual straight-line basis, instead of writing off the deferred expenses immediately and depreciating fixed assets down to their net realisable value once the going concern assumption is dropped.

Income/gainIncrease in economic benefits during the accounting period in the form of inflows or enhancement of assets or decreases in liabilities that result in increase in equity other than those relating to contributions from equity participants.
Expense/lossDecrease in economic benefits during the accounting period in the form of outflows or depletions of assets or incurrence of liabilities that result in decrease in equity other than those relating to distributions to equity participants.
Author’s Note: A common error here is describing the five elements in generic terms instead of reproducing the Framework's precise formal definitions, particularly the distinction between an asset's control (not necessarily ownership) and its expected future economic benefit.

Mille started a business on 01.04.2022 with a capital of ₹15,00,000. She purchased 1,500 units of stock at ₹1,000 each. She sold the entire stock for ₹1,500 each unit till 31.03.2023.

PYQ September 2025 · Q6(a) [OR-alt 2] · Marks: 4 · Approx Time: 8 minutes (approx.) · Topic 1.2: The five key elements - assets, liabilities, equity, income, expenses
Question:

What are the key elements of financial statements? Explain.

Answer / Solution:
  1. Assets: a resource controlled by the enterprise from past events, expected to bring future economic benefits (e.g. plant, patents, receivables).
  2. Liabilities: a present obligation arising from past events, settlement of which is expected to result in an outflow of economic benefits (e.g. borrowings, provisions).
  3. Equity: the residual interest in assets after deducting all liabilities — owners' claim (capital, reserves), distinct from liabilities (claims of parties other than owners); changes through contributions/distributions or income/expenses.
  4. Income/Gain: increases in economic benefits through inflow of assets or reduction of liabilities, increasing equity (includes revenue and gains).
  5. Expenses/Loss: decreases in economic benefits through outflows/depletion of assets or incurrence of liabilities, decreasing equity (other than distributions to owners) — expenses arise in the ordinary course (e.g. wages); losses may or may not (e.g. loss on PPE disposal), and are shown separately to aid performance assessment.
Author’s Note: A direct theory recall question; common gaps include omitting the equity definition's distinction from liabilities, or failing to note that losses (unlike ordinary expenses) may fall outside the enterprise's normal activities.

Shiva started a business on 1st April 2022 with ₹15,00,000 represented by 80,000 units of ₹25 each. During the financial year ending on 31st March, 2023, he sold the entire stock for ₹35 each. Closing equity (₹35 x 80,000 units)28,00,000 represented by cash

RTP May 2026 · Q6 · Marks: Not stated in source · Approx Time: 10–20 minutes (approx.) · Topic 9: Elements of Financial Statements
Question:

Giant Ltd. has entered into a binding agreement with Tiny Ltd. to buy a custom-made machine of ₹1,00,000 at the end of 2024-25, before delivery of the machine, Giant Ltd. had to change its method of production. The new method will not require the machine ordered and it will be scrapped after delivery. The expected scrap value is nil.

You are required to advise the accounting treatment and give necessary journal entry in the year 2024-25.

Answer / Solution:

A liability is recognized when outflow of economic resources in settlement of a present obligation can be anticipated and the value of outflow can be reliably measured.

When flow of economic benefit to the enterprise beyond the current accounting period is considered improbable, the expenditure incurred is recognised as an expense rather than as an asset.

In the given case, Giant Ltd. should recognise a liability of ₹1,00,000 to Tiny Ltd.

Also, the flow of future economic benefit from the machine to the enterprise is improbable.

Thus, the entire amount of purchase price of the machine should be recognised as an expense.

Journal Entries

ParticularsDr. (₹)Cr. (₹)
Loss on Change in Production Method A/c Dr.1,00,000
  To Tiny Ltd.1,00,000
(Being loss due to change in production method)
Profit & Loss A/c Dr.1,00,000
  To Loss on Change in Production Method1,00,000
(Being loss transferred to P&L)
Author’s Note: Many examinees treated the non-deliverable bespoke machine as a contingent liability requiring only disclosure, rather than recognising a present obligation to pay Tiny Ltd. as a liability, leading to an understatement of expenses for 2024-25.

MTP January 2026 Set 1 · Q2(a) · Marks: 7 · Approx Time: 13 minutes (approx.) · Topic 1.10: Joint products and by-products - by-product NRV deducted from joint cost, remainder allocated by relative sales value
Question:

Happy Limited is a Textile Manufacturing Company producing Polyester (P) and Nylon (N); a by-product Fiber (F) is also produced. Cost of production: Raw material for 30,000 units ₹3,50,000; Wages ₹1,60,000; Fixed overheads ₹1,20,000; Variable overheads ₹60,000. Output: Polyester 12,500 units, Nylon 10,000 units, Fiber 3,200 units. Closing inventory: Polyester 1,600 units, Nylon 400 units. Average market price: Polyester ₹100/unit, Nylon ₹60/unit; by-product Fiber sold @₹40/unit, profit of ₹8,000 on sale of by-product after separate processing expenses ₹10,000 and packing charges ₹9,000. ₹5,000 realized from sale of scrap. Compute the value of closing inventory of Polyester and Nylon.

Answer / Solution:

As per AS 2 'Valuation of Inventories', most by-products, being immaterial, are measured at net realizable value, deducted from the cost of the main product.

W.N.1 — NRV of by-product Fiber: Selling price (3,200 × ₹40) 1,28,000 − separate processing charges 10,000 − packing charges 9,000 = ₹1,09,000.

W.N.2 — Joint cost allocation: Raw material 3,50,000 + Wages 1,60,000 + Fixed OH 1,20,000 + Variable OH 60,000 = 6,90,000; less NRV of Fiber (1,09,000) and scrap sale value (5,000) = Joint cost to allocate: 5,76,000.

ParticularsPolyesterNylon
Output (units)12,50010,000
Sales price/unit₹100₹60
Sales value12,50,0006,00,000
Joint cost 5,76,000 allocated in ratio 12,50,000:6,00,0003,89,1891,86,811
Cost per unit₹31.14₹18.68
Closing inventory (units)1,600400
Value of closing inventory₹49,824₹7,472
Author’s Note: Some examinees allocated the full 6,90,000 cost between Polyester and Nylon without first deducting the by-product's net realizable value and the scrap sale proceeds, overstating the joint cost base for allocation.

MTP January 2026 Set 2 · Q6(a) [OR-alt 2] · Marks: 4 · Approx Time: 8 minutes (approx.) · Topic 1.9: Costs excluded from inventory cost - abnormal waste, storage, non-attributable admin overheads, selling/distribution
Question:

"In determining the cost of inventories, it is appropriate to exclude certain costs and recognise them as expenses in the period in which they are incurred." Provide examples of such costs as per AS 2 (Revised) 'Valuation of Inventories'.

Answer / Solution:

Examples of costs excluded from inventory cost and expensed as incurred: (a) abnormal amounts of wasted materials, labour, or other production costs; (b) storage costs, unless required by the production process itself; (c) administrative overheads that do not contribute to bringing the inventories to their present location and condition; (d) selling and distribution costs.

Author’s Note: Some examinees included all administrative overheads as excluded costs, without distinguishing those that do (production-related) vs. do not (general admin) contribute to bringing inventory to its present location and condition.

MTP May 2023 Set 1 · Q1(c) · Marks: 5 · Approx Time: 9 minutes (approx.) · Topic 1.6/1.13: Fixed overhead absorption over normal capacity plus item-by-item comparison of cost and net realisable value Compulsory
Question:
ParticularsKg.₹
Opening Inventory:Finished Goods1,00025,000
Raw Materials1,10011,000
Purchases10,0001,00,000
Labour76,500
Overheads (Fixed)75,000
Sales10,0002,80,000
Closing Inventory:Raw Materials900
Finished Goods1,200

The expected production for the year was 15,000 kg of the finished product. Due to fall in market demand the sales price for the finished goods was ₹20 per kg and the replacement cost for the raw material was ₹9.50 per kg on the closing day. You are required to calculate the closing inventory as on that date. (5 Marks)

Answer / Solution:

Calculation of cost for closing inventory

Particulars₹
Cost of Purchase (10,200 × 10)1,02,000
Direct Labour76,500
Fixed Overhead (75,000 × 10,200/15,000)51,000
Cost of Production2,29,500
Cost of closing inventory per unit (2,29,500/10,200)₹22.50
Net Realisable Value per unit₹20.00

Since net realisable value is less than cost, closing inventory will be valued at ₹20. As NRV of the finished goods is less than its cost, relevant raw materials will be valued at replacement cost i.e. ₹9.50.

Therefore, value of closing inventory: Finished Goods (1,200 × 20) ₹24,000; Raw Materials (900 × 9.50) ₹8,550; Total ₹32,550.

Author’s Note: A common error is absorbing fixed overhead over actual production (10,200 kg used) instead of the expected/normal capacity of 15,000 kg when computing cost of production, or valuing raw material at replacement cost regardless of whether the related finished goods sell below cost – AS 2 only permits marking raw material down to replacement cost when the finished product it converts into cannot recover its own cost.

MTP May 2023 Set 2 · Q1(d) · Marks: 5 · Approx Time: 9 minutes (approx.) · Topic 1.9: Abnormal waste excluded from inventory cost and expensed to P&L; normal waste absorbed into remaining good units' cost Compulsory
Question:

In a production process, normal waste is 5% of input. 5,000 MT of input were put in process resulting in wastage of 300 MT. Cost per MT of input is ₹1,000. The entire quantity of waste and finished output is in stock at the year end. State with reference to Accounting Standard, how will you value the inventories in this case? What will be treatment for normal and abnormal waste?

Answer / Solution:

As per para 13 of AS 2 (Revised), abnormal amounts of wasted materials, labour and other production costs are excluded from cost of inventories and such costs are recognized as expenses in the period in which they are incurred.

In this case, normal waste is 250 MT and abnormal waste is 50 MT. The cost of 250 MT will be included in determining the cost of inventories (finished goods) at the year end. The cost of abnormal waste (50 MT × 1,052.6315 = ₹52,632) will be charged to the profit and loss statement.

Cost per MT (Normal Quantity of 4,750 MT) = 50,00,000 / 4,750 = ₹1,052.6315

Total value of inventory = 4,700 MT × ₹1,052.6315 = ₹49,47,368.

Author’s Note: A common error is spreading the abnormal loss quantity into the cost-per-unit computation along with the normal loss, understating the abnormal loss charged to the profit and loss statement and correspondingly overstating closing inventory.

MTP May 2024 Set 2 · Q1(b) · Marks: 5 · Approx Time: 9 minutes (approx.) · Topic 1.9: Abnormal waste excluded from inventory cost and expensed; normal loss absorbed into remaining good units' cost Compulsory
Question:

Wooden Plywood Limited has a normal wastage of 5% in the production process. During the year 2023-24, the Company used 16,000 MT of Raw material costing ₹190 per MT. At the end of the year, 950 MT of wastage was in stock. The accountant wants to know how this wastage is to be treated in the books. You are required to: (1) Calculate the amount of abnormal loss. (2) Explain the treatment of normal loss and abnormal loss in the context of AS-2.

Answer / Solution:

(i) As per AS 2 'Valuation of Inventories', abnormal amounts of wasted materials, labour and other production costs are excluded from cost of inventories and such costs are recognised as expenses in the period in which they are incurred. The normal loss will be included in determining the cost of inventories (finished goods) at the year end.

(ii) Material used 16,000 MT @ ₹190 = ₹30,40,000. Normal Loss (5% of 16,000 MT) = 800 MT (included in calculation of cost of inventories). Net quantity of material = 15,200 MT.

(iii) Abnormal Loss in quantity (950 − 800) = 150 MT. Abnormal Loss = ₹30,000 [150 units @ ₹200 (₹30,40,000/15,200)]. The amount of ₹30,000 (Abnormal loss) will be charged to the Profit and Loss statement.

Author’s Note: A common error here is computing the abnormal loss quantity against the gross 16,000 MT used rather than against the 800 MT normal-loss benchmark, or valuing the abnormal loss at the original ₹190/MT purchase rate instead of the higher ₹200/MT rate that results once the normal loss is absorbed into the remaining good units.

MTP May 2025 Set 2 · Q6(c) · Marks: 5 · Approx Time: 9 minutes (approx.) · Topic 1.9: Normal loss absorbed into the cost of remaining good units, abnormal loss quantified separately and expensed
Question:

Wooden Plywood Limited has a normal wastage of 5% in the production process. During the year 2024-25, the Company used 16,000 MT of Raw material costing ₹190 per MT. At the end of the year, 950 MT of wastage was in stock. The accountant wants to know how this wastage is to be treated in the books.

You are required to: (1) Calculate the amount of abnormal loss. (2) Explain the treatment of normal loss and abnormal loss [In the context of AS-2].

Answer / Solution:

As per AS 2 (Revised) 'Valuation of Inventories', abnormal amounts of wasted materials, labour and other production costs are excluded from cost of inventories and such costs are recognised as expenses in the period in which they are incurred. The normal loss will be included in determining the cost of inventories (finished goods) at the year end.

Material used: 16,000 MT @ ₹190 = ₹30,40,000.

Normal Loss (5% of 16,000 MT) = 800 MT (included in calculation of cost of inventories).

Net quantity of material = 15,200 MT.

Abnormal Loss in quantity = (950 − 800) = 150 MT.

Abnormal Loss = ₹30,000 [150 units @ ₹200 (₹30,40,000/15,200)].

The amount of ₹30,000 (Abnormal loss) will be charged to the Profit and Loss statement.

Author’s Note: A frequent mistake here is computing the cost per MT by dividing total material cost by the full 16,000 MT used (or by the 15,050 MT actually remaining after all wastage), instead of by the 15,200 MT net quantity remaining after only the normal loss is absorbed, which is the figure AS 2 requires for costing the abnormal loss.

MTP May 2026 Set 1 · Q1(c) · Marks: 4 · Approx Time: 8 minutes (approx.) · Topic 1.11/1.12: Retail/gross-margin method of cost estimation; NRV of defective stock Compulsory
Question:

In the following cases, find the value of closing stock as per AS 2:
(i) Sonu is a retailer dealing in toys. During the year, he purchased items worth for ₹1,47,000 and made a total sale ₹1,54,000. The average percentage of gross margin is 10% on cost. Opening stock of toys at cost was ₹20,000.
(ii) On 21st March, 2026, Mohan purchased 250 chairs at ₹300 each. The selling price of the chair is ₹400 each. Owing to a manufacturing defect, net realisable value of the whole lot of chair was determined at 70% of their normal selling price. No chairs were sold during the year. (4 Marks)

Answer / Solution:

(i) Cost of closing inventory is shown below:

Sale value of opening stock and purchases (₹20,000 + ₹1,47,000) x 1.101,83,700
Sales(1,54,000)
Sale value of unsold stock29,700
Less: Gross Margin (₹29,700/1.10) x 0.10(2,700)
Cost of closing inventory27,000

Alternative presentation

Opening stock and purchases (₹20,000 + ₹1,47,000)1,67,000
Less: cost of goods sold(1,40,000)
Cost of closing inventory27,000

Calculation of cost of goods sold:

Goods sold1,54,000
Less: gross margin (1,54,000 x 10/110)(14,000)
Cost of goods sold1,40,000

(ii)

Closing stock at cost (250 x ₹300) (i)75,000
Net Realizable value of closing stock (₹280* x 250) (ii)70,000
Value of closing stock [lower of (i) and (ii)]70,000

*₹280 = 70% of ₹400 selling price.

Author’s Note: Several examinees applied the gross margin percentage directly to sales value instead of grossing up cost through the margin percentage, producing an incorrect closing stock figure in part (i) under AS 2; in part (ii), some compared cost against the normal selling price instead of the defect-adjusted net realisable value.

MTP November 2023 Set 1 · Q1(b) · Marks: 5 · Approx Time: 9 minutes (approx.) · Topic 1.13/1.14: Item-by-item comparison of cost and NRV; materials held for use written down to replacement cost only when the finished product they convert into will sell below cost Compulsory
Question:

Mr. Jatin gives the following information relating to the items forming part of the inventory as on 31.03.2023. His enterprise produces product P using Raw Material X.

  1. 900 units of Raw Material X (purchased @ ₹100 per unit). Replacement cost of Raw Material X as on 31.03.2023 is ₹80 per unit.
  2. 400 units of partly finished goods in the process of producing P. Cost incurred till date is ₹245 per unit. These units can be finished next year by incurring additional cost of ₹50 per unit.
  3. 800 units of Finished goods P and total cost incurred is ₹295 per unit.

Expected selling price of product P is ₹280 per unit, subject to a payment of 5% brokerage on selling price.

Determine how each item of inventory will be valued as on 31.03.2023. Also calculate the value of total Inventory as on 31.03.2023.

Answer / Solution:

As per AS 2 (Revised) “Valuation of Inventories”, materials and other supplies held for use in the production of inventories are not written down below cost if the finished products in which they will be incorporated are expected to be sold at cost or above cost. However, when there has been a decline in the price of materials and it is estimated that the cost of the finished products will exceed net realizable value, the materials are written down to net realizable value. In such circumstances, the replacement cost of the materials may be the best available measure of their net realizable value. In the given case, selling price of product P is ₹266 and total cost per unit for production is ₹295.

Hence the valuation will be done as under:

  1. 900 units of raw material X will be written down to replacement cost as market value of finished product is less than its cost, hence valued at ₹80 per unit.
  2. 400 units of partly finished goods will be valued at ₹216 per unit i.e., lower of cost (₹245) or Net realizable value ₹216 (Estimated selling price ₹266 per unit less additional cost of ₹50).
  3. 800 units of finished product P will be valued at NRV of ₹266 per unit since it is lower than cost ₹295.

Valuation of Total Inventory as on 31.03.2023:

ParticularsUnitsCost (₹)NRV / Replacement cost (₹)Value = units × cost or NRV whichever is less (₹)
Raw material X9001008072,000
Partly finished goods40024521686,400
Finished goods P8002952662,12,800
Value of Inventory3,71,200
Author’s Note: A common error is comparing raw material's own cost against its own replacement cost in isolation, instead of first checking whether the finished product it converts into (Product P) will sell below its own total cost – AS 2 only permits marking raw material down to replacement cost when that downstream test fails. It is also easy to compute net selling price by forgetting the 5% brokerage deduction, which changes both the partly-finished-goods NRV and the finished-goods valuation.

MTP November 2023 Set 2 · Q1(a) · Marks: 5 · Approx Time: 9 minutes (approx.) · Topic 1.3/1.9: Costs excluded from cost of inventories and expensed as incurred (abnormal waste, unnecessary storage, non-contributing admin overheads, selling/distribution costs); lower-of-cost-and-NRV valuation with the agent's selling commission deducted from expected sale value Compulsory
Question:

(i) “In determining the cost of inventories, it is appropriate to exclude certain costs and recognize them as expenses in the period in which they are incurred”. Provide examples of such costs as per AS 2 ‘Valuation of Inventories’.

(ii) X Limited purchased goods at the cost of ₹40 lakhs in October, 2022. Till March, 2023, 75% of the stocks were sold. The company wants to disclose closing stock at ₹10 lakhs. The expected sale value is ₹11 lakhs and a commission at 10% on sale is payable to the agent. Advise, what is the correct value of closing stock to be disclosed as at 31.3.2023.

Answer / Solution:

(i) As per AS 2 ‘Valuation of Inventories’, certain costs are excluded from the cost of the inventories and are recognized as expenses in the period in which incurred. Examples of such costs are:

  1. abnormal amount of wasted materials, labour, or other production costs;
  2. storage costs, unless those costs are necessary in the production process prior to a further production stage;
  3. administrative overheads that do not contribute to bringing the inventories to their present location and condition; and
  4. selling and distribution costs.

(ii) As per AS 2 “Valuation of Inventories”, the inventories are to be valued at lower of cost or net realizable value. In this case, the cost of inventory is ₹10 lakhs. The net realizable value is ₹11,00,000 × 90% = ₹9,90,000. So, the stock should be valued at ₹9,90,000.

Author’s Note: A common error is treating storage costs as always excludable rather than only when unnecessary to a further production stage in part (i); and in part (ii), comparing the disclosed cost of ₹10 lakhs against the gross expected sale value of ₹11 lakhs instead of first deducting the 10% agent's commission, which changes the net realizable value from ₹11,00,000 to ₹9,90,000 and hence which figure actually governs.

PYQ November 2023 · Q1(c) · Marks: 5 · Approx Time: 9 minutes (approx.) · Topic 1.11/1.12: Retail/gross-margin technique for estimating cost of unsold stock (Sonu), and estimating net realisable value of defective stock at the lower of cost and NRV (Mohan) Compulsory
Question:

In the following cases, find the value of closing stock as per AS 2:

(i) Sonu is a retailer dealing in toys. During the year, he purchased items worth ₹1,47,000 and made a total sale ₹1,54,000. The average percentage of gross margin is 10% on cost. Opening stock of toys at cost was ₹20,000.

(ii) On 21st March, 2023, Mohan purchased 250 chairs at ₹300 each. The selling price of the chair is ₹400 each. Owing to a manufacturing defect, net realisable value of the whole lot of chair was determined at 70% of their normal selling price. No chairs were sold during the year. (5 Marks)

Answer / Solution:

(i) Cost of closing inventory is shown below:

₹
Sale value of opening stock and purchases (₹20,000 + ₹1,47,000) × 1.101,83,700
Sales(1,54,000)
Sale value of unsold stock29,700
Less: Gross Margin (₹29,700 / 1.10) × 0.10(2,700)
Cost of closing inventory27,000

(ii)

₹
Closing stock at cost (250 × ₹300) … (i)75,000
Net Realisable value of closing stock (₹280* × 250) … (ii)70,000
Value of closing stock [lower of (i) and (ii)]70,000

* Net realisable value per chair = ₹400 × 70% = ₹280.

Author’s Note: Some examinees, in part (i), incorrectly applied the 10% gross margin directly to the sale value of unsold stock instead of first grossing it down (dividing by 1.10) before extracting the margin, overstating the closing inventory figure. In part (ii), several examinees valued the chairs at cost alone without comparing it to net realisable value, missing that AS 2 requires inventory to be carried at the lower of cost and net realisable value even when the shortfall arises from a physical defect rather than a general fall in market price.

PYQ September 2024 · Q6(a) [OR-alt 2] · Marks: 4 · Approx Time: 8 minutes (approx.) · Topic 1.9: Costs excluded from inventory valuation and expensed as incurred - abnormal waste, avoidable storage, non-contributing admin overheads, selling/distribution costs
Question:

"In determining the cost of inventories, it is appropriate to exclude certain costs and recognise them as expenses in the period in which they are incurred." Provide examples of such costs as per AS 2 (Revised) 'Valuation of Inventories'.

Answer / Solution:

In determining the cost of inventories, it is appropriate to exclude certain costs and recognise them as expenses in the period in which they are incurred. Examples of such costs are:

(a) Abnormal amounts of wasted materials, labour, or other production costs;

(b) Storage costs, unless the production process requires such storage.

(c) Administrative overheads that do not contribute to bringing the inventories to their present location and condition.

(d) Selling and distribution costs.

Author’s Note: Some examinees who selected this theory alternative listed only one or two of the four categories of cost excluded from inventory valuation under AS 2, most often omitting the distinction between avoidable and production-necessary storage costs.

PYQ September 2025 · Q1(b) · Marks: 5 · Approx Time: 9 minutes (approx.) · Topic 1.14: Finished goods at lower of cost and NRV; feeding raw material written down to replacement cost once FG NRV falls below cost Compulsory
Question:

SR Limited manufactures finished goods 'MP' from raw material 'RP'. Year ended 31st March 2025: Opening Inventory MP 4,000 units ₹1,20,000; RP 4,400 units ₹52,800. Purchase of RP 40,000 units ₹4,80,000. Labour ₹3,23,200. Fixed Overheads ₹3,15,000. Sales 40,200 units ₹11,20,000. Closing Inventory: MP 4,200 units; RP 4,000 units. Expected production 45,000 units of MP. Due to fall in market demand, sales price of MP fell to ₹22/unit; replacement cost of RP ₹11.50/unit on closing day. Calculate the value of Closing Stock of 'MP' and 'RP' as on 31st March 2025.

Answer / Solution:

W.N.1 Actual production: Sales 40,200 + Closing FG 4,200 − Opening FG 4,000 = 40,400 units.

W.N.2 RP consumed: Opening RP 4,400 + Purchases 40,000 = 44,400 available; less Closing RP 4,000 = 40,400 units consumed (1 unit RP per unit MP produced).

W.N.3 Cost per unit RP (weighted average): (Opening value 52,800 + Purchases 4,80,000) / 44,400 units = 5,32,800/44,400 = ₹12.00/unit.

Cost of Material Consumed (40,400 × ₹12)4,84,800
Direct Labour3,23,200
Fixed Overhead (3,15,000 × 40,400/45,000 — based on normal/expected production, not actual)2,82,800
Cost of Production10,90,800
Cost per unit (10,90,800/40,400)₹27
Net Realisable Value per unit (selling price)₹22

Since NRV (₹22) is less than cost (₹27), the closing MP inventory is valued at NRV. Since finished goods NRV is below cost, the raw material RP feeding it is valued at replacement cost (₹11.50), per AS 2's write-down rule.

Value of closing inventory: MP (4,200 × ₹22) = ₹92,400. RP (4,000 × ₹11.50) = ₹46,000.

Examiner’s Comment: The performance of examinees in this part was not satisfactory. A majority of them were unable to determine the value of closing inventory of finished goods (MP) and raw materials (RP) in accordance with AS 2 "Valuation of Inventories". Several examinees failed to compute the cost of production correctly, particularly where certain items required proportionate allocation. Many could ascertain only the labour cost of ₹3,23,200, while the remaining elements of cost were incorrectly computed. Further, a large number of examinees valued the closing stock of finished goods (on NRV basis) and raw materials (on replacement cost basis) incorrectly.

RTP January 2026 · Q3 · Marks: Not stated in source · Approx Time: 10–20 minutes (approx.) · Topic 1.3: Lower of cost and NRV - the NRV-only exception is limited to specific industries, not general manufacturing
Question:

A private limited company manufacturing fancy terry towels had valued its closing inventory of finished goods at realisable value, inclusive of profit and export cash incentives. Firm contracts had been received and goods were packed for export, but ownership had not been transferred to the foreign buyers. Comment on the valuation of the inventories by the company.

Answer / Solution:

AS 2 requires inventories to be valued at the lower of historical cost and net realisable value. AS 9 permits valuing goods at net realisable value only in specific industries where performance is substantially complete prior to the transaction generating revenue — e.g. harvested agricultural crops or extracted mineral ores, where a sale is assured under forward contract/government guarantee or a ready market exists with negligible risk of failure to sell.

Fancy terry towels do not fall into the agricultural-crop or mineral-ore category. Since ownership had not transferred to the foreign buyers, the sale was not yet complete. The closing inventory should therefore have been valued at the lower of cost and net realisable value, not at net realisable value. Further, export cash incentives are recognised only in the year the export sale actually takes place, not accrued into inventory valuation ahead of the sale. The company's valuation policy is therefore not correct.

Author’s Note: Some examinees accepted the NRV-inclusive-of-profit valuation on the basis of firm export contracts alone, not recognising that the AS 9 exception is limited to specific industries (agricultural/mineral) and does not extend to manufactured goods merely because a sale contract exists.

RTP September 2024 · Q3 · Marks: Not stated in source · Approx Time: 10–20 minutes (approx.) · Topic 1.6: Fixed production overheads absorbed on normal capacity, excluding interest, for standard-cost/closing-stock valuation
Question:

Kirti Ltd. is in the business of manufacturing computers. During the year ended 31st March, 2024, the company manufactured 550 computers. It has the policy of valuing finished stock of goods at a standard cost of ₹1.8 lakh per computer. The details of the costs are as under:

(₹ in lakh)
Raw material consumed400
Direct Labour250
Variable production overheads150
Fixed production overheads (including interest of ₹100 lakh)290

Compute the value cost per computer for the purpose of closing stock.

Answer / Solution:

As per para 9 of AS 2 ‘Valuation of Inventories’, for inclusion in the cost of inventory, allocation of fixed production overheads is based on the normal capacity of the production facilities.

In this case, finished stock has been valued at a standard cost of ₹1.8 lakh per computer which incidentally synchronizes with the value computed on the basis of absorption costing as under:

(₹ in lakh)
Materials400
Direct Labour250
Variable production overheads150
Fixed production overheads290
Less: Interest(100)190
Total cost990

Number of computers produced = 550 computers (Assumed to be normal production).

Cost per computer ₹990 lakh / 550 computers = ₹1.80 lakh.

Author’s Note: A common error is including the ₹100 lakh interest component within fixed production overheads when arriving at the cost of inventory, instead of excluding financing costs that are not part of bringing the inventory to its present location and condition.

RTP September 2025 · Q6 · Marks: Not stated in source · Approx Time: 10–20 minutes (approx.) · Topic 1.10: Joint products and by-products - by-product/scrap NRV deducted from joint cost; raw material stays at cost when finished goods sell above cost
Question:

Zing Ltd., 2024-25: Raw Material closing stock 700 units, cost ₹35/unit, replacement cost ₹20/unit. Finished products FP1/FP2: Production 3,000/1,600 units; Closing stock 500/300 units. Material consumed ₹3,20,000; Direct labour ₹1,60,000; Direct expenses ₹78,000 (these three cost figures pertain to combined joint production). Fixed overhead ₹95,000, including ₹15,000 godown rent (for storing finished products, not a production cost). 1,000 units of by-product BY also emerged, sold @₹12/unit after ₹2,500 expense; ₹4,800 realized from scrap sale. Average market price: FP1 ₹160/unit, FP2 ₹100/unit. Calculate the value of closing stock per AS 2.

Answer / Solution:

Per AS 2, most by-products/scrap are measured at NRV, deducted from the cost of the main product.

NRV of by-product BY: Selling price (1,000×₹12) 12,000, less separate processing charges 2,500 = ₹9,500.

Joint cost to allocate: Raw material 3,20,000 + Labour 1,60,000 + Direct expenses 78,000 + Fixed overhead (95,000−15,000 godown rent, excluded as unrelated to production) 80,000 = 6,38,000; less NRV of BY (9,500) and scrap sale value (4,800) = ₹6,23,700 to allocate between FP1 and FP2.

FP1FP2
Output (units)3,0001,600
Sales price/unit₹160₹100
Sales value4,80,0001,60,000
Allocation ratio31
Joint cost allocated (3:1)4,67,7751,55,925
Cost per unit₹155.93₹97.45

Since both FP1 (₹155.93 cost vs ₹160 selling price) and FP2 (₹97.45 vs ₹100) sell above cost, both finished goods are valued at cost, and the raw material feeding them is valued at its own cost (₹35/unit, not written down to the ₹20 replacement cost).

Closing inventory: FP1 (500×₹155.93) = ₹77,965. FP2 (300×₹97.45) = ₹29,235. Raw material (700×₹35) = ₹24,500. Total closing inventory = ₹77,965 + ₹29,235 + ₹24,500 = ₹1,31,700.

Author’s Note: Some examinees included the godown rent (storage cost unrelated to production, per AS 2's general exclusion of storage costs) in the joint cost pool, or wrote raw material down to replacement cost despite both finished goods selling above their allocated cost.

AS 10 — Property, Plant and Equipment

Every MTP/RTP/PYQ question that tests this chapter, collected in one place, with official answers and topic tags — so you can practise every question this topic has been examined with, without hunting through separate papers.

A note on accuracy (please read): This is the first edition of this book, assembled with AI assistance and reviewed as carefully as we could manage, but it has not been independently audited question-by-question. If you spot an error — a wrong figure, a wrong answer, anything that looks off — please email capranavpratiktulshyan@gmail.com with the question reference so it can be corrected in the next edition.
Scope of this book (16 questions): Covers 34 sittings: MTP Jan2025 Set1, MTP Jan2025 Set2, MTP Jan2026 Set1, MTP Jan2026 Set2, MTP May2023 Set1, MTP May2023 Set2, MTP May2024 Set1, MTP May2024 Set2, MTP May2025 Set1, MTP May2025 Set2, MTP May2026 Set1, MTP May2026 Set2, MTP Nov2023 Set1, MTP Nov2023 Set2, MTP Sep2024 Set1, MTP Sep2024 Set2, MTP Sep2025 Set1, MTP Sep2025 Set2, PYQ Jan2025, PYQ Jan2026, PYQ May2023, PYQ May2024, PYQ May2025, PYQ May2026, PYQ Nov2023, PYQ Sep2024, PYQ Sep2025, RTP Jan2025, RTP Jan2026, RTP May2024, RTP May2025, RTP May2026, RTP Sep2024, RTP Sep2025. MCQs on this chapter are deliberately not included here — practise those on the dedicated MCQ platform; this book is for descriptive/scenario practice with full worked answers.
How this book is organised: Two sections — I. Descriptive (pure AS 10) and II. Integrated (questions where AS 10 is one part of a larger question that also tests another standard). An empty Section II for a chapter is normal and expected, not a mistake — most multi-topic-looking questions are split so each topic gets its own clean entry, so genuinely combined questions are the rarer case. Each answer includes either a real Examiner's Comment (tan/orange box, quoted from ICAI's own published feedback, where one exists for that sitting) or an Author's Note (pale pink box, a likely pitfall identified by the author, not an official ICAI finding, and may not apply in every case) — see How to Read this Book.md for the full key to every colour and symbol used.

I. Descriptive & Scenario-Based Questions (pure AS 10)

Full descriptive/scenario questions where this chapter is the sole topic tested (after independent-question splitting).

MTP May 2023 Set 1 · Q6(a) · Marks: 5 · Approx Time: 9 minutes (approx.) · Topic 2.6-2.7: Initial measurement of PPE at cost - directly attributable costs and decommissioning/restoration estimate included, initial operating losses excluded
Question:

Preet Ltd. is installing a new plant at its production facility. It has incurred these costs:

Particulars₹
Cost of the plant (cost per supplier's invoice plus taxes)10,00,000
Initial delivery and handling costs80,000
Cost of site preparation2,40,000
Consultants used for advice on the acquisition of the plant2,80,000
Estimated dismantling costs to be incurred after 7 years1,20,000
Operating losses before commercial production1,60,000

Please advise Preet Ltd. on the costs that can be capitalised in accordance with AS 10 (Revised). (5 Marks)

Answer / Solution:

According to AS 10 (Revised), these costs can be capitalised:

#Particulars₹
1.Cost of the plant10,00,000
2.Initial delivery and handling costs80,000
3.Cost of site preparation2,40,000
4.Consultants' fees2,80,000
5.Estimated dismantling costs to be incurred after 7 years1,20,000
Total17,20,000

Note: Operating losses before commercial production amounting to ₹1,60,000 are not regarded as directly attributable costs and thus cannot be capitalized. They should be written off to the Statement of Profit and Loss in the period they are incurred.

Author’s Note: A common error is including the pre-commercial-production operating losses in the capitalised cost of the plant, on the mistaken reasoning that they were incurred before the asset was ready for use – AS 10 specifically excludes initial operating losses as a directly attributable cost, regardless of timing.

MTP November 2023 Set 1 · Q1(d) · Marks: 5 · Approx Time: 9 minutes (approx.) · Topic 2.5/2.6/2.9: Nil depreciation when residual value equals cost; freehold land not depreciated; depreciation on a self-constructed asset begins when ready for use, not when actually used; revised useful-life estimate spread prospectively over the remaining life Compulsory
Question:

A Ltd. had following assets. Calculate depreciation for the year ended 31st March, 2023 for each asset as per AS 10 (Revised):

  1. Machinery purchased for ₹10 lakhs on 1st April, 2018 and residual value after useful life of 5 years, based on 2018 prices is ₹10 lakhs.
  2. Land for ₹50 lakhs.
  3. A Machinery is constructed for ₹5,00,000 for its own use (useful life is 10 years). Construction is completed on 1st April, 2022, but the company does not begin using the machine until 31st March, 2023.
  4. Machinery purchased on 1st April, 2020 for ₹50,000 with useful life of 5 years and residual value is NIL. On 1st April, 2022, management decided to use this asset for further 2 years only. (4 Parts × 5 Marks = 20 Marks)
Answer / Solution:

Computation of amount of depreciation as per AS 10

AssetDepreciation (₹)
(i) Machinery purchased on 1/4/18 for ₹10 lakhs (having residual value of ₹10 lakhs).
Reason: The company considers that the residual value, based on prices prevailing at the balance sheet date, will equal the cost. Therefore, there is no depreciable amount and depreciation is correctly zero.		Nil
(ii) Land (₹50 lakhs) (considered freehold).
Reason: Land has an unlimited useful life and therefore, it is not depreciated.		Nil
(iii) Machinery constructed for own use (₹5,00,000/10).
Reason: The entity should begin charging depreciation from the date the machine is ready for use i.e. 1st April, 2022. The fact that the machine was not used for a period after it was ready to be used is not relevant in considering when to begin charging depreciation.		50,000
(iv) Machinery having revised useful life.
Reason: The entity has charged depreciation using the straight-line method at ₹10,000 per annum i.e. (50,000/5 years). On 1st April, 2022 the asset’s net book value is [50,000 − (10,000 × 2)] i.e. ₹30,000. The remaining useful life is 2 years as per revised estimate. The company should amend the annual provision for depreciation to charge the unamortized cost over the revised remaining life of 2 years. Consequently, it should charge depreciation for the next 2 years at ₹15,000 per annum i.e. (30,000/2 years).		15,000
Author’s Note: A common error on part (iii) is deferring the start of depreciation to the date the machine is actually put into use rather than the date it becomes ready for use, and on part (iv) treating the revised remaining life as a fresh 5-year period instead of amending the existing straight-line rate to spread the asset's already-reduced net book value over only the 2 years actually remaining.

MTP November 2023 Set 2 · Q1(c) · Marks: 5 · Approx Time: 9 minutes (approx.) · Topic 2.6-2.7: Costs excluded from PPE cost even though incidental to acquiring/renovating the asset - pre-opening staff costs and reorganisation-type expenditure not directly attributable to bringing the asset to its intended working condition are expensed, not capitalised Compulsory
Question:

Neon Enterprise operates a major chain of restaurants located in different cities. The company has acquired a new restaurant located at Chandigarh. The new-restaurant requires significant renovation expenditure. Management expects that the renovations will last for 3 months during which the restaurant will be closed.

Management has prepared the following budget for this period –

ParticularsAmount (₹)
Salaries of the staff engaged in preparation of restaurant before its opening7,50,000
Construction and remodelling cost of restaurant30,00,000

Explain the treatment of these expenditures as per the provisions of AS 10 "Property, Plant and Equipment".

Answer / Solution:

Constructing or acquiring a new asset may result in incremental costs that would have been avoided if the asset had not been constructed or acquired. These costs are not to be included in the cost of the asset if they are not directly attributable to bringing the asset to the location and condition necessary for it to be capable of operating in the manner intended by management. The costs to be incurred by the company are in the nature of costs of reducing or reorganizing the operations of the company. These costs do not meet that requirement of AS 10 “Property, Plant and Equipment” and cannot, therefore, be capitalized.

Author’s Note: A common error is treating the pre-opening staff salaries and the construction/remodelling cost identically merely because both fall within the same closure period, without separately testing each item against AS 10's directly-attributable-cost condition.

PYQ May 2023 · Q1(a) · Marks: 5 · Approx Time: 9 minutes (approx.) · Topic 2.9: PPE acquired in exchange for a non-monetary asset, combined with WDV-method depreciation across an acquisition/disposal/exchange within the year Compulsory
Question:

In the books of Topmaker Limited, carrying amount of Plant and Machinery as on 1st April, 2022 is ₹56,30,000.

On scrutiny, it was found that a purchase of Machinery worth ₹21,12,000 was included in the purchase of goods on 1st June, 2022. On 30th June, 2022 the company disposed a Machine having book value of ₹9,60,000 (as on 1st April, 2022) for ₹8,25,000 in part exchange of a new machine costing ₹15,65,000.

The company charges depreciation @ 10% p.a. on written down value method on Plant and Machinery.

You are required to compute: (i) Depreciation to be charged to Profit & Loss Account; (ii) Book value of Plant & Machinery as on 31st March, 2023; and (iii) Profit/Loss on exchange of Plant & Machinery. (5 Marks)

Answer / Solution:

(i) Depreciation to be charged in the Profit & Loss Account

ParticularsAmount in ₹
Depreciation on old Machinery [10% on ₹56,30,000 for 3 months (01.04.2022 to 30.06.2022)]1,40,750
Add: Depreciation on Machinery acquired on 01.06.2022 (₹21,12,000 × 10% × 10/12)1,76,000
Add: Depreciation on Machinery after adjustment of Exchange [10% of (₹56,30,000 − 9,60,000 + 15,65,000) for 9 months]4,67,625
Total Depreciation to be charged in Profit & Loss A/c7,84,375

(ii) Book value of Plant & Machinery as on 31.3.2023

ParticularsAmount in ₹
Balance as per books on 01.04.202256,30,000
Add: Included in purchases on 01.06.202221,12,000
Add: Purchases on 30.06.202215,65,00036,77,000
(subtotal)93,07,000
Less: Book value of Machine sold on 30.06.2022(9,60,000)
(subtotal)83,47,000
Less: Depreciation on Machinery in use ₹(7,84,375 − 24,000)(7,60,375)
Book Value as on 31.03.202375,86,625

Note: the computation of depreciation and book value of Plant & Machinery can be presented in the following alternative manner:

ParticularsBook Value or Cost or AcquisitionPeriodDepreciationBook Value as on 31.03.2023
Opening Value46,70,000 (56,30,000 − 9,60,000)01.04.2022 to 31.03.20234,67,000 (46,70,000 × 10%)42,03,000
Sold9,60,00001.04.2022 to 30.06.202224,000 (9,60,000 × 10% × 3/12)–

New Machinery15,65,00001.07.2022 to 31.03.20231,17,375 (15,65,000 × 10% × 9/12)14,47,625
Total7,84,37575,86,625

ParticularsAmount in ₹
Balance as per books on 01.04.20229,60,000
