Author’s Note: Many examinees computed depreciation for the exchanged machine only up to the date of disposal without also computing a full 9-month depreciation charge on the new machine's cost from the date of exchange, understating the year's total depreciation figure. Some examinees also used the exchange value (₹8,25,000) directly as the sale proceeds without first reducing the old machine's book value to its 30th June written-down value, misstating the loss transferred on exchange.

PYQ May 2025 · Q1(a) · Marks: 7 · Approx Time: 13 minutes (approx.) · Topic 2.6-2.7: Costs of relocating/reorganising operations excluded from the cost of an asset; computing the directly attributable acquisition cost of land net of recoverable GST on salvage proceeds Compulsory
Question:

Hardy Ltd. intends to extend the factory set up on the adjacent plot with disintegrated old premises. It acquired the land having an area of 250 hectares at a cost of ₹25,000 per hectare.

Hardy Ltd. incurred Stamp duty and registration charges of 5% of land value. Legal fees were paid ₹4,75,000 for land acquisition.

Hardy Ltd. incurred ₹37,85,000 for demolishing old premises thereon. A sum of ₹12,60,000 (including 5% GST thereon) was realized from the sale of material salvaged from the site.

Till the new site with extended factory premises is ready, the company needs to move the present production facilities to another (temporary) site. The following incremental costs will be incurred.

(1) Set up costs of ₹7,50,000 to install machinery in the new location. (2) Rent of ₹12,00,000. (3) Removal costs of ₹2,50,000 to transport the machinery from the old location to the temporary location.

(i) Management is of the opinion that the cost of moving the production facilities to another temporary location can be capitalised. You are required to advise. (ii) You are also required to compute the cost of land acquired. (7 Marks)

Answer / Solution:

(i) Constructing or acquiring a new asset may result in incremental costs that would have been avoided if the asset had not been constructed or acquired. These costs are not to be included in the cost of the asset if they are not directly attributable to bringing the asset to the location and condition necessary for it to be capable of operating in the manner intended by management. The costs to be incurred by the company are in the nature of costs of relocating or reorganising operations of the company and do not meet the requirement of AS 10 (Revised). Therefore, these costs cannot be capitalized.

(ii) Computation of cost of land:

Particulars₹
Purchase Price250 hectares × ₹25,000 per hectare62,50,000
Stamp Duty and Registration Charges5% of ₹62,50,0003,12,500
Legal and Consultancy Fees4,75,000
Demolition Expenses (Net of Salvage Income)₹37,85,000 − ₹12,60,000 × (100/105) [i.e. ₹37,85,000 − ₹12,00,000]25,85,000
Cost of Land96,22,500
Examiner’s Comment: A significant number of examinees displayed a lack of understanding of the provisions of AS 10 "Property, Plant and Equipment." Instead of applying the correct provisions, many examinees incorrectly based their responses on AS 16 — Borrowing Costs, especially while commenting on the capitalisation of expenses related to the relocation of production facilities. Additionally, several examinees were unable to accurately compute the cost of land.

RTP January 2025 · Q8 · Marks: Not stated in source · Approx Time: 10–20 minutes (approx.) · Topic 2.10: Replacement of a significant component: capitalise the new part's cost and derecognise the estimated carrying amount of the part replaced
Question:

MS Ltd. has acquired a heavy machinery at a cost of ₹1,00,00,000 (with no breakdown of the component parts). The estimated useful life is 10 years. At the end of the sixth year, one of the major components, the turbine requires replacement, as further maintenance is uneconomical. The remainder of the machine is perfect and is expected to last for the next four years. The cost of a new turbine is ₹45,00,000. The discount rate assumed is 5%.

Can the cost of the new turbine be recognised as an asset, and, if so, what treatment should be used?

Answer / Solution:

The new turbine will produce economic benefits to MS Ltd., and the cost is measurable. Hence, the item should be recognised as an asset. The original invoice for the machine did not specify the cost of the turbine; however, the cost of the replacement ₹45,00,000 can be used as an indication (usually by discounting) of the likely cost, six years previously.

Statement showing cost of new turbine and machine after 6th year

Cost of machine recognized on purchase1,00,00,000
Less: Depreciation charged for 6 years [(1,00,00,000/10) × 6](60,00,000)
40,00,000
Less: Current cost of turbine to be derecognized:
Cost of Turbine before 6 years [45,00,000 × {1/(1.05)6}]33,57,900
Less: Depreciation for 6 years [(33,57,900/10) × 6](20,14,740)(13,43,160)
Add: Cost of new turbine to be recognised45,00,000
Revised carrying amount of machine71,56,840
Author’s Note: A common error is expensing the replacement turbine's cost entirely, or recognising it without first derecognising the estimated carrying amount of the original turbine component being replaced, resulting in double-counting of the turbine's net book value under AS 10's component approach.

RTP January 2026 · Q9(i) · Marks: Not stated in source · Approx Time: 10–20 minutes (approx.) · Topic 2.5: Nil depreciable amount when residual value equals cost
Question:

Machinery purchased 1st April, 2020 for ₹10 lakhs, useful life 5 years, residual value (at 2020 prices) ₹10 lakhs. Calculate depreciation for the year ended 31st March, 2025 per AS 10 (Revised).

Answer / Solution:

Nil. Since the residual value (₹10 lakhs) equals the cost (₹10 lakhs), the depreciable amount is nil; depreciation is correctly zero throughout the asset's life.

Author’s Note: Some examinees computed depreciation on the full cost, ignoring the stated residual value entirely.

RTP January 2026 · Q9(ii) · Marks: Not stated in source · Approx Time: 10–20 minutes (approx.) · Topic 2.5: Freehold land is not depreciated - unlimited useful life
Question:

The company owns a piece of land acquired for ₹50 lakhs, held for use in its factory operations. Calculate depreciation for the year ended 31st March, 2025.

Answer / Solution:

Nil. Land has an unlimited useful life (unless it is a wasting asset such as a quarry) and is therefore not depreciated.

Author’s Note: A basic but recurring error is depreciating land alongside buildings without separating the two components.

RTP January 2026 · Q9(iii) · Marks: Not stated in source · Approx Time: 10–20 minutes (approx.) · Topic 2.6: Depreciation begins when the asset is ready for use, not when actual use commences
Question:

Zenith Ltd. constructed a machine for its own use, total cost ₹5,00,000, completed 1st April, 2024, useful life 10 years; the company did not commence using the machine until 31st March, 2025. Calculate depreciation for the year ended 31st March, 2025.

Answer / Solution:

₹50,000 (₹5,00,000/10 years). Depreciation begins from the date the machine is ready for use (1st April, 2024), regardless of when actual use commenced — the fact that it sat idle for a period after being ready is not relevant to when depreciation begins.

Author’s Note: Some examinees charged no depreciation at all, reasoning the machine was never actually used during the year, missing that "ready for use" (not actual use) triggers depreciation.

RTP January 2026 · Q9(iv) · Marks: Not stated in source · Approx Time: 10–20 minutes (approx.) · Topic 2.9: Revised useful-life estimate - unamortised cost spread prospectively over the revised remaining life
Question:

Another machine was purchased 1st April, 2022, for ₹50,000, useful life 5 years, nil residual value. On 1st April, 2024, management decided the machine would now be used for only two more years. Calculate depreciation for the year ended 31st March, 2025.

Answer / Solution:

Original SLM depreciation = ₹50,000/5 = ₹10,000/year. Net book value on 1st April, 2024 (after 2 years) = 50,000−20,000 = ₹30,000. With the revised remaining useful life of 2 years, the unamortised cost is spread over the revised remaining life: 30,000/2 = ₹15,000/year for the next 2 years.

Author’s Note: Some examinees continued the original ₹10,000/year rate, not recognising that a revised useful-life estimate requires recomputing the annual charge over the remaining life going forward.

RTP May 2025 · Q11 · Marks: Not stated in source · Approx Time: 10–20 minutes (approx.) · Topic 2.6-2.7: Cost of a PPE item as purchase price plus directly attributable costs, at actual cost with internal profit eliminated
Question:

Shrishti Ltd. contracted with a supplier to purchase machinery which is to be installed in its Department A in three months' time. Special foundations were required for the machinery which were to be prepared within this supply lead time. The cost of the site preparation and laying foundations were ₹1,41,870. These activities were supervised by a technician during the entire period, who is employed for this purpose at ₹45,000 per month. The technician's services were given by Department B to Department A, which billed the services at ₹49,500 per month after adding 10% profit margin.

The machine was purchased at ₹1,58,34,000 inclusive of IGST @ 12% for which input credit is available to Shrishti Ltd. ₹55,770 transportation charges were incurred to bring the machine to the factory site. An Architect was appointed at a fee of ₹30,000 to supervise machinery installation at the factory site.

Ascertain the amount at which the Machinery should be capitalized under AS 10, considering that IGST credit is availed by Shrishti Limited. Internally booked profits should be eliminated in arriving at the cost of machine.

Answer / Solution:
ParticularsBasis₹
Purchase PriceGiven (₹1,58,34,000 × 100/112, IGST credit removed)1,41,37,500
Add: Site Preparation CostGiven1,41,870
Add: Technician's SalarySpecific/attributable overhead for 3 months, at cost, no internal profit (45,000 × 3)1,35,000
Add: Transportation ChargesInitial delivery cost, given55,770
Add: Architect's FeesProfessional fees for installation, given30,000
Total Cost of Asset1,45,00,140

The technician's cost is included at its actual salary cost of ₹45,000/month (attributable overhead directly related to bringing the asset to its working condition), not the ₹49,500/month inter-departmental billing rate, since the 10% mark-up billed by Department B to Department A is an internally booked profit that must be eliminated when arriving at the cost of the machine for external financial reporting.

Author’s Note: A common error is capitalising the technician's cost at the ₹49,500/month inter-departmental billing rate rather than the actual ₹45,000/month salary cost, failing to eliminate the internally booked 10% profit margin as the question explicitly requires.

Calculate the amount to be capitalized for this machine per AS 10.

RTP September 2025 · Q12(ii) · Marks: Not stated in source · Approx Time: 10–20 minutes (approx.) · Topic 2.8: Component replacement - derecognise the replaced component's carrying amount, capitalise the new component's cost
Question:

On 1st December 2024, Precision Tools Ltd. replaced the motor of an old machine with a new one costing ₹1,20,000, improving output capacity by 15%. The old motor had cost ₹50,000 and accumulated depreciation ₹35,000. Calculate the amount to be capitalized.

Answer / Solution:

Carrying amount of the old motor = 50,000−35,000 = ₹15,000, which is derecognised (written off) since it is being replaced. The new motor's acquisition cost of ₹1,20,000 is capitalised as a separate component (component accounting under AS 10). Net effect: ₹1,20,000 capitalised, ₹15,000 carrying amount of the old motor removed/expensed.

Author’s Note: Some examinees simply added the new motor's cost to the machine's carrying value without also derecognising the replaced motor's remaining carrying amount.

RTP September 2025 · Q12(iii) · Marks: Not stated in source · Approx Time: 10–20 minutes (approx.) · Topic 2.4: Relocation/reorganisation costs are never capitalised, regardless of connection to a specific asset
Question:

On 15th March 2025, Precision Tools Ltd. shifted a machine from one factory to another, incurring: Dismantling cost ₹12,000; Transport and installation ₹18,000; Loss due to damage in transit ₹6,000. Calculate the amount to be capitalized.

Answer / Solution:

Nil is capitalised — costs of relocating or reorganising part or all of an enterprise's operations are not included in the carrying amount of PPE under AS 10. The entire ₹36,000 (12,000+18,000+6,000) is charged off to the Profit and Loss Account.

Author’s Note: Some examinees capitalised the transport and installation cost, reasoning it was directly attributable to the machine, missing AS 10's specific exclusion of relocation costs regardless of their connection to a particular asset.

II. Integrated Questions (AS 10 with Other Standards)

Questions where AS 10 judgment is one part of a larger, genuinely connected question also testing another standard.

PYQ May 2026 · Q1(b) · Marks: 5 · Approx Time: 9 minutes (approx.) · Topic 2.8: Cost of installation - directly attributable labour/supervisor/testing costs; deferred-credit interest excluded  +  Topic 7.13/7.16: Impairment loss on a revalued asset - first set off against the revaluation reserve balance, remainder to P&L Compulsory
Question:

On 1 April, 2022, Sky Limited purchased a machinery for ₹7,35,000 (inclusive of GST @5%, input credit available for entire amount). Other installation expenses: Cost of preparation of site ₹16,500; Total Labour charges ₹75,000 (200 of 500 total men hours spent on installation); Total salary of supervisor ₹34,000 (25% of time spent on installation); Interest charges paid to supplier for deferred credit ₹8,000; Test run and experimental production expenses ₹28,200; Consultancy charges to architect for plant set up ₹18,800; Depreciation on assets used for installation ₹8,000. The machine was ready for use on October 1, 2022 but was put to use from February 1, 2023 (further expenses of ₹10,800 incurred due to this delay). Estimated useful life 10 years, SLM, no residual value.

On September 30, 2025, the company revalued the machine at ₹7 lakhs, surplus credited to revaluation reserve. For the year ended March 31, 2026, conditions indicating impairment existed and the recoverable amount was ascertained to be only ₹3 Lakhs.

You are required to: (i) Calculate the value at which the machine should be capitalized and the amount of depreciation to be charged for the year ending March 31, 2023 in the books of Sky Limited. (ii) Calculate the loss on impairment of the machine and show how this loss is to be treated in the books of Sky Limited. The company had followed the policy of writing down the revaluation surplus by the increased charge of depreciation resulting from the revaluation. (5 Marks)

Answer / Solution:

(i) Calculation of Cost of Machinery:

Purchase Price7,35,000
Add: Site Preparation Cost16,500
Labour charges (75,000 × 200/500)30,000
Supervisor's Salary (25% of 34,000)8,500
Test run and experimental production charges28,200
Architect Fees for set up18,800
Depreciation on assets used for installation8,000
Total Cost of Asset8,45,000
Less: GST credit receivable(35,000)
Value to be capitalized8,10,000
Depreciation to be charged on 31.3.2023 (for 6 months, SLM 10 year)40,500

Note: (i) Further expenses of ₹10,800 from 1.10.2022 to 1.2.2023 are charged to profit and loss A/c, as the plant was ready for production on 1.10.2022 (already capitalised) – the delay in actual use does not extend capitalisation. (ii) Interest charges of ₹8,000 paid on deferred credit terms to the supplier of the plant (not a qualifying asset) are not directly attributable costs and are written off to the Statement of Profit and Loss in the period incurred.

(ii) Statement showing impairment loss and its treatment:

Carrying amount of the machine as on 01/10/20228,10,000
Less: Depreciation for 3 years (8,10,000 x 3/10)(2,43,000)
Carrying amount as on 30/09/20255,67,000
Add: Upward revaluation (credited to revaluation reserve)1,33,000
Carrying amount of the machine as on 30/09/2025 (post-revaluation)7,00,000
Less: Depreciation for 6 months up to 31/03/2026 (7,00,000 x 0.5/7)(50,000)
Carrying amount as on 31/03/20266,50,000
Less: Recoverable amount(3,00,000)
Impairment Loss3,50,000
Less: balance in revaluation reserve as on 31/03/2026 [1,33,000 − (50,000−40,500)](1,23,500)
Impairment Loss to be debited to Profit & Loss Account2,26,500

Depreciation for 01/10/2025 to 31/03/2026 (7,00,000 x 0.5/7) = ₹50,000. Depreciation set off against Revaluation Reserve = (1,33,000 x 0.5/7) = ₹9,500 (Impairment loss set off against revaluation reserve balance as per para 58 of AS 28 "Impairment of Assets").

Author’s Note: Many examinees debited the entire ₹3,50,000 impairment loss to the profit and loss account, not applying AS 28's requirement (para 58) to first set off an impairment loss on a revalued asset against the remaining balance in that asset's revaluation reserve before charging the balance to P&L. Several also capitalised the ₹10,800 delay-related expenses instead of expensing them, since the asset was already ready for use on 1st October, 2022.

RTP May 2026 · Q10 · Marks: Not stated in source · Approx Time: 10–20 minutes (approx.) · Topic 2.8: Cost of a self-constructed asset - directly attributable costs only, excluding relocation/inauguration  +  Topic 4.4/4.9: Eligible borrowing cost net of temporary-investment income, capitalisation period
Question:

On 1st April, 2024, Y Limited purchased an industrial plot of land for ₹50,00,000 for the purpose of constructing a new factory. This cost of ₹50,00,000 included legal cost of ₹2,50,000 incurred for the purpose of acquisition of this plot. The construction of the factory commenced on 1st May, 2024. Y Limited provides you with the following details of the costs incurred in relation to the above construction:

ParticularsAmount (₹)
Preparation and levelling of the land1,60,000
Employment costs of construction workers (per month)58,000
Purchase of Raw materials for the construction42,48,000
Cost of relocating the workers to new factory for work75,000
Costs of inaugural function of the new factory on 1st January, 202595,000
Overhead costs incurred directly on the construction of the factory (per month)50,000

The construction of the factory was completed on 31st December, 2024 and production could commence on 1st February, 2025. The overall useful life of the factory building was estimated at 40 years from the date of completion. However, it was estimated that the roof would need to be replaced 20 years after the date of completion. The cost of replacing the roof at current prices would be 25% of the total cost of the building. The construction of the factory was partly financed by a loan of ₹56,00,000 raised from State Bank of India on 1st April, 2024 at an interest rate of 9% per annum. During the period when the loan proceeds had been fully utilized to finance the construction, Y Limited earned an income of ₹50,000 from the temporary investment of the proceeds. Assume that all of the net finance cost needs to be allocated to the cost of factory (excluding land) and interest cost to be capitalized based on eight months' period.

You are required to compute the carrying amount (i.e. value after charging depreciation) of the Factory in the books of Y Limited as at 31 March, 2025 as per the provisions of the relevant Accounting Standard.

Answer / Solution:

Cost of construction of the factory

Cost of Industrial Plot50,00,000
Preparation and levelling of the land1,60,000
Employment costs of construction workers (₹58,000 per month) for 8 months4,64,000
Purchase of Raw materials for the construction42,48,000
Overhead costs incurred directly on the construction of the factory (₹50,000 per month) for 8 months4,00,000
Interest on ₹56,00,000 for 9 months @ 9% = ₹3,78,000 less ₹50,0003,28,000
Total Cost (A)1,06,00,000
Depreciation (B) (W.N.)43,750
Carrying amount of the factory (A−B)1,05,56,250

Working Note: Calculation of Depreciation

On land of ₹50,00,000: Nil. On remaining cost of Building i.e. ₹1,06,00,000 − ₹50,00,000 = ₹56,00,000:

  • On Building: ₹56,00,000 × 75% / 40 yrs × 3/12 = ₹26,250
  • On roof: ₹56,00,000 × 25% / 20 yrs × 3/12 = ₹17,500
  • Total Depreciation charged = ₹43,750

Cost of relocating the workers to new factory for work and cost of inaugural function of the new factory is not directly attributable to construction cost, hence not considered.

Author’s Note: Many examinees included the relocation cost and the inauguration-function cost in the capitalised cost of the factory, failing to apply AS 10's distinction between costs necessary to bring an asset to its working condition and costs merely associated with commissioning it. Several also capitalised the gross interest of ₹3,78,000 without netting the ₹50,000 temporary-investment income against it, as AS 16 requires.

AS 26 — Intangible Assets

Every MTP/RTP/PYQ question that tests this chapter, collected in one place, with official answers and topic tags — so you can practise every question this topic has been examined with, without hunting through separate papers.

A note on accuracy (please read): This is the first edition of this book, assembled with AI assistance and reviewed as carefully as we could manage, but it has not been independently audited question-by-question. If you spot an error — a wrong figure, a wrong answer, anything that looks off — please email capranavpratiktulshyan@gmail.com with the question reference so it can be corrected in the next edition.
Scope of this book (9 questions): Covers 34 sittings: MTP Jan2025 Set1, MTP Jan2025 Set2, MTP Jan2026 Set1, MTP Jan2026 Set2, MTP May2023 Set1, MTP May2023 Set2, MTP May2024 Set1, MTP May2024 Set2, MTP May2025 Set1, MTP May2025 Set2, MTP May2026 Set1, MTP May2026 Set2, MTP Nov2023 Set1, MTP Nov2023 Set2, MTP Sep2024 Set1, MTP Sep2024 Set2, MTP Sep2025 Set1, MTP Sep2025 Set2, PYQ Jan2025, PYQ Jan2026, PYQ May2023, PYQ May2024, PYQ May2025, PYQ May2026, PYQ Nov2023, PYQ Sep2024, PYQ Sep2025, RTP Jan2025, RTP Jan2026, RTP May2024, RTP May2025, RTP May2026, RTP Sep2024, RTP Sep2025. MCQs on this chapter are deliberately not included here — practise those on the dedicated MCQ platform; this book is for descriptive/scenario practice with full worked answers.
How this book is organised: Two sections — I. Descriptive (pure AS 26) and II. Integrated (questions where AS 26 is one part of a larger question that also tests another standard). An empty Section II for a chapter is normal and expected, not a mistake — most multi-topic-looking questions are split so each topic gets its own clean entry, so genuinely combined questions are the rarer case. Each answer includes either a real Examiner's Comment (tan/orange box, quoted from ICAI's own published feedback, where one exists for that sitting) or an Author's Note (pale pink box, a likely pitfall identified by the author, not an official ICAI finding, and may not apply in every case) — see How to Read this Book.md for the full key to every colour and symbol used.

I. Descriptive & Scenario-Based Questions (pure AS 26)

Full descriptive/scenario questions where this chapter is the sole topic tested (after independent-question splitting).

MTP January 2025 Set 1 · Q1(b) · Marks: 5 · Approx Time: 9 minutes (approx.) · Topic 6.17: Recognition-as-expense rule - once expensed in a prior period, a cost cannot later be capitalised even after approval/criteria are met Compulsory
Question:

As per provisions of AS-26, how would you deal to the following situations: (1) ₹23,00,000 paid by a manufacturing company to the legal advisor for defending the patent of a product is treated as a capital expenditure. (2) During the year 2023-24, a company spent ₹7,00,000 for publicity and research expenses on one of its new consumer products which was marketed in the same accounting year but proved to be a failure. (3) A company spent ₹25,00,000 in the past three years to develop a product, these expenses were charged to profit and loss account since they did not meet AS-26 criteria for capitalization. In the current year approval of the concerned authority has been received. The company wishes to capitalize ₹25,00,000 by disclosing it as a prior period item. (4) A company with a turnover of ₹200 crores and an annual advertising budget of ₹50,00,000 had taken up for the marketing of a new product by a company. It was estimated that the company would have a turnover of ₹20 crore from the new product. The company had debited to its Profit & Loss Account the total expenditure of ₹50,00,000 incurred on extensive special initial advertisement campaign for the new product.

Answer / Solution:

As per AS 26 "Intangible Assets", subsequent expenditure on an intangible asset after its purchase or its completion should be recognized as an expense when it is incurred unless (a) it is probable that the expenditure will enable the asset to generate future economic benefits in excess of its originally assessed standard of performance; and (b) expenditure can be measured and attributed to the asset reliably. If these conditions are met, the subsequent expenditure should be added to the cost of the intangible asset.

  1. In the given case, the legal expenses to defend the patent of a product amounting ₹23,00,000 should not be capitalized and be charged to Profit and Loss Statement.
  2. The company is required to expense the entire amount of ₹7,00,000 in the Profit and Loss account for the year ended 31st March, 2024 because no benefit will arise in the future.
  3. As per AS 26, expenditure on an intangible item that was initially recognized as an expense by a reporting enterprise in previous annual financial statements should not be recognized as part of the cost of an intangible asset at a later date. Thus, the company cannot capitalize the amount of ₹25,00,000 and it should be recognized as expense.
  4. Expenditure of ₹50,00,000 on advertising and promotional activities should always be charged to Profit and Loss Statement. Hence, the company has done the correct treatment by debiting the sum of ₹50 lakhs to Profit and Loss Account.
Author’s Note: A frequent mistake is capitalising defence-of-patent legal costs or attempting to retrospectively capitalise previously expensed development costs once approval is later obtained; AS 26 bars reinstating costs already recognised as an expense in an earlier period.

MTP January 2025 Set 2 · Q1(b) · Marks: 7 · Approx Time: 13 minutes (approx.) · Topic 6.24-6.25: Carrying amount from the date recognition criteria first met, then tested for impairment against recoverable amount Compulsory
Question:

Honey Ltd. is in the process of developing a new production method. During the financial year ended 31st March, 2023, total expenditure incurred on development of this production method was ₹98,00,000. On 1st Jan, 2023, the production method met the criteria as an intangible asset and expenditure incurred till this date was ₹68,00,000. Further expenditure incurred on the new method was ₹72,00,000 for the year ended 31st March, 2024 and recoverable amount of the know how embodied in the new method for this financial year is ₹52,00,000. You are required to calculate: (1) The carrying amount of the Intangible asset on 31st March, 2023. (2) The expenditure to be shown in Statement of Profit and Loss for the year ended 31st March, 2024. (3) The carrying amount of the Intangible asset on 31st March, 2024.

Answer / Solution:

As per AS 26 'Intangible Assets':

(i) Carrying value of intangible asset as on 31.03.2023: at the end of financial year, on 31st March 2023, the production process will be recognized (i.e. carrying amount) as an intangible asset at a cost of ₹30 lacs (98−68), being expenditure incurred since the date the recognition criteria were met, i.e. from 1st January, 2023.

 ₹ in lacs
Carrying Amount as on 31.03.202330
Expenditure during 2023–202472
Book Value102
Recoverable Amount(52)
Impairment loss50

(ii) ₹50 lakhs to be charged to Profit and Loss account for the year ending 31.03.2024.

 ₹ in lacs
Book Value102
Less: Impairment loss(50)
Carrying amount as on 31.03.202452

(iii) Carrying value of intangible asset as on 31.03.2024 = ₹52 lacs.

Author’s Note: A common error is treating the entire ₹98 lakhs of development expenditure as the intangible asset's cost, rather than starting the carrying amount only from the date the AS 26 recognition criteria were first met (1st January 2023), and separately, omitting the impairment test against the recoverable amount once further expenditure is added in the following year.

MTP January 2026 Set 2 · Q1(b) · Marks: 5 · Approx Time: 9 minutes (approx.) · Topic 6.5: Subsequent expenditure, previously-expensed items never later capitalized, advertising always expensed Compulsory
Question:

As per provisions of AS-26, how would you deal with the following situations: (1) ₹23,00,000 paid by a manufacturing company to the legal advisor for defending the patent of a product, treated as capital expenditure. (2) During 2024-2025, a company spent ₹7,00,000 on publicity and research expenses on a new consumer product, marketed the same year but proved a failure. (3) A company spent ₹25,00,000 over three years to develop a product, charged to P&L since AS-26 capitalization criteria were not met; in the current year approval was received and the company wishes to capitalize ₹25,00,000 as a prior period item. (4) A company (turnover ₹200 crores, annual advertising budget ₹50,00,000) debited ₹50,00,000 to P&L for an extensive special initial advertisement campaign for a new product expected to generate ₹20 crore turnover.

Answer / Solution:

(1) The legal expenses of ₹23,00,000 to defend the patent should not be capitalized — subsequent expenditure on an intangible asset is expensed unless it enables the asset to generate future economic benefits in excess of its originally assessed performance and can be reliably measured and attributed. Defending an existing right does not meet this test; charge to P&L.

(2) The full ₹7,00,000 must be expensed in the year ended 31st March, 2025, since the product failed and no future economic benefit will arise.

(3) AS 26 explicitly prohibits reinstating expenditure on an intangible item that was previously recognised as an expense — the company cannot capitalize the ₹25,00,000 even with the current-year approval; it remains an expense already recognised, not a prior period item to be restated.

(4) Advertising and promotional expenditure is always charged to the Profit and Loss Account as incurred, regardless of expected future revenue benefit — the company's treatment of debiting the full ₹50,00,000 is correct.

Author’s Note: Some examinees allowed the ₹25,00,000 to be capitalized once approval was received, missing AS 26's explicit bar on reinstating expenditure once it has been recognised as an expense in an earlier period.

MTP January 2026 Set 2 · Q6(b) · Marks: 5 · Approx Time: 9 minutes (approx.) · Topic 6.7: Amortization in the ratio of estimated future cash flows, not straight-line
Question:

Record Journal Entries for amortization in the books of Huge Ltd. for the year ended 31st March, 2025 with reference to AS-26: Patent Rights acquired for ₹340 lakhs on 01.04.2023, estimated product life 4 years, amortization decided in the ratio of estimated future cash flows: Year 1 ₹140 lakhs, Year 2 ₹350 lakhs, Year 3 ₹280 lakhs, Year 4 ₹420 lakhs.

Answer / Solution:

Amortization for the second year (2024-25, the year in question): ₹340 lakhs × 350/(140+350+280+420) = 340 × 350/1,190 = ₹100 lakhs.

Journal entry (31.3.2025): Amortization A/c Dr. 100 lakhs; To Patent Rights A/c 100 lakhs. P&L A/c Dr. 100 lakhs; To Amortization A/c 100 lakhs.

Author’s Note: Some examinees amortized the patent on a straight-line basis (₹85 lakhs/year) instead of following the cash-flow-ratio method the question specifically directs.

MTP May 2024 Set 2 · Q1(a) · Marks: 5 · Approx Time: 9 minutes (approx.) · Topic 6.17: Expenditure that fails asset-recognition criteria must be expensed, never later deferred once no future benefit is expected Compulsory
Question:

K Ltd. launched a project for producing product X in October, 2023. The Company incurred ₹40 lakhs towards Research and Development expenses upto 31st March, 2024. Due to prevailing market conditions, the Management came to conclusion that the product cannot be manufactured and sold in the market for the next 10 years. The Management hence wants to defer the expenditure write off to future years. Advise the Company as per the applicable Accounting Standard.

Answer / Solution:

As per AS 26 "Intangible Assets", expenditure on research should be recognized as an expense when it is incurred. An intangible asset arising from development (or from the development phase of an internal project) should be recognized if, and only if, an enterprise can demonstrate all of the conditions specified in para 44 of the standard. An intangible asset (arising from development) should be derecognised when no future economic benefits are expected from its use according to para 87 of the standard. Thus, the manager cannot defer the expenditure write off to future years in the given case.

Hence, the expenses amounting ₹40 lakhs incurred on the research and development project has to be written off in the current year ending 31st March, 2024.

Author’s Note: A common error here is advising deferral of the expenditure on the basis that the product might still become viable in future, rather than applying AS 26's rule that once no future economic benefit is expected, the amount cannot be carried forward or deferred, regardless of management's stated intention.

RTP January 2025 · Q19 · Marks: Not stated in source · Approx Time: 10–20 minutes (approx.) · Topic 6.15: Costs incurred before technological feasibility is established are expensed (research phase); costs from that point until product-master completion are capitalised (development phase); post-development duplication/packing costs are expensed
Question:

During 2023-2024, an enterprise incurred costs to develop and produce a routine, low risk computer software product, as follows:

Completion of detailed programme and design (Phase 1)₹25,000
Coding and Testing for establishing technical feasibility (Phase 2)₹20,000
Other coding costs (Phase 3)₹42,000
Testing costs (Phase 4)₹12,000
Product masters for training materials (Phase 5)₹13,000
Duplication of computer software and training materials, from product masters (2,000 units) (Phase 6)₹40,000
Packing the product (1,000 units) (Phase 7)₹11,000

After completion of phase 2, it was established that the computer software is technically feasible for the market. What amount should be capitalized as software costs in the books of the company, on the Balance Sheet date?

Answer / Solution:

As per para 44 of AS 26, costs incurred in creating a computer software product should be charged to research and development expense when incurred until technological feasibility/asset recognition criteria has been established for the product. Technological feasibility/asset recognition criteria have been established upon completion of detailed programme design or working model. In this case, ₹45,000 would be recorded as an expense (₹25,000 for completion of detailed programme design and ₹20,000 for coding and testing to establish technological feasibility/asset recognition criteria).

Cost incurred from the point of technological feasibility/asset recognition criteria until the time when product costs are incurred are capitalized as software cost (₹42,000 + ₹12,000 + ₹13,000) = ₹67,000. Duplication of computer software and training materials, from product masters and packing the products are costs incurred after the development phase. Hence, the same shall be expensed off during the year it is incurred.

Author’s Note: A common error is capitalising the cost of completing the detailed programme design and the coding/testing performed to establish technical feasibility, missing that AS 26 requires all costs incurred before technological feasibility is established to be expensed as research and development, with capitalisation beginning only from that point onward.

RTP January 2026 · Q17 · Marks: Not stated in source · Approx Time: 10–20 minutes (approx.) · Topic 6.7: Amortization ratio revised mid-life when future-cash-flow estimates and remaining useful life change
Question:

Swift Limited acquired patent rights to manufacture Solar Roof Top Panels for ₹600 lacs. Product life cycle estimated at 5 years; amortization decided in the ratio of future cash flows: Year 1–5: 300, 300, 300, 150, 150 (₹ lacs). After Year 3, estimated balance future life revised to 3 years, with expected cash flow after Year 5 of ₹75 lacs. Determine the amortization cost of the patent for each year per AS 26.

Answer / Solution:

Years 1–3, amortized in the ratio of the originally estimated future cash flows 300:300:300:150:150 (total 1,200): each of Years 1, 2, 3 = ₹600 × 300/1,200 = ₹150 lacs/year.

Unamortized patent cost after Year 3 = 600−450 = ₹150 lacs, now amortized over the revised remaining life of 3 years (Years 4, 5, 6) in the ratio of the revised estimated future cash flows: 150:150:75 (i.e. 2:2:1). Year 4 = 150×2/5=₹60 lacs; Year 5 = ₹60 lacs; Year 6 = 150×1/5=₹30 lacs.

Total amortized over the patent's full (revised) life: 150+150+150+60+60+30 = ₹600 lacs, fully recovering the original cost.

Author’s Note: Some examinees continued amortizing the remaining balance using the original 5-year cash-flow ratio, not re-basing the calculation on the revised 3-year remaining life and its own revised cash-flow estimates.

RTP May 2024 · Q12 · Marks: Not stated in source · Approx Time: 10–20 minutes (approx.) · Topic 6.7-6.11: Separately-acquired intangibles (franchise, patent, purchased-business goodwill) recognised at cost and amortised over their useful/contractual/economic life
Question:

Naresh Ltd. had the following transactions during the financial year 2022-2023:

  1. Naresh Ltd. acquired the running business of Sunil Ltd. for ₹10,80,000 on 15th May, 2022. The fair value of Sunil Ltd.'s net assets was ₹5,16,000. Naresh Ltd. is of the view that due to popularity of Sunil Ltd.'s product in the market, its goodwill exists.
  2. Naresh Ltd. had taken a franchise on July 2022 to operate a restaurant from Sankalp Ltd. for ₹1,80,000 and at an annual fee of 10% of net revenues (after deducting expenditure). The franchise expires after 6 years. Net revenues were ₹60,000 during the financial year 2022-2023.
  3. On 20th August, 2022, Naresh Ltd, incurred costs of ₹2,40,000 to register the patent for its product. Naresh Ltd. expects the patent's economic life to be 8 years.

Naresh Ltd. follows an accounting policy to amortize all intangibles on straight line basis over the maximum period permitted by accounting standards taking a full year amortization in the year of acquisition. Goodwill on acquisition of business to be amortized over 5 years (SLM) as per AS 14. Prepare a schedule showing the intangible assets section in Naresh Ltd. Balance Sheet at 31st March, 2023.

AS 16 — Borrowing Costs

Every MTP/RTP/PYQ question that tests this chapter, collected in one place, with official answers and topic tags — so you can practise every question this topic has been examined with, without hunting through separate papers.

A note on accuracy (please read): This is the first edition of this book, assembled with AI assistance and reviewed as carefully as we could manage, but it has not been independently audited question-by-question. If you spot an error — a wrong figure, a wrong answer, anything that looks off — please email capranavpratiktulshyan@gmail.com with the question reference so it can be corrected in the next edition.
Scope of this book (23 questions): Covers 34 sittings: MTP Jan2025 Set1, MTP Jan2025 Set2, MTP Jan2026 Set1, MTP Jan2026 Set2, MTP May2023 Set1, MTP May2023 Set2, MTP May2024 Set1, MTP May2024 Set2, MTP May2025 Set1, MTP May2025 Set2, MTP May2026 Set1, MTP May2026 Set2, MTP Nov2023 Set1, MTP Nov2023 Set2, MTP Sep2024 Set1, MTP Sep2024 Set2, MTP Sep2025 Set1, MTP Sep2025 Set2, PYQ Jan2025, PYQ Jan2026, PYQ May2023, PYQ May2024, PYQ May2025, PYQ May2026, PYQ Nov2023, PYQ Sep2024, PYQ Sep2025, RTP Jan2025, RTP Jan2026, RTP May2024, RTP May2025, RTP May2026, RTP Sep2024, RTP Sep2025. MCQs on this chapter are deliberately not included here — practise those on the dedicated MCQ platform; this book is for descriptive/scenario practice with full worked answers.
How this book is organised: Two sections — I. Descriptive (pure AS 16) and II. Integrated (questions where AS 16 is one part of a larger question that also tests another standard). An empty Section II for a chapter is normal and expected, not a mistake — most multi-topic-looking questions are split so each topic gets its own clean entry, so genuinely combined questions are the rarer case. Each answer includes either a real Examiner's Comment (tan/orange box, quoted from ICAI's own published feedback, where one exists for that sitting) or an Author's Note (pale pink box, a likely pitfall identified by the author, not an official ICAI finding, and may not apply in every case) — see How to Read this Book.md for the full key to every colour and symbol used.

MTP January 2026 Set 1 · Q1(b) · Marks: 7 · Approx Time: 13 minutes (approx.) · Topic 4.5: Specific and general borrowings combined, net of temporary-investment income, then depreciation from completion date Compulsory
Question:

On 1st April, 2024, A Limited started the construction of an Office Building (qualifying asset; land is a separate asset, not part of the qualifying asset). For construction, the company raised a specific loan of ₹14 lakhs from a Bank at 12% p.a. Interest income of ₹15,000 was earned on this loan while held in anticipation of payments. The company's other outstanding loans on 1st April, 2024: ₹20,00,000 at 15%; ₹30,00,000 at 8%. Construction started 1st April, 2024, completed 31st January, 2025 (ready for intended use). Payments to the contractor: 1st April 2024 ₹4,00,000; 1st August 2024 ₹10,00,000; 1st December 2024 ₹25,00,000; 31st January 2025 ₹5,00,000. Life of building 20 years, straight line depreciation. Required: (i) borrowing cost to be capitalized; (ii) initial journal entry (interest paid at year end); (iii) depreciation for the year ending 31st March, 2025; (iv) carrying value of building as on 31st March, 2025.

Answer / Solution:

(i) Weighted average accumulated expenses and borrowing cost capitalized:

DateAmountSourceCalculation₹
1 Apr 20244,00,000Specific4,00,000 × 12% × 10/1240,000
1 Aug 202410,00,000Specific10,00,000 × 12% × 10/121,00,000
1 Dec 202425,00,000General (10.8% w. avg.)25,00,000 × 10.8% × 2/1245,000
31 Jan 20255,00,000General0 months remainingNil
Subtotal1,85,000
Less: interest income on specific borrowing(15,000)
Total borrowing cost to be capitalized1,70,000

Working note — weighted average rate on general borrowings: (20,00,000×15%=3,00,000) + (30,00,000×8%=2,40,000) = 5,40,000 on 50,00,000 = 10.8%.

(ii) Journal entry (31.1.2025): Building A/c Dr. 45,70,000; To Bank A/c 44,00,000; To Interest Payable A/c (borrowing cost) 1,70,000. (Cost of building = 44,00,000 payments + 1,70,000 capitalised interest.)

(iii) Depreciation for year ended 31.3.2025 = 45,70,000 / 20 years × 2/12 (Feb–Mar, post-completion) = ₹38,083.33.

(iv) Carrying value as on 31.3.2025 = 45,70,000 − 38,083.33 = ₹45,31,917 (approx).

Author’s Note: Common errors: forgetting to net off the ₹15,000 temporary-investment interest income against capitalised borrowing cost, misclassifying the 1st December payment as specific-loan funded once the specific loan is fully drawn, or depreciating from the payment date rather than the date the asset was ready for use (31st January).

MTP May 2023 Set 1 · Q6(c) · Marks: 5 · Approx Time: 9 minutes (approx.) · Topic 4.4/4.6: Borrowing costs eligible for capitalisation on a specific borrowing - actual interest incurred less income earned on temporary investment of the surplus, not the weighted-average general-borrowing rate
Question:

Vital Limited borrowed an amount of ₹150 crores on 1.4.2021 for construction of boiler plant @ 10% p.a. The plant is expected to be completed in 4 years. Since the weighted average cost of capital is 13% p.a., the accountant of Vital Ltd. capitalized ₹19.50 crores for the accounting period ending on 31.3.2022. Due to surplus fund out of ₹150 crores, an income of ₹1.50 crores was earned and credited to profit and loss account. Comment on the above treatment of accountant with reference to relevant accounting standard. (5 Marks)

Answer / Solution:

Para 10 of AS 16 'Borrowing Costs' states that to the extent the funds are borrowed specifically for the purpose of obtaining a qualifying asset, the amount of borrowing costs eligible for capitalization on that asset should be determined as the actual borrowing costs incurred on that borrowing during the period less any income on the temporary investment of those borrowings. The capitalization rate should be the weighted average of the borrowing costs applicable to the borrowings of the enterprise that are outstanding during the period, other than borrowings made specifically for the purpose of obtaining a qualifying asset. Hence, in the above case, treatment of accountant of Vital Ltd. is incorrect. The amount of borrowing costs capitalized for the financial year 2021-22 should be calculated as follows:

Particulars₹
Actual interest for 2021-22 (10% of ₹150 crores)15.00 crores
Less: Income on temporary investment from specific borrowings(1.50 crores)
Borrowing costs to be capitalized during year 2021-2213.50 crores
Author’s Note: A common error is applying the enterprise's weighted average cost of capital (or the general-borrowings capitalisation rate) to a loan that was specifically raised for the qualifying asset, instead of using the actual interest rate on that specific borrowing net of any temporary-investment income earned on the surplus funds.

MTP May 2023 Set 2 · Q1(a) · Marks: 5 · Approx Time: 9 minutes (approx.) · Topic 4.7: General borrowings capitalisation rate as weighted average of period/rate-varying borrowings Compulsory
Question:

ABC Limited has started construction of an asset on 1st December, 2021, which continues till 31st March, 2022 (and is expected to go beyond a year). The entity has not taken any specific borrowings to finance the construction of the asset but has incurred finance costs on its general borrowings during the construction period. The directly attributable expenditure at the beginning of the month on this asset was ₹10 lakh in December 2021 and ₹4 lakh in each of the months of January to March 2022. At the beginning of the year, the entity had taken Inter Corporate Deposits of ₹20 lakh at 9% rate of interest and had an overdraft of ₹4 lakh, which increased to ₹8 lakh on 1st March, 2022. Interest was paid on the overdraft at 10% until 1st January, 2022 and then the rate was increased to 12%. You are required to calculate the annual capitalization rate for computation of borrowing cost in accordance with AS 16 'Borrowing Costs'.

Answer / Solution:

Calculation of capitalization rate on borrowings other than specific borrowings

Nature of general borrowingsPeriod of outstanding balanceAmount of loan (₹)Rate of interest p.a.Weighted average amount of interest (₹)
9% Debentures12 months20,00,0009%1,80,000
Bank overdraft9 months4,00,00010%30,000
Bank overdraft2 months4,00,00012%8,000
Bank overdraft1 month8,00,00012%8,000
Total36,00,0002,26,000

Weighted average cost of borrowings = {20,00,000 × (12/12)} + {4,00,000 × (11/12)} + {8,00,000 × (1/12)} = ₹24,33,334

Capitalisation rate = [(Weighted average amount of interest / Weighted average of general borrowings) × 100] = [(2,26,000 / 24,33,334) × 100] = 9.29% p.a.

Author’s Note: A common error is applying the overdraft's changed interest rate or increased balance retroactively across the full year rather than time-weighting each rate/balance segment separately, or omitting the fixed-rate borrowing from the weighted-average pool entirely.

MTP May 2025 Set 1 · Q6(a) [OR-alt 2] · Marks: 4 · Approx Time: 8 minutes (approx.) · Topic 4.11: Cessation of capitalisation - substantially complete activities; part-by-part cessation for assets completed in stages
Question:

When capitalisation of borrowing cost should cease as per Accounting Standard 16? Explain in brief.

Answer / Solution:

Capitalization of borrowing costs should cease when substantially all the activities necessary to prepare the qualifying asset for its intended use or sale are complete. An asset is normally ready for its intended use or sale when its physical construction or production is complete even though routine administrative work might still continue. If minor modifications such as the decoration of a property to the user's specification, are all that are outstanding, this indicates that substantially all the activities are complete. When the construction of a qualifying asset is completed in parts and a completed part is capable of being used while construction continues for the other parts, capitalization of borrowing costs in relation to a part should cease when substantially all the activities necessary to prepare that part for its intended use or sale are complete.

Author’s Note: A common error is assuming capitalisation continues until the asset is actually put into use or sold, rather than ceasing once the asset is merely ready for its intended use, even if routine administrative work or minor finishing touches remain outstanding.

MTP May 2026 Set 1 · Q1(a) · Marks: 5 · Approx Time: 9 minutes (approx.) · Topic 4.4/4.6/4.7: Eligible borrowing cost - specific vs general borrowings, netting temporary investment income Compulsory
Question:

Glen Ltd. began construction of a new building on 1st January, 2025. On 1st April, 2025, following two loans were obtained to fund the construction cost:
(i) Loan of ₹60,00,000 from Data Bank Ltd. was taken at interest rate of 8% per annum. This loan was fully utilized for construction of the new building.
(ii) Loan of ₹20,00,000 from Satya Bank Ltd. Out of this, loan amount of ₹6,00,000 was utilized for working capital purpose. Total interest of ₹1,92,000 were paid to Satya Bank Ltd. for the financial year 2025-26.
Construction of the new building was completed on 31st January, 2026 and was ready for its intended use on the same date.
None of the loan was repaid during the year. The building is a qualifying asset for the purpose of AS-16.
Out of loan from Data Bank Ltd., surplus funds were temporarily invested for the short period of time. This temporary investment earned interest of ₹30,000.
You are required to calculate the amount of interest (a) to be capitalized, (b) to be charged to profit and loss account from the total interest incurred as borrowing cost during the year 2025-26 (as per AS-16). (5 Marks)

Answer / Solution:

According to AS 16 “Borrowing Costs”, borrowing costs that are directly attributable to the acquisition, construction or production of a qualifying asset should be capitalized as part of the cost of that asset. The amount of borrowing costs eligible for capitalization should be determined in accordance with this Standard. Other borrowing costs should be recognised as an expense in the period in which they are incurred.

The standard also states that to the extent that funds are borrowed specifically for the purpose of obtaining a qualifying asset, the amount of borrowing costs eligible for capitalization on that asset should be determined as the actual borrowing costs incurred on that borrowing during the period less any income on the temporary investment of those borrowings.

Thus, eligible borrowing cost on Loan of data bank to be capitalized:
= ₹(60,00,000 x 8%) x 10/12 − ₹30,000
= ₹(4,80,000 x 10/12) = ₹4,00,000
= ₹4,00,000 − ₹30,000
= ₹3,70,000

LoanParticularsNature of assetsInterest to be Capitalized (₹)Interest to be charged to Profit & Loss Account (₹)
Data bankConstruction of factory buildingQualifying Asset3,70,000(4,80,000 − 4,00,000) = 80,000
Satya BankConstruction of factory buildingQualifying Asset(1,92,000 x 14/20) x 10/12 = 1,12,000(1,92,000 x 14/20) x 2/12 = 22,400
Satya BankWorking CapitalNot a Qualifying AssetNIL(1,92,000 x 6/20) = ₹57,600
Total₹4,82,000₹1,60,000

Note: Loan from Satya bank is considered to be specific borrowings.

Author’s Note: Many examinees capitalised the full interest on the Data Bank loan without deducting the ₹30,000 temporary-investment income as required under AS 16, and several also failed to apportion the Satya Bank interest between the qualifying-asset and working-capital portions, treating the entire ₹1,92,000 as eligible for capitalisation.

MTP May 2026 Set 2 · Q6(a) [OR-alt 2] · Marks: 4 · Approx Time: 8 minutes (approx.) · Topic 4.11: Cessation of capitalisation, including the part-completion case
Question:

When capitalisation of borrowing cost should cease as per Accounting Standard 16? Explain in brief. (4 Marks)

Answer / Solution:

Capitalization of borrowing costs should cease when substantially all the activities necessary to prepare the qualifying asset for its intended use or sale are complete. An asset is normally ready for its intended use or sale when its physical construction or production is complete even though routine administrative work might still continue. If minor modifications such as the decoration of a property to the user's specification, are all that are outstanding, this indicates that substantially all the activities are complete. When the construction of a qualifying asset is completed in parts and a completed part is capable of being used while construction continues for the other parts, capitalization of borrowing costs in relation to a part should cease when substantially all the activities necessary to prepare that part for its intended use or sale are complete.

Author’s Note: Several examinees described only the overall-completion cessation rule and omitted the part-completion exception, despite this being the same principle tested numerically elsewhere in this paper's Case Scenario I.

MTP November 2023 Set 1 · Q1(c) · Marks: 5 · Approx Time: 9 minutes (approx.) · Topic 4.4: Borrowing costs eligible for capitalisation - apportionment of a composite loan's interest between one qualifying asset and several non-qualifying assets Compulsory
Question:

On 15th April, 2022 RBM Ltd. obtained a Term Loan from the Bank for ₹320 lakhs to be utilized as under:

Particulars₹ (in lakhs)
Construction for factory shed240
Purchase of Machinery30
Working capital24
Purchase of Vehicles12
Advance for tools/cranes etc.8
Purchase of technical know how6

In March, 2023 construction of shed was completed and machinery was installed. Total interest charged by the bank for the year ending 31st March, 2023 was ₹40 lakhs.

In the context of provisions of AS 16 ‘Borrowing Costs’, show the treatment of interest and also explain the nature of Assets.

Answer / Solution:

As per AS 16 a qualifying asset is an asset that necessarily takes a substantial period of time to get ready for its intended use or sale. Other investments and those inventories that are routinely manufactured or otherwise produced in large quantities on a repetitive basis over a short period of time, are not qualifying assets. Assets that are ready for their intended use or sale when acquired also are not qualifying assets. Borrowing costs that are directly attributable to the acquisition, construction or production of a qualifying asset should be capitalized as part of the cost of that asset. Other borrowing costs should be recognized as an expense in the period in which they are incurred.

Construction of factory shed amounting ₹240 lakhs is a qualifying asset in the given case. The interest for this amount during the year will be added to the cost of factory shed. All others (purchase of machinery, vehicles and technical know how, working capital, advance for tools/cranes) are non-qualifying assets and related borrowing cost will be charged to Profit and Loss statement.

Qualifying Asset as per AS 16 (construction of a shed) = ₹240 lakhs
Borrowing cost to be capitalized = ₹40 lakhs × 240/320 = ₹30 lakhs
Interest to be debited to Profit or Loss account: ₹(40 − 30) = ₹10 lakhs.

Note: Assumed that construction of factory shed completed on 31st March, 2023.

Author’s Note: A common error is capitalising interest on the entire ₹320 lakh loan, or on the machinery/vehicle/technical-know-how portions as well, instead of identifying the factory shed as the only qualifying asset and apportioning the ₹40 lakh interest strictly in the ratio of that asset's own utilisation (240/320) to the total borrowing.

MTP September 2024 Set 2 · Q1(b) · Marks: 4 · Approx Time: 8 minutes (approx.) · Topic 4.5: 12-month substantial-period presumption is rebuttable when a shorter period is genuinely, technically justified Compulsory
Question:

A company incorporated in June 2023, has setup a factory within a period of 8 months with borrowed funds. The construction period of the assets had reduced drastically due to usage of technical innovations by the company and the company is able to justify the reasons for the same. Whether interest on borrowings for the period prior to the date of setting up the factory should be capitalized although it has taken less than 12 months for the assets to get ready for use. You are required to comment on the necessary treatment with reference to AS 16.

Answer / Solution:

As per AS 16 ‘Borrowing Costs’, a qualifying asset is one that necessarily takes a substantial period of time to get ready for its intended use or sale. What constitutes a substantial period of time primarily depends on the facts and circumstances of each case; ordinarily a period of twelve months is considered substantial unless a shorter or longer period can be justified. In estimating the period, the time an asset takes, technologically and commercially, to get ready for its intended use or sale is considered — there is a rebuttable presumption that 12 months constitutes a substantial period.

Under circumstances where the construction period has reduced drastically due to technical innovation, the 12-month period should be looked at as a benchmark, not a conclusive yardstick. An enterprise that completes the asset in 8 months should not be penalised for its efficiency by being denied interest capitalisation. The substantial-period criterion exists to ensure enterprises do not spend disproportionate time and effort capturing immaterial interest cost for capitalisation purposes.

Conclusion: since the factory was constructed in 8 months (a genuinely justified, technically-innovation-driven reduction), it is still considered a qualifying asset, and the interest on borrowings for the same shall be capitalised, although it took less than 12 months for the asset to get ready for use.

Author’s Note: A common error here is treating the 12-month benchmark as a rigid, non-rebuttable rule and denying capitalisation outright once construction takes under 12 months, without weighing the facts-and-circumstances test AS 16 actually applies.

MTP September 2025 Set 1 · Q5(b) · Marks: 7 · Approx Time: 13 minutes (approx.) · Topic 4.5: Specific and general borrowings combined, net of temporary-investment income, then depreciation from completion date
Question:

On 1st April, 2023, Green Limited started the construction of an Office Building (qualified asset). The land under the building is regarded as a separate asset and is not a part of qualifying asset.

For the purpose of construction of building, the company raised a specific loan of ₹14 lakhs from a Bank at an interest rate of 12% per annum. An interest income of ₹15,000 was earned on this loan while it was held in anticipation of payments.

The company's other outstanding loans on 1st April, 2023 were as follows: ₹20,00,000 at 15% per annum; ₹30,00,000 at 8% per annum.

The construction of building started on 1st April, 2023 and was completed on 31st January, 2024 when it was ready for its intended use. Up to the date of completion of the building, the following payments were made to the contractor: 1st April, 2023 ₹4,00,000; 1st August, 2023 ₹10,00,000; 1st December, 2023 ₹25,00,000; 31st January, 2024 ₹5,00,000.

The life of building is estimated to be 20 years and depreciation is calculated on straight line method. You are required to: (i) Calculate the amount of borrowing cost to be capitalized. (ii) Pass initial journal entry to recognise the cost of building. (iii) Depreciation on building for the year ending 31st March, 2024. (iv) Carrying value of building as on 31st March, 2024.

Answer / Solution:

(i) Computation of borrowing cost to be capitalized for specific and general borrowings, based on weighted average accumulated expenses:

Date of incurrence of expenditureAmount spentFinanced throughCalculation₹
1st April 20234,00,000Specific borrowing4,00,000 × 12% × 10/1240,000
1st August 202310,00,000Specific borrowing10,00,000 × 12% × 10/121,00,000
1st December 202325,00,000General borrowing25,00,000 × 10.8% × 2/1245,000
31st January 20245,00,000General borrowing5,00,000 × 10.8% × 0/12Nil
Subtotal1,85,000
Less: interest income on borrowing(15,000)
Total amount of borrowing cost to be capitalized1,70,000

(ii) Journal Entry (31.1.2024): Building account Dr. 45,70,000; To Bank account 44,00,000; To Interest payable (borrowing cost) 1,70,000. (Being expenditure incurred on construction of building and borrowing cost thereon capitalized.) Note: it is assumed that interest amount will be paid at the year end; hence entry for interest payable has been passed on 31.1.2024.

(iii) Depreciation = 45,70,000 / 20 years × 2/12 (Feb–Mar, post-completion) = ₹38,083.

(iv) Carrying amount = 45,70,000 − 38,083 = ₹45,31,917.

Author’s Note: A common error here is forgetting to net off the interest income earned on the specific borrowing while it was held in anticipation of payments, or capitalising interest for the general borrowings using a simple average rather than a weighted-average rate.

MTP September 2025 Set 2 · Q6(a) · Marks: 5 · Approx Time: 9 minutes (approx.) · Topic 4.4: Amortised bond discount is a borrowing-cost component, capitalised only for the portion of the period during which the qualifying asset's acquisition/construction/production takes place
Question:

How will interest be capitalised when qualifying assets are funded by borrowings in the nature of bonds that are issued at a discount?

Answer / Solution:

As per AS 16, "Borrowing costs are interest and other costs incurred by an enterprise in connection with the borrowing of funds." The Statement also contemplates "amortisation of discounts or premiums relating to borrowings" as a component of borrowing costs (paragraph 4(b)). Thus, borrowing costs comprise the periodic interest payable on the bonds in question and the amount of discount amortised during the period.

Paragraph 6 of the Statement states that "Borrowing costs that are directly attributable to the acquisition, construction or production of a qualifying asset should be capitalised as part of the cost of that asset." Paragraph 19 further states that "Capitalisation of borrowing costs should cease when substantially all the activities necessary to prepare the qualifying asset for its intended use or sale are complete." Thus, only that portion of the amortised discount should be capitalised as part of the cost of a qualifying asset which relates to the period during which acquisition, construction or production of the asset takes place.

Author’s Note: A common error here is treating only the coupon interest as the borrowing cost and overlooking that the periodic amortisation of a bond's issue discount is itself an explicit component of borrowing cost under AS 16.

PYQ November 2023 · Q1(a) · Marks: 5 · Approx Time: 9 minutes (approx.) · Topic 4.6/4.7: Specific borrowings (Data Bank, fully attributable) and a single general borrowing (Satya Bank) apportioned between a qualifying asset and working capital, net of temporary-investment income Compulsory
Question:

Glen Ltd. began construction of a new building on 1st January, 2022. On 1st April, 2022, following two loans were obtained to fund the construction cost:

(i) Loan of ₹60,00,000 from Data Bank Ltd. was taken at interest rate of 8% per annum. This loan was fully utilized for construction of the new building.

(ii) Loan of ₹20,00,000 from Satya Bank Ltd. Out of this, loan amount of ₹6,00,000 was utilized for working capital purpose. Total interest of ₹1,92,000 were paid to Satya Bank Ltd. for the financial year 2022-23.

Construction of the new building was completed on 31st January, 2023 and was ready for its intended use on the same date.

None of the loan was repaid during the year. The building is a qualifying asset for the purpose of AS-16.

Out of loan from Data Bank Ltd., surplus funds were temporarily invested for the short period of time. This temporary investment earned interest of ₹30,000.

You are required to calculate the amount of interest (a) to be capitalized, (b) to be charged to profit and loss account from the total interest incurred as borrowing cost during the year 2022-23 (as per AS-16). (5 Marks)

Answer / Solution:

According to AS 16 “Borrowing Costs”, borrowing costs that are directly attributable to the acquisition, construction or production of a qualifying asset should be capitalized as part of the cost of that asset. The amount of borrowing costs eligible for capitalization should be determined in accordance with this Standard. Other borrowing costs should be recognised as an expense in the period in which they are incurred.

The standard also states that to the extent that funds are borrowed specifically for the purpose of obtaining a qualifying asset, the amount of borrowing costs eligible for capitalization on that asset should be determined as the actual borrowing costs incurred on that borrowing during the period less any income on the temporary investment of those borrowings.

Thus, eligible borrowing cost on Loan of Data Bank to be capitalized:

= ₹(60,00,000 × 8%) × 10/12 − ₹30,000
= ₹4,00,000 − ₹30,000
= ₹3,70,000

LoanParticularsNature of assets(a) Interest to be Capitalized (₹)(b) Interest to be charged to Profit & Loss Account (₹)
Data BankConstruction of factory buildingQualifying Asset3,70,000(4,80,000 − 4,00,000) = 80,000
Satya BankConstruction of factory buildingQualifying Asset(1,92,000 × 14/20) × 10/12 = 1,12,000(1,92,000 × 14/20) × 2/12 = 22,400
Satya BankWorking CapitalNot a Qualifying AssetNIL(1,92,000 × 6/20) = ₹57,600
Total₹4,82,000₹1,60,000

Note: Loan from Satya Bank is considered to be specific borrowings.

Author’s Note: Many examinees correctly capitalised the Data Bank loan's borrowing cost but failed to net the ₹30,000 temporary-investment income against it before capitalising, overstating the amount eligible for capitalisation under AS 16. Several examinees also treated the entire Satya Bank interest as attributable to the qualifying asset without first apportioning it between the working-capital and construction purposes in the 6:14 ratio, and some capitalised interest for the full 12-month period instead of restricting the Data Bank capitalisation window to the construction period ending 31st January, 2023.

RTP January 2025 · Q11 · Marks: Not stated in source · Approx Time: 10–20 minutes (approx.) · Topic 4.4: Amortisation of a bond discount is a component of borrowing cost eligible for capitalisation only up to the period during which the qualifying asset is under construction
Question:

How will interest be capitalized when qualifying assets are funded by borrowings in the nature of bonds that are issued at a discount?

X Ltd. issued in year 1, a 3 year 10% p.a. (interest paid annually) bond with a face value of ₹1,00,000 at a price of ₹90,000 to finance a qualifying asset which is ready for intended use at the end of year 2. Compute the amount of borrowings costs to be capitalized if the company uses for amortization of discount straight line basis.

Answer / Solution:

As per AS 16, "Borrowing costs are interest and other costs incurred by an enterprise in connection with the borrowing of funds". Further, as per para 4(b) of the standard, "amortization of discounts or premiums relating to borrowings" is a component of borrowing costs. Thus, the borrowing costs comprise the periodic interest payable on the bonds in question and the amount of discount amortised during the period.

Paragraph 6 of the Statement, inter-alia, states that "Borrowing costs that are directly attributable to the acquisition, construction or production of a qualifying asset should be capitalized as part of the cost of that asset". Further, paragraph 19 states that "Capitalisation of borrowing costs should cease when substantially all the activities necessary to prepare the qualifying asset for its intended use or sale are complete". Thus, only that portion of the amortised discount should be capitalised as part of the cost of a qualifying asset which relates to the period during which acquisition, construction or production of the asset takes place.

Straight line basis (Amount in ₹)

YearsInterestAmortisation of discountTotal borrowing costs
Year 110,0003,33313,333
Year 210,0003,33313,333
Year 310,0003,33413,334

In the above case, the amount of borrowing costs capitalized would be ₹13,333 in Year 1 and Year 2. The borrowing costs of ₹13,334 incurred in Year 3 would be expensed since the asset is ready for its intended use at the end of Year 2.

Author’s Note: A common error is capitalising the entire annual bond discount amortisation for all three years as a borrowing cost, missing that AS 16 requires capitalisation to cease once the qualifying asset is ready for its intended use — here, at the end of Year 2 — so the Year 3 amortised discount and interest must be expensed, not capitalised.

RTP January 2026 · Q12 · Marks: Not stated in source · Approx Time: 10–20 minutes (approx.) · Topic 4.2: Interest capitalised into inventory cost only for the exceptional qualifying-asset case (substantial maturation period)
Question:

Can interest be included in the cost of inventories?

Answer / Solution:

As a general rule, AS 2 (para 12) provides that interest and other borrowing costs are usually not related to bringing inventories to their present location and condition, and are therefore usually excluded from inventory cost.

However, AS 16 (para 6) requires borrowing costs directly attributable to acquisition/construction/production of a qualifying asset to be capitalised, and para 5 specifically includes "inventories that require a substantial period of time to bring them to a saleable condition" as an example of a qualifying asset (e.g. liquor requiring 12+ months of maturation, per ASI 1). It is only in such exceptional cases — where time is a major factor in changing the condition of the inventory — that borrowing costs are included in inventory valuation. Routinely/repetitively manufactured inventory over a short period is never a qualifying asset, so its borrowing costs are never capitalised.

Author’s Note: Some examinees answered with a flat "no", missing the exceptional qualifying-asset case (e.g. maturing liquor) where AS 16 does require capitalisation into inventory cost.

RTP May 2025 · Q16 · Marks: Not stated in source · Approx Time: 10–20 minutes (approx.) · Topic 4.4: Apportionment of interest on a mixed-purpose loan between qualifying-asset capitalisation and expense, by proportion of funds actually used for each purpose
Question:

U Limited has obtained a term loan of ₹620 lacs for a complete renovation and modernisation of its Factory on 1st April, 2023. Plant and Machinery was acquired under the modernisation scheme and installation was completed on 30th April, 2024. An expenditure of ₹510 lacs was incurred on installation of Plant and Machinery, ₹54 lacs has been advanced to suppliers for additional assets which were also received and installed before 30th April, 2024 (additional asset has taken substantial period of time in its installation), and the balance loan of ₹56 lacs has been used for working capital purposes.

The company has paid total interest of ₹68.20 lacs during financial year 2023-2024 on the above loan. The accountant seeks your advice how to account for the interest paid in the books of accounts.

Answer / Solution:

As per AS 16 'Borrowing Costs', borrowing costs directly attributable to the acquisition, construction or production of a qualifying asset should be capitalized as part of the cost of that asset; other borrowing costs should be recognized as an expense in the period in which they are incurred.

Qualifying Asset: an asset that necessarily takes a substantial period of time (ordinarily 12 months, unless a shorter or longer period is justified by the facts) to get ready for its intended use or sale.

Since construction of the asset completed only on 30th April, 2024 (after the year end), the treatment for the total borrowing cost of ₹68.20 lacs is:

PurposeNatureInterest to be capitalised (₹ lacs)Interest to be charged to P&L (₹ lacs)
Modernisation and renovation of plant and machineryQualifying asset68.20 × (510/620) = 56.10—
Advance to suppliers for additional assetsAssumed as qualifying asset (took substantial time to install)68.20 × (54/620) = 5.94—
Working CapitalNot a qualifying asset—68.20 × (56/620) = 6.16
Total62.046.16
Author’s Note: A common error is capitalising interest on the entire ₹620 lacs loan without apportioning it by actual fund usage, missing that the ₹56 lacs used for working capital is not a qualifying asset and its share of interest must be expensed, not capitalised.

RTP May 2026 · Q10 · Marks: Not stated in source · Approx Time: 10–20 minutes (approx.) · Topic 2.8: Cost of a self-constructed asset - directly attributable costs only, excluding relocation/inauguration  +  Topic 4.4/4.9: Eligible borrowing cost net of temporary-investment income, capitalisation period
Question:

On 1st April, 2024, Y Limited purchased an industrial plot of land for ₹50,00,000 for the purpose of constructing a new factory. This cost of ₹50,00,000 included legal cost of ₹2,50,000 incurred for the purpose of acquisition of this plot. The construction of the factory commenced on 1st May, 2024. Y Limited provides you with the following details of the costs incurred in relation to the above construction:

ParticularsAmount (₹)
Preparation and levelling of the land1,60,000

The construction of the factory was completed on 31st December, 2024 and production could commence on 1st February, 2025. The overall useful life of the factory building was estimated at 40 years from the date of completion. However, it was estimated that the roof would need to be replaced 20 years after the date of completion. The cost of replacing the roof at current prices would be 25% of the total cost of the building. The construction of the factory was partly financed by a loan of ₹56,00,000 raised from State Bank of India on 1st April, 2024 at an interest rate of 9% per annum. During the period when the loan proceeds had been fully utilized to finance the construction, Y Limited earned an income of ₹50,000 from the temporary investment of the proceeds. Assume that all of the net finance cost needs to be allocated to the cost of factory (excluding land) and interest cost to be capitalized based on eight months' period.

You are required to compute the carrying amount (i.e. value after charging depreciation) of the Factory in the books of Y Limited as at 31 March, 2025 as per the provisions of the relevant Accounting Standard.

Answer / Solution:

Cost of construction of the factory

Cost of Industrial Plot50,00,000
Preparation and levelling of the land1,60,000
Employment costs of construction workers (₹58,000 per month) for 8 months4,64,000
Purchase of Raw materials for the construction42,48,000
Overhead costs incurred directly on the construction of the factory (₹50,000 per month) for 8 months4,00,000
Interest on ₹56,00,000 for 9 months @ 9% = ₹3,78,000 less ₹50,0003,28,000
Total Cost (A)1,06,00,000
Depreciation (B) (W.N.)43,750
Carrying amount of the factory (A−B)1,05,56,250

Working Note: Calculation of Depreciation

On land of ₹50,00,000: Nil. On remaining cost of Building i.e. ₹1,06,00,000 − ₹50,00,000 = ₹56,00,000:

  • On Building: ₹56,00,000 × 75% / 40 yrs × 3/12 = ₹26,250
  • On roof: ₹56,00,000 × 25% / 20 yrs × 3/12 = ₹17,500
  • Total Depreciation charged = ₹43,750

Cost of relocating the workers to new factory for work and cost of inaugural function of the new factory is not directly attributable to construction cost, hence not considered.

Author’s Note: Many examinees included the relocation cost and the inauguration-function cost in the capitalised cost of the factory, failing to apply AS 10's distinction between costs necessary to bring an asset to its working condition and costs merely associated with commissioning it. Several also capitalised the gross interest of ₹3,78,000 without netting the ₹50,000 temporary-investment income against it, as AS 16 requires.

Loyal Ltd. has undertaken a project for expansion of capacity as per the following details:

The company pays to its bank interest at a rate of 15% p.a., which is debited on a monthly basis. During the half year, company had ₹20 lakh overdraft up to 31st December, surplus cash in January and again overdraft of ₹14 lakh from 1.2.2024 and ₹30 lakh from 1.3.2024. The company had a strike during December and hence could not continue the work during said period. However, the substantial administrative work related to the project was continued. Onsite work was again commenced on 1st January and all the work were completed on 31st March. Assume that expenditure was incurred on 1st day of each month.

Calculate interest to be capitalized giving reason wherever necessary. Assume overdraft will be less, if there is no capital expenditure.

Answer / Solution:

Loyal Ltd.

MonthActual Expenditure (₹)Interest on outstanding amount @ 15% p.a.Interest capitalized (₹)Outstanding amount (₹)Cumulative amount (₹)
October, 20234,00,0004,00,000×15%×1/125,0004,05,0004,05,000
November, 20237,95,000(4,05,000+7,95,000)×15%×1/1215,0004,05,000+7,95,000+15,00012,15,000
December, 2023-(12,15,000)×15%×1/1215,18812,15,000+15,18812,30,188
