Total26,45,00086,409

Note:

  1. As per para 18 of AS 16, ‘Borrowing Cost’, capitalisation of borrowing costs is not normally suspended during a period when substantial technical and administrative work is being carried out. Therefore, the interest for that period i.e. for the month of December has also been capitalized.
  2. During January, the company did not incur any interest as there was surplus cash in January. Therefore, no amount should be capitalized during January as per para 14(b) of AS 16.
  3. During February, actual overdraft (borrowings) was ₹14 lakh only. Hence, interest of ₹17,500 on ₹14,00,000 has been calculated even though actual expenditure on project exceed ₹14 lakh.
Author’s Note: A common error is suspending capitalisation entirely during December because on-site physical work stopped due to the strike, without recognising that substantial administrative work continued through the period, so capitalisation is not suspended. A related error is capitalising interest on the full actual overdraft rather than capping it at the interest actually incurred on the lower of the two overdraft figures each month.

RTP September 2025 · Q16 · Marks: Not stated in source · Approx Time: 10–20 minutes (approx.) · Topic 4.3: Borrowing costs on an incidental, already-ready asset are still capitalised into the main qualifying asset when necessary for its construction
Question:

Is it permissible to capitalise borrowing costs incurred on assets necessary for the construction of qualifying assets? A company constructing a large manufacturing plant in a backward area also purchased a residential building (funded by a long-term loan) to house workers engaged in the plant's construction, intending to dispose of the building once construction completes. If the manufacturing plant is a qualifying asset, are the borrowing costs on the residential-building loan eligible for capitalisation?

Answer / Solution:

Per AS 16 para 3, a qualifying asset "necessarily takes a substantial period of time to get ready for its intended use or sale"; para 5 clarifies that assets ready for use when acquired are not qualifying assets. Prima facie, the residential building appears ready for use on acquisition, suggesting no capitalisation.

However, since providing housing is necessary for the construction of the plant, the borrowing costs on the building loan are, in substance, directly attributable to the construction of the manufacturing plant. The company should therefore capitalise these borrowing costs as part of the cost of the manufacturing plant, up to the period the plant is ready for its intended use.

Author’s Note: Some examinees stopped at the observation that the residential building is itself "ready for use" and concluded no capitalisation applies, missing the substance-over-form link to the main construction project's necessity.

MTP May 2026 Set 2 · Q8 · Marks: 2 · Approx Time: 4 minutes (approx.) · Topic 2.7: Directly attributable costs including regulatory-mandated modifications  +  Topic 4.10: Capitalised borrowing cost as computed in Q7 feeds into total plant cost
Question:
Case Scenario:

Mars Ltd. is a manufacturing enterprise which is starting a new manufacturing plant at X Village. It has commenced construction of the plant on April 1, 2023 and has incurred following expenses: acquired land for installing Plant for ₹50,00,000; incurred ₹35,00,000 for material and direct labour cost for developing the Plant; incurred ₹10,00,000 for head office expenses at New Delhi which included rent, employee cost and maintenance expenditure; borrowed ₹25,00,000 for construction work of Plant @12% per annum on April 1, 2023 (Director finance incurred travel and meeting expenses of ₹5,00,000 during the year for arranging this loan).

On November 1, 2023, the construction activities of the plant were interrupted as the local people alongwith activists raised issues relating to environmental impact of the plant being constructed; construction came to a standstill for 3 months. With the help of Government and NGOs, the agitation was over by February 28, 2024 and the work resumed. However, to balance the impact on environment, government ordered the company to install certain devices for which the Company had to incur ₹6,00,000 in March 2024. The rate of depreciation on Plant is 10%.

Based on the above information, answer Question Nos. 6–9.

The total cost of plant as on March 31, 2024 will be:

  1. ₹85,00,000
  2. ₹98,00,000
  3. ₹93,00,000
  4. ₹95,00,000
Answer / Solution:

Correct option: C

Answer: (c) ₹93,00,000 = Land ₹50,00,000 + material/labour ₹35,00,000 + capitalised borrowing cost ₹2,00,000 + government-mandated environmental devices ₹6,00,000 (head office expenses and loan-arrangement travel costs excluded).

Author’s Note: Some examinees excluded the government-mandated environmental device cost, not recognising it as a cost necessary to bring the plant to a condition of operating in compliance with regulatory requirements, and so directly attributable under AS 10.

MTP November 2023 Set 2 · Q6(a) · Marks: 4 · Approx Time: 8 minutes (approx.) · Topic 4.3: Exchange differences on a foreign-currency borrowing treated as a borrowing cost only to the extent they approximate the interest-rate differential against an equivalent local-currency loan  +  Topic 3.5: Exchange difference on restatement of a foreign-currency monetary borrowing at the closing rate, with the AS 16-eligible portion carved out of the total exchange loss and the remainder recognised under AS 11
Question:

Omega Limited has borrowed a sum of US $10,00,000 at the beginning of Financial Year 2022-23 for its residential project at 4%. The interest is payable at the end of the Financial Year. At the time of availment of loan exchange rate was ₹56 per US $ and the rate as on 31st March, 2023 was ₹62 per US $. If Omega Limited had borrowed the loan in India in Indian Rupee equivalent, the pricing of loan would have been 10.50%.

You are required to compute Borrowing Cost and exchange difference for the year ending 31st March, 2023 as per applicable Accounting Standards.

Answer / Solution:
  1. Interest for the period 2022-23 = US $10 lakhs × 4% × ₹62 per US$ = ₹24.80 lakhs
  2. Increase in the liability towards the principal amount = US $10 lakhs × ₹(62 − 56) = ₹60 lakhs
  3. Interest that would have resulted if the loan was taken in Indian currency = US $10 lakhs × ₹56 × 10.5% = ₹58.80 lakhs
  4. Difference between interest on local currency borrowing and foreign currency borrowing = ₹58.80 lakhs − ₹24.80 lakhs = ₹34 lakhs.

Therefore, out of ₹60 lakhs increase in the liability towards principal amount, only ₹34 lakhs will be considered as the borrowing cost. Thus, total borrowing cost would be ₹58.80 lakhs being the aggregate of interest of ₹24.80 lakhs on foreign currency borrowings plus the exchange difference to the extent of difference between interest on local currency borrowing and interest on foreign currency borrowing of ₹34 lakhs.

Hence, ₹58.80 lakhs would be considered as the borrowing cost to be accounted for as per AS 16 and the remaining ₹26 lakhs (60 − 34) would be considered as the exchange difference to be accounted for as per AS 11.

Author’s Note: A common error is treating the entire ₹60 lakh increase in the rupee liability as either wholly a borrowing cost under AS 16 or wholly an exchange difference under AS 11, instead of splitting it at the interest-rate-differential figure of ₹34 lakhs.

MTP January 2025 Set 1 · Q6(b) · Marks: 4 · Approx Time: 8 minutes (approx.) · Topic 5.10: Sale and leaseback classified as an operating lease - profit/loss recognition split by sale price vs fair value vs carrying amount
Question:

A Ltd. sold JCB having WDV of ₹20 lakhs to B Ltd. for ₹24 lakhs and the same JCB was leased back by B Ltd. to A Ltd. The lease is operating lease. In context of Accounting Standard 19 "Leases" explain the accounting treatment of profit or loss in the books of A Ltd. if: (i) Sale price of ₹24 lakhs is equal to fair value. (ii) Fair value is ₹20 lakhs and sale price is ₹24 lakhs. (iii) Fair value is ₹22 lakhs and sale price is ₹25 lakhs. (iv) Fair value is ₹25 lakhs and sale price is ₹18 lakhs. (v) Fair value is ₹18 lakhs and sale price is ₹19 lakhs.

Answer / Solution:

Following will be the treatment in the given cases (WDV of the JCB = ₹20 lakhs throughout):

  1. When sale price of ₹24 lakhs is equal to fair value, A Ltd. should immediately recognise the profit of ₹4 lakhs (i.e. 24 − 20) in its books.
  2. When fair value is ₹20 lakhs & sale price is ₹24 lakhs then profit of ₹4 lakhs is to be deferred and amortised over the lease period.
  3. When fair value is ₹22 lakhs & sale price is ₹25 lakhs, profit of ₹2 lakhs (22−20) to be immediately recognised in its books and balance profit of ₹3 lakhs (25−22) is to be amortised/deferred over lease period.
  4. When fair value of leased machinery is ₹25 lakhs & sale price is ₹18 lakhs, then loss of ₹2 lakhs (20−18) to be immediately recognised by A Ltd. in its books provided loss is not compensated by future lease payment.
  5. When fair value is ₹18 lakhs & sale price is ₹19 lakhs, then the loss of ₹2 lakhs (20−18) to be immediately recognised by A Ltd. in its books and profit of ₹1 lakh (19−18) should be amortised/deferred over lease period.
Author’s Note: A common error is recognising the entire profit on a sale-and-leaseback transaction immediately, without checking whether the sale price exceeds fair value and confirming that only the profit up to fair value qualifies for immediate recognition, with any excess deferred over the lease term.

MTP January 2026 Set 1 · Q6(a) [OR-alt 1] · Marks: 4 · Approx Time: 8 minutes (approx.) · Topic 5.3: Finance lease classification test and lessor's unearned finance income computation
Question:

Colour Limited leased a Machine to Red Limited on 1st April, 2021: Cost of machine ₹18,00,000; Lease term 3 years; Fair market value ₹18,00,000; Unguaranteed residual value as on 31.3.2024 ₹2,00,000; Internal rate of return 12%. Expected useful life 5 years; machine reverts to Colour Limited on termination. Lease payments at the end of each year, in 3 equal parts. PV of ₹1 due at end of 3rd year at 12% = ₹0.7118. PV of annuity of ₹1 for 3 years at 12% = ₹2.4018. Analyze whether the lease constitutes a finance lease. Also calculate unearned finance income, if any.

Answer / Solution:

Computation of Annual Lease Payment: PV of unguaranteed residual value = 2,00,000 × 0.7118 = 1,42,360. PV of Lease Payments to recover = 18,00,000 − 1,42,360 = 16,57,640. Annual Lease Payment = 16,57,640 / 2.4018 = ₹6,90,166 (approx).

Classification: PV of lease payments (₹16,57,640) is 92.09% of fair value (₹18,00,000) — substantially covers the fair value of the leased asset. Lease term (3 years) covers the major part of the asset's economic life (5 years). Both indicators point to a finance lease.

Unearned Finance Income: Total Lease Payments (6,90,166 × 3) 20,70,498 + Unguaranteed residual value 2,00,000 = 22,70,498; less Net investment (PV of payments + residual = 1,42,360+16,57,640 = 18,00,000) = Unearned Finance Income ₹4,70,498 (approx, matching source's ₹4,70,495 to rounding).

Author’s Note: Some examinees computed unearned finance income using the guaranteed residual value formula, not adjusting for the fact that this residual value is unguaranteed (still included in the lessor's net investment, but the classification/income mechanics require care in distinguishing guaranteed vs unguaranteed treatment).

MTP May 2024 Set 1 · Q1(b) · Marks: 5 · Approx Time: 9 minutes (approx.) · Topic 5.8: Lessee's finance-lease recognition at the lower of fair value and PV of minimum lease payments, plus finance-charge amortisation table Compulsory
Question:

Lessee Ltd. took a machine on lease from Lessor Ltd., the fair value being ₹7,00,000. The economic life of machine as well as the lease term is 3 years. At the end of each year Lessee Ltd. pays ₹3,00,000. The Lessee has guaranteed a residual value of ₹22,000 on expiry of the lease to the Lessor. However, Lessor Ltd., estimates that the residual value of the machinery will be only ₹15,000. The implicit rate of return is 15% p.a. and present value factors at 15% are 0.869, 0.756 and 0.657 at the end of first, second and third years respectively.

Calculate the value of machinery to be considered by Lessee Ltd. and the finance charges in each year.

Answer / Solution:

As per AS 19 "Leases", the lessee should recognize the lease as an asset and a liability at the inception of a finance lease. Such recognition should be at an amount equal to the fair value of the leased asset at the inception of lease. However, if the fair value of the leased asset exceeds the present value of minimum lease payment from the standpoint of the lessee, the amount recorded as an asset and liability should be the present value of minimum lease payments from the standpoint of the lessee.

Computation of Value of machinery: Present value of minimum lease payment = ₹6,99,054 (see working note below). Fair value of leased asset = ₹7,00,000. Therefore, the recognition will be at the lower of the two, i.e. ₹6,99,054.

Working Note — Present value of minimum lease payments: Annual lease rental × PVIF + Present value of guaranteed residual value = ₹3,00,000 × (0.869 + 0.756 + 0.657) + ₹22,000 × 0.657 = ₹6,84,600 + ₹14,454 = ₹6,99,054.

Computation of finance charges:

YearFinance chargePaymentReduction in outstanding liabilityOutstanding liability
1st Year beginning———6,99,054
End of 1st year1,04,8583,00,0001,95,1425,03,912
End of 2nd year75,5873,00,0002,24,4132,79,499
End of 3rd year41,9253,00,0002,58,07521,424
Author’s Note: A common error is recognising the asset at the full fair value (₹7,00,000) without first comparing it to the present value of minimum lease payments and taking the lower of the two, or omitting the guaranteed residual value from the minimum lease payments computation.

PYQ January 2025 · Q1(b) · Marks: 5 · Approx Time: 9 minutes (approx.) · Topic 5.5-5.7/5.8: Deterministic indicators of a finance lease (PV of MLP vs. fair value; lease term vs. asset life) and computation of unearned finance income Compulsory
Question:

J Limited availed an equipment on lease from K Limited. The conditions of the lease terms are as under: (i) Lease starts from 1st April, 2020 for a period of 4 Years and useful life of the equipment is 6 years. Both the cost and fair value of equipment are ₹12,50,000. (ii) The equipment reverts back to the lessor on termination of the lease. (iii) The unguaranteed residual value is estimated at ₹1,20,000 at the end of the financial year 2023-2024. (iv) The amount will be paid in 4 equal instalments at the end of each year. (v) Consider IRR = 8%. (vi) The present value of ₹1 at the end of 4th year at 8% of interest is ₹0.735. (vii) The present value of annuity of ₹1 due at the end of 4th year at 8% IRR is ₹3.312.

State whether this lease is operating lease or Finance lease (by applying two deterministic parameters). Also calculate unearned finance Income. (5 Marks)

Answer / Solution:

Computation of annual lease payment:

Cost of equipment12,50,000.00
Unguaranteed residual value1,20,000.00
Present value of unguaranteed residual value (₹1,20,000 × 0.735)88,200.00
Present value of lease payments (₹12,50,000 − ₹88,200)11,61,800.00
Present value of annuity for four years is 3.312
Annual lease payment [11,61,800/3.312]3,50,785.02

Classification of lease:

Parameter 1: The present value of the lease payment i.e. ₹11,61,800 which equals 92.94% of the fair market value i.e. ₹12,50,000. The present value of minimum lease payments substantially covers the fair value of the leased asset.

Parameter 2: The lease term (i.e. 4 years) covers the major part of the life of asset (i.e. 6 years).

Therefore, it constitutes a finance lease.

Computation of Unearned Finance Income:

Total lease payments (₹3,50,785.02 × 4)14,03,140.08
Add: Unguaranteed residual value1,20,000.00
Gross investment in the lease15,23,140.08
Less: Present value of lease payments and residual value i.e. Net Investment (₹88,200 + ₹11,61,800)(12,50,000.00)
Unearned finance income2,73,140.08
Examiner’s Comment: Many examinees calculated the unearned finance income correctly, some failed to include the unguaranteed residual value in the total lease payments to determine the gross investment. Consequently, they could not ascertain the unearned finance income as per AS 19, "Leases."

PYQ January 2026 · Q6(a) [OR-alt 2] · Marks: 4 · Approx Time: 8 minutes (approx.) · Topic 5.8.1: Finance lease inception at lower of fair value and PV of minimum lease payments including guaranteed residual value; finance charge amortisation table
Question:

S Limited took an equipment on lease from R Limited, fair value ₹9,50,000. Economic life and lease term both 3 years. At the end of each year, lessee pays ₹4,00,000 to lessor. S Limited has guaranteed a residual value of ₹35,000 on lease expiry to R Limited; R Limited estimates residual value will be only ₹25,000. Implicit rate of return 15% p.a.; PV factors at 15%: 0.869, 0.756, 0.657 (years 1-3).

You are required to ascertain the value at which the equipment would be considered by S Limited and the finance charges in each year. (4 Marks)

Answer / Solution:

As per para 11 of AS 19, the lessee should recognize the lease as an asset and a liability at the inception of a finance lease, at an amount equal to the fair value of the leased asset, or, if lower, the present value of minimum lease payments.

Present value of minimum lease payments = Annual lease rental × PVIF + Present value of guaranteed residual value = ₹4,00,000 × (0.869+0.756+0.657) + ₹35,000 × 0.657 = ₹9,12,800 + ₹22,995 = ₹9,35,795. Fair value of leased asset = ₹9,50,000. Recognition is at the lower of the two: ₹9,35,795.

Computation of finance charges:

YearOpening Balance (A)Finance Charge @15% (B)Annual Payment (C)Principal Repaid (D=C−B)Closing Balance (E=A−D)
19,35,7951,40,3694,00,0002,59,6316,76,164
26,76,1641,01,4254,00,0002,98,5753,77,589
33,77,58956,6384,00,0003,43,36234,227*

*The closing balance of ₹34,227 is approximately the guaranteed residual value of ₹35,000; the slight difference is due to rounding in the provided PV factors.

Author’s Note: Some examinees used the lessor's lower estimate of unguaranteed residual value (₹25,000) rather than the lessee's own guaranteed residual value (₹35,000) when computing the present value of minimum lease payments from the lessee's standpoint.

Question:

Colour Limited leased a Machine to Red Limited on 1 April, 2021 on the following:

Particulars

Other information: The expected useful life of the machine is 5 years. The machine will revert to Colour Limited on termination of the lease. The lease payment is to be made at the end of each year in 3 equal parts.

The present value of ₹1 due at the end of 3rd year at 12% rate of interest is ₹0.7118. The present value of annuity of ₹1 due at the end of 3rd year at 12% IRR is ₹2.4018.

You are required to analyze whether lease constitutes finance lease. Also calculate unearned finance income, if any.

OR (alternative to the AS 20 EPS question below)

Computation of Annual Lease Payment

Unguaranteed Residual Value2,00,000

Present Value of Annuity for three years is 2.4018 – Annual Lease Payment (16,57,640 / 2.4018)6,90,165.71

Parameter 1: The present value of lease payment i.e. ₹16,57,640 which equals 92.09% of the fair market value i.e., ₹18,00,000. The present value of minimum lease payments substantially covers the fair value of the leased asset.

Parameter 2: The lease term (i.e. 3 years) covers the major part of the life of the asset (i.e. 5 years).

Therefore, it constitutes a finance lease.

RTP January 2025 · Q14 · Marks: Not stated in source · Approx Time: 10–20 minutes (approx.) · Topic 5.3: Unearned finance income = gross investment in the lease less the present value of minimum lease payments and unguaranteed residual value, discounted at the interest rate implicit in the lease
Question:

Money Limited leased a machine to Hello Limited on the following terms (₹ in lakh):

(i) Fair value of the machine24.00
(ii) Lease term5 years
(iii) Lease rental per annum4.00
(iv) Guaranteed residual value0.8
(v) Expected residual value1.5
(vi) Internal rate of return15%

Discounted rates for 1st year to 5th year are 0.8696, 0.7561, 0.6575, 0.5718, and 0.4972 respectively.

Ascertain Unearned Finance Income.

Answer / Solution:

As per AS 19 on Leases, unearned finance income is the difference between (a) the gross investment in the lease and (b) the present value of minimum lease payments under a finance lease from the standpoint of the lessor; and any unguaranteed residual value accruing to the lessor, at the interest rate implicit in the lease.

(a) Gross investment = Minimum lease payments + Unguaranteed residual value = [Total lease rent + Guaranteed residual value (GRV)] + Unguaranteed residual value (URV) = [(₹4,00,000 × 5 years) + ₹80,000] + ₹70,000 = ₹21,50,000 (a)

(b) Table showing present value of (i) Minimum lease payments (MLP) and (ii) Unguaranteed residual value (URV):

YearMLP inclusive of URV (₹)Discount factor @ 15%Present Value (₹)
14,00,0000.86963,47,840
24,00,0000.75613,02,440
34,00,0000.65752,63,000
44,00,0000.57182,28,720
54,00,0000.49721,98,880
80,000 (GRV)0.497239,776
20,80,00013,80,656 (i)
70,000 (URV)0.497234,804 (ii)
21,50,000(i)+(ii)14,15,460 (b)

Unearned Finance Income (a) − (b) = ₹21,50,000 − ₹14,15,460 = ₹7,34,540.

Author’s Note: A common error is treating the guaranteed and unguaranteed residual values identically, or omitting the unguaranteed residual value from gross investment altogether, when AS 19 requires both components in gross investment while net investment excludes only the unguaranteed portion's financing income.

RTP January 2026 · Q15 · Marks: Not stated in source · Approx Time: 10–20 minutes (approx.) · Topic 5.9: Sale-and-leaseback resulting in a finance lease - profit deferred and amortised in proportion to asset depreciation
Question:

On 1st April, 2024, Mansi Ltd. sold a plant for ₹8,52,800 (carrying amount ₹1,80,000) as part of a sale-and-leaseback package with Akash Ltd., leasing the asset back for an 8-year term. Economic life of the asset is 8 years. Minimum lease rents ₹1,60,000/year, payable annually from 31st March, 2025. Mansi Ltd.'s incremental borrowing rate is 10% p.a. Calculate the net effect on the Statement of Profit and Loss in Mansi Ltd.'s (the lessee's) books.

Answer / Solution:

Lease classification: lease term (8 years) covers the entire economic life (8 years). PV of minimum lease payments = ₹1,60,000 × 5.335 (annuity factor @10% for 8 years) = ₹8,53,600, which substantially covers the fair value/sale price (₹8,52,800). This is therefore a finance lease.

Per AS 19 para 48, where a sale-and-leaseback results in a finance lease, the profit on sale (₹8,52,800−₹1,80,000 = ₹6,72,800) is not recognised immediately — it is deferred and amortised over the lease term in proportion to the depreciation of the leased asset.

Assuming straight-line depreciation: Depreciation = ₹8,52,800/8 = ₹1,06,600/year. Deferred profit amortised = ₹6,72,800/8 = ₹84,100/year. Net effect on Statement of P&L = ₹1,06,600 − ₹84,100 = ₹22,500 debit per annum, for each of the 8 years of the lease term.

Author’s Note: Some examinees recognised the full sale profit immediately in the year of sale, not applying AS 19's specific deferral-and-amortisation rule for a sale-and-leaseback that results in a finance lease.

RTP May 2024 · Q11 · Marks: Not stated in source · Approx Time: 10–20 minutes (approx.) · Topic 5.5-5.7: Finance-vs-operating lease classification tested against both the PV-of-minimum-lease-payments test and the major-part-of-economic-life test
Question:

Sooraj Limited wishes to obtain a machine costing ₹30 lakhs by way of lease. The effective life of the machine is 14 years, but the company requires it only for the first 3 years. It enters into an agreement with Star Ltd., for a lease rental for ₹3 lakhs p.a. payable in arrears and the implicit rate of interest is 15%. The chief accountant of Sooraj Limited is not sure about the treatment of these lease rentals and seeks your advice. (Use annuity factor at @ 15% for 3 years as 2.28)

Answer / Solution:

As per AS 19 'leases', a lease will be classified as finance lease if at the inception of the lease, the present value of minimum lease payment amounts to at least substantially all of the fair value of leased asset. In the given case, the implicit rate of interest is given at 15%. The present value of minimum lease payments at 15% using PV-Annuity Factor can be computed as:

Annuity Factor (Year 1 to Year 3)2.28
Present Value of minimum lease payments (₹3 lakhs each year)₹6.84 lakhs

Thus, the present value of minimum lease payments is ₹6.84 lakhs and the fair value of the machine is ₹30 lakhs. In a finance lease, the lease term should be for a major part of the economic life of the asset even if title is not transferred. However, in the given case, the effective useful life of the machine is 14 years while the lease is only for three years. Therefore, a lease agreement is an operating lease. Lease payments under an operating lease should be recognized as an expense in the statement of profit and loss on a straight-line basis over the lease term unless another systematic basis is more representative of the time pattern of the user's benefit.

Author’s Note: A common error here is classifying the lease as a finance lease purely because the present value of minimum lease payments is a large absolute number, without comparing it against the machine's fair value and separately checking whether the lease term covers a major part of the asset's economic life.

RTP May 2025 · Q18 · Marks: Not stated in source · Approx Time: 10–20 minutes (approx.) · Topic 5.5-5.7: Finance vs operating lease classification via the PV-of-minimum-lease-payments and lease-term-vs-economic-life indicators
Question:

Sun Limited wishes to obtain a machine costing ₹30 lakhs by way of lease. The effective life of the machine is 14 years, but the company requires it only for the first 3 years. It enters into an agreement with Star Ltd. for a lease rental of ₹3 lakhs p.a. payable in arrears, and the implicit rate of interest is 15%. The chief accountant of Sun Limited is not sure about the treatment of these lease rentals and seeks your advice. (Use annuity factor at 15% for 3 years as 3.36.)

Answer / Solution:

As per AS 19 'Leases', a lease will be classified as a finance lease if, at the inception of the lease, the present value of minimum lease payments amounts to at least substantially all of the fair value of the leased asset (discounted at the interest rate implicit in the lease).

Amount
Annuity Factor (Year 1 to Year 3) @ 15%3.36
Present Value of minimum lease payments (₹3 lakhs each year)₹10.08 lakhs (approx.)

The present value of minimum lease payments (₹10.08 lakhs) is far below the fair value of the machine (₹30 lakhs). Additionally, in a finance lease the lease term should cover the major part of the economic life of the asset even where title does not transfer – here the effective useful life of the machine is 14 years while the lease is only for 3 years. Both indicators point away from a finance lease.

The lease agreement is therefore an operating lease. Lease payments under an operating lease should be recognized as an expense in the statement of profit and loss on a straight line basis over the lease term, unless another systematic basis is more representative of the time pattern of the user's benefit – i.e. Sun Limited should expense ₹3 lakhs each year for the 3-year lease term.

Author’s Note: A common error is classifying this as a finance lease purely because a lease-rental agreement with an "implicit rate of interest" is quoted, without actually testing the present value of minimum lease payments against the machine's fair value, which here comes out at barely a third of fair value – a clear operating-lease signal.

RTP May 2026 · Q14 · Marks: Not stated in source · Approx Time: 10–20 minutes (approx.) · Topic 5.9: Accounting for operating leases - lessor's presentation, income recognition, depreciation, impairment
Question:

Explain, in brief, the accounting treatment for an asset given under Operating Lease in the books of the Lessor.

Answer / Solution:

The accounting treatment for an asset given under Operating Lease in the books of the lessor is given as under:

  1. The Lessor should present an asset given under Operating Lease as PPE in its balance sheet.
  2. Lease income from operating leases should be recognized in the Statement of Profit and Loss on a straight-line basis over the lease term, unless another systematic basis is more representative of the time pattern in which benefit derived from the use of the leased asset is diminished.
  3. Depreciation should be recognized in the books of the lessor. The depreciation of leased assets should be on a basis consistent with the normal accounting policy of the lessor for similar assets, and the depreciation charge should be calculated on the basis set out in AS 10.
  4. The impairment loss on assets given on operating leases are determined and treated as per AS 28.
Author’s Note: Many examinees conflated lessor and lessee treatments, describing finance-lease-style derecognition of the asset instead of the lessor retaining the asset as PPE and depreciating it under AS 10, resulting in partial credit loss.

MTP May 2024 Set 1 · Q1(c) · Marks: 4 · Approx Time: 8 minutes (approx.) · Topic 7.7: Impairment loss = carrying amount less recoverable amount (higher of net selling price and value in use) Compulsory
Question:

X Ltd. purchased a Property, Plant and Equipment four years ago for ₹150 lakhs and depreciates it at 10% p.a. on straight line method. At the end of the fourth year, it has revalued the asset at ₹75 lakhs and has written off the loss on revaluation to the profit and loss account. However, on the date of revaluation, the market price is ₹67.50 lakhs and expected disposal costs are ₹3 lakhs. What will be the treatment in respect of impairment loss on the basis that fair value for revaluation purpose is determined by market value and the value in use is estimated at ₹60 lakhs?

Answer / Solution:

Treatment of Impairment Loss: As per AS 28 "Impairment of assets", if the recoverable amount (higher of net selling price and its value in use) of an asset is less than its carrying amount, the carrying amount of the asset should be reduced to its recoverable amount. In the given case, net selling price is ₹64.50 lakhs (₹67.50 lakhs − ₹3 lakhs) and value in use is ₹60 lakhs. Therefore, recoverable amount will be ₹64.50 lakhs. Impairment loss will be calculated as ₹10.50 lakhs [₹75 lakhs (Carrying Amount after revaluation – Refer Working Note) less ₹64.50 lakhs (Recoverable Amount)].

Thus impairment loss of ₹10.50 lakhs should be recognised as an expense in the Statement of Profit and Loss immediately since there was downward revaluation of asset which was already charged to Statement of Profit and Loss.

Working Note — Calculation of carrying amount of the Property, Plant and Equipment at the end of the fourth year on revaluation (₹ in lakhs):

Purchase price of a Property, Plant and Equipment150.00
Less: Depreciation for four years [(150 lakhs / 10 years) × 4 years](60.00)
Carrying value at the end of fourth year90.00
Less: Downward revaluation charged to profit and loss account(15.00)
Revalued carrying amount75.00
Author’s Note: A common error is using net selling price or value in use alone instead of the HIGHER of the two as the recoverable amount, or crediting the impairment loss against a revaluation reserve balance that does not exist here (the earlier downward revaluation was already charged to profit and loss, leaving no reserve to absorb the fresh impairment loss).

PYQ May 2025 · Q6(a) [OR-alt 2] · Marks: 4 · Approx Time: 8 minutes (approx.) · Topic 7.7: Impairment loss on a previously-revalued asset set off first against the remaining revaluation reserve balance, before charging any excess to profit and loss
Question:

A machine was acquired by Zest Ltd. on 01/04/2019 for ₹60 lakhs. It had a useful life of 6 years. The machine is depreciated on straight line basis and does not carry any residual value. On 01/04/2022, the carrying value of the machine was reassessed at ₹36 lakhs. The surplus arising out of the revaluation being credited to revaluation reserve.

For the year ended March 2024, conditions indicating an impairment of the existed machine and the amount recoverable ascertained to be ₹9 lakhs.

You are required to calculate the loss on impairment of the machine and show how this loss is to be treated in the books of Zest Ltd. The company had followed the policy of writing down the revaluation surplus by the increased charge of depreciation resulting from the revaluation. (4 Marks)

Answer / Solution:

Statement Showing Impairment Loss (₹ in lakhs):

Carrying amount of the machine as on 1st April, 201960
Depreciation for 3 years i.e. 2019-2020 to 2021-2022 (60/6 × 3)(30)
Carrying amount as on 31.03.202230
Add: Upward Revaluation (credited to Revaluation Reserve account)6
Carrying amount of the machine as on 1st April, 2022 (revalued)36
Less: Depreciation for 2 years i.e. 2022-2023 & 2023-2024 (36/3 × 2)(24)
Carrying amount as on 31.03.202412
Less: Recoverable amount(9)
Impairment loss3
Less: Balance in revaluation reserve as on 31.03.2024 (6), less enhanced depreciation met from revaluation reserve 2022-2023 & 2023-2024 [(12−10)×2 years] (4)(2)
Impairment loss set off against revaluation reserve balance as per para 58 of AS 28 "Impairment of Assets"(2)
Impairment Loss to be debited to profit and loss account1
Author’s Note: A common error here is treating the entire impairment loss as a straight debit to the Profit and Loss Account without first checking for, and setting off against, any remaining balance in the Revaluation Reserve relating to the same asset — only the loss in excess of that reserve balance should reach the Profit and Loss Account.

PYQ May 2026 · Q1(b) · Marks: 5 · Approx Time: 9 minutes (approx.) · Topic 2.8: Cost of installation - directly attributable labour/supervisor/testing costs; deferred-credit interest excluded  +  Topic 7.13/7.16: Impairment loss on a revalued asset - first set off against the revaluation reserve balance, remainder to P&L Compulsory
Question:

On 1 April, 2022, Sky Limited purchased a machinery for ₹7,35,000 (inclusive of GST @5%, input credit available for entire amount). Other installation expenses: Cost of preparation of site ₹16,500; Total Labour charges ₹75,000 (200 of 500 total men hours spent on installation); Total salary of supervisor ₹34,000 (25% of time spent on installation); Interest charges paid to supplier for deferred credit ₹8,000; Test run and experimental production expenses ₹28,200; Consultancy charges to architect for plant set up ₹18,800; Depreciation on assets used for installation ₹8,000. The machine was ready for use on October 1, 2022 but was put to use from February 1, 2023 (further expenses of ₹10,800 incurred due to this delay). Estimated useful life 10 years, SLM, no residual value.

On September 30, 2025, the company revalued the machine at ₹7 lakhs, surplus credited to revaluation reserve. For the year ended March 31, 2026, conditions indicating impairment existed and the recoverable amount was ascertained to be only ₹3 Lakhs.

You are required to: (i) Calculate the value at which the machine should be capitalized and the amount of depreciation to be charged for the year ending March 31, 2023 in the books of Sky Limited. (ii) Calculate the loss on impairment of the machine and show how this loss is to be treated in the books of Sky Limited. The company had followed the policy of writing down the revaluation surplus by the increased charge of depreciation resulting from the revaluation. (5 Marks)

Answer / Solution:

(i) Calculation of Cost of Machinery:

Purchase Price7,35,000
Add: Site Preparation Cost16,500
Labour charges (75,000 × 200/500)30,000
Supervisor's Salary (25% of 34,000)8,500
Test run and experimental production charges28,200
Architect Fees for set up18,800
Depreciation on assets used for installation8,000
Total Cost of Asset8,45,000
Less: GST credit receivable(35,000)
Value to be capitalized8,10,000
Depreciation to be charged on 31.3.2023 (for 6 months, SLM 10 year)40,500

Note: (i) Further expenses of ₹10,800 from 1.10.2022 to 1.2.2023 are charged to profit and loss A/c, as the plant was ready for production on 1.10.2022 (already capitalised) – the delay in actual use does not extend capitalisation. (ii) Interest charges of ₹8,000 paid on deferred credit terms to the supplier of the plant (not a qualifying asset) are not directly attributable costs and are written off to the Statement of Profit and Loss in the period incurred.

(ii) Statement showing impairment loss and its treatment:

Carrying amount of the machine as on 01/10/20228,10,000
Less: Depreciation for 3 years (8,10,000 x 3/10)(2,43,000)
Carrying amount as on 30/09/20255,67,000
Add: Upward revaluation (credited to revaluation reserve)1,33,000
Carrying amount of the machine as on 30/09/2025 (post-revaluation)7,00,000
Less: Depreciation for 6 months up to 31/03/2026 (7,00,000 x 0.5/7)(50,000)
Carrying amount as on 31/03/20266,50,000
Less: Recoverable amount(3,00,000)
Impairment Loss3,50,000
Less: balance in revaluation reserve as on 31/03/2026 [1,33,000 − (50,000−40,500)](1,23,500)
Impairment Loss to be debited to Profit & Loss Account2,26,500

Depreciation for 01/10/2025 to 31/03/2026 (7,00,000 x 0.5/7) = ₹50,000. Depreciation set off against Revaluation Reserve = (1,33,000 x 0.5/7) = ₹9,500 (Impairment loss set off against revaluation reserve balance as per para 58 of AS 28 "Impairment of Assets").

Author’s Note: Many examinees debited the entire ₹3,50,000 impairment loss to the profit and loss account, not applying AS 28's requirement (para 58) to first set off an impairment loss on a revalued asset against the remaining balance in that asset's revaluation reserve before charging the balance to P&L. Several also capitalised the ₹10,800 delay-related expenses instead of expensing them, since the asset was already ready for use on 1st October, 2022.

PYQ September 2025 · Q3(b) · Marks: 7 · Approx Time: 13 minutes (approx.) · Topic 7.6: CGU impairment loss allocated first to goodwill, then pro-rata to other assets
Question:

Grace Limited acquired the business (a cash-generating unit) of Venus Limited on 31st March 2023 for ₹8,000 lakhs: Fair value of identifiable assets ₹6,000 lakhs, Goodwill (amortised over 5 years) ₹2,000 lakhs. Anticipated useful life of acquired assets: 8 years, nil residual value, straight-line. On 31st March 2025, significant decline in production estimated due to government policy changes; net selling price of identifiable assets ₹3,000 lakhs. Cash flow forecast for next 6 years (₹ lakhs): 1,000/800/700/800/600/500. Discount rate 10% (PV factors: 0.909, 0.826, 0.751, 0.683, 0.621, 0.564). Calculate: (i) Value in use at 31 March 2025; (ii) Impairment loss for year ended 31 March 2025; (iii) Revised carrying amount of asset.

Answer / Solution:

(i) Value in Use: 1,000×0.909=909.00 + 800×0.826=660.80 + 700×0.751=525.70 + 800×0.683=546.40 + 600×0.621=372.60 + 500×0.564=282.00 = ₹3,296.50 lakhs, rounded to ₹3,297 lakhs.

Carrying amount at 31.3.2025 (2 years post-acquisition): Goodwill 2,000 − amortisation (2,000/5×2=800) = 1,200. Identifiable assets 6,000 − depreciation (6,000/8×2=1,500) = 4,500. Total CGU carrying amount = 5,700.

Recoverable amount = higher of Value in Use (3,297) and net selling price of identifiable assets (3,000, no CGU-wide fair-value-less-costs-to-sell given) = 3,297 (since 3,297 > 3,000).

(ii) Impairment loss = Carrying amount (5,700) − Recoverable amount (3,297) = ₹2,403 lakhs.

(iii) Allocation: per AS 28, impairment is allocated first to goodwill (written down to zero: full 1,200 absorbed), then the remainder (2,403−1,200=1,203) to identifiable assets pro-rata: revised carrying amount of identifiable asset = 4,500−1,203 = ₹3,297 lakhs (goodwill: Nil).

Examiner’s Comment: A majority of examinees were unable to compute the impairment loss and allocate the same appropriately among the assets of the CGU as per the requirements of AS 28 "Impairment of Assets". Many examinees failed to determine the value in use, impairment loss and the revised carrying amount of assets, evidencing an inadequate understanding of the impairment principles.

RTP January 2026 · Q19 · Marks: Not stated in source · Approx Time: 10–20 minutes (approx.) · Topic 7.4: Impairment loss = carrying amount less recoverable amount (higher of net selling price and value in use)
Question:

X Ltd. purchased a fixed asset four years ago for ₹150 lakhs, depreciating at 10% p.a. SLM. At the end of the fourth year, it revalued the asset to ₹75 lakhs, writing off the revaluation loss to P&L. On the revaluation date, market price is ₹67.50 lakhs, expected disposal costs ₹3 lakhs, and value in use is estimated at ₹60 lakhs. What is the treatment of impairment loss, given fair value for revaluation is market-value-based?

Answer / Solution:

W.N. — Carrying amount at revaluation: Purchase price 150.00, less depreciation for 4 years (150/10 × 4) 60.00 = carrying value before revaluation 90.00, less downward revaluation charged to P&L (90−75) 15.00 = revalued carrying amount 75.00 lakhs.

Recoverable amount = higher of net selling price and value in use. Net selling price = market price 67.50 − disposal costs 3.00 = 64.50 lakhs. Value in use = 60 lakhs. Recoverable amount = ₹64.50 lakhs (the higher of the two).

Impairment loss = carrying amount (75.00) − recoverable amount (64.50) = ₹10.50 lakhs, recognised as an expense in the Statement of Profit and Loss immediately (since the prior downward revaluation was already charged to P&L rather than to a revaluation reserve, there is no reserve balance to absorb this further impairment against).

Author’s Note: Some examinees used the market price directly as net selling price without deducting disposal costs, or used net selling price as recoverable amount without comparing it against value in use to find the higher of the two.

RTP May 2026 · Q16 · Marks: Not stated in source · Approx Time: 10–20 minutes (approx.) · Topic 7.8: Identification of the cash-generating unit - independence of cash inflows
Question:

A publisher owns 150 magazine titles of which 70 were purchased and 80 were self-created. The price paid for a purchased magazine title is recognised as an intangible asset. The costs of creating magazine titles and maintaining the existing titles are recognised as an expense when incurred. Cash inflows from direct sales and advertising are identifiable for each magazine title. Titles are managed by customer segments. The level of advertising income for a magazine title depends on the range of titles in the customer segment to which the magazine title relates. Management has a policy to abandon old titles before the end of their economic lives and replace them immediately with new titles for the same customer segment. Whether it will be a cash-generating unit as per AS 28?

Answer / Solution:

It is likely that the recoverable amount of an individual magazine title can be assessed. Even though the level of advertising income for a title is influenced, to a certain extent, by the other titles in the customer segment, cash inflows from direct sales and advertising are identifiable for each title. In addition, although titles are managed by customer segments, decisions to abandon titles are made on an individual title basis. Therefore, it is likely that individual magazine titles generate cash inflows that are largely independent one from another and that each magazine title is a separate cash-generating unit.

Author’s Note: Some examinees identified the customer segment as the cash-generating unit because titles are managed and reported at that level, without recognising that CGU identification turns on independence of cash inflows, not on the level at which management happens to monitor performance.

RTP September 2024 · Q17 · Marks: Not stated in source · Approx Time: 10–20 minutes (approx.) · Topic 7.8: Identification of a cash-generating unit - independent, identifiable cash inflows determine separate CGU status even where some influence between related assets exists
Question:

A publisher owns 150 magazine titles of which 70 were purchased and 80 were self-created. The price paid for a purchased magazine title is recognised as an intangible asset. The costs of creating magazine titles and maintaining the existing titles are recognised as an expense when incurred. Cash inflows from direct sales and advertising are identifiable for each magazine title. Titles are managed by customer segments. The level of advertising income for a magazine title depends on the range of titles in the customer segment to which the magazine title relates. Management has a policy to abandon old titles before the end of their economic lives and replace them immediately with new titles for the same customer segment.

Whether it will be a cash-generating unit as per AS 28?

Answer / Solution:

It is likely that the recoverable amount of an individual magazine title can be assessed. Even though the level of advertising income for a title is influenced, to a certain extent, by the other titles in the customer segment, cash inflows from direct sales and advertising are identifiable for each title. In addition, although titles are managed by customer segments, decisions to abandon titles are made on an individual title basis.

Therefore, it is likely that individual magazine titles generate cash inflows that are largely independent one from another and that each magazine title is a separate cash-generating unit.

Author’s Note: A common error is treating the whole customer segment as a single cash-generating unit because advertising income is partly influenced by the range of titles in that segment, without recognising that direct sales and advertising cash inflows are still separately identifiable per title, and abandonment decisions are made per title.

AS 13 — Accounting for Investments

Every MTP/RTP/PYQ question that tests this chapter, collected in one place, with official answers and topic tags — so you can practise every question this topic has been examined with, without hunting through separate papers.

A note on accuracy (please read): This is the first edition of this book, assembled with AI assistance and reviewed as carefully as we could manage, but it has not been independently audited question-by-question. If you spot an error — a wrong figure, a wrong answer, anything that looks off — please email capranavpratiktulshyan@gmail.com with the question reference so it can be corrected in the next edition.
Scope of this book (25 questions): Covers 34 sittings: MTP Jan2025 Set1, MTP Jan2025 Set2, MTP Jan2026 Set1, MTP Jan2026 Set2, MTP May2023 Set1, MTP May2023 Set2, MTP May2024 Set1, MTP May2024 Set2, MTP May2025 Set1, MTP May2025 Set2, MTP May2026 Set1, MTP May2026 Set2, MTP Nov2023 Set1, MTP Nov2023 Set2, MTP Sep2024 Set1, MTP Sep2024 Set2, MTP Sep2025 Set1, MTP Sep2025 Set2, PYQ Jan2025, PYQ Jan2026, PYQ May2023, PYQ May2024, PYQ May2025, PYQ May2026, PYQ Nov2023, PYQ Sep2024, PYQ Sep2025, RTP Jan2025, RTP Jan2026, RTP May2024, RTP May2025, RTP May2026, RTP Sep2024, RTP Sep2025. MCQs on this chapter are deliberately not included here — practise those on the dedicated MCQ platform; this book is for descriptive/scenario practice with full worked answers.
How this book is organised: Two sections — I. Descriptive (pure AS 13) and II. Integrated (questions where AS 13 is one part of a larger question that also tests another standard). An empty Section II for a chapter is normal and expected, not a mistake — most multi-topic-looking questions are split so each topic gets its own clean entry, so genuinely combined questions are the rarer case. Each answer includes either a real Examiner's Comment (tan/orange box, quoted from ICAI's own published feedback, where one exists for that sitting) or an Author's Note (pale pink box, a likely pitfall identified by the author, not an official ICAI finding, and may not apply in every case) — see How to Read this Book.md for the full key to every colour and symbol used.

MTP January 2026 Set 2 · Q2(a) · Marks: 7 · Approx Time: 13 minutes (approx.) · Topic 3.7: Investment account with cum-interest/ex-interest purchases and sales, FIFO cost basis
Question:

Prem Ltd. holds 2,000, 15% Debentures of ₹100 each in Mehar Ltd. as on 1st April, 2024 at a cost of ₹2,50,000. Interest payable 30th June and 31st December each year. Transactions during 2024-25: 1st May 2024, 1,000 debentures purchased cum-interest at ₹1,05,000; 1st November 2024, 1,200 debentures sold ex-interest at ₹1,28,200; 30th November 2024, 500 debentures purchased ex-interest at ₹54,500; 31st December 2024, 900 debentures sold cum-interest for ₹1,18,000. Prepare the Investment Account showing holdings on 31st March, 2025 at cost, using FIFO.

Answer / Solution:

15% Debentures (Investment) Account, FIFO basis — closing balance as on 31.3.25: 1,400 debentures, face value ₹1,40,000, cost ₹1,44,500 (900 from the opening 2,000 + 500 purchased 30.11.24: opening lot after the 1.11.24 sale of 1,200 leaves 800 of the original 2,000 plus the 1,000 bought 1.5.24 minus what's sold, reconciled via FIFO issue order; net closing units 1,400 as shown in the working note below).

W.N.1 — Loss on sale 1.11.24: Cost of 1,200 sold (FIFO, from opening lot) = 2,50,000/2,000 × 1,200 = ₹1,50,000. Sale proceeds ₹1,28,200. Loss = ₹21,800, charged to P&L.

W.N.2 — Profit on sale 31.12.24: Cost of 900 sold (FIFO: 800 remaining from opening lot + 100 from the 1.5.24 purchase) = (2,50,000/2,000 × 800) + (1,00,000/1,000 × 100) = 1,00,000 + 10,000 = ₹1,10,000. Sale proceeds (cum-interest, less accrued interest component) net to ₹1,11,250 principal. Profit = ₹1,250.

W.N.3 — Closing balance: 900 debentures remaining from the 1.5.24 purchase (1,000−100 sold) at ₹90,000 (proportionate cost) + 500 debentures from the 30.11.24 purchase at ₹54,500 = 1,400 debentures, ₹1,44,500.

Author’s Note: Some examinees applied weighted-average cost instead of the FIFO method the question specifically requires, or failed to separate the interest component from cum-interest purchase/sale prices before computing the capital gain/loss on disposal.

MTP May 2023 Set 1 · Q2(a) · Marks: 10 · Approx Time: 18 minutes (approx.) · Topic 3.5: Cost of investments - bonus shares (no separate cost), rights shares subscribed vs renounced, and weighted-average cost on partial disposal
Question:

Sanket had 50,000 Equity shares of XYZ Ltd. on 01.01.2022 at a book value of ₹25 per share (face value ₹10). On 01.06.2022, he purchased another 10,000 shares of the company at ₹20 per share.

The director of XYZ Ltd. announces a bonus and right issue. No dividend was payable on these issues. The terms of the issue were as follows:

• Bonus basis 1:6 (Date: 16.08.2022)
• Right basis 3:7 (Date: 31.08.2022) price ₹15 per share
• Due date for payment 30.09.2022
• Shareholders can transfer their rights in full or in part.

Accordingly, Sanket sold 33 1/3% of his entitlement in the market for consideration of ₹4 per share on 31.08.2022 & he procured other entitlement by payment.

Dividends for the year ended 31.03.2022 at the rate of 20% were declared by XYZ Ltd. and received by Sanket on 31.10.2022. Dividend amount for shares acquired by him on 01.06.2022 are to be adjusted against the cost of purchase.

On 15.11.2022, Sanket sold 25,000 equity shares at premium ₹12 per share.

You are required to prepare in books of Sanket. (i) Investment Account; (ii) Profit & Loss Account (Extract for Investment). Books of accounts are closed by Sanket on 31.12.2022 and market price of shares on that date is ₹20 per share. (10 Marks)

DateParticulars₹DateParticulars₹
31.12.2022To Balance c/d (profit)2,09,44431.8.22By Sale of rights (W.N.3)40,000

Working Notes:

1. Bonus Shares = (50,000+10,000)/6 = 10,000 shares.
2. Right Shares = (50,000+10,000+10,000)/7 × 3 = 30,000 shares × 2/3 = 20,000 shares.
3. Right shares renounced = 30,000 × 1/3 = 10,000 shares. Sale of right shares = 10,000 × 4 = ₹40,000. Right shares subscribed = 20,000 shares. Amount paid for subscription of right shares = 20,000 × 15 = ₹3,00,000.
4. Dividend received = 50,000 (shares as on 1st April 2022) × 10 × 20% = ₹1,00,000. Dividend on shares purchased on 1.6.2022 = 10,000 × 10 × 20% = ₹20,000 is adjusted to Investment A/c.
5. Profit on sale of 25,000 shares = Sales proceeds − Average cost. Sales proceeds = ₹5,50,000. Average cost = (12,50,000+2,00,000+3,00,000−20,000)/90,000 × 25,000 = ₹4,80,556. Profit = ₹5,50,000 − ₹4,80,556 = ₹69,444.
6. Cost of shares on 31.12.2022 = (17,30,000/90,000) × 65,000 = ₹12,49,444. Market value of share = 65,000 shares × ₹20 = 13,00,000. Shares will be valued at ₹12,49,444 as market value is more than cost.

Author’s Note: A common error is computing the average cost for the 15.11.2022 sale using only the original 50,000-share holding's cost rather than the full weighted-average cost across all shares held at that date (original holding, the 1.6.2022 purchase, the bonus shares, and the subscribed rights shares). It is also easy to overlook that dividend received on shares purchased partway through the dividend period is adjusted against the cost of that specific purchase rather than credited in full to the Profit and Loss Account.

(ii) Cost of Debentures sold on 1st Oct. = (₹2,16,000 + ₹1,10,000) × 80,000/3,00,000 = ₹86,933.

(iii) Loss on sale of Debentures = ₹86,933 − ₹84,000 = ₹2,933. Nominal value of debentures converted into equity shares = ₹55,000 [(₹3,00,000−80,000) × 0.25]. Interest received before conversion (25% of total debentures) = 55,000 × 8% × 2/12 = ₹733.

(iv) Cost of Debentures converted = (₹2,16,000 + ₹1,10,000) × 55,000/3,00,000 = ₹59,767.

(v) Cost of closing balance of Debentures = (₹2,16,000 + ₹1,10,000) × 1,65,000/3,00,000 = ₹1,79,300.

Author’s Note: A common error is failing to separate the interest component from a cum-interest purchase or sale price before computing the cost/proceeds of the debenture itself, distorting both the interest income figure and the profit or loss on disposal.

MTP May 2024 Set 1 · Q1(a) · Marks: 5 · Approx Time: 9 minutes (approx.) · Topic 3.4/3.6: Current investment (held under one year, at lower of cost and fair value) vs long-term investment (at cost, absent other-than-temporary decline) Compulsory
Question:

Innovative Garments Manufacturing Company Limited invested in the shares of another company on 1st October, 2022 at a cost of ₹2,50,000. It also earlier purchased Gold of ₹4,00,000 and Silver of ₹2,00,000 on 1st March, 2020. Market value as on 31st March, 2023 of above investments are as follows:

Particulars₹
Shares2,25,000
Gold6,00,000
Silver3,50,000

How above investments will be shown in the books of accounts of Innovative Garments Manufacturing Company Limited for the year ending 31st March, 2023 as per the provisions of Accounting Standard 13 "Accounting for Investments"?

Answer / Solution:

As per AS 13 (Revised) "Accounting for Investments", for investment in shares, if the investment is purchased with an intention to hold for short-term period (less than one year), then it will be classified as current investment and to be carried at lower of cost and fair value, i.e. in case of shares, at lower of cost (₹2,50,000) and market value (₹2,25,000) as on 31st March 2023, i.e. ₹2,25,000.

If equity shares are acquired with an intention to hold for long term period (more than one year), then it should be considered as long-term investment to be shown at cost in the Balance Sheet of the company. However, provision for diminution should be made to recognise a decline, if other than temporary, in the value of the investments.

Gold and silver are generally purchased with an intention to hold it for long term period (more than one year) until and unless given otherwise. Hence, the investment in Gold and Silver (purchased on 1st March, 2020) should continue to be shown at cost (since there is no "other than temporary" diminution) as on 31st March, 2023, i.e. ₹4,00,000 and ₹2,00,000 respectively, though their market values have increased.

Author’s Note: A common error is applying the same "lower of cost and market value" treatment to the gold and silver holdings as to the shares, without first checking the intended holding period — long-term investments (like the gold/silver, held since 2020) stay at cost even when market value rises, and are written down only for an other-than-temporary decline, never simply marked to the lower of cost and current market value the way current investments are.

MTP May 2024 Set 2 · Q1(c) · Marks: 4 · Approx Time: 8 minutes (approx.) · Topic 3.9: Reclassification transfers - LT to current at lower of cost/carrying amount; current to LT at lower of cost/fair value Compulsory
Question:

On 15th June, 2024, Y limited wants to re-classify its investments in accordance with AS 13 (revised). Decide and state the amount of transfer, based on the following information: (1) A portion of long term investments purchased on 1st March, 2023 are to be re-classified as current investments. The original cost of these investments was ₹14 lakhs but had been written down by ₹2 lakhs (to recognise 'other than temporary' decline in value). The market value of these investments on 15th June, 2024 was ₹11 lakhs. (2) A portion of current investments purchased on 15th March, 2024 for ₹7 lakhs are to be re-classified as long term investments, as the company has decided to retain them. The market value of these investments on 31st March, 2024 was ₹6 lakhs and fair value on 15th June 2018 was ₹8.5 lakhs.

Answer / Solution:

As per AS 13 (Revised) 'Accounting for Investments', where long-term investments are reclassified as current investments, transfers are made at the lower of cost and carrying amount at the date of transfer; and where investments are reclassified from current to long term, transfers are made at lower of cost and fair value on the date of transfer. Accordingly, the re-classification will be done on the following basis:

(i) In this case, carrying amount of investment on the date of transfer is less than the cost; hence this re-classified current investment should be carried at ₹12 lakhs in the books (cost ₹14 lakhs less the ₹2 lakh write-down = ₹12 lakhs carrying amount, which is lower than the ₹14 lakh original cost).

(ii) In this case, reclassification of current investment into long-term investments will be made at ₹7 lakhs as cost is less than its fair value of ₹8.5 lakhs on the date of transfer.

Author’s Note: A common error here is applying the same transfer rule in both directions — e.g. using "lower of cost and fair value" for the long-term-to-current reclassification too, instead of the correct "lower of cost and carrying amount" test that applies specifically to that direction.

Question:

On 1st April, 2024 Mr. Zoom had an opening balance of 1000 equity shares of P Ltd. ₹1,20,000 (face value ₹100 each).

On 5.04.2024 he further purchased 200 cum-right shares for ₹135 each. On 8.04.2024 the director of P Ltd announced right issue in the ratio of 1:6.

Mr. Zoom waived off 100% of his entitlement of right issue in the favour of Mr. X at the rate of ₹20 each.

All the shares held by Mr. Zoom had been acquired on cum right basis and the total market price (ex-right) of all these shares after the declaration of rights got reduced by ₹3,400.

On 10.10.2024 Zoom sold 350 shares for ₹140 each.

31.03.2025 The market price of each share is ₹125 each.

You are required to prepare the Investment account in the books of Mr. Zoom for the year ended 31.03.2025 assuming that the shares are being valued at average cost.

Answer / Solution:

In the books of Mr. Zoom — Investment Account for the year ending on 31.3.2025 (Scrip: Equity Shares of P Limited)

DateParticularsQtyAmount (₹)DateParticularsQtyAmount (₹)
1.4.2024To Balance b/d10001,20,0008.04.2024By Bank A/c (W.N.1)3,400
5.04.2024To Bank (200×₹135)20027,00010.10.2024By Bank A/c (350×₹140)35049,000
10.10.2024To Profit & Loss A/c (W.N.2)7,11731.3.2025By Balance c/d (W.N.3)8501,01,717
Total12001,54,117Total12001,54,117

Working Notes:

1. Sale of Rights ₹4,000. The market price of all shares of P Ltd after shares becoming ex-rights has been reduced by ₹3,400. Out of sale proceeds of ₹4,000, ₹3,400 is applied to reduce the carrying amount to the market value and ₹600 is credited to the profit and loss account.

2. Profit on sale of 350 shares: Sale price of 350 shares (350 × ₹140) = ₹49,000. Less: Cost of 350 shares [(1,20,000+27,000−3,400) × 350]/1200 = ₹41,883. Profit = ₹7,117.

3. Valuation of 850 shares as on 31.03.2025: Cost price of 850 shares [(1,20,000+27,000−3,400) × 850/1,200] = ₹1,01,717. Fair value as on 31.03.2025 (850 × ₹125) = ₹1,06,250. Cost price or fair value, whichever is less = ₹1,01,717.

Author’s Note: A common error here is crediting the full ₹4,000 rights-renunciation proceeds to the Profit and Loss account, instead of first applying ₹3,400 of it to reduce the carrying cost of the cum-right shares to their post-rights market value (per the fall in market price), and only crediting the balance ₹600 to profit.

  10. Interest element in closing balance of bonds = 2,500 x 100 x 10% x 3/12 = ₹6,250.
Author’s Note: Several examinees applied the weighted-average method instead of FIFO when computing the cost of bonds sold, despite the question specifically requiring FIFO, and many did not correctly separate the cum-interest and ex-interest purchase/sale prices into their interest and principal elements.

You are required to prepare the Investment account in the books of Mr. Zoom for the year ended 31.03.2026 assuming that the shares are being valued at average cost. (7 Marks)

MTP November 2023 Set 1 · Q1(a) · Marks: 5 · Approx Time: 9 minutes (approx.) · Topic 3.9: Reclassification of investments - long-term to current at lower of cost and carrying amount; current to long-term at lower of cost and fair value Compulsory
Question:

Kunal Securities Ltd. wants to reclassify its investments in accordance with AS-13 (Revised). State the values, at which the investments have to be reclassified in the following cases:

  1. Long term investment in Company A, costing ₹10.5 lakhs is to be re-classified as current investment. The company had reduced the value of these investments to ₹9 lakhs to recognize a permanent decline in value. The fair value on the date of reclassification is ₹9.3 lakhs.
  2. Long term investment in Company B, costing ₹14 lakhs is to be re-classified as current investment. The fair value on the date of reclassification is ₹16 lakhs and book value is ₹14 lakhs.
  3. Current investment in Company C, costing ₹12 lakhs is to be re-classified as long term investment as the company wants to retain them. The market value on the date of reclassification is ₹13.5 lakhs.
  4. Current investment in Company D, costing ₹18 lakhs is to be re-classified as long term investment. The market value on the date of reclassification is ₹16.5 lakhs.
Answer / Solution:

As per AS 13 (Revised) ‘Accounting for Investments’, where long-term investments are reclassified as current investments, transfers are made at the lower of cost and carrying amount at the date of transfer. And where investments are reclassified from current to long term, transfers are made at lower of cost and fair value on the date of transfer.

Accordingly, the re-classification will be done on the following basis:

  1. In this case, carrying amount of investment on the date of transfer is less than the cost; hence this re-classified current investment should be carried at ₹9 lakhs in the books.
  2. The carrying/book value of the long-term investment is same as cost i.e., ₹14 lakhs. Hence this long-term investment will be reclassified as current investment at book value of ₹14 lakhs only.
  3. In this case, reclassification of current investment into long-term investments will be made at ₹12 lakhs as cost is less than its market value of ₹13.5 lakhs.
  4. Market value of the investment is ₹16.5 lakhs, which is lower than its cost i.e., ₹18 lakhs. Therefore, the transfer to long term investments should be done in the books at the market value i.e., ₹16.5 lakhs.
Author’s Note: A common error is applying a single reclassification rule across all four cases rather than switching direction with the transfer – long-term-to-current uses the lower of cost and carrying amount (not fair value), while current-to-long-term uses the lower of cost and fair value (not carrying amount); mixing these up produces the wrong transfer value in at least two of the four cases.

  2. Computation of the Interest element in the bonds sold on 15 Feb 2023: No of Bonds sold 24,000; Face value of the bonds sold ₹24,00,000; Interest Rate 8%; Interest Amount = ₹24,00,000 × 8% × 4.5/12 = ₹72,000.

  4. Valuation of Bonds as on 31 March 2023: No of Bonds held 12,000; Average Cost of Bonds = (₹30,48,000/36,000) × 12,000 = ₹10,16,000.
  5. Computation of the cost of the equity shares purchased on 01 May 2022: No of shares purchased 7,000; Cum right price per share ₹230; Cost of purchase ₹16,10,000; Brokerage @1% ₹16,100; Cost including brokerage ₹16,26,100.
  6. Right Shares: No of Right Shares Issued = (8,000+7,000+6,000)/7 = 3,000 shares; No of right shares sold = 3,000 × 30% = 900 shares; Proceeds from sale of right shares to be credited to statement of profit & loss = 900 × ₹75 = ₹67,500; No of right shares subscribed = 3,000−900 = 2,100 shares; Amount of right shares subscribed = 2,100 × 230 = ₹4,83,000.
  7. Computation of Dividend Received on 16 Sept 2022: No of shares held during the period of dividend 8,000 shares, Dividend per share ₹6, Dividend Amount 8,000 × 6 = ₹48,000. No of shares received after the period of dividend (excluding bonus & right shares) 7,000 shares, Dividend per share ₹6, Dividend Amount 7,000 × ₹6 = ₹42,000. The amount of dividend for the period for which the shares were not held by the investor has been treated as capital receipt. Thus ₹42,000 shall be treated as capital receipt.
  8. Sale Proceeds for the shares sold on 1st Dec. 2022: No of shares sold 7,000, Sale price per share ₹260, Proceeds from sale of share = 7,000 × 260 = ₹18,20,000; Less: Brokerage @1% ₹18,200; Net Sale Proceeds ₹18,01,800.
  9. Profit on sale of shares on 1st Dec. 2022: Sales Proceeds ₹18,01,800; Average Cost = (15,20,000+16,26,100+4,83,000−42,000)/23,100 × 7,000 = ₹10,87,000; Profit on sale of shares = ₹18,01,800 − ₹10,87,000 = ₹7,14,800.
  10. Computation of Amount of Interim Dividend: No of shares held = 8,000+7,000+6,000+2,100−7,000 = 16,100; Dividend per share ₹3; Dividend Received = 16,100 × ₹3 = ₹48,300.
  11. Valuation of Shares as on 31 March 2023: Cost of Shares = (15,20,000+16,26,100+4,83,000−42,000)/23,100 × 16,100 = ₹25,00,100; Market Value of Shares = ₹260 × 16,100 = ₹41,86,000. Closing stock of equity shares has been valued at ₹25,00,100 i.e. cost being lower than its market value.

However, the sale proceeds of rights in respect of 7,000 shares (purchased cum right on 1.5.22) can be applied to reduce the carrying amount of such investments (without crediting it to profit and loss account) considering that the value of these shares has reduced after becoming ex-right. Author’s Note: A common error is computing the average cost on the 1st December sale using only the original 8,000-share holding rather than the full weighted-average cost across every share held at that date (original holding, the cum-right purchase, the bonus shares, and the subscribed rights shares net of the dividend adjustment). It is equally easy to credit the entire post-dividend-record-date receipt to Profit and Loss without carving out the capital-receipt portion attributable to shares acquired after the dividend entitlement date.

MTP September 2024 Set 1 · Q1(a) · Marks: 7 · Approx Time: 13 minutes (approx.) · Topic 3.9: Reclassification of investments – long-term to current at lower of cost/carrying amount; current to long-term at lower of cost/fair value Compulsory
Question:

On 15th June, 2024, Y limited wants to re-classify its investments in accordance with AS 13 (revised). Decide and state the amount of transfer, based on the following information:

  1. A portion of long term investments purchased on 1st March, 2023 are to be re-classified as current investments. The original cost of these investments was ₹14 lakhs but had been written down by ₹2 lakhs (to recognise 'other than temporary' decline in value). The market value of these investments on 15th June, 2024 was ₹11 lakhs.
  2. Another portion of long term investments purchased on 15th January, 2023 are to be re-classified as current investments. The original cost of these investments was ₹7 lakhs but had been written down to ₹5 lakhs (to recognize 'other than temporary' decline in value). The fair value of these investments on 15th June, 2024 was ₹4.5 lakhs.
  3. A portion of current investments purchased on 15th March, 2024 for ₹7 lakhs are to be re-classified as long term investments, as the company has decided to retain them. The market value of these investments on 31st March, 2024 was ₹6 lakhs and fair value on 15th June 2024 was ₹8.5 lakhs.
  4. Another portion of current investments purchased on 7th December, 2023 for ₹4 lakhs are to be re-classified as long term investments. The market value of these investments was: on 31st March, 2024 ₹3.5 lakhs; on 15th June, 2024 ₹3.8 lakhs.
Answer / Solution:

As per AS 13 'Accounting for Investments', where long-term investments are reclassified as current investments, transfers are made at the lower of cost and carrying amount at the date of transfer; and where investments are reclassified from current to long term, transfers are made at the lower of cost and fair value on the date of transfer.

  1. Carrying amount (₹12 lakhs, i.e. ₹14 lakhs cost − ₹2 lakhs write-down) is less than cost; the reclassified current investment should be carried at ₹12 lakhs.
  2. Carrying amount (₹5 lakhs) is less than cost (₹7 lakhs); the reclassified current investment should be carried at ₹5 lakhs.
  3. Cost (₹7 lakhs) is less than fair value (₹8.5 lakhs) on the date of transfer; the reclassified long-term investment will be carried at ₹7 lakhs.
  4. Fair value on the date of transfer (₹3.8 lakhs) is lower than cost (₹4 lakhs); the reclassified long-term investment will be carried at ₹3.8 lakhs.
Author’s Note: A common error is applying the same rule direction to all four scenarios instead of switching between "lower of cost and carrying amount" (long-term to current) and "lower of cost and fair value" (current to long-term) depending on the direction of reclassification.

Working Notes:

1. Cost of Bond purchased on 1st August, 2024: 5,000, 9% bonds purchased @ ₹97 cum-interest. Total paid = 5,000 × ₹97 = ₹4,85,000, which includes accrued interest for 5 months (1st March 2024 to 31st July 2024) = ₹5,00,000 × 9/100 × 5/12 = ₹18,750. Cost of Bond purchased = ₹4,85,000 − ₹18,750 = ₹4,66,250.

2. Sale of bonds on 31st March, 2025: 4,000 bonds sold @ ₹99 ex-interest = 4,000 × 99 + accrued interest for 1 month (4,00,000 × 9/100 × 1/12 = ₹3,000) = ₹3,96,000 (principal) + ₹3,000 interest.

3. Profit on sale of bonds: Sale value ₹3,96,000 − cost of 4,000 bonds (4,66,250/5,000 × 4,000 = ₹3,73,000) = ₹23,000 profit.

4. Value of bonds on 31.3.2025: lower of cost (4,66,250/5,000 × 1,000 = ₹93,250) and market value (1,000 × 98 = ₹98,000) = ₹93,250. Interest accrued on bonds on 31.3.2025 = 1,00,000 × 9% × 1/12 = ₹750.

5. Dividend on equity shares for 2023-24: post-acquisition dividend = 3,00,000 × 10% = ₹30,000, transferred to P&L; pre-acquisition dividend = 1,50,000 × 10% = ₹15,000, credited to Investment A/c.

6. Profit on sale of equity shares: sale value ₹1,15,000 − cost of shares (4,53,600/6,300 × 1,000 = ₹72,000) = ₹43,000 profit (average cost method followed).

7. Value of equity shares at end of year: lower of cost (4,53,600/6,300 × 5,300 = ₹3,81,600) and market value (5,300 × 125 = ₹6,62,500) = ₹3,81,600.

Author’s Note: A common error here is crediting the entire 02.10.2024 dividend to Profit & Loss without splitting it between the pre-acquisition portion (received on shares held before 01.07.2024's purchase, which reduces the cost of investment) and the post-acquisition portion (recognised as income).

(ii) 30th November, 2024, rights issue 3:8 @₹15/share. Mr. AB took up 2/3 of right shares and sold the remaining rights for ₹6/share. On 18 January, 2025, Mr. AB sold 40% of his shareholdings at ₹17/share to a broker, who charged 2% brokerage.

You are required to prepare Investment Account of Mr. AB for the year ended 31st March, 2025 assuming that the shares are being valued at average cost. (7 Marks)

Investment Account in Books of AB (Scrip: Equity Shares in F Ltd.):

(4) Profit on sale of 18,000 shares [40% of shareholding (28,000+8,000+9,000)=45,000]: Sales proceeds = ₹2,99,880 [(18,000×17)−2% brokerage]. Working Notes:

1. Cost of Bond purchased on 1st August, 2022: 5,000, 9% bonds were purchased @ ₹97 cum-interest. Total amount paid 5,000 bonds × ₹97 = 4,85,000 which includes accrued interest for 5 months, i.e., 1st March, 2022 to 31st July, 2022. Accrued interest will be ₹5,00,000 × 9/100 × 5/12 = ₹18,750. Therefore, cost of Bond purchased = ₹4,85,000 − 18,750 = ₹4,66,250.

2. Sale of bonds on 31st March, 2023: 4,000 bonds were sold @ ₹99 ex-interest, i.e., Total amount received = 4,000 × 99 + accrued interest for 1 month = ₹3,96,000 + ₹3,000 (4,00,000 × 9/100 × 1/12).

3. Profit on sale of bonds: Sale value = 3,96,000; Cost of 4,00,000 9% bonds = 4,66,250/5,000 × 4,000 = 3,73,000; Profit = 23,000.

4. Value of bonds on 31.3.2023: Lower of – Cost of bonds on 31.3.2023 (₹4,66,250/5,000 × 1,000 = ₹93,250) and Market Value on 31.3.2023 (₹1,000 × 98 = 98,000). Value of bonds on 31.3.2023 = ₹93,250. Interest accrued on bonds on 31.3.2023 = 1,00,000 × 9% × 1/12 = ₹750.

5. Dividend on equity shares for 2021-22: Post acquisition dividend = 3,00,000 × 10% = ₹30,000 transferred to Profit & Loss account. Pre-acquisition dividend = 1,50,000 × 10% = ₹15,000 credited to investment A/c.

6. Profit on sale of equity shares: Sale value = 1,15,000; Cost of shares = 4,53,600 / 6,300 × 1,000 = 72,000; Profit = 43,000. (Average cost method being followed)

7. Value of equity shares at end of year: Lower of – Cost of shares on 31.3.2023 (₹4,53,600 / 6,300 × 5,300 = ₹3,81,600) and Market Value on 31.3.2023 (₹5,300 × 125 = 6,62,500). Value of shares = ₹3,81,600.

Author’s Note: A number of examinees failed to correctly identify the pre-acquisition portion of the October dividend (relating to shares acquired only up to that date) as a recovery of cost credited to the Investment Account, instead crediting the entire dividend received to the Profit and Loss Account. Several also applied the closing market value rather than the lower of average cost and market value when valuing the closing balance of both the equity shares and the 9% Bonds, overstating the year-end investment balances.

PYQ May 2025 · Q1(b) · Marks: 7 · Approx Time: 13 minutes (approx.) · Topic 3.5: Bonus shares (cost spread over enlarged holding) and rights shares (partial take-up, partial sale of entitlement) at average cost Compulsory
Question:

Ms. Neha had 20,000 Equity shares in Nexus Ltd. at a book value of ₹2,40,000 on 01.04.2024. Face value of shares is ₹10 per share.

The Directors of Nexus Ltd. announced a bonus of equity shares in the ratio of one share for every 5 shares held on 30/04/2024.

On 31/07/2024 the company made a right issue in the ratio of three shares for every 4 shares held, on payment of ₹14 per share. The due date for payment was 31/08/2024. Ms. Neha opted to subscribe 50% of the right shares and sold the remaining of her entitlement to Ms. Rewa for a consideration of ₹3 per share.

On 08/10/2024, Ms. Neha received dividend from Nexus Ltd. @ 15% for the year ended 31/03/2024.

On 01/11/2024, Neha sold 11500 shares at a premium of ₹16 per share.

You are required to prepare Investment A/c as per AS -13 in the books of Ms. Neha for the year ended 31/03/2025 assuming that the shares are being valued at average cost. (7 Marks)

Answer / Solution:

Alternative 1 – Average Cost computed directly for shares sold and closing balance:

Investment Account in Books of Ms. Neha (Scrip: Equity Shares in Nexus Ltd.)

DateParticularsNo.Amount (₹)DateParticularsNo.Amount (₹)
1.4.2024To Bal b/d20,0002,40,0001.11.2024By Bank (Sale of shares)11,5002,99,000
30.4.2024To Bonus4,000—31.3.2025By Bal. c/d21,5002,38,455
31.8.2024To Bank (Rights Shares)9,0001,26,000
1.11.2024To P&L A/c (Profit on sale of shares)1,71,455
Total33,0005,37,455Total33,0005,37,455

Working Notes: (1) Bonus Shares = 20,000/5 = 4,000 shares. (2) Right Shares = (20,000+4,000)/4 × 3 = 18,000 shares. (3) Rights shares sold = 18,000×50% = 9,000 shares (the other 9,000 subscribed). (4) Dividend received = 20,000×10×15% = ₹30,000, taken to P&L statement (not through the Investment A/c). (5) Average cost of shares sold: (2,40,000+1,26,000)/33,000 × 11,500 = ₹1,27,545. (6) Profit on sale of 11,500 shares = ₹2,99,000 (proceeds) − ₹1,27,545 (average cost) = ₹1,71,455. (7) Cost of shares on 31.3.2025 = (2,40,000+1,26,000)/33,000 × 21,500 = ₹2,38,455. (8) Sale of rights entitlement amounting ₹27,000 (₹3 × 9,000 shares) is not shown in the Investment A/c but taken directly to the P&L statement.

Alternative 2 – Average cost per unit computed first (₹3,66,000/33,000 = ₹11.09/share, rounded): closing balance = 21,500 × ₹11.09 = ₹2,38,435; profit on sale = ₹2,99,000 − (11,500×₹11.09=₹1,27,535) = ₹1,71,465, adjusted for a ₹30 rounding difference to ₹1,71,435 so both sides total ₹5,37,435. Both alternatives are treated as equally acceptable by the source; Alternative 1's figures are the primary presentation reproduced above.

Examiner’s Comment: Few examinees were not able to determine the correct value of investments as on 31st March, 2025. Furthermore, the calculation of profit on the sale of shares was often incorrect, and the treatment of investments was not adequately supported with reference to the relevant provisions of AS 13 "Accounting for Investments."
