MTP May 2023 Set 1 · Q1(d) · Marks: 5 · Approx Time: 9 minutes (approx.) · Topic 2.5: Change in the method of estimating a provision is not a change in accounting policy, and the required disclosure note when the change is nonetheless made Compulsory
Question:

ABC Ltd. was making provision for non-moving inventories based on no issues for the last 12 months up to 31.3.2021.

The company wants to provide during the year ending 31.3.2022 based on technical evaluation:

Particulars₹
Total value of inventory100 lakhs
Provision required based on 12 months issue3.5 lakhs
Provision required based on technical evaluation2.5 lakhs

Does this amount to change in Accounting Policy? Can the company change the method of provision? (5 Marks)

Answer / Solution:

The decision of making provision for non-moving inventories on the basis of technical evaluation does not amount to change in accounting policy. Accounting policy of a company may require that provision for non-moving inventories should be made. The method of estimating the amount of provision may be changed in case a more prudent estimate can be made. In the given case, considering the total value of inventory, the change in the amount of required provision of non-moving inventory from ₹3.5 lakhs to ₹2.5 lakhs is also not material. The disclosure can be made for such change in the following lines by way of notes to the accounts in the annual accounts of ABC Ltd. for the year 2021-22:

“The company has provided for non-moving inventories on the basis of technical evaluation unlike preceding years. Had the same method been followed as in the previous year, the profit for the year and the corresponding effect on the year end net assets would have been lower by ₹1 lakh.”

Author’s Note: A common error is treating any change in the basis of a provision estimate as automatically a change in accounting policy requiring restatement, without distinguishing a genuine policy change from a change in accounting estimate (moving to a more prudent estimation method for an existing policy of providing for non-moving inventory).

PYQ May 2026 · Q6(b) · Marks: 4 · Approx Time: 8 minutes (approx.) · Topic 2.5: Distinguishing a change in accounting estimate, a policy for new/immaterial transactions, and a genuine change in accounting policy
Question:

The accountant of Moon Limited provides you the following information: (i) Provision for doubtful debts was created @3% till 31st March, 2025; from FY 2025-26, the rate has been changed to 5%. (ii) During the year ended 31st March, 2026 the management has introduced a formal gratuity scheme in place of ad-hoc ex-gratia payments to employees on retirement. (iii) During 2025-26, there was change in cost formula in measuring the cost of inventories. (iv) Management decided to pay pension to employees who have retired after completing 5 years of service (₹25,000 per month); earlier there was no such pension scheme.

You are required to advise the accountant of Moon Limited, with valid reasons, whether the above transactions would be treated as change in accounting policy or not, for the year ended 31st March, 2026 in the context of AS 5. (4 Marks)

Answer / Solution:

As per para 21 of AS 5, the preparation of financial statements involves making estimates based on circumstances existing when the statements are prepared; it may be necessary to revise an estimate in a subsequent period if circumstances change. Revision of an estimate, by its nature, does not bring the adjustment within the definitions of a prior period item or an extraordinary item. Change in Accounting estimate is not a change in accounting policy.

(i) Provision for doubtful debts rate change (3% to 5%): this is a change in accounting estimate, not a change in accounting policy. Per para 27 of AS 5, a change in estimate with a material effect in the current period should be disclosed and quantified; any change expected to have a material effect in later periods should also be disclosed and quantified.

(ii) As per AS 5, adopting an accounting policy for events or transactions that differ in substance from previously occurring events or transactions is not considered a change in accounting policy. Accordingly, introduction of a formal retirement gratuity scheme in place of ad hoc ex-gratia payments is not a change in accounting policy.

(iii) As per AS 2 and AS 5: the method of determining cost (FIFO/Weighted Average) is an accounting policy choice, and any change in it affects measurement of inventory and profit. Hence a change in cost formula in measuring the cost of inventories IS a change in Accounting Policy.

(iv) The adoption of a new accounting policy for events or transactions which did not occur previously, or that were immaterial, will not be treated as a change in accounting policy. Introducing a pension scheme where none previously existed is therefore not a change in accounting policy.

Author’s Note: Many examinees classified the provision-rate change and the new gratuity/pension schemes as changes in accounting policy, not recognising AS 5's distinction between a genuine policy change (like the inventory cost-formula change) and a change in estimate or the adoption of a policy for a genuinely new type of transaction.

PYQ September 2025 · Q6(a) [OR-alt 1] · Marks: 4 · Approx Time: 8 minutes (approx.) · Topic 2.3: Prior period item vs current-year expense - depends on whether the underlying adjustment was determinable in the prior period or only becomes so via a later event
Question:

Sneha, an employee of Omre Limited, went on paid maternity leave for 9 months, 1st January 2024 to 30th September 2024, monthly pay ₹1,50,000. While preparing FY2023-24 financial statements, her salary for 3 months (Jan–Mar 2024) was omitted. When she joined 1st October 2024, the whole 9-month salary was paid. With reference to AS-5, determine if this is a prior period item and pass the FY2024-25 journal entry. Variant: Suppose Sneha was terminated 1st January 2024 and reinstated by court order on 30th September 2024, with the 9-month salary paid 1st October 2024 — what is the AS-5 treatment here, with journal entry?

Answer / Solution:

Original scenario: Per AS 5, prior period items are income/expenses arising in the current period from errors or omissions in preparing prior periods' financial statements. The 3 months' salary (Jan–Mar 2024, ₹4,50,000) omitted from FY2023-24 is a prior period item in FY2024-25.

Journal entry (FY2024-25): Salary A/c (₹1,50,000×6) Dr. 9,00,000; Prior Period Item A/c (₹1,50,000×3) Dr. 4,50,000; To Bank A/c 13,50,000.

Variant (termination/reinstatement): AS 5 states "prior period items" does not include adjustments necessitated by circumstances that, though related to prior periods, are determined only in the current period. Since Sneha's reinstatement (with retrospective salary) was ordered by the court only in FY2024-25, the ₹4,50,000 (Jan–Mar 2024) is not a prior period item — the entire ₹13,50,000 is a current-year expense.

Journal entry (variant): Salary A/c (₹1,50,000×9) Dr. 13,50,000; To Bank A/c 13,50,000.

Examiner’s Comment: A majority of examinees were unable to determine whether the given item constituted a prior period item under AS 5 "Net Profit or Loss for the Period, Prior Period Items and Changes in Accounting Policies". Many of them also failed to pass the correct journal entry.

RTP January 2025 · Q5 · Marks: Not stated in source · Approx Time: 10–20 minutes (approx.) · Topic 2.2: Prior period items arise only from errors or omissions in preparing earlier financial statements - a provision write-back from a genuinely unusual event is an extraordinary item instead
Question:

During the course of the last three years, a company owning and operating Helicopters lost four Helicopters. The company's accountant felt that after the crash, the maintenance provision created in respect of the respective helicopters was no longer required, and proposed to write it back to the Profit and Loss account as a prior period item.

Is the company's proposed accounting treatment correct? Discuss.

Answer / Solution:

The balance amount of maintenance provision written back to profit and loss account, no longer required due to crash of the helicopters, is not a prior period item because there was no error in the preparation of previous periods' financial statements. The term "prior period items", as defined in AS 5 (revised) "Net Profit or Loss for the Period, Prior Period Items and Changes in Accounting Policies", refer only to income or expenses which arise in the current period as a result of errors or omissions in the preparation of the financial statements of one or more prior periods. The balance amount left in the provision created earlier is not as a result of error in the past. So it will not be considered as a prior period item. Such write back of provision is not an ordinary feature of the business; it shall be considered as an extra-ordinary item.

As per paragraph 8 of AS 5, extraordinary items should be disclosed in the Statement of Profit and Loss as a part of net profit or loss for the period. The nature and the amount of each extraordinary item should be separately disclosed in the Statement of Profit and Loss in a manner that its impact on current profit or loss can be perceived. Hence, the amount so written-back (if material) should be disclosed as an extraordinary item as per AS 5 rather than as a prior period item.

Author’s Note: A common error is treating the reversal of a no-longer-required provision as a prior period item merely because the original provision was created in an earlier year, missing AS 5's requirement that prior period items arise specifically from errors or omissions in preparing earlier financial statements — a provision correctly created and later found unnecessary due to a genuinely unusual event is an extraordinary item, not a prior period correction.

RTP January 2026 · Q5 · Marks: Not stated in source · Approx Time: 10–20 minutes (approx.) · Topic 2.3: Classification exercise across accounting policy changes, estimate changes, extraordinary items, and prior period items
Question:

Identify each of the following as Change in Accounting Policy / Change in Accounting Estimate / Extraordinary Item / Prior Period Item / Ordinary Activity: (i) Non-provision for salary already due in an earlier year. (ii) Attachment of the property of the enterprise. (iii) Introduction of a new pension scheme for employees. (iv) Change in Reserve for obsolete inventory. (v) Settlement of a litigation case. (vi) Legislative changes with long-term retrospective application. (vii) Change from Cost Model to Revaluation Model for PPE measurement. (viii) Government-sanctioned grant received this year for expenses incurred in a previous year.

Answer / Solution:
  1. Prior period item.
  2. Extraordinary item.
  3. Ordinary activity (not a change in accounting policy).
  4. Change in accounting estimate.
  5. Ordinary activity, but requires separate disclosure.
  6. Extraordinary item requiring separate disclosure.
  7. Change in accounting policy.
  8. Prior period item.
Author’s Note: Some examinees classified the change from Cost to Revaluation Model as a change in estimate rather than a change in accounting policy, and conversely treated the pension-scheme introduction as a policy change rather than recognising it as a new ordinary business decision, not a change to an existing policy.

RTP January 2026 · Q6 · Marks: Not stated in source · Approx Time: 10–20 minutes (approx.) · Topic 2.4: Tax demands from ordinary business activity are not extraordinary items
Question:

Best Ltd., a consultancy services provider, received a GST department demand notice of ₹2,50,000 on consultancy services provided; the company paid the demand and recorded it as extraordinary expenditure. Can this payment of a tax demand be recognised as an extraordinary item?

Answer / Solution:

No. Per AS 5, extraordinary items arise from events clearly distinct from ordinary activities and are not expected to recur frequently or regularly. Providing consultancy services is Best Ltd.'s ordinary business activity, and the GST liability arises directly from these ordinary transactions. Paying a tax demand raised by the taxation authority is part of normal business operations. Recording it as extraordinary is therefore not correct — it should be recognised as part of profit or loss from ordinary activities.

Author’s Note: Some examinees accepted the company's own extraordinary-item classification uncritically, not testing it against AS 5's actual definition (an event clearly distinct from, and not part of, the ordinary business activity).

RTP May 2025 · Q8 · Marks: Not stated in source · Approx Time: 10–20 minutes (approx.) · Topic 2.5: Classification exercise distinguishing accounting-estimate changes, non-policy-changes (new events), and genuine accounting-policy changes
Question:

The Accountant of Heera Ltd. has sought your opinion with relevant reasons, whether the following transactions will be treated as change in Accounting Policy or not for the year ended 31st March, 2024. Please advise him in the following situations in accordance with the provisions of relevant Accounting Standard:

  1. Till the previous year the furniture was depreciated on straight line basis over a period of 5 years. From current year, the useful life of furniture has been changed to 3 years.
  2. Management decided to pay pension to those employees who have retired after completing 5 years of service in the organization. Such employees will get pension of ₹20,000 per month. Earlier there was no such scheme of pension in the organization.
  3. During the year ended 31st March, 2024, there was change in cost formula in measuring the cost of inventories.
Answer / Solution:
  1. Change in useful life of furniture from 5 years to 3 years is a change in accounting estimate, not a change in accounting policy.
  2. Adoption of a new accounting policy for events or transactions which did not occur previously (there was no pension scheme before) should not be treated as a change in an accounting policy. The introduction of the new pension scheme is therefore not a change in accounting policy.
  3. Change in the cost formula used in measuring the cost of inventories is a change in accounting policy.
Author’s Note: A common error is classifying the new pension scheme as a change in accounting policy simply because it is a new accounting treatment being adopted, missing AS 5's specific rule that adopting a policy for an event that did not previously occur is not a change in an existing policy.

RTP September 2024 · Q6 · Marks: Not stated in source · Approx Time: 10–20 minutes (approx.) · Topic 2.5: Adoption of a policy for events/transactions that did not previously occur is not a change in accounting policy
Question:

Explain whether the following will constitute a change in accounting policy or not as per AS 5:

  1. Introduction of a formal retirement gratuity scheme by an employer in place of ad hoc ex-gratia payments to employees on retirement.
  2. Management decided to pay pension to those employees who have retired after completing 5 years of service in the organistaion. Such employees will get pension of ₹20,000 per month. Earlier there was no such scheme of pension in the organization.
Answer / Solution:

As per para 31 of AS 5 ‘Net Profit or Loss for the Period, Prior Period Items and Changes in Accounting Policies’, the adoption of an accounting policy for events or transactions that differ in substance from previously occurring events or transactions, will not be considered as a change in accounting policy.

  1. Accordingly, introduction of a formal retirement gratuity scheme by an employer in place of ad hoc ex-gratia payments to employees on retirement is not a change in an accounting policy.
  2. Similarly, the adoption of a new accounting policy of paying pension to retired employees is a policy for events or transactions which did not occur previously. Hence, it will not be treated as a change in an accounting policy.
Author’s Note: A common error is treating both scenarios as changes in accounting policy simply because the amount charged to profit or loss will differ going forward, without checking whether the underlying event or transaction itself is genuinely new rather than merely a change in the treatment of the same recurring event.

RTP September 2025 · Q9(a) · Marks: Not stated in source · Approx Time: 10–20 minutes (approx.) · Topic 2.3: Definition of a prior period item - errors/omissions in prior financial statements, not later-determined adjustments
Question:

When can an item qualify to be a prior period item as per AS 5?

Answer / Solution:

Per AS 5 para 16, prior period items are income or expenses that arise in the current period as a result of errors or omissions in the preparation of financial statements of one or more prior periods. The term does not include other adjustments necessitated by circumstances that, though related to prior periods, are determined only in the current period (e.g. arrears payable to workers from a retrospective wage revision).

Author’s Note: A direct definitional question; the key nuance examinees often miss is the exclusion for items only determinable in the current period despite relating to an earlier one.

RTP September 2025 · Q9(b) · Marks: Not stated in source · Approx Time: 10–20 minutes (approx.) · Topic 2.4: Correcting an omitted-inventory error from a prior period, added to opening stock as a prior period item
Question:

A Ltd. finds that the stock sheets of 31.3.2024 did not include two pages containing details of inventory worth ₹20 lakhs. How should this be dealt with in the accounts for the year ended 31st March, 2025, per AS 5?

Answer / Solution:

This omission is a prior period item under AS 5 para 16. Per para 19, prior period items are normally included in determining the current period's net profit or loss — so ₹20 lakhs should be added to the opening stock as at 1.4.2024. Alternatively, such items may be shown in the statement of profit and loss after the current period's net profit/loss has been determined. Either presentation must clearly indicate the effect of the item on the current period's profit or loss.

Author’s Note: Some examinees treated the omission as a current-year adjustment to closing stock rather than correcting the prior year's opening stock figure, misplacing the correction in the wrong period.

II. Integrated Questions (AS 5 with Other Standards)

Questions where AS 5 judgment is one part of a larger, genuinely connected question also testing another standard.

MTP January 2025 Set 2 · Q1(a) · Marks: 7 · Approx Time: 13 minutes (approx.) · Topic 1.4: Adjusting versus non-adjusting events after the balance sheet date, across five distinct fact patterns  +  Topic 2.2: Extraordinary item discovered after financial statements are approved, treated in the subsequent period Compulsory
Question:

State with reasons, how the following events would be dealt with in the financial statements of Hari Ltd. for the year ended 31st March, 2024 (accounts were approved on 25th July, 2024):

  1. Negotiations with another company for acquisition of its business was started on 21st January, 2024. Hari Ltd. invested ₹40 lakh on 22nd April, 2024.
  2. The company made a provision for bad debts @ 4% of its total debtors (as per trend followed from the previous years). In the second week of March 2024, a debtor for ₹2,50,000 had suffered heavy loss due to an earthquake; the loss was not covered by any insurance policy. In May, 2024 the debtor became bankrupt.
  3. During the year 2023-24, Hari Ltd. was sued by a competitor for ₹13 lakhs for infringement of a trademark. Based on the advice of the company's legal counsel, Hari Ltd. provided for a sum of ₹8 lakhs in its financial statements for the year ended 31st March, 2024. On 26th May, 2024, the Court decided in favour of the party alleging infringement of the trademark and ordered Hari Ltd. to pay the aggrieved party a sum of ₹12 lakhs.
  4. Cashier of Hari Ltd. embezzled cash amounting to ₹3,00,000 during March, 2024. However the same comes to the notice of Company management during August, 2024.
  5. Cheques dated 31st March, 2024 collected in the month of April, 2024. All cheques are presented to the bank in the month of April, 2024 and are also realized in the same month in the normal course after deposit in the bank.
Answer / Solution:
  1. As per AS 4 'Contingencies and Events Occurring After the Balance Sheet Date', disclosure should be made in the report of the approving authority of those events occurring after the balance sheet date that represent material changes and commitments affecting the financial position of the enterprise; the investment of ₹40 lakhs in April, 2024 in the acquisition of another company should be disclosed in the report of the Board of Directors to enable users of financial statements to make proper evaluations and decisions.
  2. As per AS 4, adjustment to assets and liabilities are required for events occurring after the balance sheet date that provide additional information materially affecting the determination of the amounts relating to conditions existing at the Balance Sheet date. A debtor for ₹2,50,000 suffered heavy loss due to earthquake in the second week of March, 2024 which was not covered by insurance. This information with its implications was already known to the company. The fact that he became bankrupt in May, 2024 (after the balance sheet date) is only an additional information related to the existing condition on the balance sheet date. Accordingly, full provision for bad debts amounting ₹2,50,000 should be made, to cover the loss arising due to the insolvency of a debtor, in the final accounts for the year ended 31st March 2024.
  3. As per AS 4, adjustments to assets and liabilities are required for events occurring after the balance sheet date that provide additional information materially affecting the determination of the amounts relating to conditions existing at the balance sheet date. In the given case, since Hari Ltd. was sued by a competitor for infringement of a trademark during the year 2023-24 for which the provision was also made by it, the decision of the Court on 26th May, 2024, for payment of the penalty will constitute as an adjusting event because it is an event occurred before approval of the financial statements. Therefore, Hari Ltd. should adjust the provision upward by ₹4 lakhs to reflect the award decreed by the Court to be paid by them to its competitor.
  4. As the embezzlement of cash comes to the notice of company management only after approval of financial statements by board of directors of the company, then the treatment will be done as per the provisions of AS 5 "Net Profit or Loss for the Period, Prior Period Items and Changes in Accounting Policies" and the same will not be adjusted in the financial statements for the year ended 31st March, 2024. This being an extra-ordinary item should be disclosed in the statement of profit and loss as a part of loss for the year ending March, 2025, in a manner, that its impact on current profit or loss can be perceived.
  5. Collection of cheques after balance sheet date is not an adjusting event even if the cheques bear the date of 31st March. Recognition of cheques in hand is therefore not consistent with requirements of AS 4. Moreover, the collection of cheques after balance sheet date does not represent any material change or commitments affecting financial position of the enterprise and no disclosure of such collections in the Directors' Report is necessary.
Author’s Note: A common error is treating all five items uniformly as either "always adjust" or "always disclose only", rather than separately testing each event against AS 4's adjusting-versus-non-adjusting distinction on its own facts — in particular, confusing the Court's post-year-end decision (an adjusting event, since it relates to a liability that already existed and was already provided for at the balance sheet date) with the cashier's embezzlement discovered after the accounts were approved (a subsequent-period item under AS 5, not an adjustment to the year already closed).

AS 11 — The Effects of Changes in Foreign Exchange Rates

Every MTP/RTP/PYQ question that tests this chapter, collected in one place, with official answers and topic tags — so you can practise every question this topic has been examined with, without hunting through separate papers.

A note on accuracy (please read): This is the first edition of this book, assembled with AI assistance and reviewed as carefully as we could manage, but it has not been independently audited question-by-question. If you spot an error — a wrong figure, a wrong answer, anything that looks off — please email capranavpratiktulshyan@gmail.com with the question reference so it can be corrected in the next edition.
Scope of this book (13 questions): Covers 34 sittings: MTP Jan2025 Set1, MTP Jan2025 Set2, MTP Jan2026 Set1, MTP Jan2026 Set2, MTP May2023 Set1, MTP May2023 Set2, MTP May2024 Set1, MTP May2024 Set2, MTP May2025 Set1, MTP May2025 Set2, MTP May2026 Set1, MTP May2026 Set2, MTP Nov2023 Set1, MTP Nov2023 Set2, MTP Sep2024 Set1, MTP Sep2024 Set2, MTP Sep2025 Set1, MTP Sep2025 Set2, PYQ Jan2025, PYQ Jan2026, PYQ May2023, PYQ May2024, PYQ May2025, PYQ May2026, PYQ Nov2023, PYQ Sep2024, PYQ Sep2025, RTP Jan2025, RTP Jan2026, RTP May2024, RTP May2025, RTP May2026, RTP Sep2024, RTP Sep2025. MCQs on this chapter are deliberately not included here — practise those on the dedicated MCQ platform; this book is for descriptive/scenario practice with full worked answers.
How this book is organised: Two sections — I. Descriptive (pure AS 11) and II. Integrated (questions where AS 11 is one part of a larger question that also tests another standard). An empty Section II for a chapter is normal and expected, not a mistake — most multi-topic-looking questions are split so each topic gets its own clean entry, so genuinely combined questions are the rarer case. Each answer includes either a real Examiner's Comment (tan/orange box, quoted from ICAI's own published feedback, where one exists for that sitting) or an Author's Note (pale pink box, a likely pitfall identified by the author, not an official ICAI finding, and may not apply in every case) — see How to Read this Book.md for the full key to every colour and symbol used.

I. Descriptive & Scenario-Based Questions (pure AS 11)

Full descriptive/scenario questions where this chapter is the sole topic tested (after independent-question splitting).

MTP January 2026 Set 2 · Q1(a) · Marks: 5 · Approx Time: 9 minutes (approx.) · Topic 3.6: Forward contract premium amortised over the contract period; monetary item restated at each balance sheet date and on settlement Compulsory
Question:

Jared Limited purchased a machine for US$20,000 on 31st December 2024, payment due after four months. The company entered a four-month forward contract at ₹78.85 per US$; the spot rate on 31st December 2024 was ₹77.50 per US$. (i) How should Jared recognise the profit or loss on the forward contract for the year ended 31st March, 2025? (ii) Trade payables include an amount due to Sterling Limited of ₹9,75,000, recorded at US$1=₹75.00 on the purchase date. Exchange rate on balance-sheet date (31st March 2025): US$1=₹79.00. Payment made 1st May 2025 at US$1=₹78.30. Calculate the exchange difference as at 31st March 2025 and on settlement (1st May 2025), and explain the accounting treatment per AS 11.

Answer / Solution:

(i) Forward contract premium/loss: Forward rate 78.85 − Spot rate 77.50 = premium of ₹1.35/US$. Total loss on contract = 20,000 × 1.35 = ₹27,000. Contract period 4 months, of which 3 months fall in the year ended 31st March, 2025: loss to be recognised = 27,000 × 3/4 = ₹20,250 in the year ended 31st March, 2025 (the balance ₹6,750 recognised in the following year).

(ii) Exchange difference on trade payable to Sterling Ltd.: Initial recognition: US$13,000 (9,75,000/75) at ₹75. Balance sheet date rate ₹79 — exchange loss = 13,000 × (79−75) = ₹52,000, charged to the Statement of Profit & Loss for the year ended 31st March, 2025 (per AS 11, monetary item restatement differences are recognised as they arise). Settlement date rate ₹78.30 — exchange gain on settlement = 13,000 × (79−78.30) = ₹9,100, credited to the Statement of Profit & Loss for the year ended 31st March, 2026 (the year of settlement).

Author’s Note: Some examinees recognised the full forward-contract loss in the year of inception rather than time-apportioning it over the contract period falling in each accounting year, or netted the balance-sheet-date exchange loss against the later settlement-date gain instead of recognising each in its own accounting period.

MTP May 2023 Set 2 · Q6(a) [OR-alt 2] · Marks: 5 · Approx Time: 9 minutes (approx.) · Topic 3.2/3.4: Definition of monetary item and reporting of foreign currency monetary/non-monetary items at each balance sheet date
Question:

"Explain "monetary item" as per Accounting Standard 11. How are foreign currency monetary items to be recognized at each Balance Sheet date? Classify the following as monetary or non-monetary item: (i) Share Capital (ii) Trade Receivables (iii) Investments (iv) Fixed Assets.

Answer / Solution:

As per AS 11 'The Effects of Changes in Foreign Exchange Rates', Monetary items are money held and assets and liabilities to be received or paid in fixed or determinable amounts of money.

Foreign currency monetary items should be reported using the closing rate at each balance sheet date. However, in certain circumstances, the closing rate may not reflect with reasonable accuracy the amount in reporting currency that is likely to be realised from, or required to disburse, a foreign currency monetary item at the balance sheet date. In such circumstances, the relevant monetary item should be reported in the reporting currency at the amount which is likely to be realised from or required to disburse, such item at the balance sheet date.

ItemClassification
Share capitalNon-monetary
Trade receivablesMonetary
InvestmentsNon-monetary
Fixed assetsNon-monetary
Author’s Note: A common error is classifying Investments as a monetary item because they are eventually realised in cash, missing that AS 11 tests whether the amount to be received is fixed or determinable in monetary terms at the reporting date, not merely whether the asset will ultimately convert to cash.

MTP May 2023 Set 2 · Q6(d) · Marks: 5 · Approx Time: 9 minutes (approx.) · Topic 3.5: Exchange differences on restatement of a monetary trade receivable at the balance sheet date are recognised in the Statement of Profit and Loss
Question:

Trade receivables of PP Ltd. include amount receivable from Preksha Ltd., ₹20,00,150 recorded at the prevailing exchange rate on the date of sales, transaction recorded at US $1 = ₹73.40. The exchange rate on balance sheet date (31.03.2023) is US $1 = ₹73.60. Exchange rate on 1st April, 2022 is US $1 = ₹74.00. You are required to calculate the amount of exchange difference and also explain the accounting treatment needed in the above two cases as per AS 11 in the books of PP Ltd.

Answer / Solution:

Trade Receivables

Foreign Currency / Rate₹
Initial recognitionUS $27,250 (20,00,150/73.40) at 1 US $ = ₹73.4020,00,150
Rate on Balance sheet date1 US $ = ₹73.60
Exchange Difference Gain [US $27,250 × (73.60−73.40)]5,450

As per AS 11 "The Effects of Changes in Foreign Exchange Rates", exchange differences on trade receivables amounting ₹5,450 is required to be transferred to Profit and Loss A/c.

Treatment needed in this case: Credit Profit and loss account by ₹5,450.

Author’s Note: A common error is recognising the exchange gain on the monetary trade receivable directly in a reserve, rather than crediting the full amount to the Statement of Profit and Loss for the period as AS 11 requires for monetary-item restatement differences.

MTP May 2025 Set 1 · Q6(b) · Marks: 5 · Approx Time: 9 minutes (approx.) · Topic 3.2/3.5: Monetary vs non-monetary classification, and exchange difference on restatement of a monetary trade payable recognised in profit and loss
Question:

(i) Classify the following items into Monetary and Non-monetary: Share capital; Trade Payables; Cash balance; Property, plant and equipment.

(ii) Trade payables of CAT Ltd. include amount payable to JBB Ltd., ₹10,00,000 recorded at the prevailing exchange rate on the date of transaction, transaction recorded at US $1 = ₹80.00. The exchange rate on balance sheet date (31.03.2024) was US $1 = ₹85.00. You are required to calculate the amount of exchange difference and also explain the accounting treatment needed for this as per AS 11 in the books of CAT Ltd.

Answer / Solution:

(i) Share capital – Non-monetary; Trade Payables – Monetary; Cash balance – Monetary; Property, plant and equipment – Non-monetary.

(ii) Amount of Exchange difference and its Accounting Treatment

ParticularsForeign Currency / Rate₹
Trade payables — Initial recognitionUS $12,500 (₹10,00,000/80), 1 US $ = ₹8010,00,000
Rate on Balance sheet date1 US $ = ₹85
Exchange Difference lossUS $12,500 × ₹(85−80)62,500

Treatment: Debit Profit and Loss A/c by ₹62,500 and Credit Trade Payables. Thus, the Exchange Difference on trade payables amounting ₹62,500 is required to be transferred to Profit and Loss.

Author’s Note: A common error is classifying Property, Plant and Equipment as monetary because it has a determinable rupee value, confusing "monetary" (a fixed or determinable number of currency units) with simply "having a value"; a second common error is deferring or capitalising the exchange loss instead of recognising it in profit and loss for the period.

MTP May 2026 Set 1 · Q1(b) · Marks: 5 · Approx Time: 9 minutes (approx.) · Topic 3.4/3.5: Balance sheet valuation of monetary/non-monetary items and exchange gain/loss on settlement Compulsory
Question:

Karna Ltd., an Indian Company, has the following foreign currency transactions during the financial year 2025-26:
(i) On 1st July, 2025, imported goods from Try Ltd., a German based company, amounting to ₹30,96,000.
(ii) On 1st October, 2025, imported plant and machinery from Lucy Ltd., a German based company, for €18,500. The amount was paid on the date of import itself. (Ignore depreciation).
(iii) On 1st December, 2025, exported good on credit to Cream Ltd., a German based company, amounting to ₹50,40,000.
All the above transactions were recorded in the books of account at the prevailing exchange rate on the date of the transactions. Ignore taxes and duty on the above transactions.
Payment due from Cream Ltd. and payment due to Try Ltd. is outstanding as on 31st March, 2026.
Rate of exchange between reporting currency (₹) and foreign currency (€) on different dates are as under: On 1st July, 2025, 1€ = ₹86; On 1st October, 2025, 1€ = ₹88; On 1st December, 2025, 1€ = ₹84; On 31st March, 2026, 1€ = ₹90.
You are required, as per AS-11: (i) To show value at which above items will appear in Balance sheet as on 31st March, 2026; (ii) To calculate the amount of gain/loss on each of above transactions on account of exchange differences, if any. (5 Marks)

Answer / Solution:

As per AS 11 “The Effects of Changes in Foreign Exchange Rates”, Foreign currency monetary items should be reported using the closing rate. Non-monetary items which are carried in terms of historical cost denominated in a foreign currency should be reported using the exchange rate at the date of the transaction. Exchange differences arising on the settlement of monetary items or on reporting an enterprise's monetary items at rates different from those at which they were initially recorded during the period, or reported in previous financial statements, should be recognised as income or as expenses in the period in which they arise.

(i) Items given in the question will appear in the Balance Sheet at the following values:
Trade Payables (30,96,000/86 = 36,000 German Currency) x ₹90 = ₹32,40,000
Plant and Machinery 18,500 German Currency x ₹88 = ₹16,28,000
Trade Receivables (50,40,000/84 = 60,000 German Currency) x ₹90 = ₹54,00,000

(ii) Amount of gain/loss on each transaction on account of exchange difference:
Exchange loss on Transaction of import of goods from Try Ltd. = ₹(1,44,000) [36,000 German Currency x ₹4 (i.e. 90−86)]
Exchange gain on Transaction of export of goods to Cream Ltd = ₹3,60,000 [60,000 German Currency x ₹6 (i.e. 90−84)]

Author’s Note: A significant number of examinees used the transaction-date rate instead of the closing rate to restate the outstanding trade payable and trade receivable at year end under AS 11, and some failed to translate the plant and machinery paid for on the date of import at the transaction-date rate.

MTP November 2023 Set 2 · Q6(a) · Marks: 4 · Approx Time: 8 minutes (approx.) · Topic 4.3: Exchange differences on a foreign-currency borrowing treated as a borrowing cost only to the extent they approximate the interest-rate differential against an equivalent local-currency loan  +  Topic 3.5: Exchange difference on restatement of a foreign-currency monetary borrowing at the closing rate, with the AS 16-eligible portion carved out of the total exchange loss and the remainder recognised under AS 11
Question:

Omega Limited has borrowed a sum of US $10,00,000 at the beginning of Financial Year 2022-23 for its residential project at 4%. The interest is payable at the end of the Financial Year. At the time of availment of loan exchange rate was ₹56 per US $ and the rate as on 31st March, 2023 was ₹62 per US $. If Omega Limited had borrowed the loan in India in Indian Rupee equivalent, the pricing of loan would have been 10.50%.

You are required to compute Borrowing Cost and exchange difference for the year ending 31st March, 2023 as per applicable Accounting Standards.

Answer / Solution:
  1. Interest for the period 2022-23 = US $10 lakhs × 4% × ₹62 per US$ = ₹24.80 lakhs
  2. Increase in the liability towards the principal amount = US $10 lakhs × ₹(62 − 56) = ₹60 lakhs
  3. Interest that would have resulted if the loan was taken in Indian currency = US $10 lakhs × ₹56 × 10.5% = ₹58.80 lakhs
  4. Difference between interest on local currency borrowing and foreign currency borrowing = ₹58.80 lakhs − ₹24.80 lakhs = ₹34 lakhs.

Therefore, out of ₹60 lakhs increase in the liability towards principal amount, only ₹34 lakhs will be considered as the borrowing cost. Thus, total borrowing cost would be ₹58.80 lakhs being the aggregate of interest of ₹24.80 lakhs on foreign currency borrowings plus the exchange difference to the extent of difference between interest on local currency borrowing and interest on foreign currency borrowing of ₹34 lakhs.

Hence, ₹58.80 lakhs would be considered as the borrowing cost to be accounted for as per AS 16 and the remaining ₹26 lakhs (60 − 34) would be considered as the exchange difference to be accounted for as per AS 11.

Author’s Note: A common error is treating the entire ₹60 lakh increase in the rupee liability as either wholly a borrowing cost under AS 16 or wholly an exchange difference under AS 11, instead of splitting it at the interest-rate-differential figure of ₹34 lakhs.

PYQ May 2023 · Q1(b) · Marks: 5 · Approx Time: 9 minutes (approx.) · Topic 3.3/3.4: Measurement of a foreign-currency monetary payable at the transaction/settlement exchange rate, compared under two settlement options Compulsory
Question:

Trower Limited is an Indian importer. It imports goods from True View Limited situated at London. Trower Limited has a payable of £50,000 to True View Limited as on 31st March, 2023. True View Limited has given Trower Limited the following two options:

(i) Pay immediately with a cash discount of 1% on the payable.
(ii) Pay after 6 months with interest @ 5% p.a. on the payable.

The borrowing rate for Trower Limited in rupees is 15% p.a.

The following are the exchange rates:

Date₹/£
31st March, 202397
30th September, 202399

You are required to give your opinion to Trower Limited on which of the above two options to be chosen. (5 Marks)

Answer / Solution:

Option (i) Pay immediately with Cash discount of 1% on the payable

₹
Total amount payable as on 31.3.2023 (50,000 × ₹97)48,50,000
Less: Cash discount(48,500)
(subtotal)48,01,500
Add: Borrowing cost @ 15% p.a. for 6 months3,60,112.50
If payment made immediate51,61,612.50

Option (ii) Pay after 6 months with interest @ 5% p.a. on the payable

₹
Total amount payable as on 31.3.2023 (50,000 × ₹99)49,50,000
Interest for 6 months @ 5%1,23,750
If payment made after 6 months50,73,750

Thus, Option (ii) is beneficial to Trower Limited as the Rupee outflow will be lower by ₹(51,61,612 − 50,73,750) = ₹87,862 in option (ii).

Note: the source presents an alternative worked route to the identical figures – Option (i): 50,000 less cash discount (500) = 49,500 units × ₹97 = 48,01,500, plus borrowing cost 3,60,112.50 = ₹51,61,612.50. Option (ii): 50,000 + interest for 6 months @5% (50,000×5/100×6/12=1,250) = 51,250 units × ₹99 = ₹50,73,750. Same conclusion.

Author’s Note: A significant number of examinees omitted the notional borrowing cost of paying immediately (interest on funds foregone at the company's own 15% p.a. rate) when comparing the two options, effectively comparing only the cash discount against the deferred interest without placing both options on a common date. This led many to conclude that immediate payment was cheaper, missing that Trower Limited's own high borrowing rate outweighs the 1% cash discount once time value is properly reflected.

PYQ May 2026 · Q6(a) [OR-alt 2] · Marks: 4 · Approx Time: 8 minutes (approx.) · Topic 3.13: Para 46A option - exchange difference on foreign-currency loan capitalised to a depreciable asset, or accumulated in FCMITD if not asset-linked
Question:

ABC Ltd, borrowed 10,000 US $ in foreign currency on 1st April, 2025 at 6% p.a. annual interest and acquired a depreciable asset. Exchange rates: 01-04-2025 ₹85.00/US$; 31-03-2026 ₹90.00/US$. (Assume interest accrued on 31st March, 2026 is paid on the same date.)

You are required to: (i) Pass the journal entries in case the option under Para 46A of AS 11 is availed by the company. (ii) Explain the difference in treatment of exchange difference if Para 46A of AS 11 is not availed. (iii) Would your answer be different regarding treatment of exchange difference if the loan was taken to finance the operations of the entity, not to procure a depreciable asset, and option under Para 46A of AS 11 is availed by the company? (4 Marks)

Answer / Solution:

(i) Option under Para 46A availed – Journal Entries in the Books of ABC Ltd.:

DateParticulars₹ Dr.₹ Cr.
2025 Apr. 01Bank Account (10,000×85) Dr.
  To Foreign Loan Account		8,50,0008,50,000
2026 Mar 31Finance Cost (USD 10,000×6%×₹90) Dr.
  To Bank Account		54,00054,000
2026 Mar 31Foreign Exchange Difference Account Dr.
  To Foreign Loan Account [10,000×(90−85)]		50,00050,000
2026 Mar 31Property, Plant and Equipment Dr.
  To Foreign Exchange Difference Account		50,00050,000

Since the option under Para 46A is availed, the Exchange Loss of ₹50,000 is capitalized in the cost of PPE, indirectly recognized in the P&L by way of increased depreciation over the remaining useful life of the asset.

(ii) If Para 46A is NOT availed: the Exchange Loss of ₹50,000 is recognised as an expense in the Statement of Profit and Loss for the year ending 31 March 2026 instead.

(iii) If the loan financed operations (not a depreciable asset) and Para 46A is availed: the Exchange Loss of ₹50,000 is accumulated in the FCMITD A/c, subsequently spread over and debited to P&L over the tenure of the loan (since there is no qualifying asset to capitalise it against).

Author’s Note: Many examinees applied the same asset-capitalisation treatment to part (iii) as part (i), not recognising that Para 46A's asset-linked capitalisation route is only available when the borrowing financed a depreciable asset; where it instead financed operations, the FCMITD accumulation-and-amortisation route applies.

PYQ November 2023 · Q1(b) · Marks: 5 · Approx Time: 9 minutes (approx.) · Topic 3.3/3.4/3.5: Trade payable/receivable restated at closing rate vs. a non-monetary asset (plant, settled same day) held at transaction-date rate; exchange gain/loss recognised on each outstanding monetary item Compulsory
Question:

Karna Ltd., an Indian Company, has the following foreign currency transactions during the financial year 2022-23:

(i) On 1st July, 2022, imported goods from Try Ltd., a German based company, amounting to ₹30,96,000.

(ii) On 1st October, 2022, imported plant and machinery from Lucy Ltd., a German based company, for €18,500. The amount was paid on the date of import itself. (Ignore depreciation).

(iii) On 1st December, 2022, exported goods on credit to Cream Ltd., a German based company, amounting to ₹50,40,000.

All the above transactions were recorded in the books of account at the prevailing exchange rate on the date of the transactions. Ignore taxes and duty on the above transactions.

Payment due from Cream Ltd. and payment due to Try Ltd. is outstanding as on 31st March, 2023.

Rate of exchange between reporting currency (₹) and foreign currency (€) on different dates are as under:

Date₹/€
1st July, 202286
1st October, 202288
1st December, 202284
31st March, 202390

You are required, as per AS-11: (i) To show value at which above items will appear in Balance sheet as on 31st March, 2023; (ii) To calculate the amount of gain/loss on each of above transactions on account of exchange differences, if any. (5 Marks)

Answer / Solution:

As per AS 11 “The Effects of Changes in Foreign Exchange Rates”, Foreign currency monetary items should be reported using the closing rate. Non-monetary items which are carried in terms of historical cost denominated in a foreign currency should be reported using the exchange rate at the date of the transaction. Exchange differences arising on the settlement of monetary items or on reporting an enterprise’s monetary items at rates different from those at which they were initially recorded during the period, or reported in previous financial statements, should be recognised as income or as expenses in the period in which they arise.

(i) Items given in the question will appear in the Balance Sheet at the following values:

Trade Payables (30,96,000/86 = 36,000 German Currency) × ₹90 = ₹32,40,000
Plant and Machinery 18,500 German Currency × ₹88 = ₹16,28,000
Trade Receivables (50,40,000/84 = 60,000 German Currency) × ₹90 = ₹54,00,000

(ii) Amount of gain/loss on each transaction on account of exchange difference:

Exchange loss on Transaction of import of goods from Try Ltd. = ₹(1,44,000) [36,000 German Currency × ₹4 (i.e. 90−86)]

Exchange gain on Transaction of export of goods to Cream Ltd = ₹3,60,000 [60,000 German Currency × ₹6 (i.e. 90−84)]

Author’s Note: Many examinees correctly applied the closing rate to the trade receivable and trade payable but incorrectly restated the plant and machinery – a non-monetary item already settled in cash on the date of import – to the 31st March closing rate as well, not recognising that AS 11 requires non-monetary items carried at historical cost to remain at the transaction-date rate. Some examinees also computed the exchange gain/loss by comparing the transaction-date rupee value to the closing-rate rupee value directly rather than isolating the per-unit rate movement on the outstanding foreign-currency amount, occasionally producing the correct final figure by an incorrect method.

RTP January 2025 · Q9 · Marks: Not stated in source · Approx Time: 10–20 minutes (approx.) · Topic 3.4: Monetary items restated at the closing rate at each balance sheet date; the resulting exchange difference goes to profit and loss, never adjusted against the non-monetary cost already recorded
Question:

Bansal Company Ltd. imported raw material worth US Dollars 12,000 on 15th January, 2024 when the exchange rate was ₹68 per US Dollar. The payment for the transaction was made on 5th May, 2024 when exchange rate was ₹64 per US Dollar. At the year end, 31st March, 2024, the rate of exchange was ₹65 per US Dollar. The accountant of the company passed entry on 31st March, 2024 adjusting the cost of raw material consumed for the difference between ₹64 and ₹68 per US Dollar.

Discuss whether this treatment is justified as per the provisions of AS-11 (Revised).

Answer / Solution:

As per AS 11, "The Effects of Changes in Foreign Exchange Rates", initial recognition of a foreign currency transaction is done in the reporting currency by applying the exchange rate at the date of the transaction. Accordingly, on 15th January, 2024, the raw material purchased and its creditors will be recorded at US dollar 12,000 × ₹68 = ₹8,16,000.

Also, on balance sheet date such transaction is reported at closing rate of exchange, hence it will be valued at the closing rate i.e. ₹65 per US dollar (USD 12,000 × ₹65 = ₹7,80,000) at 31st March, 2024, irrespective of the payment made for the same subsequently at a lower rate in the next financial year.

The difference of ₹3 (65 − 68) per US dollar i.e. ₹36,000 (USD 12,000 × ₹3) will be shown as an exchange gain in the profit and loss account for the year ended 31st March, 2024 and will not be adjusted against the cost of raw materials.

In the subsequent year on settlement date, the company would recognize or provide in the Profit and Loss account an exchange gain of ₹1 per US dollar, i.e. the difference from balance sheet date to the date of settlement between ₹65 and ₹64 per US dollar i.e. ₹12,000.

Hence, the accounting treatment adopted by the Accountant of the company is incorrect i.e. it is not in accordance with the provisions of AS 11.

Author’s Note: A common error is adjusting the cost of raw material consumed for the exchange difference between the transaction-date and settlement-date rates, missing that AS 11 requires monetary items to be restated at the closing rate at each balance sheet date, with the resulting exchange difference recognised in the Statement of Profit and Loss, not adjusted against the non-monetary cost of raw material already recorded.

RTP May 2025 · Q12 · Marks: Not stated in source · Approx Time: 10–20 minutes (approx.) · Topic 3.5: Para 46A option to capitalise exchange differences on long-term foreign-currency monetary items into a depreciable asset's cost
Question:

Legal Ltd. is engaged in the manufacturing of rubber. For its plant, it required machineries of latest technology. It usually resorts to Long Term Foreign Currency Borrowings for its fund requirements. On 1st April, 2023, it borrowed US $1 million from International Funding Agency, USA when the exchange rate was 1$ = ₹63. The funds were used for acquiring machineries, on the same date, to be used in three different plants. The useful life of the machineries is 10 years and their residual value is ₹30,00,000.

Earlier also the company used to purchase machineries out of foreign borrowings. The exchange differences arising on such borrowings were charged to profit and loss account and were not capitalized, even though the company had an option to capitalize it as per notified AS 11.

Now for this new purchase of machinery, Legal Ltd. is interested to avail the option of capitalizing the same to the cost of asset. Exchange rate on 31st March, 2024 is 1 US$ = ₹62. Assume that on 31st March, 2024, Legal Ltd. is not having any old long term foreign currency borrowings except for the amount borrowed for machinery purchased on 1st April, 2023.

Comment whether Legal Ltd. can capitalize the exchange difference to the cost of asset on 31st March, 2024. If yes, then calculate the depreciation amount on machineries as on 31st March, 2024.

Answer / Solution:

As per paragraph 46A of AS 11, in respect of accounting periods commencing on or after 1st April, 2011, an enterprise (whether or not it had earlier exercised the option under paragraph 46, the option being irrevocable and applied to all such foreign currency monetary items) may add to or deduct from the cost of a depreciable capital asset the exchange differences arising on reporting long-term foreign currency monetary items relating to its acquisition, and depreciate this over the balance life of the asset.

Accordingly, though Legal Ltd. had not earlier exercised the option, it can still avail the option to capitalize the exchange difference to the cost of machinery by virtue of para 46A of AS 11. Further, since Legal Ltd. has no other long term foreign currency borrowings, it is not required to apply the capitalization option to any earlier borrowing.

Exchange difference to be capitalized and depreciation amount₹
Cost of the asset in $ (1 million); Exchange rate on 1st April, 2023 (₹63 = $1)—
Cost of the asset in ₹ (1 million × ₹63)63 million
Less: Exchange difference as on 31st March, 2024 – (63−62) × $1 million (Gain)(1 million)
Revised cost of asset62 million
Less: Depreciation for 2023-2024 – (62 million − 3 million) / 10 years(5.90 million)
Carrying amount as on 31st March, 202456.10 million
Author’s Note: A common error is assuming the para 46A option is unavailable to Legal Ltd. because it never exercised it in earlier years, missing that the option is available for this new borrowing on its own facts, since Legal Ltd. has no other long-term foreign-currency borrowings that would otherwise force the irrevocable-election issue.

RTP September 2024 · Q9 · Marks: Not stated in source · Approx Time: 10–20 minutes (approx.) · Topic 3.5: Exchange differences on restatement/repayment of a long-term foreign-currency loan financing PPE, capitalised into the asset's carrying amount
Question:

Alfa Ltd. purchased an item of property, plant and equipment for US $ 50 lakh on 01.04.2023 and the same was fully financed by the foreign currency loan [i.e. US $] repayment in five equal instalments annually. (Exchange rate at the time of purchase was 1 US $ = ₹60]. As on 31.03.2024 the first instalment was paid when 1 US $ fetched ₹62.00. The entire loss on exchange was included in cost of goods sold. Alfa Ltd. normally provides depreciation on an item of property, plant and equipment at 20% on WDV basis and exercised the option to adjust the cost of asset for exchange difference arising out of loan restatement and payment. Calculate the amount of exchange loss and its treatment and depreciation.

Answer / Solution:

Exchange differences arising on restatement or repayment of liabilities incurred for the purpose of acquiring an item of property, plant and equipment should be adjusted in the carrying amount of the respective item of property, plant and equipment as Alfa Ltd. has exercised the option and it is long term foreign currency monetary item.

Thus, the entire exchange loss due to variation of ₹20 lakh on 31.03.2023 on payment of US $ 10 lakh, should be added to the carrying amount of an item of property, plant and equipment and not to the cost of goods sold. Further, depreciation on the unamortized depreciable amount should also be provided.

Calculation of Exchange loss:

Foreign currency loan (in ₹) = (50 lakh $ × ₹60) = ₹3,000 lakh

Exchange loss on outstanding loan on 31.03.2024 = ₹40 lakh US $ × (62.00−60.00) = ₹80 lakh.

So, ₹80 lakh should also be added to cost of an item of property, plant and equipment with corresponding credit to outstanding loan in addition to ₹20 lakh on account of exchange loss on payment of instalment. The total cost of an item of property, plant and equipment to be increased by ₹100 lakh.

Total depreciation to be provided for the year 2023-2024 = 20% of (₹3,000 lakh + 100 lakh) = ₹620 lakh.

Author’s Note: A common error is leaving the exchange loss in the cost of goods sold (as the company's own initial treatment had done) rather than capitalising it into the carrying amount of the property, plant and equipment once the long-term-monetary-item option has been exercised, and consequently missing the resulting increase in the depreciation charge.

AS 9 — Revenue Recognition

Every MTP/RTP/PYQ question that tests this chapter, collected in one place, with official answers and topic tags — so you can practise every question this topic has been examined with, without hunting through separate papers.

A note on accuracy (please read): This is the first edition of this book, assembled with AI assistance and reviewed as carefully as we could manage, but it has not been independently audited question-by-question. If you spot an error — a wrong figure, a wrong answer, anything that looks off — please email capranavpratiktulshyan@gmail.com with the question reference so it can be corrected in the next edition.
Scope of this book (20 questions): Covers 34 sittings: MTP Jan2025 Set1, MTP Jan2025 Set2, MTP Jan2026 Set1, MTP Jan2026 Set2, MTP May2023 Set1, MTP May2023 Set2, MTP May2024 Set1, MTP May2024 Set2, MTP May2025 Set1, MTP May2025 Set2, MTP May2026 Set1, MTP May2026 Set2, MTP Nov2023 Set1, MTP Nov2023 Set2, MTP Sep2024 Set1, MTP Sep2024 Set2, MTP Sep2025 Set1, MTP Sep2025 Set2, PYQ Jan2025, PYQ Jan2026, PYQ May2023, PYQ May2024, PYQ May2025, PYQ May2026, PYQ Nov2023, PYQ Sep2024, PYQ Sep2025, RTP Jan2025, RTP Jan2026, RTP May2024, RTP May2025, RTP May2026, RTP Sep2024, RTP Sep2025. MCQs on this chapter are deliberately not included here — practise those on the dedicated MCQ platform; this book is for descriptive/scenario practice with full worked answers.
How this book is organised: Two sections — I. Descriptive (pure AS 9) and II. Integrated (questions where AS 9 is one part of a larger question that also tests another standard). An empty Section II for a chapter is normal and expected, not a mistake — most multi-topic-looking questions are split so each topic gets its own clean entry, so genuinely combined questions are the rarer case. Each answer includes either a real Examiner's Comment (tan/orange box, quoted from ICAI's own published feedback, where one exists for that sitting) or an Author's Note (pale pink box, a likely pitfall identified by the author, not an official ICAI finding, and may not apply in every case) — see How to Read this Book.md for the full key to every colour and symbol used.

I. Descriptive & Scenario-Based Questions (pure AS 9)

Full descriptive/scenario questions where this chapter is the sole topic tested (after independent-question splitting).

MTP January 2025 Set 1 · Q1(c) · Marks: 5 · Approx Time: 9 minutes (approx.) · Topic 2.8: Conditions for recognising revenue on sale of goods - delayed delivery at buyer's request still recognised if buyer accepts billing and goods are ready Compulsory
Question:

Indicate in each case whether revenue can be recognized and when it will be recognized as per AS-9. (1) Trade discount and volume rebate received. (2) Where goods are sold to distributors or others for resale. (3) Where seller concurrently agrees to repurchase the same goods at a later date. (4) Insurance agency commission for rendering services. (5) On 11-03-2024 cloths worth ₹50,000 were sold to X mart, but due to refurbishing of their showroom being underway, on their request, clothes were delivered on 12-04-2024.

Answer / Solution:
  1. Trade discounts and volume rebates received are not encompassed within the definition of revenue, since they represent a reduction of cost. Trade discounts and volume rebates given should be deducted in determining revenue.
  2. When goods are sold to distributor or others, revenue from such sales can generally be recognized if significant risks of ownership have passed; however, in some situations the buyer may in substance be an agent and in such cases the sale should be treated as a consignment sale.
  3. For transactions, where seller concurrently agrees to repurchase the same goods at a later date that are in substance a financing agreement, the resulting cash inflow is not revenue as defined and should not be recognized as revenue.
  4. Insurance agency commissions should be recognized on the effective commencement or renewal dates of the related policies.
  5. On 11.03.2024, if X mart takes title and accepts billing for the goods then it is implied that the sale is complete and all risk and reward on ownership has been transferred to the buyers. Revenue should be recognized for the year ended 31st March, 2024 notwithstanding that physical delivery has not been completed so long as there is every expectation that delivery will be made and items were ready for delivery to the buyer at the time.
Author’s Note: A common error is recognising revenue on the physical delivery date rather than the date the buyer accepted billing with goods ready for delivery, or failing to identify a sale-with-repurchase arrangement as a financing transaction rather than a sale.

MTP January 2025 Set 2 · Q3(a) · Marks: 4 · Approx Time: 8 minutes (approx.) · Topic 2.8: Revenue recognition timing across five distinct transaction types - approval-basis sale, delayed delivery, sale-repurchase, interest/royalty, consignment
Question:

Given the following information of Rainbow Ltd., you are required to advise, with valid reasons, the amount to be recognized as revenue under the provisions of AS-9: (i) On 15th November, goods worth ₹5,00,000 were sold on approval basis. The period of approval was 4 months after which they were considered sold. Buyer sent approval for 75% goods sold upto 31st January and no approval or disapproval received for the remaining goods till 31st March. (ii) On 31st March, goods worth ₹2,40,000 were sold to Bright Ltd. but due to refurnishing of their show-room being underway, on their request, goods were delivered on 10th April. (iii) Rainbow Ltd. supplied goods worth ₹6,00,000 to Shyam Ltd. and concurrently agrees to re-purchase the same goods on 14th April. (iv) Dew Ltd, used certain assets of Rainbow Ltd. Rainbow Ltd. received ₹7.5 lakhs and ₹12 as interest and royalties respectively from Dew Ltd. during the year 2023-24. (v) On 25th December, goods of ₹4,00,000 were sent on consignment basis of which 40% of the goods unsold are lying with the consignee at the year-end on 31st March.

Answer / Solution:
  1. As per AS 9 "Revenue Recognition", in case of goods sold on approval basis, revenue should not be recognized until the goods have been formally accepted by the buyer or the buyer has done an act adopting the transaction or the time period for rejection has elapsed or where no time has been fixed, a reasonable time has elapsed. Therefore, revenue should be recognized for the total sales amounting ₹5,00,000 as the time period for rejecting the goods had expired.
  2. The sale is complete but delivery has been postponed at buyer's request. The entity should recognize the entire sale of ₹2,40,000 for the year ended 31st March.
  3. Sale/repurchase agreements i.e. where seller concurrently agrees to repurchase the same goods at a later date, such transactions that are in substance a financing agreement, the resulting cash inflow is not revenue as defined and should not be recognized as revenue. Hence no revenue to be recognized in the given case.
  4. Revenue arising from the use by others of enterprise resources yielding interest and royalty should be recognized when no significant uncertainty as to measurability or collectability exists. The interest should be recognized on time proportion basis taking into account the amount outstanding and rate applicable. The royalty should be recognized on accrual basis in accordance with the terms of relevant agreement.
  5. 40% goods lying unsold with consignee should be treated as closing inventory and sales should be recognized for ₹2,40,000 (60% of ₹4,00,000). In case of consignment sale revenue should not be recognized until the goods are sold to a third party.
Author’s Note: A common error is treating goods sold on approval as sold immediately at the point of delivery instead of waiting for buyer acceptance or expiry of the approval period, and separately, recognising revenue on a sale-and-repurchase arrangement instead of identifying it as a financing transaction outside the scope of AS 9 revenue.

MTP January 2026 Set 2 · Q6(a) [OR-alt 1] · Marks: 4 · Approx Time: 8 minutes (approx.) · Topic 1.6: Revenue recognition timing across five distinct transaction types
Question:

Indicate in each case whether revenue can be recognized and when, as per AS-9: (i) Delivery is delayed at buyer's request but buyer takes title and accepts billing. (ii) Instalment Sales. (iii) Trade discounts and volume rebates. (iv) Insurance agency commission for rendering services. (v) Advertising commission.

Answer / Solution:

(i) Revenue is recognised notwithstanding the delayed physical delivery, so long as delivery is expected and the goods are on hand, identified, and ready for delivery at the time of sale recognition (not merely an intention to acquire/manufacture in time).

(ii) When consideration is receivable in instalments, revenue attributable to the sale price (excluding interest) is recognised at the date of sale; the interest element is recognised as revenue proportionately to the unpaid balance.

(iii) Trade discounts and volume rebates received are not revenue (they reduce cost); those given are deducted in determining revenue.

(iv) Insurance agency commissions are recognised on the effective commencement or renewal dates of the related policies.

(v) Advertising commission is recognised when the service is completed — media commission when the advertisement appears before the public (with the agency's intimation received); production commission when the project is completed.

Author’s Note: Some examinees deferred revenue on the delayed-delivery sale entirely, missing that the goods being on-hand and ready is what matters, not the physical transfer date itself.

MTP May 2024 Set 1 · Q3(a) · Marks: 4 · Approx Time: 8 minutes (approx.) · Topic 2.7: Income from other sources - interest on a time-proportion basis, royalties on an accrual basis per the agreement
Question:

Y Ltd. used certain resources of X Ltd. In return X Ltd. received ₹10 lakhs and ₹15 lakhs as interest and royalties respectively from Y Ltd. during the year 2022-23. You are required to state whether and on what basis these revenues can be recognized by X Ltd.

Answer / Solution:

As per AS 9 on Revenue Recognition, revenue arising from the use by others of enterprise resources yielding interest and royalties should only be recognized when no significant uncertainty as to measurability or collectability exists. These revenues are recognized on the following bases: (i) Interest: on a time proportion basis taking into account the amount outstanding and the rate applicable. Therefore X Ltd. should recognize interest revenue of ₹10 Lakhs. (ii) Royalties: on an accrual basis in accordance with the terms of the relevant agreement. X Ltd. therefore should recognize royalty revenue of ₹15 Lakhs.

Author’s Note: A common error is applying the same recognition basis to both interest and royalty income, when AS 9 prescribes two distinct bases — time-proportion for interest, accrual per the agreement's terms for royalties.

MTP September 2025 Set 1 · Q6(b) · Marks: 5 · Approx Time: 9 minutes (approx.) · Topic 2.8: Five specific-scenario tests for revenue recognition timing
Question:

Indicate in each case whether revenue can be recognized and when it will be recognized as per AS-9.

  1. Trade discount and volume rebate received.
  2. Where goods are sold to distributors or others for resale.
  3. Where seller concurrently agrees to repurchase the same goods at a later date.
  4. Insurance agency commission for rendering services.
  5. On 11-03-2024 cloths worth ₹50,000 were sold to X mart, but due to refurbishing of their showroom being underway, on their request, clothes were delivered on 12-04-2024.
Answer / Solution:
  1. Trade discounts and volume rebates received are not encompassed within the definition of revenue, since they represent a reduction of cost. Trade discounts and volume rebates given should be deducted in determining revenue.
  2. When goods are sold to distributor or others, revenue from such sales can generally be recognized if significant risks of ownership have passed; however, in some situations the buyer may in substance be an agent and in such cases the sale should be treated as a consignment sale.
  3. For transactions, where seller concurrently agrees to repurchase the same goods at a later date that are in substance a financing agreement, the resulting cash inflow is not revenue as defined and should not be recognized as revenue.
  4. Insurance agency commissions should be recognized on the effective commencement or renewal dates of the related policies.
  5. On 11.03.2024, if X mart takes title and accepts billing for the goods then it is implied that the sale is complete and all risk and reward on ownership has been transferred to the buyers. Revenue should be recognized for year ended 31st March, 2024 notwithstanding that physical delivery has not been completed so long as there is every expectation that delivery will be made and items were ready for delivery to the buyer at the time.
Author’s Note: A common error here is treating a sale to a distributor for resale, or a delayed-delivery sale made at the buyer's own request, as ineligible for revenue recognition, without checking whether the substantive risk-and-reward transfer conditions have actually been met.

PYQ September 2025 · Q1(c-i) · Marks: 1 · Approx Time: 2 minutes (approx.) · Topic 1.4: Trade discounts deducted from revenue, regardless of the reason for the discount Compulsory
Question:

AB Limited purchased goods on credit from XY Limited for ₹150 lakhs for export. The export order was cancelled; AB Limited decided to sell the same goods locally with a price discount. XY Limited agreed to a 12% price discount requested by AB Limited. XY's chief accountant wants to adjust the sales figure to the extent of the discount. Discuss whether this treatment is as per the relevant Accounting Standard.

Answer / Solution:

Correct. Per AS 9, trade discounts given should be deducted in determining revenue. The 12% discount should be deducted from the turnover figure for revenue recognition purposes — XY Limited's adjustment of the sales figure to the extent of the discount is correct as per AS 9.

Examiner’s Comment: The responses of examinees to the requirements of AS 9 "Revenue Recognition" were unsatisfactory. Many were unable to correctly comment on the treatment of the four independent situations provided in the question, indicating inadequate conceptual clarity on timing and basis of revenue recognition.

PYQ September 2025 · Q1(c-ii) · Marks: 1 · Approx Time: 2 minutes (approx.) · Topic 1.5: Dividend income recognised only when the right to receive payment is established (declaration, not mere proposal) Compulsory
Question:

XY Limited recognized dividend income of ₹10 lakhs on accrual basis on securities of face value ₹100 lakhs held at 31st March 2025. The dividend (10%) was declared on 30th April 2025, having been proposed on 30th March 2025. Comment.

Answer / Solution:

Incorrect. Dividends from investments in securities are not recognised in the Statement of Profit and Loss until the right to receive payment is established. Here, the dividend is proposed 30th March 2025 but declared only 30th April 2025 — the right to receive payment is established only on 30th April 2025. Recognising ₹10 lakhs on accrual basis at 31st March 2025 is not correct as per AS 9.

Examiner’s Comment: The responses of examinees to the requirements of AS 9 "Revenue Recognition" were unsatisfactory. Many were unable to correctly comment on the treatment of the four independent situations provided in the question, indicating inadequate conceptual clarity on timing and basis of revenue recognition.

PYQ September 2025 · Q1(c-iii) · Marks: 1 · Approx Time: 2 minutes (approx.) · Topic 1.6: Sale on approval - revenue recognised on acceptance or expiry of the approval period, not at dispatch Compulsory
Question:

XY Limited sold goods of ₹1,50,000 on approval basis on 15th December 2024; approval period 3 months, after which goods are considered sold. Buyer approved 60% of goods by 31st January 2025; no approval/disapproval received for the remainder by 31st March 2025. The accountant recognised ₹1,50,000 as revenue on 15th December, 2024. Comment.

Answer / Solution:

Incorrect as recognised. For goods sold on approval, revenue should not be recognised until formal acceptance, an act adopting the transaction, or expiry of the rejection period. Revenue for ₹90,000 (60%) should be recognised on 31st January, 2025 (date of approval); the remaining ₹60,000 should be recognised on 15th March, 2025, when the 3-month approval period lapsed without response (deemed acceptance) — not the full ₹1,50,000 on 15th December, 2024 as the accountant did.

Examiner’s Comment: The responses of examinees to the requirements of AS 9 "Revenue Recognition" were unsatisfactory. Many were unable to correctly comment on the treatment of the four independent situations provided in the question, indicating inadequate conceptual clarity on timing and basis of revenue recognition.

PYQ September 2025 · Q1(c-iv) · Marks: 1 · Approx Time: 2 minutes (approx.) · Topic 1.7: Consignment sales - revenue recognised only when the consignee sells to a third party Compulsory
Question:

In 2024-2025, XY Limited supplied goods worth ₹80,000 on consignment basis to ABC (a retail outlet). ABC sold goods worth ₹60,000 during the year; the rest remains in its store. XY recognizes ₹60,000 revenue in its books for 2024-2025. Comment.

Answer / Solution:

Correct. Unsold consignment goods (₹20,000) remain XY Limited's closing inventory; revenue on a consignment sale is recognised only when the goods are sold to a third party by the consignee. XY's recognition of ₹60,000 revenue is correct as per AS 9.

RTP January 2025 · Q7 · Marks: Not stated in source · Approx Time: 10–20 minutes (approx.) · Topic 2.8: Sale and repurchase arrangement with a pre-determined, holding-cost-covering resale price is accounted for as financing, not a sale
Question:

Mithya Ltd. entered into agreement with Satya Ltd. for sale of goods costing ₹8 lakh at a profit of 20% on cost. The sale transaction took place on 1st February, 2024. On the same day, Satya Ltd. entered into another agreement with Mithya Ltd. to resell the same goods at ₹10.80 lakh on 1st August, 2024. State the treatment of this transaction in the financial statements of Mithya Ltd. as on 31.03.2024. The predetermined re-selling price covers the holding cost of Satya Ltd. Give the Journal Entries as on 31.03.2024 in the books of Mithya Ltd.

Answer / Solution:

In the given case, Mithya Ltd. concurrently agreed to repurchase the same goods from Satya Ltd. on 1st February, 2024. Also the re-selling price is pre-determined and covers purchasing and holding costs of Satya Ltd. Hence, the transaction between Mithya Ltd. and Satya Ltd. on 1st February, 2024 should be accounted for as financing rather than sale. The resulting cash flow of ₹9.60 lakh received by Mithya Ltd. cannot be considered as revenue as per AS 9 "Revenue Recognition".

Journal Entries in the books of Mithya Ltd. (₹ in lakh)

DateParticularsDr.Cr.
1.2.2024Bank Account Dr. To Advance from Satya Ltd. (Being advance received from Satya Ltd. amounting [₹8 lakh + 20% of ₹8 lakh = 9.60 lakh] under sale and re-purchase agreement)9.609.60
31.3.2024Financing Charges Account Dr. To Satya Ltd. (Financing charges for 2 months [(10.80 − 9.60) × 2/6])0.400.40
31.3.2024Profit and Loss Account Dr. To Financing Charges Account (Being amount of finance charges transferred to P&L Account)0.400.40

Note: the balance of Satya Ltd.'s account will be disclosed as an advance under the heading liabilities in the balance sheet of Mithya Ltd. as on 31st March, 2024.

Author’s Note: A common error is recognising the ₹9.60 lakh received by Mithya Ltd. as sale revenue, missing that a concurrent agreement to repurchase the same goods at a pre-determined price covering the buyer's holding cost converts the arrangement into a financing transaction under AS 9, not a genuine sale.

RTP January 2026 · Q8 · Marks: Not stated in source · Approx Time: 10–20 minutes (approx.) · Topic 1.2: Property sale by a real-estate dealer is ordinary-activity revenue, not extraordinary, even at unusual scale
Question:

Class Ltd., a real-estate developer, purchased land for ₹225 crore in FY2025 intending a residential complex, then sold it a few months later for ₹360 crore due to a strategic reallocation and favourable market conditions. All legal formalities completed. Advise on revenue recognition for the year ended 31st March, 2025.

Answer / Solution:

AS 9 recognises revenue when earned with reasonable certainty of collection, arising from the enterprise's ordinary activities. Class Ltd. is in the business of buying and selling properties; the land forms part of its inventory. The ₹360 crore sale is therefore a transaction arising from ordinary activities, and revenue is recognised when the sale is completed and collection is reasonably certain.

Per AS 5, this is not an extraordinary item, since it arises in the ordinary course of business — though given its size, its nature and amount should be separately disclosed if relevant to explaining the enterprise's performance. The ₹360 crore is recognised as revenue in the year the sale is completed.

Author’s Note: Some examinees treated the large, unusual sale as an extraordinary item given its size and the company's stated change in strategy, missing that dealing in land is Class Ltd.'s core ordinary business, so scale alone does not make a transaction extraordinary.

RTP May 2024 · Q16(i) · Marks: Not stated in source · Approx Time: 10–20 minutes (approx.) · Topic 2.8: Revenue recognised where the sale is complete and only physical delivery is postponed at the buyer's own request, buyer having accepted billing
Question:

Goods of ₹2,00,000 sold to Den Ltd. on 20-03-2023 but at the request of the buyer these were delivered on 10-04-2023. You are required to advise the accountant of BS Products Ltd., with valid reasons, the amount to be recognized as revenue in this case in the context of AS 9.

Answer / Solution:

The sale is complete, but delivery has been postponed at buyer's request. BS Products Ltd. should recognize the entire sale of ₹2,00,000 for the year ended 31st March, 2023.

Author’s Note: A common error here is deferring revenue recognition to the actual delivery date, missing that the sale itself was already complete and delivery was postponed purely at the buyer's own request.
