RTP May 2024 · Q16(ii) · Marks: Not stated in source · Approx Time: 10–20 minutes (approx.) · Topic 2.8: Consignment sale - revenue recognised only on sale by the consignee to a third party; unsold consignment goods remain closing inventory
Question:

On 15-01-2023 goods of ₹3,00,000 were sent on consignment basis, of which 20% of the goods unsold are lying with the consignee as on 31-03-2023. You are required to advise the accountant of BS Products Ltd., with valid reasons, the amount to be recognized as revenue in this case in the context of AS 9.

Answer / Solution:

20% goods lying unsold with consignee should be treated as closing inventory and sales should be recognized for ₹2,40,000 (80% of ₹3,00,000). In the case of consignment sale revenue should not be recognized until the goods are sold to a third party.

Author’s Note: A common error here is recognising the full ₹3,00,000 as revenue on the date goods are sent on consignment, treating dispatch to the consignee as equivalent to a sale to the end customer.

RTP May 2024 · Q16(iii) · Marks: Not stated in source · Approx Time: 10–20 minutes (approx.) · Topic 2.8: Sale on approval basis - revenue recognised once formally accepted, an adopting act occurs, or the approval/rejection period has elapsed, whichever governs
Question:

₹4,00,000 worth of goods were sold on approval basis on 01-12-2022. The period of approval was 3 months after which they were considered as sold. Buyer sent approval for 75% goods upto 31-01-2023 and no approval or disapproval received for the remaining goods till 31-03-2023. You are required to advise the accountant of BS Products Ltd., with valid reasons, the amount to be recognized as revenue in this case in the context of AS 9.

Answer / Solution:

In case of goods sold on approval basis, revenue should not be recognized until the goods have been formally accepted by the buyer or the buyer has done an act adopting the transaction or the time period for rejection has elapsed or where no time has been fixed, a reasonable time has elapsed. Therefore, revenue should be recognized for the total sales amounting to ₹4,00,000 as the time period for rejecting the goods had expired.

Author’s Note: A common error here is recognising revenue only for the 75% expressly approved by the buyer and continuing to treat the remaining 25% as unsold, missing that the stated 3-month approval period had already lapsed for that portion by the year end, which itself triggers recognition.

RTP May 2024 · Q16(iv) · Marks: Not stated in source · Approx Time: 10–20 minutes (approx.) · Topic 2.9: Effect of collection uncertainty on revenue recognition - recognised only to the extent collection is reasonably certain, based on past collection experience
Question:

Apart from the above, BS Products Ltd. sells goods to dealers also. One of the conditions of sale is that interest is payable @ 2% p.m. for delayed payments by dealers. The percentage of interest recovery is only 10% i.e. ₹50,000 on such overdue outstanding due to various reasons. During the year 2022-23, the company wants to recognize the entire interest receivable of ₹60,000. You are required to advise the accountant of BS Products Ltd., with valid reasons, the amount to be recognized as revenue in this case in the context of AS 9, and also determine the total revenue to be recognized for the year ending 31-03-2023.

Answer / Solution:

As per the standard, "where the ability to assess the ultimate collection with reasonable certainty is lacking at the time of raising any claim, the revenue recognition is postponed to the extent of uncertainty involved. In such cases, the revenue is recognized only when it is reasonably certain that the ultimate collection will be made". In this case, interest should be recognized only if the ultimate collection is certain and the company expects to realize interest for the delayed payments for ₹50,000 only. Hence, based on the past experience, the realization of interest for the delayed payments by the agent is certain only to the extent of this amount and not ₹60,000. Therefore, the interest income of ₹50,000 should be recognized in the books for the year ended 31st March, 2023.

Thus, total revenue amounting ₹8,90,000 (2,00,000 + 2,40,000 + 4,00,000 + 50,000) will be recognized for the year ended 31st March, 2023 in the books of BS Products Ltd.

Author’s Note: A common error here is recognising the full contractually-computed interest of ₹60,000 rather than limiting recognition to the ₹50,000 actually supported by past collection experience, and separately failing to aggregate all four cases into the single total revenue figure the question asks for.

RTP May 2025 · Q10 · Marks: Not stated in source · Approx Time: 10–20 minutes (approx.) · Topic 2.8: Revenue-recognition timing across delayed delivery, consignment sale, and sale-on-approval scenarios
Question:

Given below are the following information of B.S. Ltd.:

  1. Goods of ₹50,000 were sold on 18-03-2024 but at the request of the buyer these were delivered on 15-04-2024.
  2. On 13-01-2024 goods of ₹1,25,000 are sent on consignment basis, of which 20% of the goods unsold are lying with the consignee as on 31-03-2024.
  3. ₹1,00,000 worth of goods were sold on approval basis on 01-12-2023. The period of approval was 3 months after which they were considered sold. Buyer sent approval for 75% goods up to 31-01-2024 and no approval or disapproval received for the remaining goods till 31-03-2024.

You are required to advise the accountant of B.S. Ltd., with valid reasons, the amount to be recognized as revenue for the year ended 31st March, 2024 in the above cases in the context of AS-9.

Answer / Solution:

As per AS 9 'Revenue Recognition', in a transaction involving the sale of goods, performance should be regarded as being achieved when: (a) the seller has transferred to the buyer the property in the goods for a price, or all significant risks and rewards of ownership have been transferred and the seller retains no effective control of the goods to a degree usually associated with ownership; and (b) no significant uncertainty exists regarding the amount of consideration to be derived from the sale.

Case (i): The sale is complete but delivery has been postponed at the buyer's request. B.S. Ltd. should recognize the entire sale of ₹50,000 for the year ended 31st March, 2024.

Case (ii): In case of a consignment sale, revenue should not be recognized until the goods are sold by the consignee to a third party. The 20% of goods lying unsold with the consignee should be treated as closing inventory, and sales should be recognized for ₹1,00,000 (80% of ₹1,25,000).

Case (iii): In case of goods sold on approval basis, revenue should not be recognized until the goods have been formally accepted by the buyer, or the buyer has done an act adopting the transaction, or the time period for rejection has elapsed (or, where no time has been fixed, a reasonable time has elapsed). Since the 3-month approval period had already expired by 31st March, 2024, revenue should be recognized for the full ₹1,00,000 (including the portion neither approved nor disapproved, since the approval window itself had lapsed).

Thus, total revenue amounting to ₹2,50,000 (50,000 + 1,00,000 + 1,00,000) will be recognized for the year ended 31st March, 2024 in the books of B.S. Ltd.

Author’s Note: A common error in case (iii) is withholding revenue recognition on the un-responded-to 25% of goods on the reasoning that no explicit acceptance was received, missing that AS 9 treats the mere expiry of the stated rejection period as itself sufficient for revenue recognition, with no separate acceptance needed.

RTP September 2024 · Q8 · Marks: Not stated in source · Approx Time: 10–20 minutes (approx.) · Topic 2.2: No revenue recognized on inter-divisional transfers since risks/rewards remain within the enterprise and there is no external consideration
Question:

When will the revenue be recognized in the case of inter divisional transfers?

Answer / Solution:

The Accounting Standard Board of ICAI has come up with an announcement in the earlier years wherein it clarified that the inter-divisional transfers/sales are not revenue as per AS 9 "Revenue Recognition". According to it, in case of inter-divisional transfers, risks and rewards remain within the enterprise and also there is no consideration from the point of view of the enterprise as a whole. Therefore, the recognition criteria for revenue recognition are also not fulfilled in respect of inter-divisional transfers. Hence, no revenue is recognized in the case of inter-divisional transfers.

Author’s Note: A common error is treating an inter-divisional transfer priced at a notional transfer price as genuine revenue, without recognising that the enterprise as a whole has not transacted with any outside party.

RTP September 2025 · Q11(i) · Marks: Not stated in source · Approx Time: 10–20 minutes (approx.) · Topic 1.7: Consignment sales - revenue recognised only on the consignee's actual sale to a third party
Question:

Tonk Tanners (leather shoes): On 31st December, 2024, shoes worth ₹3,20,000 were sent to Mohan Shoes for sale on consignment; 25% remained unsold with Mohan Shoes as on 31st March, 2025. Advise when revenue is recognised in 2024-25 per AS 9.

Answer / Solution:

Mohan Shoes is a consignee (agent), not a buyer — risk and reward remain with Tonk Tanners until Mohan Shoes sells to a third party. Revenue is recognised only for the goods actually sold by the consignee: ₹3,20,000 × 75% = ₹2,40,000 recognised as revenue in 2024-25; the remaining 25% (unsold) stays as Tonk Tanners' closing inventory.

Author’s Note: Some examinees recognised the full ₹3,20,000 upon dispatch to the consignee, treating the consignment shipment itself as a completed sale.

RTP September 2025 · Q11(ii) · Marks: Not stated in source · Approx Time: 10–20 minutes (approx.) · Topic 1.8: Sale-and-repurchase arrangements treated as financing, not revenue
Question:

On 10th January, 2025, Tonk Tanners supplied shoes worth ₹4,50,000 to Shani Shoes and concurrently agreed to repurchase the same goods on 11th April, 2025. Advise on revenue recognition.

Answer / Solution:

A sale with a concurrent agreement to repurchase the same goods is, in substance, a financing arrangement, not a genuine sale. The resulting cash inflow is not revenue and should not be recognised as revenue in 2024-25.

Author’s Note: Some examinees recognised the ₹4,50,000 as ordinary sales revenue, not recognising the repurchase commitment as converting the transaction into a financing arrangement in substance.

RTP September 2025 · Q11(iii) · Marks: Not stated in source · Approx Time: 10–20 minutes (approx.) · Topic 1.4: Delivery delayed at buyer's request - revenue still recognised once title/billing acceptance occurs
Question:

On 21st March, 2025, shoes worth ₹1,60,000 were sold to Shoe Shine, but due to their showroom refurbishment, delivery was made on 12th April, 2025 at their request. Advise on revenue recognition.

Answer / Solution:

If, on 21st March 2025, Shoe Shine took title and accepted billing for the goods, the sale is complete and all risks/rewards of ownership have transferred, even though physical delivery was delayed at the buyer's own request. Provided no significant uncertainty exists over the consideration, revenue is recognised in 2024-25, regardless of the delayed physical delivery.

Author’s Note: Some examinees deferred revenue recognition to the actual delivery date (April 2025), not recognising that title transfer and billing acceptance, not physical delivery, is what matters here.

MTP September 2025 Set 1 · Q3(a) · Marks: 7 · Approx Time: 13 minutes (approx.) · Topic 1.6/1.9/1.10: Percentage-of-completion method with a mid-contract variation changing total contract value and estimated cost
Question:

Constructions Limited is engaged in the business of constructing Flyovers and Railway over bridges. It obtained a contract from Railway Authorities to construct a railway over bridge for ₹400 crores. The construction of the railway over bridge is expected to be completed in 4 years.

At the outset of the contract, it was estimated that the total costs to be incurred will be ₹370 crores but by the end of year 1, this estimate stands revised to ₹375 crores.

During year 3, the Construction Limited has requested for a variation in the contract which is approved by Railway Authorities and accordingly the total contract value will increase by ₹10 crores and costs will increase by ₹7 crores.

The Constructions Limited decided to measure the stage of completion on the basis of the proportion of contract costs incurred to the total estimated contract costs. Contract costs incurred at the end of each year is: Year 1 ₹98.8 crores; Year 2 ₹202.4 crores; Year 3 ₹310 crores (including unused material of 3 crores); Year 4 ₹382 crores.

You are required to: (1) Calculate stage of completion of contract for each year; (2) Profit to be recognised for each year.

Answer / Solution:

(i) Stage of completion = Costs incurred to date / Total estimated costs

YearCalculationStage of completion
Year 198.8 crore / 375 crore26.35%
Year 2202.4 crore / 375 crore53.97%
Year 3(310 crore − 3 crore) / (375+7) crore80.37%
Year 4382 crore / 382 crore100%

(ii) Profit to be recognized each year:

ParticularsYear 1Year 2Year 3Year 4
Contract Revenue (1)105.40 crore (400 crore × 26.35%)110.48 crore (400 crore × 53.97% − 105.40 crore)113.64 crore (410 crore × 80.37% − 105.40 crore − 110.48 crore)80.48 crore (410 crore × 100% − 105.40 − 110.48 − 113.64 crore)
Contract Cost (2)98.8 crore103.60 crore (202.40 − 98.80 crore)104.60 crore (307 crore − 98.8 crore − 103.60 crore)75 crore (382 crore − 98.8 crore − 103.6 crore − 104.6 crore)
Contract Profit (1)−(2)6.60 crore6.88 crore9.04 crore5.48 crore
Author’s Note: A common error here is failing to re-base the stage-of-completion percentage each year against the year's own revised total estimated cost, particularly once a contract variation changes both the total contract value and the total estimated cost part-way through the project.

PYQ May 2024 · Q3(a) · Marks: 7 · Approx Time: 13 minutes (approx.) · Topic 1.6/1.9/1.10: Percentage of completion method - stage of completion via costs-incurred-to-date/total-estimated-costs, revision of contract price and cost estimates mid-contract (change in estimate), profit recognised as revenue less cost incurred each year
Question:

Constructions Limited is engaged in the business of constructing Flyovers and Railway over bridges. It obtained a contract from Railway Authorities to construct a railway over bridge for ₹400 crores. The construction of the railway over bridge is expected to be completed in 4 years.

At the outset of the contract, it was estimated that the total costs to be incurred will be ₹370 crores but by the end of year 1, this estimate stands revised to ₹375 crores.

During year 3, the Construction Limited has requested for a variation in the contract which is approved by Railway Authorities and accordingly the total contract value will increase by ₹10 crores and costs will increase by ₹7 crores.

The Constructions Limited decided to measure the stage of completion on the basis of the proportion of contract costs incurred to the total estimated contract costs. Contract costs incurred at the end of each year is:

YearContract costs incurred
Year 1₹98.8 crores
Year 2₹202.4 crores
Year 3₹310 crores (including unused material of ₹3 crores)
Year 4₹382 crores

You are required to:

  1. Calculate stage of completion of contract for each year
  2. Profit to be recognised for each year.
Answer / Solution:

(a) Stage of completion = Costs incurred to date / Total estimated costs

Year 1: 98.8 crore / 375 crore = 26.35%
Year 2: 202.4 crore / 375 crore = 53.97%
Year 3: (310 crore − 3 crore) / (375+7) crore = 80.37%
Year 4: 382 crore / 382 crore = 100%

(b) Profit to be recognized each year

Year 1Year 2Year 3Year 4
Contract Revenue (1)105.40 crore

RTP January 2025 · Q6 · Marks: Not stated in source · Approx Time: 10–20 minutes (approx.) · Topic 1.6: Percentage of completion method - stage of completion, revenue and profit recognition, updated for a contract-price escalation clause
Question:

Rose Constructions undertake to construct a bridge for the Government of Uttar Pradesh. The construction commenced during the financial year ending 31.03.2024 and is likely to be completed by the next financial year. The contract is for a fixed price of ₹12 crore with an escalation clause. You are given the following information for the year ended 31.03.2024:

Cost incurred upto 31.03.2024₹4 crore
Cost estimated to complete the contract₹6 crore

Escalation in cost was by 5%. Hence, the contract price is also increased by 5%.

You are required to ascertain the stage of completion and compute the amount of revenue and profit to be recognized for the year as per AS 7.

Answer / Solution:
Cost of construction of bridge incurred upto 31.3.2024₹4.00 crore
Add: Estimated future cost₹6.00 crore
Total estimated cost of construction₹10.00 crore
Contract Price (12 crore × 1.05)₹12.60 crore

Stage of completion: Percentage of completion till date to total estimated cost of construction = (4/10)×100 = 40%.

Revenue and Profit to be recognized for the year ended 31st March, 2024 as per AS 7:

Proportion of total contract value recognized as revenue = Contract price × percentage of completion = ₹12.60 crore × 40% = ₹5.04 crore.

Profit for the year ended 31st March, 2024 = ₹5.04 crore − ₹4 crore = ₹1.04 crore.

Author’s Note: A common error is computing the percentage of completion using the original (pre-escalation) contract price or cost estimates instead of updating both cost incurred/estimated-to-complete and contract price for the 5% escalation before applying AS 7's percentage of completion formula.

RTP January 2026 · Q7 · Marks: Not stated in source · Approx Time: 10–20 minutes (approx.) · Topic 3.4: Percentage of completion method - unused stored materials excluded from the cost-incurred-to-date figure used to measure progress
Question:

A construction contractor entered a fixed-price contract of ₹18,000 lacs to construct a bridge within 3 years, with provisions for variations. (₹ in lacs): Year 1/2/3 — Initial revenue agreed 18,000/18,000/18,000; Variation in revenue (+)400/400 (Years 2,3); Contract costs incurred to date 4,186/12,336*/16,200**; Estimated profit for whole contract 1,900/2,000/2,000. *includes ₹200 lacs standard materials stored at site for use in Year 3. **excludes ₹200 lacs standard material brought forward from Year 2. Year 2's variation was approved by the customer. Compute year-wise: revenue recognised, expenses recognised, contract costs to complete, and profit/loss recognised.

Answer / Solution:

Working — degree of completion each year (costs incurred, excluding unused stored materials, ÷ estimated total cost): Year 1: revenue after variations 18,000, less estimated profit 1,900 = estimated total cost 16,100; actual cost incurred 4,186; degree of completion = 4,186/16,100 = 26%. Year 2: revenue 18,400, less profit 2,000 = total cost 16,400; cost incurred (excluding the ₹200 lacs stored materials not yet used) 12,336−200=12,136; degree of completion = 12,136/16,400 = 74%. Year 3: revenue 18,400, total cost 16,400; cost incurred 16,200+200 (bringing forward the previously-excluded stored material, now used) = 16,400; degree of completion 100%.

YearRevenue recognised (cumulative × %)Recognised in prior yearsRecognised in current year
118,000×26%=4,680—4,680
218,400×74%=13,6164,6808,936
318,400×100%=18,40013,6164,784
YearExpenses recognised (cumulative)Prior yearsCurrent year
116,100×26%=4,186—4,186
216,400×74%=12,1364,1867,950
316,400×100%=16,40012,1364,264

Profit recognised each year: Year 1: 494 (4,680−4,186). Year 2 cumulative 1,480, current year 986 (1,480−494). Year 3 cumulative 2,000, current year 520 (2,000−1,480).

Contract costs to complete the remaining work: Year 1: 16,100−4,186=11,914. Year 2: 16,400−12,136=4,264 (plus the ₹200 lacs stored materials earmarked for Year 3, held separately). Year 3: Nil (contract complete).

Author’s Note: Some examinees included the ₹200 lacs of unused stored materials in Year 2's cost-incurred-to-date figure when computing the degree of completion, overstating progress since those materials had not yet been consumed in construction.

RTP May 2024 · Q15 · Marks: Not stated in source · Approx Time: 10–20 minutes (approx.) · Topic 1.6: Percentage of completion computed as cost incurred to date (excluding unused materials, including specific/sub-contract costs, excluding advances) over total estimated contract cost
Question:

The following data is provided for M/s. Raj Construction Co.

  1. Contract Price - ₹85 lakhs
  2. Materials issued - ₹21 Lakhs out of which Materials costing ₹4 Lakhs is still lying unused at the end of the period.
  3. Labour Expenses for workers engaged at site - ₹16 Lakhs (out of which ₹1 Lakh is still unpaid)
  4. Specific Contract Costs = ₹5 Lakhs
  5. Sub-Contract Costs for work executed - ₹7 Lakhs, Advances paid to Sub-Contractors - ₹4 Lakhs
  6. Further Cost estimated to be incurred to complete the contract - ₹35 Lakhs

You are required to compute the Percentage of Completion, the Contract Revenue and Cost to be recognized as per AS-7.

Answer / Solution:

Computation of contract cost

₹ Lakh₹ Lakh
Material cost incurred on the contract (net of closing stock)21-417
Add: Labour cost incurred on the contract (including outstanding amount)16
Specified contract costgiven5
Sub-contract cost (advances should not be considered)7
Cost incurred (till date)45
Add: further cost to be incurred35
Total contract cost80

Percentage of completion = Cost incurred till date/Estimated total cost = ₹45,00,000/₹80,00,000 = 56.25%

Contract revenue and costs to be recognized:

Contract revenue (₹85,00,000 x 56.25%) = ₹47,81,250

Contract costs = ₹45,00,000

Author’s Note: A common error here is including unused materials and advances paid to sub-contractors in the cost-incurred-to-date figure, overstating the percentage of completion since neither represents cost actually incurred on work performed.

RTP May 2025 · Q9(i) · Marks: Not stated in source · Approx Time: 10–20 minutes (approx.) · Topic 1.3: Conditions under which one contract document covering multiple assets is treated as separate construction contracts
Question:

AP Ltd., a construction contractor, undertakes the construction of a commercial complex for Kay Ltd. AP Ltd. submitted separate proposals for each of 3 units of the commercial complex. A single agreement is entered into between the two parties. The agreement lays down the value of each of the 3 units, i.e. ₹50 Lakh, ₹60 Lakh and ₹75 Lakh respectively. The agreement also lays down the completion time for each unit. Comment, with reference to AS-7, whether AP Ltd. should treat it as a single contract or three separate contracts.

Answer / Solution:

As per AS 7 'Construction Contracts', when a contract covers a number of assets, the construction of each asset should be treated as a separate construction contract when: (a) separate proposals have been submitted for each asset; (b) each asset has been subject to separate negotiation and the contractor and customer have been able to accept or reject that part of the contract relating to each asset; and (c) the costs and revenues of each asset can be identified.

In the given case, AP Ltd. submitted separate proposals for each of the 3 units, the agreement lays down a separate value and separate completion time for each unit, and the costs/revenues of each unit are identifiable. Therefore, AP Ltd. is required to treat the construction of each unit as a separate construction contract, as the above-mentioned conditions of AS 7 are fulfilled in the given case – notwithstanding that a single agreement document was used.

Author’s Note: A common error is concluding it must be a single contract simply because only one agreement document was signed, missing that AS 7 looks at the three specific conditions (separate proposals, separate negotiability, identifiable costs/revenues) rather than the number of physical documents.

RTP May 2025 · Q9(ii) · Marks: Not stated in source · Approx Time: 10–20 minutes (approx.) · Topic 1.6: Percentage-of-completion revenue recognition together with immediate recognition of the entire foreseeable loss on a loss-making contract
Question:

On 1st December, 2023, GR Construction Co. Ltd. undertook a contract to construct a building for ₹45 lakhs. On 31st March, 2024, the company found that it had already spent ₹32.50 lakhs on the construction. Additional cost of completion is estimated at ₹15.10 lakhs. What amount should be charged to revenue in the final accounts for the year ended 31st March, 2024 as per provisions of AS-7?

Answer / Solution:
₹ in lakhs
Cost of construction incurred till date32.50
Add: Estimated future cost15.10
Total estimated cost of construction47.60

Percentage of completion till date to total estimated cost of construction = (32.50/47.60) × 100 = 68.28%.

Proportion of total contract value recognised as revenue for the year ended 31st March, 2024 per AS 7 (Revised) = Contract price × percentage of completion = ₹45 lakh × 68.28% = ₹30.73 lakhs.

₹ in lakhs
Total cost of construction47.60
Less: Total contract price(45.00)
Total foreseeable loss to be recognized as expense2.60

According to AS 7, when it is probable that total contract costs will exceed total contract revenue, the expected loss should be recognized as an expense immediately (in full, not spread by percentage of completion).

Author’s Note: A common error is recognising only the current period's proportionate share of the ₹2.60 lakh foreseeable loss (via the 68.28% completion rate) rather than the entire foreseeable loss immediately, once it becomes probable that total costs will exceed total contract revenue.

RTP September 2025 · Q10 · Marks: Not stated in source · Approx Time: 10–20 minutes (approx.) · Topic 3.5: Expected loss on a construction contract recognised immediately in full, regardless of stage of completion
Question:

A company took a construction contract for ₹100 lakhs in January 2024; 80% completed at cost ₹92 lakhs by 31.3.2025; further ₹23 lakhs estimated to complete; expected loss ₹15 lakhs. Can the company recognise the loss in the FY2024-25 financial statements?

Answer / Solution:

Yes. Per AS 7 paras 31 and 35, an expected loss on a construction contract must be recognised as an expense immediately, regardless of (i) whether work has commenced; (ii) the stage of completion; or (iii) profits expected on other contracts. The company must recognise the ₹15 lakh loss immediately in the year ended 31.3.2025.

Author’s Note: Some examinees deferred the loss recognition to future periods or spread it across the remaining completion percentage, missing AS 7's requirement for immediate full recognition.

MTP May 2023 Set 1 · Q1(b) · Marks: 5 · Approx Time: 9 minutes (approx.) · Topic 1.6: Presentation of grants related to specific fixed assets - Method I (grant deducted from asset's gross value), and treatment when the deducted grant exceeds the asset's remaining book value Compulsory
Question:

D Ltd. acquired a machine on 01-04-2017 for ₹20,00,000. The useful life is 5 years. The company had applied on 01-04-2017, for a subsidy to the tune of 80% of the cost. The sanction letter for subsidy was received in November 2020. The Company's Fixed Assets Account for the financial year 2020-21 shows a credit balance as under:

Particulars₹
Machine (Original Cost)20,00,000
Less: Accumulated Depreciation (from 2017-18 to 2019-20 on Straight Line Method)12,00,000
8,00,000
Less: Grant received(16,00,000)
Balance(8,00,000)

You are required to explain how should the company deal with this asset in its accounts for 2020-21? (5 Marks)

Answer / Solution:

From the above account, it is inferred that the Company has deducted grant from the book value of asset for accounting of Government Grants. Accordingly, out of the ₹16,00,000 that has been received, ₹8,00,000 (being the balance in Machinery A/c) should be credited to the machinery A/c.

The balance ₹8,00,000 may be credited to P&L A/c, since already the cost of the asset to the tune of ₹12,00,000 had been debited to P&L A/c in the earlier years by way of depreciation charge, and ₹8,00,000 transferred to P&L A/c now would be partial recovery of that cost.

There is no need to provide depreciation for 2020-21 or 2021-22 as the depreciable amount is now Nil.

Author’s Note: A frequent slip is treating the entire ₹16,00,000 grant as available to write down the asset's book value below zero, without recognising that once the asset's book value is reduced to nil, the excess grant amount must instead be recognised as income (a partial recovery of the depreciation already charged in earlier years) rather than left as a negative asset balance.

MTP May 2023 Set 2 · Q1(c) · Marks: 5 · Approx Time: 9 minutes (approx.) · Topic 1.9: Refund of a government grant related to a specific fixed asset increases the asset's book value, depreciated prospectively Compulsory
Question:

Caseworker Limited received a specific grant of ₹6 crore for acquiring the plant of ₹30 crore on 1.4.2016 having useful life of 10 years. At the beginning of the financial year 2021-2022, due to non-compliance of conditions laid down for the grant of ₹6 crore, the company had to refund the grant to the Government. What should be the treatment of the refund if grant was deducted from the cost of the plant during financial year 2016-2017? Assume depreciation is charged on fixed assets as per Straight Line Method.

Answer / Solution:

As per AS 12, the amount refundable in respect of grant related to specific fixed assets should be recorded by increasing the book value of the asset or by reducing the capital reserve or the deferred income balance, as appropriate, by the amount refundable. Where the book value of the asset is increased, depreciation on the revised book value should be provided prospectively over the residual useful life of the asset.

Where grant was deducted from the cost of the asset, initial value of the plant after deduction of grant amount of ₹6 crore would have been = ₹30 crore − ₹6 crore = ₹24 crore.

Carrying value of the plant after 5 years on 1.4.2021 = [(₹24 crore / 10 years) × 5 years] = ₹12 crore.

Annual depreciation charge would be ₹2.4 crore.

On refund of grant to the Government, the book value of the plant shall be increased by ₹6 crore i.e. ₹12 crore + ₹6 crore = ₹18 crore. The increased cost of ₹18 crore of the plant should be amortised prospectively over remaining 5 years of useful residual life. Depreciation charge in the year 2021-2022 would be ₹18 crore / 5 years = ₹3.6 crore instead of earlier ₹2.4 crore.

Author’s Note: A common error is reversing the refund entry against the original grant-deduction entry retrospectively (restating prior years), rather than increasing the asset's current book value prospectively and depreciating the revised amount only over the remaining useful life.

MTP November 2023 Set 2 · Q1(b) · Marks: 5 · Approx Time: 9 minutes (approx.) · Topic 1.6/1.9: Refund of a grant credited to Deferred Grant Account under the deferred-income method - refund entry splitting the outstanding deferred-grant balance and the shortfall to Profit and Loss, with the related fixed asset's own carrying amount and remaining depreciation charge unaffected by the refund Compulsory
Question:

Ram Ltd. purchased machinery for ₹80 lakhs (useful life 4 years and residual value ₹8 lakhs). Government grant received was ₹32 lakhs. The grant had to be refunded at the beginning of third year. Show the Journal Entry to be passed at the time of refund of grant and the value of the fixed assets in the third year and the amount of depreciation for remaining two years, if the grant had been credited to Deferred Grant A/c.

Answer / Solution:

As per AS 12 ‘Accounting for Government Grants,’ income from Deferred Grant Account is allocated to Profit and Loss account usually over the periods and in the proportions in which depreciation on related assets is charged. Accordingly, in the first two years (₹32 lakhs /4 years) = ₹8 lakhs x 2 years = ₹16 lakhs will be credited to Profit and Loss Account and ₹16 lakhs will be the balance of Deferred Grant Account after two years. Therefore, on refund of grant, following entry will be passed:

Particulars₹₹
Deferred Grant A/cDr.16 lakhs
Profit & Loss A/cDr.16 lakhs
  To Bank A/c32 lakhs
(Being Government grant refunded)

1. Value of Fixed Assets after two years but before refund of grant

Fixed assets initially recorded in the books = ₹80 lakhs
Depreciation for each year = (₹80 lakhs − ₹8 lakhs)/4 years = ₹18 lakhs per year
Book value of fixed assets after two years = ₹80 lakhs − (₹18 lakhs x 2 years) = ₹44 lakhs

2. Value of Fixed Assets after refund of grant

On refund of grant the balance of deferred grant account will become nil. The fixed assets will continue to be shown in the books at ₹44 lakhs.

3. Amount of depreciation for remaining two years

Depreciation will continue to be charged at ₹18 lakhs per annum for the remaining two years.

Author’s Note: A common error is writing the refund entry entirely against the Deferred Grant Account balance without recognising that only ₹16 lakhs remains there after two years' amortisation, forcing the shortfall of ₹16 lakhs to be debited to Profit and Loss; a related error is reducing the fixed asset's own book value on refund, when AS 12 requires the asset's carrying amount and future depreciation to continue unchanged since the grant was never netted against the asset's cost under the deferred-income method.

Question:

Smile Ltd. purchased machinery for ₹80 lakhs (useful life 4 years and residual value ₹8 lakhs). Government grant received was ₹32 lakhs. The grant had to be refunded at the beginning of third year. Show the Journal Entry to be passed at the time of refund of grant and the value of the fixed assets in the third year and the amount of depreciation for remaining two years, if the grant had been credited to Deferred Grant A/c.

Answer / Solution:

As per AS 12 ‘Accounting for Government Grants’, income from a Deferred Grant Account is allocated to Profit and Loss usually over the periods and in the proportions in which depreciation on the related asset is charged. In the first two years, (₹32 lakhs/4 years) = ₹8 lakhs × 2 years = ₹16 lakhs is credited to P&L, leaving ₹16 lakhs as the balance of the Deferred Grant Account after two years. On refund of the grant:

AccountDr (₹ lakhs)Cr (₹ lakhs)
Deferred Grant A/c Dr.16
Profit & Loss A/c Dr.16
  To Bank A/c32
(Being Government grant refunded)

1. Value of fixed assets after two years but before refund of grant: initial cost ₹80 lakhs; depreciation per year = (₹80 lakhs − ₹8 lakhs)/4 years = ₹18 lakhs; book value after two years = 80 − (18×2) = ₹44 lakhs.

2. Value of fixed assets after refund of grant: on refund the Deferred Grant Account balance becomes nil, but the fixed asset continues to be shown in the books at ₹44 lakhs (unchanged — the refund does not restate the asset's carrying amount).

3. Depreciation for remaining two years: continues to be charged at ₹18 lakhs per annum for the remaining two years.

Author’s Note: A common error here is restating the fixed asset's carrying amount upward on refund of the grant, rather than recognising that the refund is charged to the Deferred Grant Account balance and Profit and Loss, leaving the asset's carrying amount unaffected.

MTP September 2025 Set 2 · Q1(a) · Marks: 7 · Approx Time: 13 minutes (approx.) · Topic 1.6: Depreciation impact of the asset-deduction, deferred-income and promoter's-contribution presentation methods, including a mid-life grant refund Compulsory
Question:

On 1st April 2023, Eleanor Limited purchased a manufacturing Plant for ₹60 lakhs, which has an estimated useful life of 10 years with a salvage value of ₹10 lakhs. On purchase of the Plant, a grant of ₹20 lakhs was received from the government. You are required to calculate the amount of depreciation as per AS 12 for the financial year 2024-25 in the following cases: (i) If the grant amount is deducted from the value of Plant. (ii) If the grant is treated as deferred income. (iii) If the grant amount is deducted from the value of Plant, but at the end of the year 2024-2025 grant is refunded to the extent of ₹4 lakhs, due to non-compliance of certain conditions. (iv) If the grant is treated as the promoter's contribution. (Assume depreciation on the basis of Straight-Line Method.)

Answer / Solution:

(i) If the grant amount is deducted from the value of Plant, depreciation = (₹60,00,000 − ₹10,00,000 − ₹20,00,000) ÷ 10 years = ₹3,00,000 p.a.

(ii) If the grant is treated as deferred income, depreciation = (₹60,00,000 − ₹10,00,000) ÷ 10 years = ₹5,00,000 p.a.

(iii) If the grant amount is deducted from the value of Plant, but at the end of the year 2024-25 grant is refunded to the extent of ₹4 lakh: depreciation for year 2023-24 remains (₹60,00,000 − ₹10,00,000 − ₹20,00,000) ÷ 10 years = ₹3,00,000; for the year 2024-25, depreciation = (₹60,00,000 − ₹10,00,000 − ₹20,00,000 − ₹3,00,000) ÷ 9 years = ₹3,00,000.

Note: It is assumed that the depreciation for the year has been charged on the book value of the plant before making adjustment for the grant refund. Alternatively, if depreciation is charged after making adjustment for the grant refund, depreciation for 2024-25 will be (₹60,00,000 − ₹10,00,000 − ₹20,00,000 + ₹4,00,000 − ₹3,00,000) ÷ 9 years = ₹3,44,444.

(iv) If the grant is treated as the promoter's contribution, depreciation = (₹60,00,000 − ₹10,00,000) ÷ 10 years = ₹5,00,000 p.a.

Author’s Note: A common error here is treating the partial grant refund in case (iii) as a fresh transaction requiring the original 10-year schedule to be unwound, rather than simply adding the refunded amount back to the asset's remaining book value and re-spreading it over the remaining useful life.

PYQ May 2023 · Q1(c) · Marks: 5 · Approx Time: 9 minutes (approx.) · Topic 1.6/1.9: Four presentation methods for a fixed-asset grant (deducted from cost / deferred income / refunded / promoter's contribution) and refund treatment Compulsory
Question:

On 1st April 2021, Eleanor Limited purchased a manufacturing Plant for ₹60 lakhs, which has an estimated useful life of 10 years with a salvage value of ₹10 lakhs. On purchase of the Plant, a grant of ₹20 lakhs was received from the government.

You are required to calculate the amount of depreciation as per AS-12 for the financial year 2022-23 in the following cases: (i) If the grant amount is deducted from the value of Plant. (ii) If the grant is treated as deferred income. (iii) If the grant amount is deducted from the value of Plant, but at the end of the year 2022-2023 grant is refunded to the extent of ₹4 lakhs, due to non-compliance of certain conditions. (iv) If the grant is treated as the promoter's contribution. (Assume depreciation on the basis of Straight-Line Method.) (5 Marks)

Answer / Solution:

Calculation of depreciation as per AS 12 for the financial year 2022-23:

(i) If the grant amount is deducted from the value of Plant, then the amount of depreciation will be ₹3,00,000 p.a. (₹60,00,000 − ₹10,00,000 − ₹20,00,000) / 10 year.

(ii) If the grant is treated as deferred income, then amount of depreciation will be ₹5,00,000 p.a. (₹60,00,000 − ₹10,00,000) / 10 year.

(iii) If the grant amount is deducted from the value of plant, but at the end of the year 2022-23 grant is refunded to the extent of ₹4 lakh then the amount of depreciation will be ₹3,00,000 p.a. (₹60,00,000 − ₹10,00,000 − ₹20,00,000) /10 year for year 2021-22 and for the year 2022-23 depreciation will be ₹3,00,000 calculated as follows, (₹60,00,000 − ₹10,00,000 − ₹20,00,000 − ₹3,00,000) / 10 years.

Note: It is assumed that the depreciation for the year has been charged on the book value on the plant before making adjustment for grant. Alternatively, if it is considered otherwise then the depreciation will be charged after making adjustment for grant. In that case depreciation for the year 2022-23 will be ₹3,44,444 calculated as follows: [(₹60,00,000 − ₹10,00,000 − ₹20,00,000 + 4,00,000 − ₹3,00,000) / 9 years].

(iv) If the grant is treated as promoter's contribution, then the amount of depreciation will be ₹5,00,000 p.a. (₹60,00,000 − 10,00,000) /10 year.

Note: the answer can be presented in the following alternative manner:

A few also confused the promoter's-contribution treatment with the deferred-income treatment, incorrectly deducting the grant from the asset's cost under case (iv) as well.

RTP January 2026 · Q10 · Marks: Not stated in source · Approx Time: 10–20 minutes (approx.) · Topic 1.7: Refund of a grant previously deducted from asset cost - added back to the asset's carrying amount
Question:

Mediwell Hospitals Ltd. acquired 40 Doppler Scan Machines from Holiver Inc., USA, at US$1,65,100/unit at the start of FY2022-23, exchange rate ₹50/US$. Partly financed by a government grant of ₹5 crores (specific condition: refund on change in management/ownership control). In April 2025, 51% shareholding acquired by an overseas investor — management control changed, grant refund now due. Useful life 5 years, SLM at 20% p.a. Also: Bank charges US$4,000 (whole import), Sea freight ₹7,500/unit. No Capital Reserve or Deferred Income Account was maintained for the grant. Advise the accounting treatment for the grant refund per AS 12.

Answer / Solution:

The grant was received towards a fixed asset; the capital (deduction-from-cost) approach was adopted (confirmed by the absence of a Capital Reserve or Deferred Income Account).

Cost of asset (1,65,100 × 40 units × ₹50)3,302 lakhs
Add: Freight and other charges (4,000×50 bank charges + 7,500×40 sea freight)5 lakhs
Total cost3,307 lakhs
Less: Grant received(500 lakhs)
Cost as per AS 10 (net of grant)2,807 lakhs
Less: Depreciation for 3 years (2,807 × 20% × 3)(1,684.2 lakhs)
Carrying amount as on 1.4.2025 (before refund)1,122.8 lakhs
Add: Grant refunded500 lakhs
Revised carrying amount1,622.8 lakhs

Per AS 12, when a grant that was deducted from an asset's cost becomes refundable, the amount refundable is added back to the carrying amount of the asset (or the gross book value increased), rather than expensed — increasing the future depreciation charge over the asset's remaining life.

Author’s Note: Some examinees expensed the refunded grant amount directly to the P&L, not applying AS 12's specific rule that a refund of a grant deducted from asset cost is added back to the carrying amount of that asset.

RTP May 2025 · Q13 · Marks: Not stated in source · Approx Time: 10–20 minutes (approx.) · Topic 1.8: Grants in the nature of promoters' contribution credited to Capital Reserve, never treated as revenue/deferred income
Question:

XYZ Limited has set-up its business in a designated backward area which entitles the company to receive from the Government of India a subsidy of 20% of the cost of investment. Having fulfilled all the conditions under the scheme, the company on its investment of ₹75 crore received ₹15 crore as subsidy from the Government in January 2024. The company wants to treat this receipt as an item of revenue and thereby reduce the losses for the year ended on 31st March, 2024. Keeping in view the relevant Accounting Standard, examine whether this action is justified or not.

Answer / Solution:

As per para 10 of AS 12 'Accounting for Government Grants', where government grants are in the nature of promoters' contribution – i.e. they are given with reference to the total investment in an undertaking, or by way of contribution towards its total capital outlay, and no repayment is ordinarily expected in respect thereof – the grants are treated as Capital Reserve, which can be neither distributed as dividend nor considered as deferred income.

In the given case, the subsidy received (20% of the cost of investment) is neither in relation to a specific fixed asset nor in relation to revenue – it is linked to the total investment made in the backward-area undertaking. It is therefore inappropriate to recognise this government grant in the profit and loss statement, since it is not earned but represents an incentive provided by the government without related costs.

The correct treatment is to credit the ₹15 crore subsidy to Capital Reserve. Therefore, the accounting treatment (treating it as revenue to reduce the reported loss) followed by the company is not proper.

Author’s Note: A common error is treating any cash subsidy received as revenue income by default, without first testing whether it meets AS 12's specific "promoters' contribution" characterisation (tied to total investment, not a specific asset or specific revenue item), which mandates Capital Reserve treatment instead.

RTP September 2024 · Q10 · Marks: Not stated in source · Approx Time: 10–20 minutes (approx.) · Topic 1.4: Recognition of a government grant requires reasonable assurance of both compliance and receipt - mere application is insufficient
Question:

Energy Ltd. has acquired a generator on 1.4.2023 for ₹100 lakh. On 2.4.2023, it applied to Indian Renewal Energy Development Authority (IREDA) for a subsidy. The subsidy was granted in June, 2024 after the accounts for 2023-2024 were finalized. The company has not accounted for the subsidy for the year ended 31.3.2024.

State

  1. Is this a prior period item?
  2. How should the subsidy be accounted in the accounting year 2024-2025?
Answer / Solution:

The answer is in para 13 of AS 12 "Accounting for Government Grants" which permits recognition of grant only when there is reasonable assurance that –

  1. the enterprise will comply with the conditions attached to them and
  2. the subsidy will be received.

Mere making of an application does not provide the reasonable assurance that the subsidy will be received. Letter of sanction from IREDA is required to provide this assurance. Since, the subsidy was granted in June, 2024 after approval of accounts, non-recognition of grant in 2023-2024 will not be considered as an error. Hence, this is not a prior period item. Therefore, the company was right in not recognizing the grant.

Further, AS 4 requires adjustment of events occurring after the balance sheet date only upto the date of approval of accounts by the Board of Directors. In view of this, the company is correct in not adjusting the same in the accounts in the year 2023-2024.

(ii) The subsidy should be deducted from the cost of the generator. The revised unamortised amount of generator should be written off over the remaining useful life.

Alternatively, the same may be treated as ‘deferred income’ and allocated over the remaining useful life in the proportion in which depreciation is charged.

Author’s Note: A common error is treating the mere filing of a subsidy application as sufficient grounds to recognize the grant, or alternatively treating the later grant of the subsidy as a prior period item requiring restatement of the already-approved 2023-2024 accounts.

RTP September 2025 · Q13(i) · Marks: Not stated in source · Approx Time: 10–20 minutes (approx.) · Topic 1.3: Revenue grants credited to P&L (or netted against the related expense)
Question:

Zenith Industries Ltd. received ₹65 lakhs from a local authority to develop medical facilities for employees at its new township. Explain the accounting treatment per AS 12.

Answer / Solution:

This is a grant in the nature of a revenue grant (related to employee welfare expenditure, not a specific fixed asset). Such grants are generally presented as a credit in the Statement of Profit and Loss, either separately or under "Other Income." Alternatively, the ₹65 lakhs may be deducted from the related expense (employee benefit expenses) instead.

Author’s Note: Some examinees treated this as a capital grant since it funds facilities at a "newly built" site, missing that the grant's purpose (employee welfare) rather than the site's newness determines its revenue-grant classification.

RTP September 2025 · Q13(ii) · Marks: Not stated in source · Approx Time: 10–20 minutes (approx.) · Topic 1.8: Promoters'-contribution grants credited to Capital Reserve
Question:

Zenith Industries Ltd. also received ₹82 lakhs as a Central Government subsidy for establishing a new production unit in a notified backward area, classified as being in the nature of promoters' contribution, intended to support long-term development. Explain the treatment per AS 12.

Answer / Solution:

Per AS 12, grants in the nature of promoters' contribution — given with reference to total investment/capital outlay, with no repayment ordinarily expected — are treated as Capital Reserve, which can neither be distributed as dividend nor treated as deferred income. Since this ₹82 lakh subsidy is neither tied to a specific fixed asset nor to revenue, the full amount should be credited to Capital Reserve.

Author’s Note: Some examinees treated this as deferred income to be amortised, not recognising the promoters'-contribution characterisation that requires direct Capital Reserve treatment.

MTP May 2025 Set 2 · Q6(a) [OR-alt 2] · Marks: 4 · Approx Time: 8 minutes (approx.) · Topic 4.3: Definitions of Timing Difference and Permanent Difference
Question:

Write short note on Timing difference and Permanent Difference as per AS 22.

Answer / Solution:

Matching of taxes against revenue for a period poses special problems arising from the fact that in a number of cases, taxable income may be different from the accounting income. The divergence between taxable income and accounting income arises due to two main reasons: firstly, there are differences between items of revenue and expenses as appearing in the statement of profit and loss and the items which are considered as revenue, expenses or deductions for tax purposes, known as Permanent Difference. Secondly, there are differences between the amount in respect of a particular item of revenue or expense as recognised in the statement of profit and loss and the corresponding amount which is recognised for the computation of taxable income, known as Timing Difference.

Permanent differences are the differences between taxable income and accounting income which arise in one accounting period and do not reverse subsequently. For example, an income exempt from tax or an expense that is not allowable as a deduction for tax purposes.

Timing differences are those differences between taxable income and accounting income which arise in one accounting period and are capable of reversal in one or more subsequent periods. For e.g., Depreciation, Bonus, etc.

Author’s Note: A common error here is treating any book-tax gap as a timing difference by default; only differences capable of reversing in a future period (like depreciation) are timing differences, while items that never reverse (like a permanently tax-exempt income) are permanent differences and never generate deferred tax.

RTP January 2025 · Q16 · Marks: Not stated in source · Approx Time: 10–20 minutes (approx.) · Topic 4.5: Deferred tax liability remeasured each year using the tax rate enacted or substantively enacted as at that balance sheet date
Question:

ABC Ltd. prepares its accounts annually on 31st March. On 1st April, 2022, it purchases a machine at a cost of ₹1,50,000. The machine has a useful life of three years and an expected scrap value of zero. Although it is eligible for a 100% first year depreciation allowance for tax purposes, the straight line method is considered appropriate for accounting purposes. ABC Ltd. has profits before depreciation and taxes of ₹2,00,000 each year and corporate tax rate is 40 percent each year.

The purchase of machine at a cost of ₹1,50,000 in 2022 gives rise to a tax saving of ₹60,000. The corporate tax rate has been assumed to be same in each of the three years. Calculate deferred tax and pass necessary journal entries.

What will be the amount of deferred tax, if the substantively enacted tax rates for 2022, 2023 and 2024 are 40%, 35% and 38% respectively.

Answer / Solution:

If the cost of machine is spread over three years of its life for accounting purposes, the amount of the tax saving should also be spread over the same period as shown below:

Statement of Profit and Loss (for the three years ending 31st March, 2022, 2023, 2024), (₹ in thousand)

Particulars202220232024
Profit before depreciation and taxes200200200
Less: Depreciation for accounting purposes505050
Profit before taxes150150150
Current tax208080
Deferred tax (originating/reversing)40(20)(20)
Tax expense606060
Profit after tax909090
Net timing differences100500
Deferred tax liability balance40200

In 2022, the amount of depreciation allowed for tax purposes exceeds the amount of depreciation charged for accounting purposes by ₹1,00,000 and, therefore, taxable income is lower than the accounting income — giving rise to a deferred tax liability of ₹40,000. In 2023 and 2024, accounting income is lower than taxable income because the amount of depreciation charged for accounting purposes exceeds the amount allowed for tax purposes by ₹50,000 each year; deferred tax liability is reduced by ₹20,000 in each of those years.

Journal Entries

YearParticularsDr. (₹)Cr. (₹)
2022Profit and Loss A/c Dr. To Current tax A/c20,00020,000
2022Profit and Loss A/c Dr. To Deferred tax liability A/c (originating timing difference ₹1,00,000)40,00040,000
2023Profit and Loss A/c Dr. To Current tax A/c80,00080,000
2023Deferred tax liability A/c Dr. To Profit and Loss A/c (reversing timing difference ₹50,000)20,00020,000
2024Profit and Loss A/c Dr. To Current tax A/c80,00080,000
2024Deferred tax liability A/c Dr. To Profit and Loss A/c (reversing timing difference ₹50,000)20,00020,000

Presentation: the balance of deferred tax liability account (₹40,000 in 2022, ₹20,000 in 2023, nil in 2024) is shown separately from the current tax payable for the year, per paragraph 30 of AS 22.

If the rate of tax changes (40%, 35%, 38% for 2022/2023/2024 respectively), the deferred tax liability carried forward each year is remeasured by applying the tax rate enacted or substantively enacted by the balance sheet date on accumulated timing differences: 31st March, 2022 = 0.40 × 1,00,000 = ₹40,000; 31st March, 2023 = 0.35 × 50,000 = ₹17,500; 31st March, 2024 = 0.38 × 0 = ₹Zero. The amount debited (credited) to the profit and loss account for each year is accordingly: 31st March, 2022 Debit ₹40,000; 31st March, 2023 (Credit) ₹(22,500); 31st March, 2024 (Credit) ₹(17,500).

Author’s Note: A common error is applying the tax rate prevailing at the time the timing difference originates to the entire deferred tax balance carried forward, missing that AS 22 requires the deferred tax liability to be remeasured each year using the tax rate enacted or substantively enacted as at that balance sheet date.

MTP January 2025 Set 1 · Q3(a) · Marks: 4 · Approx Time: 8 minutes (approx.) · Topic 5.5: Basic EPS restated for a rights issue's bonus element using the theoretical ex-rights fair value adjustment factor
Question:

Following information is supplied by K Ltd.: Number of shares outstanding prior to right issue - 2,50,000 shares. Right issue - two new share for each 5 outstanding shares (i.e. 1,00,000 new shares). Right issue price - ₹98. Last date of exercising rights - 30-06-2023. Fair value of one equity share immediately prior to exercise of right on 30-06-2023 is ₹102. Net Profit to equity shareholders: 2022-2023 - ₹50,00,000; 2023-2024 - ₹75,00,000. You are required to calculate the basic earnings per share as per AS-20 Earnings per Share.

Answer / Solution:

Theoretical ex-rights fair value per share = (Fair value of shares immediately prior to exercise of rights + Total amount received from exercise) / (Number of shares outstanding prior to exercise + Number of shares issued in the exercise) = (₹102 × 2,50,000 shares + ₹98 × 1,00,000 shares) / 3,50,000 shares = ₹100.86.

Computation of adjustment factor = Fair value per share prior to exercise of rights / Theoretical ex-rights value per share = 102/100.86 = 1.01.

Computation of earnings per share:

EPS for the year 2022-23 as originally reported: ₹50,00,000/2,50,000 shares = ₹20.

EPS for the year 2022-23 restated for rights issue: ₹50,00,000/(2,50,000 shares × 1.01) = ₹19.80.

EPS for the year 2023-24 including effects of rights issue: EPS = ₹75,00,000/3,25,625* = ₹23.03.

* [(2,50,000 × 1.01 × 3/12) + (3,50,000 × 9/12)] = 63,125 + 2,62,500 = 3,25,625 shares.

Note: Financial year (ended 31st March) is considered as accounting year while giving the above answer.

Author’s Note: A common error is using the raw share count and nominal rights-issue price directly, without first computing the theoretical ex-rights fair value and applying the resulting adjustment factor to the pre-rights weighted average.

MTP January 2026 Set 1 · Q6(a) [OR-alt 2] · Marks: 4 · Approx Time: 8 minutes (approx.) · Topic 5.6: Diluted EPS from convertible debentures, with partly-paid shares weighted by proportion paid
Question:

On 1st April, 2025, ABC Limited: 50,000 equity shares of ₹100 each (₹80 paid up by all shareholders) ₹40,00,000; 2,00,000 8% Preference shares of ₹10 each ₹20,00,000; 10,000 12% Debentures of ₹100 each (each convertible into 3 equity shares of ₹100 each) ₹10,00,000. On 1st July 2025, remaining ₹20 called up and paid by all shareholders except one holding 10,000 equity shares. Profit after tax for 2025-26: ₹3,44,000. Tax rate 30%. Compute Basic and Diluted EPS.

Answer / Solution:

Basic EPS: Net profit attributable to equity = 3,44,000 − preference dividend (8% × 20,00,000 = 1,60,000) = 1,84,000. Weighted average equity shares: 1 Apr–30 Jun (50,000 shares × 80/100 paid × 3/12) = 10,000 + 1 Jul–31 Mar (40,000 fully-paid shares × 9/12) = 30,000 + (10,000 shares still ₹80-paid × 80/100 × 9/12) = 6,000; total = 46,000. Basic EPS = 1,84,000 / 46,000 = ₹4 per share.

Diluted EPS: Interest on 10,000 12% debentures = 1,20,000; tax relief @30% = 36,000; net interest add-back = 84,000. Adjusted net profit = 1,84,000 + 1,20,000 − 36,000 = 2,68,000. Shares from conversion (10,000 debentures × 3) = 30,000. Diluted shares = 46,000 + 30,000 = 76,000. Diluted EPS = 2,68,000 / 76,000 = ₹3.53 per share (approx).

Author’s Note: Some examinees forgot to add back the after-tax interest saving on the convertible debentures to net profit when computing diluted EPS, or omitted weighting the partly-paid shares by the proportion actually paid up.

MTP May 2025 Set 1 · Q6(c) · Marks: 5 · Approx Time: 9 minutes (approx.) · Topic 5.3: Weighted average number of shares - the effective date to use for shares issued under six different circumstances
Question:

In the following list of shares issued, for the purpose of calculation of weighted average number of shares, from which date, weight is to be considered:

  1. Equity Shares issued in exchange of cash,
  2. Equity Shares issued as a result of conversion of a debt instrument,
  3. Equity Shares issued in exchange for the settlement of a liability of the enterprise,
  4. Equity Shares issued for rendering of services to the enterprise,
  5. Equity Shares issued in lieu of interest and/or principal of an other financial instrument,
  6. Equity Shares issued as consideration for the acquisition of an asset other than in cash.
Answer / Solution:

The following dates should be considered for weights for the purpose of calculation of weighted average number of shares in the given situations:

  1. Date of Cash receivable
  2. Date of conversion
  3. Date on which settlement becomes effective
  4. When the services are rendered
  5. Date when interest ceases to accrue
  6. Date on which the acquisition is recognised.
Author’s Note: A common error is defaulting to "date of allotment" for every scenario, without distinguishing situations where AS 20 specifies a different effective date, e.g. shares issued in lieu of interest are weighted from when interest ceases to accrue, not the allotment date.

Question:

In the following list of shares issued, for the purpose of calculation of weighted average number of shares, from which date, weight is to be considered: (i) Equity Shares issued in exchange of cash, (ii) Equity Shares issued as a result of conversion of a debt instrument, (iii) Equity Shares issued in exchange for the settlement of a liability of the enterprise, (iv) Equity Shares issued for rendering of services to the enterprise, (v) Equity Shares issued in lieu of interest and/or principal of an other financial instrument, (vi) Equity Shares issued as consideration for the acquisition of an asset other than in cash. (5 Marks)

Answer / Solution:

(i) Date of Cash receivable. (ii) Date of conversion. (iii) Date on which settlement becomes effective. (iv) When the services are rendered. (v) Date when interest ceases to accrue. (vi) Date on which the acquisition is recognised.

Author’s Note: Many examinees used the date of the board resolution or agreement for several of these cases instead of the specific triggering event AS 20 identifies (e.g. date of conversion, date services are rendered), inflating or understating the weighted average share count.

PYQ January 2026 · Q1(c) · Marks: 5 · Approx Time: 9 minutes (approx.) · Topic 5.5: Rights issue with a bonus element - theoretical ex-rights value, adjustment factor, and restatement of the comparative year's EPS Compulsory
Question:

From the financial records of P Limited: Profit before tax FY2023-24 ₹25,00,000; FY2024-25 ₹32,50,000. Number of Equity Shares (Face Value ₹5) outstanding as on 31st March, 2024: 12,00,000. Applicable Tax Rate for both years: 20%. On 1st June, 2024, Directors announced a rights issue: 1 share for every 6 held @ ₹20/share, exercisable to 30th June, 2024, fully subscribed. Fair value of one equity share immediately prior to exercise of right (30th June, 2024) was ₹25.

You are required to calculate the Basic Earnings per Share to be reported in the financial statements of P Limited for the year ended 31st March, 2025, including the comparative figure for the year ended 31st March, 2024, in accordance with AS 20. (5 Marks)

Answer / Solution:

Computation of Basic Earnings Per Share (as per paragraphs 10 and 26 of AS 20):

Working Note 1 – Net Profit after tax (NPAT): 2024 = 25,00,000 − 20% tax = ₹20,00,000. 2025 = 32,50,000 − 20% tax = ₹26,00,000.

Working Note 2 – Theoretical ex-rights fair value per share: (Fair value of all outstanding shares immediately prior to rights + Total received from exercise) / (Shares outstanding prior + Shares issued in exercise) = (25×12,00,000 + 20×2,00,000) / (12,00,000+2,00,000) = 3,40,00,000/14,00,000 = ₹24.29.

Working Note 3 – Adjustment factor: Fair value per share prior to exercise / Theoretical ex-rights value = 25/24.29 = 1.029 (approx.).

ParticularsYear 2024 (₹)Year 2025 (₹)
EPS for the year 2024 as originally reported (20,00,000/12,00,000 shares)1.67
EPS for the year 2024 restated for rights issue [20,00,000/(12,00,000×1.029)] = 20,00,000/12,35,2801.62 (approx.)
EPS for the year 2025 including effects of rights issue: 26,00,000 / [(12,00,000×1.029×3/12)+(14,00,000×9/12)] = 26,00,000/13,58,700 shares1.91 (approx.)
Examiner’s Comment: Many examinees were unable to compute Earnings Per Share correctly in accordance with AS 20 "Earnings Per Share." A common error was the use of profit before tax instead of profit after tax for EPS calculation. Additionally, some examinees failed to determine the correct number of equity shares for computation. Mistakes were also observed in calculating profit after tax, the weighted average number of shares, and the bonus element in rights issues.

PYQ May 2024 · Q6(a) [OR-alt 2] · Marks: 4 · Approx Time: 8 minutes (approx.) · Topic 5.3/5.4/5.6-5.8: Basic EPS with a partly-paid-share weighting adjustment, and diluted EPS incorporating the as-if-converted effect of convertible debentures on both numerator (interest add-back net of tax) and denominator
Question:

OR

On 1 April 2023, ABC Limited has given the following information:

Particulars₹
50,000 equity shares of ₹100 each (₹80 paid up by all shareholders)40,00,000
2,00,000 8% Preference shares of ₹10 each20,00,000
10,000, 12% Debentures of ₹100 each (Each debenture is convertible into 3 equity shares of ₹100 each)10,00,000

On 1st July 2023, the remaining ₹20 was called up and paid by all the shareholders except one shareholder holding 10,000 equity shares. During the year 2023-24 the company had a profit after tax of ₹3,44,000. Tax rate is 30%.

You are required to compute Basic and Diluted EPS.

Answer / Solution:

Basic Earnings per share (EPS) = Net profit attributable to equity shareholders / Weighted average number of equity shares outstanding during the year = 1,84,000 / 46,000 Shares (as per working note) = ₹4 per share.

Diluted earnings per share

ParticularsAmount
Net profit for the current year₹3,44,000
No. of equity shares outstanding50,000
Basic earnings per share₹4
No. of 12% convertible debentures of ₹100 each; each debenture convertible into 3 equity shares10,000
Interest expense for the current year₹1,20,000
Tax relating to interest expense (30%)₹36,000
Adjusted net profit for the current year ₹(1,84,000 + 1,20,000 − 36,000)₹2,68,000
No. of equity shares resulting from conversion of debentures30,000
No. of equity shares used to compute diluted earnings per share46,000 + 30,000 = 76,000
Diluted earnings per share2,68,000 / 76,000 = ₹3.53

Working Notes

1. Net profit attributable to equity share holders = Net profit less preference dividends = ₹3,44,000 − ₹(8% x 20,00,000) = ₹3,44,000 − ₹1,60,000 = ₹1,84,000.

2. Calculation of weighted average number of equity shares

As per AS 20 'Earnings Per Share', partly paid equity shares are treated as a fraction of equity share to the extent that they were entitled to participate in dividend relative to a fully paid equity share during the reporting period. Assuming that the partly paid shares are entitled to participate in the dividend to the extent of amount paid, weighted average number of shares will be calculated as follows:

DateNo. of equity sharesAmount paid per share (₹)Weighted average no. of equity shares (₹)
01.04.202350,0008050,000 x 80/100 x 3/12 = 10,000
01.07.202340,00010040,000 x 9/12 = 30,000
01.07.202310,0008010,000 x 80/100 x 9/12 = 6,000
Total weighted average equity shares46,000
Examiner’s Comment: In the AS 20 question, some examinees could not calculate the number of shares and also made mistake in calculating net profit.

RTP January 2025 · Q15 · Marks: Not stated in source · Approx Time: 10–20 minutes (approx.) · Topic 5.9: Anti-dilutive potential equity shares (those that would decrease loss per share) are excluded from diluted EPS
Question:

XYZ Limited has a wholly owned subsidiary BC Limited. The Group prepares consolidated Financial Statements for the year ended 31st March, 2024. XYZ Limited (in its separate financial statements) has incurred a loss of ₹2 crore during the year, while the consolidated profit for the group during the year is ₹40 lakh.

XYZ Limited has 5,00,000 shares outstanding as at 31st March, 2024. Further, it has granted options to issue equity shares as at that date. In respect of such options, 1,00,000 shares are considered to be the shares issued for no consideration. There are no changes in income or expenses that are expected from the issue of equity shares on exercise of these options.

Calculate Basic and Diluted EPS for XYZ Limited for separate financial statements and for the Group.

Answer / Solution:

Computation of earnings per share

ParticularsConsolidated financial statementsStandalone financial statements of XYZ Limited
Basic earnings/(loss) per share₹8 [40,00,000/5,00,000](₹40) [2,00,00,000/5,00,000]
Diluted earnings/(loss) per share₹6.66 [40,00,000/6,00,000](₹40) [2,00,00,000/5,00,000]

As per paragraph 39 of AS 20, "Potential equity shares should be treated as dilutive when, and only when, their conversion to equity shares would decrease net profit per share from continuing ordinary operations."

In the above case, if the exercise of options was considered for the separate financial statements of XYZ Limited, the diluted loss per share would have reduced to ₹33.33 [2,00,00,000/6,00,000]. As this is anti-dilutive, the options would not be treated as potentially dilutive equity shares. Accordingly, in the separate financial statements of XYZ Limited, the Diluted EPS would be the same as Basic EPS.

Author’s Note: A common error is including the anti-dilutive effect of the share options in the standalone diluted EPS computation because it appears to reduce the reported loss per share, missing that AS 20 requires potential equity shares to be excluded from diluted EPS whenever their inclusion would be anti-dilutive from the standpoint of continuing ordinary operations.

RTP January 2026 · Q16 · Marks: Not stated in source · Approx Time: 10–20 minutes (approx.) · Topic 5.2: Mandatory-reserve appropriations remain attributable to equity shareholders and are not excluded from the EPS numerator
Question:

Should appropriation to mandatory reserves be excluded from net profit attributable to equity shareholders? AB Limited must, per an agreement with debenture holders, appropriate profits each year to a specific reserve such that, at redemption, the reserve equals at least half the debenture value. Since these appropriations aren't available for distribution to equity shareholders, AB Limited excluded them from the Basic EPS numerator. Is this correct?

Answer / Solution:

The appropriation to such a mandatory reserve should be included in net profit attributable to equity shareholders for computing Basic EPS — AB Limited's treatment is not correct.

AS 20 para 11 defines the numerator as net profit/loss for the period "attributable to equity shareholders" — after deducting preference dividends and attributable tax, but nothing else. Emphasis on "attributable to equity shareholders" (not "available for distribution") means amounts appropriated to mandatory reserves, though not distributable as dividend, remain attributable to equity shareholders in substance (the reserve still belongs to them, merely earmarked). They should therefore be included in the Basic EPS computation.

Author’s Note: Some examinees conflated "attributable to equity shareholders" with "distributable to equity shareholders," incorrectly excluding non-distributable mandatory-reserve appropriations from the EPS numerator.

RTP May 2025 · Q19 · Marks: Not stated in source · Approx Time: 10–20 minutes (approx.) · Topic 5.6-5.8: Diluted EPS: numerator add-back of post-tax interest on dilutive convertible debentures, denominator inclusion of shares issuable on conversion
Question:

The following information relates to XYZ Limited for the year ended 31st March, 2024: Net Profit for the year after tax: ₹37,50,000. Number of Equity Shares of ₹10 each outstanding: 5,00,000. Convertible Debentures issued by the Company (at the beginning of the year):

ParticularsNos.
8% Convertible Debentures of ₹100 each50,000
Equity Shares to be issued on conversion55,000

The Rate of Income Tax: 30%. You are required to calculate Basic and Diluted Earnings Per Share (EPS).

Answer / Solution:

Basic EPS = Net profit for the current year / Weighted average number of equity shares outstanding = ₹37,50,000 / 5,00,000 = ₹7.50 per share.

Diluted EPS = Adjusted net profit for the current year / Weighted average number of equity shares (including dilutive potential equity shares):

Adjusted net profit for the current year₹
Net profit for the current year37,50,000
Add: Interest expense for the current year (8% × ₹50,00,000 face value)4,00,000
Less: Tax relating to interest expense (30% of ₹4,00,000)(1,20,000)
Adjusted net profit for the current year40,30,000

Number of equity shares resulting from conversion of debentures = 55,000 (given in the question). Weighted average number of equity shares for diluted EPS = 5,00,000 + 55,000 = 5,55,000 shares.

Diluted EPS = ₹40,30,000 / 5,55,000 = ₹7.26 per share.

Note: Conversion of the convertible debentures into equity shares is a dilutive potential equity share. To compute the adjusted profit, the (post-tax) interest paid on the debentures is added back, since it would not be payable if the debentures were converted into equity shares.

Author’s Note: A common error is adding back the full pre-tax interest expense to the numerator without deducting the related tax effect, overstating the adjusted net profit used for diluted EPS.

RTP September 2024 · Q14 · Marks: Not stated in source · Approx Time: 10–20 minutes (approx.) · Topic 5.5: Rights issue EPS restatement using the theoretical ex-rights fair value adjustment factor
Question:

The following information is available in respect of High-end Ltd. for the accounting year 2022-2023 and 2023-2024:

Net profit for₹
Year2022-202322,00,000
Year2023-202430,00,000

Number of shares outstanding prior to right issue 10,00,000 shares.

Right issue: One new share for each five shares outstanding i.e. 2,00,000 shares.

: Right issue price ₹25

: Last date to exercise right 31st July, 2023.

Fair value of one equity share immediately prior to exercise of rights on 31.07.2023 is ₹32.

You are required to compute, as per AS 20:

  1. Basic earnings per share for the year 2022-2023.
  2. Restated basic earnings per share for the year 2022-20223 for right issue.
  3. Basic earnings per share for the year 2023-2024.
Answer / Solution:

Computation of basic earnings per share

2022-2023 (₹)2023-2024 (₹)
EPS for the year 2022-2023 as originally reported = Net profit for the year attributable to equity shareholders / weighted average number of equity shares outstanding during the year = ₹22,00,000 / 10,00,000 shares2.20
EPS for the year 2022-2023 restated for the right issue = ₹22,00,000 / (10,00,000 × 1.04)2.12
EPS for the year 2023-2024 (including effect of right issue) = ₹30,00,000 / {(10,00,000 × 1.04 × 4/12) + (12,00,000 × 8/12)}2.62

Working Notes:

  1. Computation of theoretical ex-rights fair value per share = (fair value of all outstanding shares immediately prior to exercise of rights + Total value received from exercise of rights) / (number of shares outstanding prior to exercise + number of shares issued on the exercise)
    = (₹32 × 10,00,000 + ₹25 × 2,00,000) / (10,00,000 + 2,00,000)
    = ₹30.83
  2. Computation of adjustment factor
    = Fair value per share prior to exercise of rights / Theoretical ex-right value per share
    = ₹32/₹30.83
    = 1.04 (approx.)
Author’s Note: A common error is applying the rights-issue adjustment factor only to the current year's weighted average share count and forgetting to restate the prior year's (2022-2023) EPS by the same factor for comparability.

MTP May 2023 Set 2 · Q1(b) · Marks: 5 · Approx Time: 9 minutes (approx.) · Topic n/a: Change in basis of estimating a provision is a change in accounting estimate, not a change in accounting policy; materiality and disclosure Compulsory
Question:

HIL Ltd. was making provision for non-moving stocks based on no issues having occurred for the last 12 months upto 31.03.2021. The company now wants to change it and make provision based on technical evaluation during the year ending 31.03.2022. Total value of stock on 31.3.2022 is ₹120 lakhs. Provision required based on technical evaluation amounts ₹3.00 lakhs. However, provision required based on 12 months (no issues) is ₹4.00 lakhs. You are required to discuss the following points in the light of Accounting Standard (AS)-1: (i) Does this amount to change in accounting policy? (ii) Can the company change the method of accounting? (iii) Explain how it will be disclosed in the annual accounts of HIL Ltd. for the year 2021-2022.

Answer / Solution:

The decision of making provision for non-moving inventories on the basis of technical evaluation does not amount to change in accounting policy. Accounting policy of a company may require that provision for non-moving inventories should be made but the basis for making provision will not constitute accounting policy. The method of estimating the amount of provision may be changed in case a more prudent estimate can be made.

In the given case, considering the total value of inventory, the change in the amount of required provision of non-moving inventory from ₹4 lakhs to ₹3 lakhs is also not material. The disclosure can be made for such change in the following lines by way of notes to the accounts in the annual accounts of HIL Ltd. for the year 2021-22 in the following manner:

"The company has provided for non-moving inventories on the basis of technical evaluation unlike preceding years. Had the same method been followed as in the previous year, the profit for the year and the value of net assets at the end of the year would have been lower by ₹1 lakh."

Author’s Note: A common error is treating a change in the basis of estimating a provision (technical evaluation vs. the historical no-issues test) as a change in accounting policy requiring retrospective restatement, rather than recognising it as a change in accounting estimate needing only prospective disclosure.
