MTP May 2026 Set 1 · Q6(b) · Marks: 5 · Approx Time: 9 minutes (approx.) · Topic n/a: Disclosure cannot cure an incorrect accounting treatment; disclosure of material policy changes
Question:

Discuss Disclosure requirements in following cases as per AS 1.
(i) Accountant of A Ltd. charges a probable loss of losing a suit in books of accounts and also disclosed the same fact in financial statements. The probability of losing the suit is 25%.
(ii) Accountant of A Ltd. capitalized all the revenue expenses of repair and maintenance during the year to Plant & Machinery and is also disclosing the same as company policy in financial statements.
(iii) A Ltd. has followed accrual basis of accounting since incorporation. The chief accountant also disclosed this fact in financial statements.
(iv) A Ltd. was providing for after sales expenses @ 2% of sales for covering expenses during the warranty period. Now A Ltd. observes that actual after sales expenses were much less as compared to provision because of better technology used in manufacturing of the products. Now, the Board of A Ltd. decides to account for these expenses as and when they occur. Sales during the period are ₹50 crores. (5 Marks)

Answer / Solution:

(i) In this case, accountant of company created a provision for damages of probability of losing a suit by a charge against profits. Unless the probability of losing the suit is more than probability of not losing it, there should not be any creation of provision for such probable losses. So there is no need to charge such loss against profit and disclosing the same in financial statements.

(ii) Repairs and maintenance are revenue expenditure and should not be added to the value of assets, as these expenses do not increase the capacity of asset. Hence such expenses should be charged to profit & loss statement. Further the chief accountant also disclosed its policy of adding repairs to value of assets by way of notes to accounts. As per AS 1 disclosure is not a method to correct the wrong treatments. So the contention of chief accountant is wrong.

(iii) Accrual is one of the Fundamental accounting assumptions. If fundamental accounting assumptions are followed properly then no specific disclosure is required. Disclosure is required only when there is deviation and the company is not following fundamental accounting assumptions. So the company need not disclose this in financial statements.

(iv) As per AS 1, any change in the accounting policies which has a material effect in the current period or which is reasonably expected to have a material effect in later periods should be disclosed. Accordingly, the notes on accounts should properly disclose the change and its effect.

Note: So far, the company has been providing 2% of sales for meeting after sales expenses during the warranty period. Now the company has improved the quality of its products with better technology and has been observing that actual expenses are very less than the provision, Hence, the company has decided not to make provision for such expenses but to account for the same as and when expenses are incurred. Due to this change, the profit for the year is increased by ₹1 crore than would have been the case if the old policy were to continue.

Author’s Note: Several examinees agreed with the accountant's policy of capitalising repairs and maintenance merely because it had been disclosed as an accounting policy, not recognising that disclosure under AS 1 cannot cure a treatment that is otherwise incorrect.

MTP November 2023 Set 2 · Q1(d) · Marks: 5 · Approx Time: 9 minutes (approx.) · Topic n/a: Fundamental accounting assumptions (Going Concern, Consistency, Accrual) presumed and not usually separately disclosed unless not followed; disclosure of all significant accounting policies at one place; disclosure of material changes in accounting policy including where the effect is not ascertainable Compulsory
Question:

State whether the following statements are 'True' or 'False' in line with the provisions of AS 1. Also give reason for your answer.

  1. Certain fundamental accounting assumptions underline the preparation and presentation of financial statements. They are usually specifically stated because their acceptance and use are not assumed.
  2. If fundamental accounting assumptions are not followed in presentation and preparation of financial statements, a specific disclosure is not required.
  3. All significant accounting policies adopted in the preparation and presentation of financial statements should form part of the financial statements.
  4. Any change in an accounting policy, which has a material effect should be disclosed. Where the amount by which any item in the financial statements is affected by such change is not ascertainable, wholly or in part, the fact need not to be indicated.
  5. There is no single list of accounting policies which are applicable to all circumstances.
Answer / Solution:
  1. False; As per AS 1 “Disclosure of Accounting Policies”, certain fundamental accounting assumptions underlie the preparation and presentation of financial statements. They are usually not specifically stated because their acceptance and use are assumed. Disclosure is necessary if they are not followed.
  2. False; As per AS 1, if the fundamental accounting assumptions, viz. Going Concern, Consistency and Accrual are followed in financial statements, specific disclosure is not required. If a fundamental accounting assumption is not followed, the fact should be disclosed.
  3. True; To ensure proper understanding of financial statements, it is necessary that all significant accounting policies adopted in the preparation and presentation of financial statements should be disclosed. The disclosure of the significant accounting policies as such should form part of the financial statements and they should be disclosed at one place.
  4. False; Any change in the accounting policies which has a material effect in the current period or which is reasonably expected to have a material effect in later periods should be disclosed. Where such amount is not ascertainable, wholly or in part, the fact should be indicated.
  5. True; As per AS 1, there is no single list of accounting policies which are applicable to all circumstances. The differing circumstances in which enterprises operate in a situation of diverse and complex economic activity make alternative accounting principles and methods of applying those principles acceptable.
Author’s Note: A common error is inverting statements (i) and (ii), reasoning that fundamental accounting assumptions must be specifically stated precisely because they are so foundational, when AS 1's actual rule is the opposite – they are presumed and go unstated unless departed from, at which point disclosure becomes mandatory.

Question:

Given below is the Balance Sheet of Sky and Associates as on 31st March, 2023:

(2) The sale and purchase of the firm for the year 2023-24 amounts to ₹8,20,000 and ₹6,50,000 respectively. (3) The value of Closing Stock as on 31-3-2024 was ₹65,000. The net realizable value is estimated at 120% of cost. (4) Other expenses for the period amount to ₹25,000. (5) Deferred expenditure is getting amortized over 5 years starting from 31-3-2022. (6) The remaining life of Machinery is expected to be 3 years. The realizable value of Machine is expected at ₹1,65,000, an expense of ₹5,000 is to be incurred to realize the same. (7) Out of trade receivables, ₹5,000 is expected to be unrealizable due to an ongoing dispute. (8) Bank has charged a penalty of ₹2,500 for crossing the overdraft limit. (9) The lender has agreed to forgo 50% of interest charge for the year. (10) The firm is expecting a discount of ₹4,000 from creditors at the time of full and final settlement.

You are required to prepare a Profit & Loss A/c for the year ended 31st March, 2024 to ascertain its Profit/Loss for the period. (4 Marks)

Answer / Solution:

Profit and Loss Account of Sky & Associates for the year ended 31st March, 2024

Particulars₹Particulars₹
To Opening Stock1,15,000By Sales8,20,000
To Purchases6,50,000By Closing Stock78,000
To Gross Profit*1,33,000
Total8,98,000Total8,98,000
To Deferred Expense9,000By Gross Profit1,33,000
To Other Expenses25,000By Discount4,000
To Bad Debts5,000
To Penalty2,500
To Depreciation (1,80,000 − 1,60,000)20,000
To Interest on loan1,600
To Net Profit73,900
Total1,37,000Total1,37,000

*Closing Stock ₹65,000 written down to net realisable value; Machinery restated to its net realisable value of ₹1,80,000 − ₹5,000 (cost to realise) = ₹1,60,000 (i.e. ₹1,65,000 less the ₹5,000 cost to realise), a ₹20,000 reduction from the ₹1,80,000 book value, reflecting that since the firm is not a going concern, assets are stated at realisable rather than historical-cost values.

Author’s Note: Some examinees prepared this Profit & Loss Account on the usual historical-cost/going-concern basis, missing that the firm's planned shutdown from 1st April, 2024 required Machinery and Closing Stock to be restated to realisable value rather than carried at cost or the lower-of-cost-and-NRV rule used for an ongoing business.

PYQ May 2023 · Q6(a) · Marks: 5 · Approx Time: 9 minutes (approx.) · Topic n/a: Substance over form, fundamental accounting assumptions (accrual), and disclosure not being a remedy for non-compliance
Question:

You are required to comment on the following cases as per the provisions of Accounting Standard-1 ‘Disclosure of Accounting Policies’:

(1) Bee Limited has not complied with AS-2 "Valuation of inventories" and the same is disclosed in the Notes on Accounts. Management is of the view that the financial statements give a true and fair view as non-compliance with AS-2 is disclosed.

(2) Cee Limited sold its Office Building for ₹10,00,000 on 1st March, 2023. The buyer has paid the full amount and taken possession of the building. The book value of the Office Building is ₹4,00,000. On 31st March 2023, documentation and legal formalities are pending. The company has not recorded the disposal and the amount received is shown as an advance.

(3) Dee Limited has prepared its accounts on cash basis and the same is not disclosed.

(4) Jee Limited disclosed significant accounting policies adopted in the preparation of financial statements, in the Directors' Report. (5 Marks)

Answer / Solution:

(1) As per AS-I disclosure of accounting policies is not a remedy for wrong or inappropriate treatment in accounting. In the given case the financial statement does not give a true and fair view as they are not in compliance with AS-2.

(2) Considering the substance over form as per AS-I, documentation and legal formalities represent the form of the transaction, although the legal title has not been transferred, the economic reality and substance are that the rights and beneficial interest in the Office Building have been transferred. Therefore, recording of acquisition/disposal (by the transferee and transferor respectively) would in substance represent the transaction entered into.

(3) Accrual is a fundamental accounting assumption. If it is not followed by the company, the facts should be disclosed under AS-I. Hence the company should disclose the fact that the cash basis of accounting has been followed in the notes on accounts.

(4) The practice followed by the company is not correct. It should be disclosed as part of financial statements (The director's report is not part of financial statements).

Author’s Note: A number of examinees, when asked to comment on the AS 1 disclosure scenarios, incorrectly concluded that disclosing a departure from a specific standard such as AS 2 in the notes cures the non-compliance and preserves a true-and-fair view, not recognising that AS 1 disclosure is a transparency requirement and never a substitute for correct accounting treatment. Some also failed to identify that accounting policy disclosure belongs in the financial statements themselves, not the Directors' Report.

PYQ November 2023 · Q5(b) · Marks: 5 · Approx Time: 9 minutes (approx.) · Topic unindexed: Disclosure requirements across four illustrations: a sub-probable contingent loss, mis-stated capitalisation policy disclosed rather than corrected, disclosure of a followed fundamental accounting assumption, and disclosure of a material accounting-policy change
Question:

Discuss Disclosure requirements in following cases as per AS 1:

(i) Accountant of A Ltd. charges a probable loss of losing a suit in books of accounts and also disclosed the same fact in financial statements. The probability of losing the suit is 25%.

(ii) Accountant of A Ltd. capitalized all the revenue expenses of repair and maintenance during the year to Plant & Machinery and is also disclosing the same as company policy in financial statements.

(iii) A Ltd. has followed accrual basis of accounting since incorporation. The chief accountant also disclosed this fact in financial statements.

(iv) A Ltd. was providing for after sales expenses @ 2% of sales for covering expenses during the warranty period. Now A Ltd. observes that actual after sales expenses were much less as compared to provision because of better technology used in manufacturing of the products. Now, the Board of A Ltd. decides to account for these expenses as and when they occur. Sales during the period are ₹50 crores. (15 + 5 = 20 Marks)

Answer / Solution:

(i) In this case, accountant of company created a provision for damages of probability of losing a suit by a charge against profits. Unless the probability of losing the suit is more than the probability of not losing it, there should not be any creation of provision for such probable losses. So there is no need to charge such loss against profit and disclosing the same in financial statements.

(ii) Repairs and maintenance are revenue expenditure and should not be added to the value of assets, as these expenses do not increase the capacity of asset. Hence such expenses should be charged to profit & loss statement. Further the chief accountant also disclosed its policy of adding repairs to value of assets by way of notes to accounts. As per AS 1 disclosure is not a method to correct the wrong treatments. So the contention of chief accountant is wrong.

(iii) Accrual is one of the Fundamental accounting assumptions. If fundamental accounting assumptions are followed properly then no specific disclosure is required. Disclosure is required only when there is deviation and the company is not following fundamental accounting assumptions. So the company need not disclose this in financial statements.

(iv) As per AS 1, any change in the accounting policies which has a material effect in the current period or which is reasonably expected to have a material effect in later periods should be disclosed. Accordingly, the notes on accounts should properly disclose the change and its effect.

Note: So far, the company has been providing 2% of sales for meeting after sales expenses during the warranty period. Now the company has improved the quality of its products with better technology and has been observing that actual expenses are very less than the provision, hence, the company has decided not to make provision for such expenses but to account for the same as and when expenses are incurred. Due to this change, the profit for the year is increased by ₹1 crore than would have been the case if the old policy were to continue.

Author’s Note: Some examinees, in part (i), incorrectly concluded that disclosing the probable loss in the financial statements was sufficient without first questioning whether a provision should have been recognised at all, given the disputed suit had only a 25% probability of being lost. In part (ii), several examinees accepted the chief accountant's own disclosure of the wrong capitalisation policy as adequate compliance, missing AS 1's rule that disclosure is never a substitute for correcting a treatment that is itself wrong. In part (iv), many examinees failed to recognise that a material change expected to affect future periods still requires disclosure of the change and its effect, even though no restatement of prior years was needed.

RTP January 2025 · Q3 · Marks: Not stated in source · Approx Time: 10–20 minutes (approx.) ·
Question:

ABC Ltd. was making provision for non-moving inventories based on no issues for the last 12 months up to 31.3.2023. The company wants to provide during the year ending 31.3.2024 based on technical evaluation:

Total value of inventory₹100 lakhs
Provision required based on 12 months issue₹3.5 lakhs
Provision required based on technical evaluation₹2.5 lakhs

Does this amount to change in Accounting Policy? Can the company change the method of provision?

Answer / Solution:

The decision of making provision for non-moving inventories on the basis of technical evaluation does not amount to a change in accounting policy. Accounting policy of a company may require that provision for non-moving inventories should be made; the method of estimating the amount of provision may be changed in case a more prudent estimate can be made — this is a change in accounting estimate, not a change in accounting policy.

In the given case, considering the total value of inventory, the change in the amount of required provision of non-moving inventory from ₹3.5 lakhs to ₹2.5 lakhs is also not material. The disclosure can be made for such change in the following lines by way of notes to the accounts in the annual accounts of ABC Ltd. for the year 2023-24:

"The company has provided for non-moving inventories on the basis of technical evaluation unlike preceding years. Had the same method been followed as in the previous year, the profit for the year and the corresponding effect on the year end net assets would have been lower by ₹1 lakh."

Author’s Note: A common error is treating a switch to a more scientifically-grounded estimation basis (technical evaluation) for an existing provision as a change in accounting policy requiring restatement, rather than recognising it as a change in accounting estimate, applied prospectively with disclosure only if material.

RTP May 2025 · Q4 · Marks: Not stated in source · Approx Time: 10–20 minutes (approx.) · Definition of 'Accrual' and the rationale for accrual-basis accounting
Question:

What do you mean by 'Accrual' in reference to AS-1? Also, specify any three reasons for 'Accrual Basis of Accounting'.

Answer / Solution:

The term "Accrual" has been explained in AS 1 on Disclosure of Accounting Policies, as "Revenues and costs are accrued, that is, recognised as they are earned or incurred (and not as money is received or paid) and recorded in the financial statements of the periods to which they relate."

Reasons for Accrual Basis of Accounting (any three):

  1. Accrual basis of accounting attempts to record the financial effects of the transactions, events, and circumstances of an enterprise in the period in which they occur, rather than recording them in the period(s) in which cash is received or paid by the enterprise.
  2. Receipts and payments of the period will not coincide with the buying, producing or selling events and other economic events that affect entity performance.
  3. The goal of accrual basis of accounting is to follow the matching concept of income and expenditure so that reported net income measures an enterprise's performance during a period instead of merely listing its cash receipts and payments.
  4. Accrual basis of accounting recognizes assets, liabilities or components of revenues and expenses for amounts received or paid in cash in the past, and amounts expected to be received or paid in cash in the future.
  5. An important point of difference between accrual accounting and accounting based on cash receipts and outlay is the timing of recognition of revenues, expenses, gains and losses.
Author’s Note: A common error here is reciting a generic textbook definition of accrual accounting rather than AS 1's own precise wording, and listing reasons that describe accounting standards generally instead of accrual accounting specifically.

RTP September 2025 · Q5 · Marks: Not stated in source · Approx Time: 10–20 minutes (approx.) · Topic 1.5: Disclosure requirements for accounting policy changes and the limits of a materiality-based non-disclosure defence
Question:

Lion Ltd. (manufacturing/construction contracts), FY ended 31st March 2025, follows historical cost, FIFO, and percentage-of-completion. During the year, management changes: (i) inventory valuation FIFO→Weighted Average (citing raw-material price volatility); (ii) depreciation SLM→WDV (citing better usage reflection). The company discloses the inventory-method change in notes but not the depreciation-method change (calling it immaterial), and has not disclosed its accounting policy on government grants despite receiving a significant subsidy this year. (a) Identify AS 1 violations, if any. (b) Critically evaluate whether "materiality" justifies non-disclosure of a change in accounting policy. (c) Is the FIFO→Weighted Average change an estimate or policy change under AS 1?

Answer / Solution:

(a) AS 1 requires all significant accounting policies to be disclosed, and any material change in policy to be disclosed along with its nature and reasons (with the effect indicated if ascertainable). Applying this: (1) Inventory method change (FIFO→Weighted Average) is a change in accounting policy, correctly disclosed with justification — compliant, provided the quantified effect is also disclosed or noted as unascertainable. (2) Depreciation method change (SLM→WDV) is technically a change in accounting estimate under AS 10, but AS 1 still requires disclosure of material items affecting the financial statements — depreciation affects profit, asset values, and return ratios; non-disclosure on unsubstantiated "immateriality" grounds is not appropriate without clear quantitative evidence. (3) Government grants policy non-disclosure: AS 1 requires disclosure of all significant accounting policies, including for government grants received — non-disclosure here is a violation of AS 1.

(b) Materiality is assessed by an item's potential to influence users' economic decisions. A depreciation-method change affects profit, asset values, and tax, and even a quantitatively modest impact may carry qualitative significance for comparability/trend analysis. The company's blanket reliance on "materiality" to justify non-disclosure is not valid unless supported by concrete evidence that the impact is immaterial both quantitatively and qualitatively.

(c) The change from FIFO to Weighted Average is a change in accounting policy (not a change in accounting estimate) — it is a change in the cost formula used to measure inventory, and its nature and financial impact should be properly disclosed.

Author’s Note: Some examinees classified the depreciation-method change purely as an "estimate change" and concluded no AS 1 disclosure duty arose at all, missing that AS 1's materiality-based disclosure requirement applies regardless of whether the underlying item is technically a policy or an estimate change.

MTP January 2025 Set 1 · Q6(a) [OR-alt 2] · Marks: 4 · Approx Time: 8 minutes (approx.) · Topic 1.5: Schedule III bonus-share disclosure requirement - source of a bonus issue is not mandated to be disclosed
Question:

In the financial statements of the financial year 2023-2024, Alpha Ltd. has mentioned in the notes to accounts that during financial year, 24,000 equity shares of ₹10 each were issued as fully paid bonus shares. However, the source from which these bonus shares were issued has not been disclosed. Is such non-disclosure a violation of the Schedule III to the Companies Act? Comment.

Answer / Solution:

Schedule III has come into force for the Balance Sheet and Profit and Loss Account prepared for the financial year commencing on or after 1st April, 2023. As per Part I of the Schedule III, a company should, inter alia, disclose in notes to accounts for the period of 5 years immediately preceding the balance sheet date (31st March, 2024 in the instant case) the aggregate number and class of shares allotted as fully paid-up bonus shares. Schedule III does not require a company to disclose the source from which bonus shares have been issued. Therefore, non-disclosure of source from which bonus shares have been issued does not violate the Schedule III to the Companies Act.

Author’s Note: A frequent misconception is assuming Schedule III requires disclosure of the specific reserve a bonus issue was funded from, when only the aggregate number and class of bonus shares over the preceding five years must be disclosed.

Question:

Trial Balance of AT Ltd as on 31st March, 2025 (₹'000): Land at Cost 148 Dr.; Plant & Machinery at Cost 520 Dr.; Debtors 65 Dr.; Closing Stock 58 Dr.; Bank 14 Dr.; Adjusted Purchases 226 Dr.; Factory Expenses 40 Dr.; Administration Expenses 22 Dr.; Selling Expenses 20 Dr.; Debenture Interest 14 Dr. — Equity Share of ₹10 each 200 Cr.; 10% Debenture of ₹100 each 135 Cr.; General Reserve 90 Cr.; Profit & Loss A/c 48 Cr.; Security Premium 27 Cr.; Sales 473 Cr.; Creditors 35 Cr.; Provision for Depreciation 116 Cr.; Suspense A/c 3 Cr. Prepare Statement of Profit & Loss and Balance Sheet as per the Companies Act, 2013 (ignore previous year figures).

Answer / Solution:

Statement of Profit and Loss for the year ended 31st March, 2025 (₹ in '000):

MTP January 2026 Set 1 · Q6(b) · Marks: 4 · Approx Time: 8 minutes (approx.) · Topic 1.6: Declaration of dividend out of accumulated reserves - three-condition test under the Dividend Rules
Question:

Z Limited as on 31st March, 2024: Equity shares of ₹100 each ₹500 lakhs; General Reserve ₹100 lakhs; Loss for the year ₹5 lakhs. Due to absence of profits, management recommends a 10% dividend on equity share capital out of general reserve. Rates of equity dividend for the last 5 years preceding 2023-24: 2022-23 12%, 2021-22 14%, 2020-21 10%, 2019-20 10%, 2018-19 7%. As an accountant, suggest whether the recommendation is justified; if not, suggest the rate of dividend.

Answer / Solution:

Three conditions govern declaring dividend out of free reserves (Companies (Declaration and Payment of Dividend) Rules): (1) Rate ≤ average rate of last 3 years: 10% < 12% [(12+14+10)/3] — satisfied. (2) Amount drawn ≤ 10% of (paid-up capital + free reserves): 55,00,000 drawn (10% dividend 50,00,000 + loss 5,00,000) vs. maximum 60,00,000 [10% of (500+100) lakhs] — satisfied. (3) Reserves after withdrawal ≥ 15% of paid-up capital: balance after withdrawal (100−55=45 lakhs) is less than 75 lakhs (15% of 500 lakhs) — not satisfied.

Since condition (3) fails, the 10% recommendation is not justified. Maximum permissible withdrawal = opening reserves (100 lakhs) − minimum reserves to retain (75 lakhs, i.e. 15% of paid-up capital) = 25 lakhs; less current year's loss (5 lakhs) = 20 lakhs maximum divisible profit. Permissible dividend rate = 20,00,000 / 5,00,00,000 = 4%.

Author’s Note: Some examinees checked only the rate-cap and amount-cap conditions, missing the third condition (post-withdrawal reserves must remain at least 15% of paid-up capital), which is the one that actually fails here.

MTP September 2024 Set 2 · Q6(a) [OR-alt 2] · Marks: 4 · Approx Time: 8 minutes (approx.) · Topic 1.6: Dividend from accumulated reserves under the Companies (Declaration and Payment of Dividend) Rules, 2014 - three conditions
Question:

XYZ Ltd. proposes to declare 10% dividend out of General Reserves due to inadequacy of profits in the year ending 31-03-2024. From the following particulars ascertain the amount that can be utilized from general reserves, according to the Companies Rules, 2014: 8,00,000 Equity Shares of ₹10 each fully paid up ₹80,00,000; General Reserves ₹25,00,000; Revaluation Reserves ₹6,50,000; Net profit for the year ₹1,42,500. Average rate of dividend during the last five years has been 12%.

Answer / Solution:

Amount required for 10% dividend on ₹80,00,000 = ₹8,00,000. Profit available for the current year = ₹1,42,500. Amount to be utilized from reserves = ₹8,00,000 − ₹1,42,500 = ₹6,57,500.

Conditions as per Companies (Declaration and Payment of Dividend) Rules, 2014:

Condition I: since the proposed rate (10%) is lower than the average rate of dividend over the last five years (12%), a 10% dividend can be declared.

Condition II: the maximum amount that can be drawn from accumulated profits and reserves must not exceed 10% of paid-up capital plus free reserves = 10% × (₹80,00,000 + ₹25,00,000) = ₹10,50,000 — the required ₹6,57,500 is within this cap.

Condition III: the balance of reserves after the drawal, ₹18,42,500 (₹25,00,000 − ₹6,57,500), must not fall below 15% of paid-up capital, i.e. ₹12,00,000 (15% of ₹80,00,000) — satisfied.

All three conditions being satisfied, XYZ Ltd. can withdraw ₹6,57,500 from the accumulated General Reserve. (Revaluation Reserve, not being a free reserve, is not counted in this computation.)

Author’s Note: A common error here is including the Revaluation Reserve as part of free reserves when applying the three conditions, when it is explicitly excluded because it represents an unrealised, notional gain.

MTP September 2025 Set 1 · Q6(a) [OR-alt 2] · Marks: 4 · Approx Time: 8 minutes (approx.) · Topic 1.5: Schedule III bonus-share disclosure requirement (aggregate number/class only, not source)
Question:

In the financial statements of the financial year 2023-2024, Alpha Ltd. has mentioned in the notes to accounts that during financial year, 24,000 equity shares of ₹10 each were issued as fully paid bonus shares. However, the source from which these bonus shares were issued has not been disclosed. Is such non-disclosure a violation of the Schedule III to the Companies Act? Comment.

Answer / Solution:

Schedule III has come into force for the Balance Sheet and Profit and Loss Account prepared for the financial year commencing on or after 1st April, 2023. As per Part I of the Schedule III, a company should, inter alia, disclose in notes to accounts for the period of 5 years immediately preceding the balance sheet date (31st March, 2024 in the instant case) the aggregate number and class of shares allotted as fully paid-up bonus shares. Schedule III does not require a company to disclose the source from which bonus shares have been issued. Therefore, non-disclosure of source from which bonus shares have been issued does not violate the Schedule III to the Companies Act.

Author’s Note: A common error here is assuming that Schedule III requires disclosure of the source from which bonus shares were issued, when the actual requirement is limited to disclosing the aggregate number and class of bonus shares allotted in the preceding five years.

PYQ January 2026 · Q6(b) · Marks: 4 · Approx Time: 8 minutes (approx.) · Topic 1.6: Three-condition test for declaring dividend out of accumulated reserves - rate cap, 10% draw-down limit, 15% minimum residual reserve balance
Question:

Figures from the financial statements of MC Limited for the year ended 31st March, 2025: Issued, Subscribed and Paid-up Share Capital – 8,00,000 Equity Shares of ₹5 each ₹40,00,000; 1,25,000, 8% Preference Shares of ₹10 each ₹12,50,000. Reserves and Surplus – Securities Premium Reserve ₹5,00,000; Capital Reserve ₹3,00,000; Capital Redemption Reserve ₹2,50,000; General Reserve ₹11,75,000. Net Profit for 2024-25 ₹2,25,000. Equity Dividend paid: 2019-20 10%, 2020-21 11%, 2021-22 12%, 2022-23 13%, 2023-24 14%. Constrained by inadequate profits in 2024-25, management proposes a dividend of 12.5% out of reserves.

You are required to ascertain the amount that can be utilized by the company out of its reserves in accordance with the Companies (Declaration of dividend out of Reserves) Rules, 2014. (4 Marks)

Answer / Solution:

Three conditions apply under the Rules: (1) Rate declared must not exceed the average of rates declared in the three years immediately preceding (2021-22, 2022-23, 2023-24: average = (12%+13%+14%)/3 = 13%); the proposed 12.5% is lower, satisfying condition 1. (2) Maximum amount drawn from accumulated profits and reserves must not exceed 10% of paid-up capital and free reserves = 10% of (40,00,000+12,50,000+11,75,000) = ₹6,42,500 (as printed) – alternatively computed as 10% of ₹66,50,000 (including current year profit in free reserves) = ₹6,65,000. (3) Balance of reserves after drawal must not fall below 15% of paid-up capital = 15% of ₹52,50,000 = ₹7,87,500.

12.5% Dividend on ₹40,00,000 equity capital = ₹5,00,000. Current year profit ₹2,25,000 less 8% preference dividend on ₹12,50,000 (₹1,00,000) leaves ₹1,25,000 available from current profit; the remaining ₹3,75,000 must come from accumulated reserves. Since all three conditions are satisfied and the required ₹5,00,000 (or, on the alternative computation, ₹3,75,000 needed against a maximum usable ₹6,12,500 after maintaining the 15% minimum reserve balance) is within the permitted limits, the company can utilize ₹5,00,000 in total (₹1,25,000 from current year profit and ₹3,75,000 from accumulated reserves) as per the Companies (Declaration of Dividend out of Reserves) Rules, 2014.

Examiner’s Comment: Many examinees were unfamiliar with the three conditions for declaring dividends from accumulated profits. They failed to compute the dividend amount correctly. While some examinees were able to apply the provisions relating to declaration of dividend under the Companies (Declaration of Dividend out of Reserves) Rules, 2014, several committed errors in determining the distributable amount and related adjustments. Although many could correctly calculate the average rate of dividend for the preceding three years and the dividend on preference shares, they failed to correctly apply the limits of 10% and 15%.

PYQ May 2024 · Q6(b) · Marks: 4 · Approx Time: 8 minutes (approx.) · Topic 1.6: Conditions for declaring dividend out of free reserves under the Companies (Declaration and Payment of Dividend) Rules, 2014 - rate capped at 3-year average, quantum capped at 1/10th of paid-up capital + free reserves, post-withdrawal reserves must remain at least 15% of paid-up capital
Question:

Following information are available in respect of Z Limited as on 31st March, 2024:

  1. Equity shares of ₹100 each ₹500 lakhs
  2. General Reserve ₹100 lakhs
  3. Loss for the year ending 31st March, 2024 ₹5 lakhs

Due to absence of profits during the year 2023-24, the management recommends to declare dividend of 10% on equity share capital out of general reserve.

The rates of equity dividend for the last 5 years immediately preceding the year 2023-24 are as follows:

2022-232021-222020-212019-202018-19
12%14%10%10%7%

As an accountant of the company, you are required to suggest whether the recommendation of the management is justified? If, you do not agree, then suggest the rate of dividend.

Answer / Solution:

In case of declaration of dividend out of free reserves, there are 3 conditions:

(1) Dividend Rate < Average Rate of last 3 years: 10% < 12% [(12+14+10)/3] – Condition is Satisfied.

(2) Dividend Distributed < 10% of PUSC + Reserve and Surplus: 50,00,000 < 59,50,000 [(5,00,00,000 + 1,00,00,000 − 5,00,000) × 10%] – Condition is Satisfied.

(3) Reserves after dividend > 15% of PUSC: 45,00,000 not > 75,00,000 (5,00,00,000 × 15%) – Condition is Not Satisfied.

(4) The closing balance of reserves after payment of dividend and set off of loss = ₹75,00,000. Therefore, amount that can be utilized = 20,00,000 (1,00,00,000 − 5,00,000 − 75,00,000). Thus, rate of dividend = (20,00,000/5,00,00,000) = 4%.

Alternatively: To judge the recommendation of management, the satisfaction of all three conditions is to be checked:

Condition I: The proposed dividend of 10% is less than the average rate of dividend being 12% (i.e.) (12+14+10)/3 = 12%. Hence, this condition is satisfied.

Condition II – Amount to be withdrawn: 10% dividend on Equity share capital 50,00,000 + Loss of Current year 5,00,000 = Amount to be drawn from General Reserve 55,00,000. Maximum amount that can be withdrawn should not exceed 10% of paid-up share capital + free reserves = 10% of [₹500 lakhs + ₹100 lakhs] = ₹60,00,000. As the amount to be withdrawn is within the maximum limit, this condition is also satisfied.

Condition III: Balance of reserves after withdrawal (100−55) = ₹45,00,000; 15% of paid-up capital = ₹75,00,000. As the balance of reserves should not be less than 15% of its paid-up share capital, but here the balance of reserves after withdrawal is less than 15% of paid-up share capital, this condition is not satisfied – hence 10% dividend cannot be declared.

Maximum withdrawal of Reserve if condition III is to be satisfied: Opening balance of Reserves at the beginning of the year = ₹1,00,00,000; Less: Closing balance of reserves being 15% of paid-up capital = ₹75,00,000; Reserves available = ₹25,00,000.

Maximum permissible Divisible Profits: Permissible withdrawal as above = ₹25,00,000; Less: Current Year's Loss = ₹5,00,000; Maximum permissible Divisible profit = ₹20,00,000.

Actual permissible rate of Dividend = (₹20,00,000 / ₹5,00,00,000) x 100 = 4%.

Therefore, the recommendation of management is not justified and a dividend only up to a rate of 4% can be declared.

Examiner’s Comment: Most of the examinees wrote the first condition and its testing correctly but many of them got confused between the second and third condition. Additionally, a few examinees failed to deduct the loss when determining the amount available for the declaration of dividends.

PYQ May 2025 · Q6(b) · Marks: 4 · Approx Time: 8 minutes (approx.) · Topic 1.6: Companies (Declaration and Payment of Dividend) Rules 2014 - three-condition test for drawing dividend from accumulated reserves, excluding Revaluation Reserve from free reserves
Question:

Due to inadequacy of profits during the year ended 31st March, 2025, DAY Ltd proposes to declare 9% dividend out of General reserves. From the following particulars, ascertain the amount that can be utilized from the General reserves according to the Companies (Declaration of dividend) rules, 2014.

9,50,000 Equity Shares of ₹10 each fully paid up ₹95,00,000; General reserves as on 1st April, 2024 ₹18,50,000; Revaluation Reserve as on 1st April, 2024 ₹4,25,000; Net profit for the year ended 31st March, 2025 ₹3,75,000; Average rate of dividend during the last 3 years has been 12.5%. (4 Marks)

Answer / Solution:

Amount that can be drawn from reserves for 9% dividend: 9% dividend on ₹95,00,000 = ₹8,55,000; less current year profit available (₹3,75,000) = amount which can be utilised from reserves ₹4,80,000.

Conditions per Companies (Declaration and Payment of Dividend) Rules, 2014:

Condition I: Since 9% is lower than the average rate of dividend (12.5%), 9% dividend can be declared — satisfied.

Condition II: Maximum amount that can be drawn from accumulated profits and reserves must not exceed 10% of paid-up capital plus free reserves, i.e. ₹11,35,000 [10% of (95,00,000+18,50,000)] — satisfied.

Condition III: The balance of reserves after drawal, ₹13,70,000 (₹18,50,000−₹4,80,000), must not fall below 15% of paid up capital, i.e. ₹14,25,000 (15% of ₹95,00,000) — NOT satisfied.

Conclusion: Since Condition III is not satisfied, DAY Ltd cannot declare dividend @ 9%. For all three conditions to be satisfied, DAY Ltd. can maximum utilize ₹4,25,000 (bringing General Reserve down to exactly ₹14,25,000, the 15% floor) and pay dividend only to that extent. (Revaluation Reserve is not a Free Reserve and is excluded from this computation throughout.)

Examiner’s Comment: Many examinees were unfamiliar with the three conditions for declaring dividends from accumulated profits. They failed to compute the dividend amount correctly. Some incorrectly considered Revaluation Reserves as Free Reserves, which led to wrong calculations of available profits and post-withdrawal reserve balances. As a result, they could not determine the permissible withdrawal from General Reserves under the Companies (Declaration and Payment of Dividend) Rules, 2014.

PYQ November 2023 · Q6(b) [OR-alt 2] · Marks: 5 · Approx Time: 9 minutes (approx.) · Topic 1.1: Meaning of Company - the five cumulative conditions defining a Small and Medium-Sized Company (SMC) under the Companies (Accounting Standards) Rules, 2021
Question:

List down the applicable criteria under the Companies (Accounting Standards) Rules, 2021, to classify a company as Small and Medium Sized Company (SMC).

Answer / Solution:

Criteria for classification of Companies under the Companies (Accounting Standards) Rules, 2021 to classify a company as Small and Medium-Sized Company (SMC):

“Small and Medium Sized Company” (SMC) means, a company –

(i) whose equity or debt securities are not listed or are not in the process of listing on any stock exchange, whether in India or outside India;

(ii) which is not a bank, financial institution or an insurance company;

(iii) whose turnover (excluding other income) does not exceed rupees two-fifty crores in the immediately preceding accounting year;

(iv) which does not have borrowings (including public deposits) in excess of rupees fifty crores at any time during the immediately preceding accounting year; and

(v) which is not a holding or subsidiary company of a company which is not a small and medium-sized company.

Author’s Note: A few examinees omitted one or more of the five cumulative SMC conditions, most often the borrowings ceiling and the holding/subsidiary-company condition, recalling only the more commonly cited listing-status and turnover criteria.

The final dividend will not be recognized as a liability at the balance sheet date (even if it is declared after reporting date but before approval of the financial statements) as per Accounting Standards. Hence, it has not been recognized in the financial statements for the year ended 31 March 2024. Such dividends will be disclosed in notes only.

Working note – Bonus Shares Issue: Bonus shares are issued in a 1:2 ratio, so for every 2 equity shares, 1 bonus share is issued. Equity Share Capital = ₹2,00,000 / ₹10 = 20,000 shares. Bonus Shares = 20,000 / 2 = 10,000 shares × ₹10 = ₹1,00,000. Alternatively, since the amount of interest on 10% ₹1,35,000 Debentures comes to ₹13,500 while the Debenture Interest in the trial balance is listed as ₹14,000, the difference of ₹500 (₹13,500 − ₹14,000) may be treated as an advance payment.

Examiner’s Comment: Most of the examinees were not able to classify the various items in the Balance Sheet and Statement of Profit and Loss as per Schedule III format prescribed under the Companies Act, 2013. They also missed adjusting for the issue of bonus shares from general reserves and the securities premium account. A few examinees incorrectly showed the transfer to general reserves on the face of the Statement of Profit and Loss rather than disclosing it under the Notes on Reserves and Surplus. In the Statement of Profit and Loss, many examinees made errors in calculating the amount of other income and depreciation, resulting in an incorrect profit for the year.

RTP September 2025 · Q20 · Marks: Not stated in source · Approx Time: 10–20 minutes (approx.) · Topic 1.2: Full Schedule III financial statements with land revaluation and mid-year machinery disposal
Question:

Trial balance of ABC Limited as on 31.3.2025 (₹'000): Land at cost 800 Dr.; Calls in arrears 5 Dr.; Cash in hand 2 Dr.; Plant & Machinery at cost 824 Dr.; Trade receivables 120 Dr.; Inventories 96 Dr.; Cash at Bank 28 Dr.; Adjusted Purchases 400 Dr.; Factory expenses 80 Dr.; Administrative expenses 45 Dr.; Selling expenses 25 Dr.; Debenture Interest 30 Dr. — Equity capital (₹10 each) 500 Cr.; 10% Debentures 300 Cr.; General reserve 150 Cr.; P&L A/c (FY2023-24) 75 Cr.; Securities premium 40 Cr.; Sales 1200 Cr.; Trade payables 30 Cr.; Provision for depreciation 150 Cr.; Suspense Account 10 Cr. Additional: authorised capital 80,000 shares of ₹10; land revalued to ₹9,60,000; equity capital includes ₹50,000 issued for non-cash consideration; Suspense ₹10,000 = cash from machinery sale on 1.4.2024 (cost ₹24,000, accumulated depreciation ₹20,000); depreciation on P&M at 10% on cost; bank balance includes ₹5,000 with a non-scheduled bank. Prepare the Balance Sheet and Statement of Profit and Loss with Notes to Accounts as per Schedule III (ignore previous year figures and taxation).

Answer / Solution:

Balance Sheet of ABC Limited as at 31.3.2025 (₹ in '000): Share Capital 495.00 (500 issued − 5 calls in arrears); Reserves and Surplus 971.00 (Securities Premium 40 + General Reserve 150 + P&L 621 [75 opening + 546 current profit] + Revaluation Reserve 160 [960−800]); Long Term Borrowings 300.00 (10% Debentures); Trade Payables 30.00. Total 1,796.00. Assets: PPE 1,550.00 (Land 960 [800+160 revaluation] + Plant & Machinery 590 [824−24 disposed=800, less depreciation (150−20+80)=210, =590]); Inventories 96.00; Trade Receivables 120.00; Cash and cash equivalents 30.00 (Bank: scheduled 23 + non-scheduled 5; Cash in hand 2). Total 1,796.00.

Statement of Profit and Loss for the year ended 31st March 2025 (₹ in '000): Revenue from Operations 1,200.00; Other Income 6.00 (profit on sale of machinery: sale value 10 − book value [24−20]=4, profit=6); Total Revenue 1,206.00. Expenses: Purchases 400.00; Finance Costs 30.00 (Debenture Interest); Depreciation (10% of 800) 80.00; Other expenses 150.00 (Factory 80+Selling 25+Admin 45). Total Expenses 660.00. Profit for the period: 546.00.

Author’s Note: Some examinees depreciated the full opening Plant & Machinery balance (824) at 10% instead of first removing the disposed machine's cost (24) from the depreciation base, overstating the depreciation charge.

Cash Flow Statement — Cash Flow Statement

Every MTP/RTP/PYQ question that tests this chapter, collected in one place, with official answers and topic tags — so you can practise every question this topic has been examined with, without hunting through separate papers.

A note on accuracy (please read): This is the first edition of this book, assembled with AI assistance and reviewed as carefully as we could manage, but it has not been independently audited question-by-question. If you spot an error — a wrong figure, a wrong answer, anything that looks off — please email capranavpratiktulshyan@gmail.com with the question reference so it can be corrected in the next edition.
Scope of this book (27 questions): Covers 34 sittings: MTP Jan2025 Set1, MTP Jan2025 Set2, MTP Jan2026 Set1, MTP Jan2026 Set2, MTP May2023 Set1, MTP May2023 Set2, MTP May2024 Set1, MTP May2024 Set2, MTP May2025 Set1, MTP May2025 Set2, MTP May2026 Set1, MTP May2026 Set2, MTP Nov2023 Set1, MTP Nov2023 Set2, MTP Sep2024 Set1, MTP Sep2024 Set2, MTP Sep2025 Set1, MTP Sep2025 Set2, PYQ Jan2025, PYQ Jan2026, PYQ May2023, PYQ May2024, PYQ May2025, PYQ May2026, PYQ Nov2023, PYQ Sep2024, PYQ Sep2025, RTP Jan2025, RTP Jan2026, RTP May2024, RTP May2025, RTP May2026, RTP Sep2024, RTP Sep2025. MCQs on this chapter are deliberately not included here — practise those on the dedicated MCQ platform; this book is for descriptive/scenario practice with full worked answers.
How this book is organised: Two sections — I. Descriptive (pure Cash Flow Statement) and II. Integrated (questions where Cash Flow Statement is one part of a larger question that also tests another standard). An empty Section II for a chapter is normal and expected, not a mistake — most multi-topic-looking questions are split so each topic gets its own clean entry, so genuinely combined questions are the rarer case. Each answer includes either a real Examiner's Comment (tan/orange box, quoted from ICAI's own published feedback, where one exists for that sitting) or an Author's Note (pale pink box, a likely pitfall identified by the author, not an official ICAI finding, and may not apply in every case) — see How to Read this Book.md for the full key to every colour and symbol used.

MTP January 2026 Set 1 · Q1(a) · Marks: 7 · Approx Time: 13 minutes (approx.) · Topic 2.4.2: Indirect method with debenture interest, tax paid, and investment-income adjustments Compulsory
Question:

The following information is provided for More Limited (figures in ₹):

Particulars31st March 202431st March 2025
Profit and Loss a/c(5,400) Dr.37,800
Provision for Taxation2,21,4001,35,000
General Reserve54,00081,000
12% Debentures1,18,8002,91,600

8% Current Investments54,0001,08,000

Trade Receivables (Gross)81,0002,61,360
Provision for Doubtful Debts27,00054,000
Inventories1,35,00081,000
Cash and Cash Equivalents5,40030,240

Additional information: (i) Income tax provided during the year ₹1,62,000. (ii) New debentures have been issued at the end of the current financial year. (iii) New investments have been acquired at the end of the current financial year. You are required to calculate net Cash Flow from Operating Activities.

Answer / Solution:

Cash Flow from Operating Activities

Difference between P&L balances (37,800 + 5,400)43,200
Add: Transfer to General Reserve (81,000−54,000)27,000
Add: Provision for taxation charged during the year1,62,000

Add: Depreciation (1,62,000−1,29,600)32,400
Add: Provision for doubtful debts (54,000−27,000)27,000
Add: Debenture interest paid (1,18,800 × 12%)14,256
Less: Income from investments (54,000 × 8%)(4,320)
Operating Profit before Working Capital changes3,01,536

Cash generated from operations1,64,376
Income tax paid(2,48,400)

Working note — Provision for Taxation account: To Cash (paid, balancing figure) 2,48,400 + To Balance c/d 1,35,000 = 3,83,400; By Balance b/d 2,21,400 + By P&L A/c 1,62,000 = 3,83,400.

Author’s Note: Some examinees missed adding back debenture interest paid (since it is a financing cost, not an operating outflow, even though deducted in arriving at reported profit) or forgot to net off income from the 8% current investments before arriving at operating profit before working capital changes.

MTP May 2023 Set 1 · Q1(a) · Marks: 5 · Approx Time: 9 minutes (approx.) · Topic 2.3: Classification of six mixed disclosure items across operating/investing/financing cash flow activities Compulsory
Question:

How will you disclose following items while preparing Cash Flow Statement of Gagan Ltd. as per AS-3 for the year ended 31st March, 2022?

(i) 10% Debentures issued: As on 01-04-2021 ₹1,10,000; As on 31-03-2022 ₹77,000.
(ii) Debentures were redeemed at 5% premium at the end of the year. Premium was charged to the Profit & Loss Account for the year.
(iii) Unpaid Interest on Debentures: As on 01-04-2021 ₹275; As on 31-03-2022 ₹1,175.
(iv) Debtors of ₹36,000 were written off against the Provision for Doubtful Debts A/c during the year.
(v) 10% Bonds (Investments): As on 01-04-2021 ₹3,50,000; As on 31-03-2022 ₹3,50,000.
(vi) Accrued Interest on Investments: As on 31-03-2022 ₹10,500. (5 Marks)

Answer / Solution:

Cash Flow Statement of Gagan Ltd. for the year ended March 31, 2022

Particulars₹
A. Cash Flow from Operating Activities
Net Profit as per Profit & Loss A/c—
Add: Premium on Redemption of Debentures1,650
Add: Interest on 10% Debentures11,000
Less: Interest on 10% Investments(35,000)
B. Cash Flow from Investing Activities
Interest on Investments [35,000 − 10,500]24,500
C. Cash Flow from Financing Activities
Interest on Debentures paid [11,000 − (1,175 − 275)](10,100)
Redemption of Debentures [(1,10,000 − 77,000) at 5% premium](34,650)

Note: Debtors written off against provision for doubtful debts does not require any further adjustment in Cash Flow Statement.

Author’s Note: A common error here is classifying the debenture redemption premium or the interest accrued/unpaid movements as operating items rather than isolating the true operating adjustment (interest income/expense add-back) from the financing-activity cash movements (actual redemption outflow, interest actually paid). Care is also needed not to net the accrued-interest-on-investments closing balance directly into the operating section instead of routing it through investing activities.

Author’s Note: A common error is netting the car and investment disposal proceeds directly into operating profit instead of separately reversing the profit-on-disposal figures from operating activities and showing the full gross proceeds under investing activities. (13) Depreciation on furniture amounts to ₹40,000. (14) Depreciation on other PPE amounts to ₹20,000. (15) Plant and Machinery purchased on 15th November, 2023 for ₹3,50,000. Further information related to Profit and loss A/c for the year ended March, 2025: (i) Profit before tax is ₹45,000. One old furniture item was sold for ₹17,000 and the profit on such disposal amounting to current year ₹8,000 was booked in the current year.

Moon Ltd. – Cash Flow Statement for the year ended 31st March, 2025

Working Note 1 – Income taxes paid: Income tax expense for the year 15,000 + Income tax liability at beginning of year 10,000 = 25,000; less Income tax liability at end of year (15,000); less DTL (6,000) = 4,000.

Examiner’s Comment: Several examinees made mistakes in calculating income taxes paid and showed a lack of conceptual clarity regarding the treatment of Deferred Tax Liability. RTP January 2025 · Q4 · Marks: Not stated in source · Approx Time: 10–20 minutes (approx.) · Topic 2.3: Classification of cash flow activities - operating, investing, financing, and cash equivalents
Question:

Classify the following activities as (1) Operating Activities, (2) Investing Activities, (3) Financing Activities (4) Cash Equivalents.

  1. Proceeds from long-term borrowings.
  2. Proceeds from Trade receivables.
  3. Trading Commission received.
  4. Redemption of Preference Shares.
  5. Proceeds from sale of investment
  6. Interim Dividend paid on equity shares.
  7. Interest received on debentures held as investment.
  8. Dividend received on shares held as investments.
  9. Rent received on property held as investment.
  10. Dividend paid on Preference shares.
  11. Marketable Securities
Answer / Solution:

Operating Activities: b, c.

Investing Activities: e, g, h, i.

Financing Activities: a, d, f, j.

Cash Equivalents: k

Author’s Note: A common error is classifying interest and dividend received on investments as operating activities because they arise from routine treasury income, missing that AS 3 classifies these as investing activities from the recipient's perspective, reserving operating classification for the enterprise's principal revenue-generating activities.

RTP September 2024 · Q4 · Marks: Not stated in source · Approx Time: 10–20 minutes (approx.) · Topic 2.3: Classification of cash flows across operating, investing and financing activities for loans/advances, investment/dividend and insurance-claim items
Question:

Purse Ltd., a non financial company has the following entries in its Bank Account. It has sought your advice on the treatment of the same for preparing Cash Flow Statement.

  1. Loans and Advances given to the following and interest earned on them:
    1. to suppliers
    2. to employees
    3. to its subsidiaries companies
  2. Investment made in subsidiary Wallet Ltd. and dividend received
  3. Dividend paid for the year
  4. Insurance claim received against loss of property, plant and equipment by fire.

Discuss in the context of AS 3 ‘Cash Flow Statement’.

Answer / Solution:
ItemClassification
(i)(1) Loans/advances and interest — to suppliersCash flows from operating activities
(i)(2) Loans/advances and interest — to employeesCash flows from operating activities
(i)(3) Loans/advances and interest — to its subsidiary companiesCash flows from investing activities
(ii) Investment made in subsidiary company and dividend receivedCash flows from investing activities
(iii) Dividend paid for the yearCash flows from financing activities
(iv) Insurance claim received against loss of property, plant and equipment by fire(no classification stated — see extraction note)
Author’s Note: A common error is classifying loans/advances to subsidiaries the same way as loans to suppliers or employees (operating activity), without recognising that an inter-company loan of this kind is an investing activity from the lending company's perspective.

RTP September 2025 · Q7 · Marks: Not stated in source · Approx Time: 10–20 minutes (approx.) · Topic 2.4.2: Indirect method with interest/dividend reclassification and fixed-asset purchase derived from the balance sheet movement
Question:

Kiran Ltd. Balance Sheets (2024/2025): Share capital 12,00,000/12,00,000; P&L A/c 8,50,000/10,00,000; Long Term Loans 10,00,000/10,60,000; Trade payables 3,50,000/4,00,000; Fixed Assets 17,00,000/20,00,000; Investment in shares 2,00,000/2,00,000; Inventory 6,80,000/7,00,000; Trade receivables 7,20,000/6,60,000; Cash 60,000/70,000; Bills Receivable 40,000/30,000. Income Statement 2025: Sales 40,80,000; Cost of sales 27,20,000; Gross Profit 13,60,000; Admin expenses 4,60,000; Depreciation 2,20,000; Operating Profit 6,80,000; Dividend received 50,000; Interest paid 1,40,000; PBT 5,90,000; Tax 2,60,000; PAT 3,30,000. Retained earnings: Opening 8,50,000 + Profit 3,30,000 − Dividend paid 1,80,000 = Closing 10,00,000. Prepare the Cash Flow Statement using the indirect method.

Answer / Solution:

(i) Cash flows from operating activities: PBT 5,90,000 + Depreciation 2,20,000 + Interest (non-operating) 1,40,000 = 9,50,000; less Dividend received (non-operating) (50,000) = Operating Profit before WC changes 9,00,000; add Decrease in Bills Receivable 10,000, Decrease in Trade receivables 60,000, Increase in Trade payables 50,000 = 10,20,000; less Increase in inventory (20,000) = Cash flow from operations before tax 10,00,000; less Tax paid (2,60,000) = Cash flow from operating activities: ₹7,40,000.

(ii) Cash flows from investing activities: Purchase of fixed assets (20,00,000+2,20,000 depreciation−17,00,000 opening = 5,20,000) outflow (5,20,000); Dividend on investments received 50,000 = Cash used in investing activities: ₹(4,70,000).

(iii) Cash flows from financing activities: Long term loan taken 60,000; Interest paid (1,40,000); Dividend paid (1,80,000) = Cash used in financing activities: ₹(2,60,000).

Net increase in cash: ₹10,000 (7,40,000−4,70,000−2,60,000). Opening cash 60,000 + 10,000 = Closing cash balance ₹70,000 (matches given).

Author’s Note: Some examinees computed the fixed-asset purchase figure without adding back the year's depreciation to the net book value movement, understating the actual cash outflow for the purchase.

RTP September 2025 · Q8 · Marks: Not stated in source · Approx Time: 10–20 minutes (approx.) · Topic 2.6: Fixed asset acquisitions and disposals reported gross, not netted, in the cash flow statement
Question:

Garden Ltd. acquired plant and machinery for ₹20 lakhs and sold furniture and fixtures for ₹5 lakhs in the same year. Can the company disclose net cash outflow towards purchase of fixed assets in the cash flow statement per AS 3?

Answer / Solution:

No. Per AS 3 para 21, major classes of gross cash receipts and gross cash payments from investing and financing activities must be reported separately, except for the specific items permitted to be reported net under paras 22 and 24 — acquisition and disposal of fixed assets is not among those permitted items. The company cannot net the ₹20 lakh purchase against the ₹5 lakh disposal; both must be shown as separate gross cash flow lines.

Author’s Note: Some examinees assumed netting was acceptable since both items relate to fixed assets, not checking the specific, limited list of items AS 3 actually permits to be reported net.

MTP May 2025 Set 2 · Q6(b) · Marks: 5 · Approx Time: 9 minutes (approx.) · Topic 3.5: Treatment of interest for segment reporting, including overdraft/operating-liability interest and interest capitalised into segment-asset inventory
Question:

Whether interest expense relating to overdrafts and other operating liabilities identified to a particular segment should be included in the segment expense or not?

In case interest is included as a part of the cost of inventories where it is so required as per AS 16, read with AS 2, and those inventories are part of segment assets of a particular segment, state whether such interest would be considered as a segment expense.

Answer / Solution:

The interest expense relating to overdrafts and other operating liabilities identified to a particular segment should not be included as a part of the segment expense unless the operations of the segment are primarily of a financial nature or unless the interest is included as a part of the cost of inventories.

In case interest is included as part of the cost of inventories where it is so required as per AS 16 "Borrowing Costs", read with AS 2 "Valuation of Inventories", and those inventories are part of segment assets of a particular segment, such interest should be considered as a segment expense.

In this case, the amount of such interest and the fact that the segment result has been arrived at after considering such interest should be disclosed by way of a note to the segment result.

Author’s Note: A common error here is treating all segment-identified interest expense the same way, without recognising the specific carve-out where interest capitalised into inventory cost under AS 16/AS 2 does count as a segment expense even though ordinary overdraft interest generally does not.

MTP May 2026 Set 1 · Q6(c) · Marks: 4 · Approx Time: 8 minutes (approx.) · Topic 3.9: Identifying reportable segments - 10% revenue/asset threshold and 75% cumulative external revenue test
Question:

Garnet Limited has 4 operating segments. The total revenue (internal and external) and assets are set out as below:

SegmentInter Segment SalesExternal SalesTotal Assets
Fan3,20010,90023,700
Light2001,40013,200
Lamp01,5004,200
Printer1,1002003,400
TOTAL4,50014,00044,500

How many reportable segments does Garnet Limited have as per the Revenue and Assets criteria given in AS 17? State Reasons for your answer. (4 Marks)

Answer / Solution:

As per AS 17 ‘Segment Reporting’, a business segment or geographical segment should be identified as a reportable segment if: its revenue from sales to external customers and from other transactions with other segments is 10% or more of the total revenue – external and internal of all segments; or its segment assets are 10% or more of the total assets of all segments.

If the total external revenue attributable to reportable segments constitutes less than 75% of total enterprise revenue, additional segments should be identified as reportable segments even if they do not meet the 10% thresholds until at least 75% of total enterprise revenue is included in reportable segments. This is not applicable in the given case. In the given case 75% of External Revenue is ₹10,500 Lakhs (₹14,000 × 75%) and the total External Revenue from Reportable segments is ₹12,300 Lakhs. So, no need to add Reportable segments.

On the basis of turnover criteria segment Fan is reportable segment as its sales are more than 1,850 lakhs (10% of ₹18,500 lakhs). Moreover, total external revenue attributable to reportable segment is also more than 75% of the total enterprise revenue.

On the basis of asset criteria, Fan and Light are reportable segments as their assets are more than 4,450 lakhs (10% of ₹44,500 lakhs).

Author’s Note: Many examinees applied only the 10% revenue or asset threshold test and omitted to check the 75% cumulative external-revenue test for identifying reportable segments under AS 17.

RTP January 2025 · Q12 · Marks: Not stated in source · Approx Time: 10–20 minutes (approx.) · Topic 3.6: Inter-segment transfer pricing may be based on any consistently-applied and disclosed basis - cost, below cost, or market price
Question:

A Company has an inter-segment transfer pricing policy of charging at cost less 5%. The market prices are generally 20% above cost.

You are required to examine whether the policy adopted by the company is correct or not?

Answer / Solution:

AS 17 "Segment Reporting" requires that inter-segment transfers should be measured on the basis that the enterprise actually used to price these transfers. The basis of pricing inter-segment transfers and any change therein should be disclosed in the financial statements. Hence, the enterprise can have its own policy for pricing inter-segment transfers and hence, inter-segment transfers may be based on cost, below cost or market price. However, whichever policy is followed, the same should be disclosed and applied consistently. Therefore, in the given case the inter-segment transfer pricing policy adopted by the company is correct if followed consistently.

Author’s Note: A common error is concluding that any inter-segment transfer price other than market price is automatically non-compliant with AS 17, missing that the standard permits any consistently-applied and disclosed pricing basis, including cost, below cost, or market price.

RTP January 2026 · Q13 · Marks: Not stated in source · Approx Time: 10–20 minutes (approx.) · Topic 3.3: Reportable segment thresholds - 10% revenue or assets test, plus the 75% external-revenue coverage check
Question:

Garnet Limited has 4 operating segments (₹ in appropriate units): Fan — Inter-segment sales 3,200, External sales 10,900, Total assets 23,700; Light — 200, 1,400, 13,200; Lamp — 0, 1,500, 4,200; Printer — 1,100, 200, 3,400; Total — 4,500, 14,000, 44,500. How many reportable segments does Garnet Limited have per the Revenue and Assets criteria in AS 17? State reasons.

Answer / Solution:

A segment is reportable if its revenue (external + inter-segment) is ≥10% of total revenue (external + internal, all segments), OR its assets are ≥10% of total assets.

Total revenue basis (external 14,000 + internal 4,500 = 18,500): 10% threshold = 1,850. Fan's total revenue (3,200+10,900=14,100) far exceeds 1,850 — Fan is reportable. (Light: 200+1,400=1,600, below threshold; Lamp: 0+1,500=1,500, below; Printer: 1,100+200=1,300, below.)

Assets basis (total 44,500): 10% threshold = 4,450. Fan (23,700) and Light (13,200) both exceed this — both are reportable on the assets criterion.

75% external-revenue test: reportable segments' external revenue must cover ≥75% of total external revenue (75% × 14,000 = 10,500). Fan and Light's combined external revenue (10,900+1,400=12,300) already exceeds 10,500, so no additional segments need to be added to meet the 75% threshold.

Conclusion: Garnet Limited has 2 reportable segments — Fan and Light (Fan qualifies on both revenue and assets; Light qualifies on assets only, but that alone is sufficient).

Author’s Note: Some examinees tested the 10% revenue threshold against external sales alone, omitting inter-segment sales from the revenue base used for that specific test.

RTP May 2026 · Q13 · Marks: Not stated in source · Approx Time: 10–20 minutes (approx.) · Topic 3.5: Treatment of interest for segment reporting - overdraft/operating-liability interest
Question:

Whether interest expense relating to overdrafts and other operating liabilities identified to a particular segment should be included in the segment expense or not?

Answer / Solution:

The interest expense relating to overdrafts and other operating liabilities identified to a particular segment should not be included as a part of the segment expense unless the operations of the segment are primarily of a financial nature or unless the interest is included as a part of the cost of inventories.

Author’s Note: Some examinees included all interest expense indiscriminately in segment expense, overlooking the two exceptions (segment primarily financial in nature, or interest forming part of inventory cost) under which such interest is included.

Whether interest expense relating to overdrafts and other operating liabilities identified to a particular segment should be included in the segment expense or not?

RTP September 2025 · Q17 · Marks: Not stated in source · Approx Time: 10–20 minutes (approx.) · Topic 3.3: A segment need only satisfy one of the three reportability tests - checking all three can expand the reportable set well beyond the most obvious single segment
Question:

Cotton Garments Limited, 5 segments (₹ Crore): Segment Assets A/B/C/D/E 40/15/10/10/5 (Total 80); Segment Results (95)/5/5/(5)/15 (Total −75); Segment Revenue 310/40/30/40/30 (Total 450). The Chief Accountant believes only segment "A" should be reported. Examine this opinion per AS 17.

Answer / Solution:

Per AS 17 para 27, a segment is reportable if: (i) its revenue (external+internal) is ≥10% of total revenue; or (ii) its result (profit or loss) is ≥10% of the combined result of all profit-making segments or all loss-making segments, whichever is greater in absolute amount; or (iii) its assets are ≥10% of total assets. If reportable segments cover <75% of total external revenue, additional segments must be added until 75% is reached.

(a) Revenue test (10% of 450 = 45): only A (310) qualifies.

(b) Result test: combined profit-segments (B+C+E = 5+5+15=25) vs. combined loss-segments (A+D = 95+5=100, in absolute terms); greater = 100; 10% = 10. Segments with |result| ≥10: A (95) and E (15) qualify.

(c) Assets test (10% of 80 = 8): A, B, C, D (40,15,10,10) qualify; only E (5) falls short.

Since every segment (A through E) satisfies at least one of the three tests, all five segments must be reported per AS 17. The Chief Accountant's opinion that only segment A is reportable is therefore wrong.

Author’s Note: Some examinees checked only the revenue test (which favours only segment A) and stopped there, missing that the result and assets tests bring in the remaining segments too.

I. Descriptive & Scenario-Based Questions (pure AS 18)

Full descriptive/scenario questions where this chapter is the sole topic tested (after independent-question splitting).

MTP September 2025 Set 2 · Q1(b) · Marks: 7 · Approx Time: 13 minutes (approx.) · Topic 4.3/4.4: Related-party status ceasing mid-year, directors serving in an individual professional capacity, and sole-customer economic dependence not amounting to related-party status Compulsory
Question:

Answer the following with respect to AS 18: (i) ABC Ltd. sold goods of ₹2,00,000 to its associate company for the 1st quarter ending 30.06.2025. After that the related party relationship ceased to exist. However, goods were supplied to any other ordinary customer. Decide whether transactions of the entire year have to be disclosed as related party transaction. (ii) If the majority of directors of Arjun Ltd. constitute the majority of the Board of another Company Bheem Ltd. in their individual capacity as professionals (and not by virtue of their being Directors in Arjun Ltd.). Are both the companies related? (iii) Asha Ltd. sells all the manufactured furniture of ₹1,00,00,000 to Sasha Ltd, as per agreement. Sasha Ltd. is the only customer to Asha Ltd. In the financial statements, Asha Ltd. wants to present Sasha company as a related party. Comment on the disclosure requirement.

Answer / Solution:

(i) As per AS 18, parties are considered related if at any time during the reporting period one party has the ability to control the other or exercise significant influence over the other. Transactions of ABC Ltd. with its associate company for the first quarter ending 30.06.2025 only are required to be disclosed as related party transactions, as the company had the ability to exercise significant influence only until 30.6.2025. The transactions for the period in which the related party relationship did not exist need not be reported.

(ii) Arjun Ltd. cannot be said to control the composition of the board of directors of Bheem Ltd., as the directors have been appointed in their individual capacity as professionals and not by virtue of their being directors in Arjun Ltd. Hence, it cannot be concluded that the companies are related merely because the majority of the directors of one company became the majority of the directors of the second in their individual capacity as professionals.

(iii) In the context of AS 18, a single customer, supplier, franchiser, distributor, or general agent with whom an enterprise transacts a significant volume of business cannot be construed as a Related Party Relationship merely by virtue of the resulting economic dependence. There is economic dependence between the companies, but no one controls or exercises significant influence on the other. Asha Ltd. need not report Sasha Company as its related party in its financial statements.

Author’s Note: A common error here is over-extending "related party" to any relationship of economic significance — mere economic dependence on a sole customer, or directors overlapping only in an unrelated individual professional capacity, does not by itself create control or significant influence under AS 18.

PYQ January 2025 · Q6(a) [OR-alt 1] · Marks: 4 · Approx Time: 8 minutes (approx.) · Topic 4.3: Related party relationships as per AS 18, including indirect significant influence through an intermediate holding and disclosure limited to the period the relationship existed
Question:

The following information is provided for the year ended 31st March, 2024: (i) AX Limited holds 70% shares of BX Limited. (ii) BX Limited holds 30% shares of CX Limited. (iii) DX Limited holds 40% shares of in CX Limited. (iv) DX Limited holds 49% shares in EX Limited.

You are required to: (i) Identify the related parties for the reporting entities – AX Limited, CX Limited and EX Limited. (ii) If DX Limited would have sold its investment in EX Limited on 1st October, 2023, but goods were continued to be supplied by DX Limited to EX Limited throughout the year, will this scenario change your answer with respect to any of the reporting entity mentioned in point (i)? Give reasons for your answer as per AS 18. (4 Marks)

Answer / Solution:

(i)

Reporting entityRelated party
AX LimitedBX Limited (AX Limited controls BX Limited directly as holding company); CX Limited (AX Limited has significant influence in CX Limited indirectly through BX Limited)
CX LimitedAX Limited (AX Limited has significant influence in CX Limited indirectly through BX Limited); BX Limited (BX Limited has significant influence in CX Limited); DX Limited (DX Limited holds 40% shares, means substantial interest of more than or equal to 20%, hence significant influence exists in this case)
EX LimitedDX Limited (DX Limited holds 49% shares, means substantial interest of more than or equal to 20%, hence significant influence exists in this case)

(ii) No, DX would still be a related party of EX Limited. EX Limited will report DX Limited as a related party as per AS 18. However, the transaction for the period in which the related party relationship exists will only be disclosed.

Examiner’s Comment: Some examinees failed to correctly identify the related parties for the three reporting entities.

RTP January 2025 · Q13 · Marks: Not stated in source · Approx Time: 10–20 minutes (approx.) · Topic 4.6: A related party transaction requires disclosure whether or not a price is actually charged for the transfer of resources or obligations
Question:

Will transactions with related parties, for services provided/received free of cost, be required to be disclosed?

A Limited has a corporate communications department, which centralises the public relations function for the whole group of A Limited and its subsidiaries. No charges are, however, levied by A Limited on its subsidiaries and accordingly, these transactions are not given accounting recognition. Would these constitute related party transactions requiring disclosure under AS 18 in the standalone financial statements of A Limited?

Answer / Solution:

These transactions would require disclosure under AS 18 in the standalone financial statements of A Limited. As per paragraph 10 of AS 18, a related party transaction is "a transfer of resources or obligations between related parties, regardless of whether or not a price is charged". In the given situation, there is a transfer of resources from A Limited to its subsidiaries, though no price is charged for the same. Hence, it will constitute a related party transaction and will require disclosure in the financial statements of A Ltd.

Author’s Note: A common error is concluding that a related party transaction requires disclosure under AS 18 only if a price is actually charged, missing that the standard's own definition explicitly covers a transfer of resources or obligations between related parties regardless of whether or not a price is charged.

RTP January 2026 · Q14 · Marks: Not stated in source · Approx Time: 10–20 minutes (approx.) · Topic 4.6: Expense reimbursement to a KMP is not remuneration and does not require AS 18 disclosure
Question:

Mr. Rajiv, a KMP of Raijada Limited, received a cheque of ₹70,000 towards reimbursement of expenses incurred on hotel stay, conference expenses, etc. while attending a meeting on behalf of the company. Is this transaction covered under AS-18?

Answer / Solution:

Mr. Rajiv, as a KMP, is a related party of Raijada Limited under AS 18. However, a reimbursement of expenses actually incurred on the company's behalf is not in the nature of remuneration or a related-party transaction requiring disclosure — it is simply the company bearing its own cost, routed through the KMP. Hence, this reimbursement need not be disclosed as a related-party transaction under AS 18.

Author’s Note: Some examinees concluded disclosure was required simply because Mr. Rajiv is a related party, without separately testing whether the specific transaction (a cost reimbursement, not remuneration) actually falls within AS 18's disclosure scope.
