RTP May 2024 · Q7(i) · Marks: Not stated in source · Approx Time: 10–20 minutes (approx.) · Topic 4.3: Related-party status requires either a voting-power interest giving control/significant influence, or the ability to direct/instruct the board (key management personnel) - day-to-day management alone under a fee contract does not qualify
Question:

A Ltd. enters into an agreement with Mr. Bhola for running a business for a fixed amount payable to the later every year. The contract states that the day-to-day management of the business will be handled by Mr. Bhola, while all financial and operating policy decisions are taken by the Board of Directors of the Company. Mr. Bhola does not have any voting power in A Limited. You are required to suggest how this transaction will be treated as at the closing date i.e. on 31st March, 2023 for the purposes of AS 18 'Related Party Disclosures'.

Answer / Solution:

Mr. Bhola will not be considered as a related party of A Ltd. in view of provisions of AS 18 "Related Party Disclosures" which states, "individuals owning, directly or indirectly, an interest in the voting power of the reporting enterprise that gives them control or significant influence over the enterprise, and relatives of any such individual are related parties". In the given case, in the absence of share ownership, Mr. Bhola would not be considered to exercise significant influence on A Limited, even though there is an agreement giving him the power to manage the company. Further, the fact that Mr Bhola does not have the ability to direct or instruct the board of directors does not qualify him as a key management personnel.

Author’s Note: A common error here is treating anyone contractually responsible for day-to-day management as automatically a related party, without checking for an actual voting-power interest or the ability to control the board's financial and operating policy decisions.

RTP May 2024 · Q7(ii) · Marks: Not stated in source · Approx Time: 10–20 minutes (approx.) · Topic 4.7: Related-party disclosure applies if the relationship existed at any time during the reporting period, even if it has since ended before year-end
Question:

Shri Manoj a relative of key management personnel received remuneration of ₹3,50,000 for his services in the company for the period from 1st April, 2022 to 30th June, 2022. On 1st July, 2022, he left the service. You are required to suggest how this transaction will be treated as at the closing date i.e. on 31st March, 2023 for the purposes of AS 18 'Related Party Disclosures'.

Answer / Solution:

According to AS 18 on 'Related Party Disclosures', parties are considered to be related if at any time during the reporting period one party has the ability to control the other party or exercise significant influence over the other party in making financial and/or operating decisions. Hence, Shri Manoj, a relative of key management personnel should be identified as related party for disclosure in the financial statements for the year ended 31.3.2023 as he received remuneration for his services in the company for the period from 1st April, 2022 to 30th June, 2022.

Author’s Note: A common error here is excluding the transaction from disclosure on the reasoning that Shri Manoj was no longer employed as at the balance sheet date, missing that AS 18's "at any time during the reporting period" test is satisfied by the relationship having existed for even part of the year.

RTP May 2025 · Q17 · Marks: Not stated in source · Approx Time: 10–20 minutes (approx.) · A day-to-day hotel manager with no voting power and no control over financial/operating policy decisions is not a related party under AS 18
Question:

SP Hotels Limited enters into an agreement with Mr. A for running its hotel for a fixed return payable to the latter every year. The contract involves the day-to-day management of the hotel, while all financial and operating policy decisions are taken by the Board of Directors of the company. Mr. A does not own any voting power in SP Hotels Limited. Would he be considered as a related party of SP Hotels Limited?

Answer / Solution:

Mr. A will not be considered as a related party of SP Hotels Limited, in view of paragraph 3(c) of AS 18, which states: "individuals owning, directly or indirectly, an interest in the voting power of the reporting enterprise that gives them control or significant influence over the enterprise, and relatives of any such individual." In the given case, in the absence of share ownership, Mr. A would not be considered to exercise significant influence over SP Hotels Limited, even though there is an agreement giving him the power to manage the day-to-day operations of the company. Further, the fact that Mr. A does not have the ability to direct or instruct the Board of Directors (which retains all financial and operating policy decisions) means he does not qualify as a key management personnel either.

Author’s Note: A common error is treating Mr. A as a related party simply because he has day-to-day management authority over the hotel, without separately testing whether he has the voting power or board-level control that AS 18 actually requires for related-party or key-management-personnel status.

RTP September 2025 · Q18 · Marks: Not stated in source · Approx Time: 10–20 minutes (approx.) · Topic 4.4: Only transactions during the period the related party relationship actually existed require disclosure
Question:

X Ltd. sold goods to its associate company for the 1st quarter ending 30.6.2024, priced as it would for any ordinary customer. After that quarter, the related party relationship ceased to exist. Decide whether transactions for the entire year have to be disclosed as related party transactions.

Answer / Solution:

No. Per AS 18 para 23, only the transactions during the period the related party relationship actually existed — here, the first quarter ending 30.6.2024 — need be disclosed as related party transactions. Transactions in the remaining periods, after the relationship ceased, need not be disclosed as such.

Author’s Note: Some examinees required disclosure for the whole year merely because a related party relationship existed at some point during it, not applying the period-specific test AS 18 actually uses.

I. Descriptive & Scenario-Based Questions (pure AS 24)

Full descriptive/scenario questions where this chapter is the sole topic tested (after independent-question splitting).

MTP January 2026 Set 2 · Q1(c) · Marks: 4 · Approx Time: 8 minutes (approx.) · Topic 6.2: Gradual phasing out without a formal approved plan does not meet the discontinuing-operation definition Compulsory
Question:

Kumar Ltd. manufactures both passenger cars and commercial vehicles. Management has an informal long-term strategic vision to shift focus toward commercial vehicles over 5 years, reducing passenger car production by ~20% annually and establishing a new commercial-vehicle facility, with employees to be transferred in phases. However, no specific or approved plan exists for sale, closure, or discontinuance of the passenger car division; no formal disposal plan, no Board approval; the new factory has not commenced operations, no binding commitments made. Comment on whether this gradual scaling down, without a formal approved plan, can be regarded as a 'Discontinuing Operation' under AS 24.

Answer / Solution:

Mere gradual phasing out is not considered a discontinuing operation as defined under AS 24. Examples of activities that do not necessarily satisfy the definition on their own (though they might in combination with other circumstances) include: gradual/evolutionary phasing out of a product line; discontinuing several products within an ongoing line of business; shifting production/marketing activities between locations; and closing a facility for productivity improvements or cost savings.

On these facts: the strategic plan has no final Board approval via resolution; there is no specific, time-bound plan for asset/employee transfer; and the new commercial-vehicle segment has not started operations. Kumar Ltd.'s passenger-car scale-down is therefore not a discontinuing operation under AS 24.

Author’s Note: Some examinees treated the mere existence of a strategic intention as sufficient for AS 24 classification, missing that a specific, Board-approved plan with a defined implementation timeline is required.

MTP May 2025 Set 2 · Q1(a) · Marks: 7 · Approx Time: 13 minutes (approx.) · Topic 6.2-6.3: Gradual phasing out without a formal approved plan vs. a time-bound Board-resolved closure plan Compulsory
Question:

Arzoo Ltd. is in the business of manufacture of Passenger cars and commercial vehicles. The company is working on a strategic plan to shift from the Passenger car segment over the coming 5 years. However, no specific plans have been drawn up for sale of neither the division nor its assets. As part of its plan it will reduce the production of passenger cars by 20% annually. It also plans to commence another new factory for the manufacture of commercial vehicles plus transfer of employees in a phased manner.

  1. You are required to comment if mere gradual phasing out in itself can be considered as a ‘Discontinuing Operation' within the meaning of AS 24.
  2. If the company passes a resolution to sell some of the assets in the passenger car division and also to transfer few other assets of the passenger car division to the new factory, does this trigger the application of AS 24?
  3. Would your answer to the above be different if the company resolves to sell the assets of the Passenger Car Division in a phased but time bound manner?
Answer / Solution:

Mere gradual phasing out is not considered as discontinuing operation as defined under para 3 of AS 24, ‘Discontinuing Operations'.

Examples of activities that do not necessarily satisfy criterion of the definition, but that might do so in combination with other circumstances, include: (1) Gradual or evolutionary phasing out of a product line or class of service; (2) Discontinuing, even if relatively abruptly, several products within an ongoing line of business; (3) Shifting of some production or marketing activities for a particular line of business from one location to another; and (4) Closing of a facility to achieve productivity improvements or other cost savings.

A Reportable business segment or geographical segment as defined in AS 17, would normally satisfy criteria (b) of the definition.

In view of the above the answers are:

(i) No, the companies' strategic plan has no final approval from the board through a resolution and there is no specific time bound activities like shifting of assets and employees. Above all, the new segment i.e. commercial vehicle production line in a new factory has not started.

(ii) No, the resolution is salient about stoppage of the Car segment in definite time period. Though, sale of some assets and some transfer proposal were passed through a resolution to the new factory, closure road map and new segment starting roadmap are missing. Hence, AS 24 will not be applicable.

(iii) Yes, phased and time bound programme resolved in the board clearly indicates the closure of the passenger car segment in a definite time frame and will constitute a clear roadmap. Hence, this action will attract compliance of AS 24.

Author’s Note: A common error across all three parts of this question is treating any board resolution touching the passenger car division as sufficient to trigger AS 24, without checking whether it actually specifies a definite, time-bound closure roadmap for the division as a whole, as distinct from partial asset sales/transfers alongside an ongoing, open-ended strategic shift.

MTP May 2026 Set 1 · Q6(a) [OR-alt 1] · Marks: 5 · Approx Time: 9 minutes (approx.) · Topic 6.5: Presentation and disclosure requirements for a discontinuing operation
Question:

Analyse the disclosure and presentation requirements of AS 24 for Discontinuing Operations (any five). (5 Marks)

Answer / Solution:

An enterprise should include the following information relating to a discontinuing operation in its financial statements beginning with the financial statements for the period in which the initial disclosure event occurs:

  1. A description of the discontinuing operation(s).
  2. The business or geographical segment(s) in which it is reported as per AS 17.
  3. The date and nature of the initial disclosure event.
  4. The date or period in which the discontinuance is expected to be completed if known or determinable.
  5. The carrying amounts, as of the balance sheet date, of the total assets to be disposed of and the total liabilities to be settled.
  6. The amounts of revenue and expenses in respect of the ordinary activities attributable to the discontinuing operation during the current financial reporting period.
  7. The amount of pre-tax profit or loss from ordinary activities attributable to the discontinuing operation during the current financial reporting period, and the income tax expense related thereto.
  8. The amounts of net cash flows attributable to the operating, investing, and financing activities of the discontinuing operation during the current financial reporting period.
Author’s Note: Many examinees omitted the requirement to disclose the amount of net cash flows attributable to the operating, investing and financing activities of the discontinuing operation, listing only the descriptive disclosures under AS 24.

PYQ January 2026 · Q6(a) [OR-alt 1] · Marks: 4 · Approx Time: 8 minutes (approx.) · Topic 6.5: Initial disclosure event - the eight required disclosure items
Question:

What is the initial disclosure information of AS-24 for discontinuing operations? (4 Marks)

Answer / Solution:

An enterprise should include the following information relating to a discontinuing operation in its financial statements beginning with the financial statements for the period in which the initial disclosure event occurs: (a) A description of the discontinuing operation(s). (b) The business or geographical segment(s) in which it is reported as per AS 17. (c) The date and nature of the initial disclosure event. (d) The date or period in which the discontinuance is expected to be completed if known or determinable. (e) The carrying amounts, as of the balance sheet date, of the total assets to be disposed of and the total liabilities to be settled. (f) The amounts of revenue and expenses in respect of the ordinary activities attributable to the discontinuing operation during the current financial reporting period. (g) The amount of pre-tax profit or loss from ordinary activities attributable to the discontinuing operation during the current financial reporting period, and the income tax expense related thereto. (h) The amounts of net cash flows attributable to the operating, investing, and financing activities of the discontinuing operation during the current financial reporting period.

Examiner’s Comment: Many examinees faced difficulty in stating the initial disclosure requirements for discontinuing operations as per AS 24. Instead of addressing the required disclosures, they described the circumstances under which a business may be discontinued.

PYQ May 2026 · Q5(b) · Marks: 10 · Approx Time: 18 minutes (approx.) · Topic 6.2: Definition of a discontinuing operation - single plan, piecemeal disposal, separate major line of business
Question:

Oasis Limited runs a famous chain of super markets and restaurants. Restaurant division constitutes 35% of total group revenue. The management of the company decides to close the business of restaurants as the company has been experiencing declining profitability due to increased competition. On 1st April, 2025, the management announced its intention to discontinue the restaurant business and concentrate on Super market segment only. The decision was made through strategic review and the management started actively seeking buyers for the restaurant division. During the year 2025-26, the company has sold 5 restaurants out of 12 restaurants so far as part of the sale.

Comment, whether it will be considered as discontinuing operation or not as per the provisions of AS-24? (10 Marks)

Answer / Solution:

As per AS 24, a discontinuing operation is a component of an enterprise: that the enterprise, pursuant to a single plan, is disposing of substantially in its entirety, or disposing of piecemeal, or terminating through abandonment; and which represents a separate major line of business or geographical area of operations.

Hence the restaurant division's closure by Oasis Limited will be considered a discontinuing operation as per the provisions of AS 24. This is due to the fact that the assets are sold off as part of a single plan, and that the business represents a separate major line of business, and can be distinguished both operationally and for financial reporting purposes.

Author’s Note: Some examinees concluded this was not a discontinuing operation because the disposal was piecemeal (5 of 12 restaurants sold rather than the whole division at once), not recognising that AS 24 explicitly includes piecemeal disposal pursuant to a single plan within its definition.

RTP January 2025 · Q18 · Marks: Not stated in source · Approx Time: 10–20 minutes (approx.) · Topic 6.5: Disclosure and presentation requirements for a discontinuing operation, and activities that only satisfy the AS 24 criteria in combination with other circumstances
Question:

What are the disclosure and presentation requirements of AS 24 for discontinuing operations?

Give four examples of activities that do not necessarily satisfy criterion (a) of paragraph 3 of AS 24, but that might do so in combination with other circumstances.

Answer / Solution:

(i) An enterprise should include the following information relating to a discontinuing operation in its financial statements beginning with the financial statements for the period in which the initial disclosure event (as defined in paragraph 15) occurs:

  1. a description of the discontinuing operation(s);
  2. the business or geographical segment(s) in which it is reported as per AS 17, Segment Reporting;
  3. the date and nature of the initial disclosure event;
  4. the date or period in which the discontinuance is expected to be completed if known or determinable;
  5. the carrying amounts, as of the balance sheet date, of the total assets to be disposed of and the total liabilities to be settled;
  6. the amounts of revenue and expenses in respect of the ordinary activities attributable to the discontinuing operation during the current financial reporting period;
  7. the amount of pre-tax profit or loss from ordinary activities attributable to the discontinuing operation during the current financial reporting period, and the income tax expense related thereto; and
  8. the amounts of net cash flows attributable to the operating, investing, and financing activities of the discontinuing operation during the current financial reporting period.

(ii) Para 3 of AS 24 "Discontinuing Operations" explains the criteria for determination of discontinuing operations. According to Paragraph 9 of AS 24, examples of activities that do not necessarily satisfy criterion (a) of paragraph 3, but that might do so in combination with other circumstances, include:

  1. Gradual or evolutionary phasing out of a product line or class of service;
  2. Discontinuing, even if relatively abruptly, several products within an ongoing line of business;
  3. Shifting of some production or marketing activities for a particular line of business from one location to another; and
  4. Closing of a facility to achieve productivity improvements or other cost savings.

An example in relation to consolidated financial statements is selling a subsidiary whose activities are similar to those of the parent or other subsidiaries.

Author’s Note: A common error is treating any product-line phase-out or facility closure as an automatic discontinuing operation under AS 24, missing that paragraph 9's listed activities only qualify in combination with other circumstances that independently satisfy the AS 24 criteria for a distinct, separately identifiable major line of business or geographical area.

RTP May 2024 · Q8 · Marks: Not stated in source · Approx Time: 10–20 minutes (approx.) · Topic 6.2: Gradual/evolutionary phasing out of a product line does not by itself meet the definition of a discontinuing operation; needs a specific plan, board approval, and time-bound implementation
Question:

Arzoo Ltd. is in the business of manufacture of passenger cars and commercial vehicles. The company is working on a strategic plan to shift from the passenger car segment to the commercial vehicles segment over the coming 5 years. However, no specific plans have been drawn up for sale of neither the division nor its assets. As part of its plan, it has planned that it will reduce the production of passenger cars by 20% annually. It also plans to commence another new factory for the manufacture of commercial vehicles plus transfer of employees in a phased manner. These plans have not been approved from the Board of Directors and the new factory for manufacture of commercial vehicles has not yet started. You are required to comment if mere gradual phasing out in itself can be considered as a 'Discontinuing Operation' within the meaning of AS 24.

Answer / Solution:

Mere gradual phasing out is not considered as discontinuing operation as defined under AS 24, 'Discontinuing Operations'. Examples of activities that do not necessarily satisfy criterion of the definition, but that might do so in combination with other circumstances, include:

  1. Gradual or evolutionary phasing out of a product line or class of service;
  2. Discontinuing, even if relatively abruptly, several products within an ongoing line of business;
  3. Shifting of some production or marketing activities for a particular line of business from one location to another; and
  4. Closing of a facility to achieve productivity improvements or other cost savings.

In view of the above, mere gradual phasing out in itself cannot be considered as discontinuing operation. The companies' strategic plan also has no final approval from the board through a resolution and there is no specific time bound activities like shifting of assets and employees. Moreover, the new segment, i.e. the commercial vehicle production line in a new factory has not started.

Author’s Note: A common error here is concluding that any strategic segment shift automatically meets AS 24's discontinuing-operation definition, without checking for a formally approved, specific, time-bound plan for disposal or discontinuance of the operation and its assets.

RTP May 2026 · Q15 · Marks: Not stated in source · Approx Time: 10–20 minutes (approx.) · Topic 6.2/6.3: Definition of a discontinuing operation and what triggers the initial disclosure event
Question:

Arzoo Ltd. is in the business of manufacture of Passenger cars and commercial vehicles. The company is working on a strategic plan to shift from the Passenger car segment over the coming 5 years. However, no specific plans have been drawn up for sale of neither the division nor its assets. As part of its plan it will reduce the production of passenger cars by 20% annually. It also plans to commence another new factory for the manufacture of commercial vehicles plus transfer of employees in a phased manner.

(i) You are required to comment if mere gradual phasing out in itself can be considered as a ‘Discontinuing Operation' within the meaning of AS 24.

(ii) If the company passes a resolution to sell some of the assets in the passenger car division and also to transfer few other assets of the passenger car division to the new factory, does this trigger the application of AS 24?

(iii) Would your answer to the above be different if the company resolves to sell the assets of the Passenger Car Division in a phased but time bound manner?

Answer / Solution:

Mere gradual phasing out is not considered as discontinuing operation as defined under para 3 of AS 24, ‘Discontinuing Operations'.

Examples of activities that do not necessarily satisfy criterion of the definition, but that might do so in combination with other circumstances, include: (1) Gradual or evolutionary phasing out of a product line or class of service; (2) Discontinuing, even if relatively abruptly, several products within an ongoing line of business; (3) Shifting of some production or marketing activities for a particular line of business from one location to another; and (4) Closing of a facility to achieve productivity improvements or other cost savings.

In view of the above the answers are:

(i) No, the companies' strategic plan has no final approval from the board through a resolution and there is no specific time bound activities like shifting of assets and employees. Above all, the new segment i.e. commercial vehicle production line in a new factory has not started.

(ii) No, the resolution is salient about stoppage of the Car segment in definite time period. Though, sale of some assets and some transfer proposal were passed through a resolution to the new factory, closure road map and new segment starting roadmap are missing. Hence, AS 24 will not be applicable.

(iii) Yes, phased and time bound programme resolved in the board clearly indicates the closure of the passenger car segment in a definite time frame and will constitute a clear roadmap. Hence, this action will attract compliance of AS 24.

Author’s Note: Some examinees answered part (iii) without properly building on the reasoning already established in parts (i) and (ii), missing that a phased-but-time-bound board resolution is precisely the missing ingredient (a definite closure roadmap) that parts (i) and (ii) found absent, and so overlooked the requirement for a clear sale plan with time-bound actions when applying AS 24.

Question:

Arzoo Ltd. is in the business of manufacture of Passenger cars and commercial vehicles. The company is working on a strategic plan to shift from the Passenger car segment over the coming 5 years. However, no specific plans have been drawn up for sale of neither the division nor its assets. As part of its plan it will reduce the production of passenger cars by 20% annually. It also plans to commence another new factory for the manufacture of commercial vehicles plus transfer of employees in a phased manner.

  1. You are required to comment if mere gradual phasing out in itself can be considered as a ‘Discontinuing Operation' within the meaning of AS 24.
  2. If the company passes a resolution to sell some of the assets in the passenger car division and also to transfer few other assets of the passenger car division to the new factory, does this trigger the application of AS 24?
  3. Would your answer to the above be different if the company resolves to sell the assets of the Passenger Car Division in a phased but time bound manner?
Answer / Solution:

Mere gradual phasing out is not considered as discontinuing operation as defined under para 3 of AS 24, ‘Discontinuing Operations’.

Examples of activities that do not necessarily satisfy criterion of the definition, but that might do so in combination with other circumstances, include:

  1. Gradual or evolutionary phasing out of a product line or class of service;
  2. Discontinuing, even if relatively abruptly, several products within an ongoing line of business;
  3. Shifting of some production or marketing activities for a particular line of business from one location to another; and
  4. Closing of a facility to achieve productivity improvements or other cost savings.

In view of the above the answers are:

  1. No, the companies' strategic plan has no final approval from the board through a resolution and there is no specific time bound activities like shifting of assets and employees. Above all, the new segment i.e. commercial vehicle production line in a new factory has not started.
  2. No, the resolution is salient about stoppage of the Car segment in definite time period. Though, sale of some assets and some transfer proposal were passed through a resolution to the new factory, closure road map and new segment starting roadmap are missing. Hence, AS 24 will not be applicable.
  3. Yes, phased and time bound programme resolved in the board clearly indicates the closure of the passenger car segment in a definite time frame and will constitute a clear roadmap. Hence, this action will attract compliance of AS 24.
Author’s Note: A common error is treating the mere existence of a strategic plan and a board resolution touching some assets as sufficient to trigger AS 24, without checking whether the resolution actually sets out a definite, time-bound closure roadmap for the whole segment.

MTP January 2025 Set 1 · Q5 · Marks: 14 · Approx Time: 26 minutes (approx.) · Topic 1.17: Restating a subsidiary's balance sheet to uniform accounting policies (inventory method, doubtful-debt provision rate, deferred-expenditure write-off period) before consolidation
Question:

Consider the following summarized Balance Sheets of subsidiary MNT Ltd.:

Other Information: (1) MNT Ltd. is a subsidiary of LTC Ltd. (2) LTC Ltd. values inventory on FIFO basis, while MNT Ltd. used LIFO basis. To bring MNT Ltd.'s inventories values in line with those of LTC Ltd., its value of inventory is required to be reduced by ₹5,000 at the end of 2022-2023 and increased by ₹12,000 at the end of 2023-2024. (Inventory of 2022-23 has been sold out during the year 2023-24). (3) MNT Ltd. deducts 2% from Trade Receivables as a general provision against doubtful debts. (4) Prepaid expenses in MNT Ltd. include Sales Promotion expenditure carried forward of ₹25,000 in 2022-23 and ₹12,500 in 2023-24 being part of initial Sales Promotion expenditure of ₹37,500 in 2022-23, which is being written off over three years. Similar nature of Sales Promotion expenditure of LTC Ltd. has been fully written off in 2022-23.

Restate the balance sheet of MNT Ltd. as on 31st March, 2024 after considering the above information for the purpose of consolidation. Such restatement is necessary to make the accounting policies adopted by LTC Ltd. and MNT Ltd. uniform.

Answer / Solution:

Restated Balance Sheet of MNT Ltd. as at 31st December, 2024:

ParticularsNote No.(₹)
Share Capital7,50,000
Reserves and Surplus17,18,500
Short term borrowings21,70,000
Trade Payables2,46,000
Short-term provision34,30,000
Total23,14,500
Property, Plant & Equipment46,37,500
Non-current Investment5,30,000
Inventories (6,90,000+12,000)57,02,000
Trade Receivables (3,43,000/98 × 100)3,50,000
Cash & Cash Equivalents42,500
Other current assets652,500
Total23,14,500

Notes to Accounts: 1. Reserves and Surplus: Revenue Reserve (refer W.N.) 5,11,500 + Securities Premium 2,07,000 = 7,18,500. 2. Short term borrowings: Bank overdraft 1,70,000. 3. Short-term provision: Provision for taxation 4,30,000. 4. PPE: Cost 9,20,000 − Depreciation to date 2,82,500 = 6,37,500. 5. Inventories: 6,90,000 + increase in value as per FIFO 12,000 = 7,02,000. 6. Other current assets: Prepaid expenses (after adjusting sales promotion expenses to be written off each year) 65,000−12,500 = 52,500.

Working Note — Adjusted revenue reserves of MNT Ltd.: Revenue reserves as given 5,05,000; Add: Provision for doubtful debts [3,43,000 × 2/98] 7,000; Add: Increase in value of inventory 12,000 (subtotal add-back 19,000); = 5,24,000; Less: Sales Promotion expenditure to be written off (12,500); Adjusted revenue reserve = 5,11,500.

Author’s Note: A recurring error is adjusting only the inventory-valuation difference for uniform accounting policies while forgetting that the doubtful-debts provision rate and the deferred sales-promotion write-off period also need to be restated to the parent's policy before consolidation.

MTP January 2025 Set 2 · Q2(a) · Marks: 7 · Approx Time: 13 minutes (approx.) · Topic 1.11: Cost of control - goodwill/capital reserve against revalued net assets, net of pre-acquisition dividend
Question:

Exe Ltd. acquires 70% of equity shares of Zed Ltd. as on 31st March, 2024 at a cost of ₹70 lakhs. The following information is available from the balance sheet of Zed Ltd. as on 31st March, 2024: Property, plant and equipment ₹120 lakhs, Investments ₹55 lakhs, Current Assets ₹70 lakhs, Loans & Advances ₹15 lakhs, 15% Debentures ₹90 lakhs, Current Liabilities ₹50 lakhs. The following revaluations have been agreed upon (not included in the above figures): Property, plant and equipment up by 20%, Investments down by 10%. Zed Ltd. declared and paid dividend @ 20% on its equity shares as on 31st March, 2024 (Face value – ₹10 per share). Exe Ltd. purchased the shares of Zed Ltd. @ ₹20 per share. Calculate the amount of goodwill/capital reserve on acquisition of shares of Zed Ltd.

Answer / Solution:

Revalued net assets of Zed Ltd. as on 31.03.2024:

Particulars₹ in lakhs
Property Plant & Equipment [120 × 120%]144.0
Investments [55 × 90%]49.5
Current Assets70.0
Loans & Advances15.0
Total Assets after revaluation278.5
Less: 15% Debentures (90.0) and Current Liabilities (50.0)(140.0)
Equity / Net Worth138.50
Exe Ltd.'s share of net assets (70% of 138.50)96.95
Exe Ltd.'s cost of acquisition of shares of Zed Ltd. (₹70 lakhs − ₹7 lakhs pre-acquisition dividend*)63.00
Capital Reserve33.95

*Total Cost of 70% Equity of Zed Ltd. ₹70 lakhs; Purchase Price of each share ₹20; Number of shares purchased (70 lakhs/20) 3.50 lakhs; Dividend @ 20% i.e. ₹2/share = ₹7 lakhs. Since dividend received is for the pre-acquisition period, it has been reduced from the cost of investment in the subsidiary company.

Author’s Note: A common error is comparing the cost of investment against the subsidiary's unrevalued net assets, or failing to net the pre-acquisition dividend against the cost of investment before computing goodwill or capital reserve.

MTP January 2025 Set 2 · Q2(b) · Marks: 7 · Approx Time: 13 minutes (approx.) · Topic 1.12: Minority interest computed separately at acquisition date and at consolidation date across five cases
Question:

From the following data, determine Minority Interest on the date of acquisition and on the date of consolidation in each case:

CaseSubsidiary Company% of Share OwnedCost (₹)Share Capital, 01-01-2024 (₹)Profit and Loss A/c, 01-01-2024 (₹)Share Capital, 31-12-2024 (₹)Profit and Loss A/c, 31-12-2024 (₹)
Case-iX85%1,85,0001,35,00060,0001,35,00070,000
Case-iiY70%1,60,0001,25,00045,0001,25,0005,000

Case-ivM90%60,00045,00020,00045,00040,000
Case-vN100%85,00025,00025,00025,00050,000
Answer / Solution:

Minority Interest = Equity attributable to minorities. Equity is the residual interest in the assets of an enterprise after deducting all its liabilities, i.e. in this case, it should be equal to Share Capital + Profit & Loss A/c.

CaseMinority %Minority Interest at Date of Acquisition (₹)Minority Interest at Date of Consolidation (₹)
Case i [100−85]15%29,25030,750
Case ii [100−70]30%51,00039,000
Case iii [100−65]35%10,50010,500
Case iv [100−90]10%6,5008,500
Case v [100−100]NILNILNIL
Author’s Note: A common error is computing minority interest only at the date of acquisition and not separately recomputing it at the date of consolidation using the later Share Capital and Profit & Loss balances, since the minority's proportionate share of accumulated profits changes between the two dates even where share capital does not.

MTP January 2026 Set 1 · Q3 · Marks: 14 · Approx Time: 26 minutes (approx.) · Topic 1.9: Minority interest turning negative - losses absorbed by holding company, recouped from future minority profits
Question:

GB Limited acquired 80% of equity shares of TB Limited on 1st April, 2018 at a cost of ₹58,00,000, when TB Limited had Equity Share Capital of ₹50,00,000 and Reserves and Surplus of ₹4,64,000. Yearly profit/(loss) of TB Limited: 2018-19 (14,50,000); 2019-20 (23,20,000); 2020-21 (29,00,000); 2021-22 (6,96,000); 2022-23 1,90,000; 2023-24 6,80,000; 2024-25 12,70,000. You are required to calculate the minority interest and cost of control at the end of each year for the purpose of consolidation.

Answer / Solution:

W.N. — Minority Interest and Goodwill on 1.4.2018: Share Capital 50,00,000 (80%: 40,00,000; 20%: 10,00,000) + Reserves 4,64,000 (80%: 3,71,200; 20%: 92,800) = Holding's share 43,71,200, Minority 10,92,800. Cost of investment 58,00,000 − 43,71,200 = Goodwill 14,28,800.

Since minority interest (20%) turns negative during the loss-making years 2018-19 through 2020-21, AS 21 requires losses beyond the minority's own interest to be absorbed by the holding company (Cost of Control account), then recouped from future minority profits before minority interest is credited again:

YearProfit/(Loss)Minority share (20%)Minority interest balanceCost of Control (holding co. absorption)
2018-19(14,50,000)(2,90,000)8,02,800—
2019-20(23,20,000)(4,64,000)3,38,800—
2020-21(29,00,000)(5,80,000)Nil (excess 2,41,200 absorbed by holding co.)2,41,200
2021-22(6,96,000)(1,39,200)Nil (absorbed by holding co.)3,80,400 (cumulative)
2022-231,90,00038,000Nil (profit share adjusted against losses absorbed by holding co.)3,42,400 (cumulative)
2023-246,80,0001,36,000Nil (profit share adjusted against holding co.'s absorbed balance)2,06,400 (cumulative)
2024-2512,70,0002,54,00047,600 (2,54,000 − 2,06,400 remaining absorbed balance recouped)Nil

Cumulative Minority Interest at 31.3.2025 (Balance Sheet figure, excluding the P&L movement column): ₹12,22,400 (i.e. opening 10,92,800 plus the net minority share of profits across the full period, after the loss-absorption/recoupment mechanism above).

Author’s Note: A very common error across multiple sittings on this exact pattern: continuing to show a negative (debit) minority interest balance in the consolidated balance sheet, instead of transferring the excess loss to the holding company (Cost of Control) and recouping it against the minority's later profit shares before crediting minority interest again.

Reserves and Surplus – General Reserve: Virat Ltd. 1,00,000, Anushka Ltd. 1,00,000. 3. Non-current investments – Shares in Anushka Ltd.: Virat Ltd. 3,20,000.

Consolidated Balance Sheet of Virat Ltd. and its Subsidiary Anushka Ltd. as at 31st March, 2023

ParticularsNoteAmount (₹)
I. Equity and Liabilities
(1) Shareholders' Funds – (a) Share Capital16,00,000
   (b) Reserve and Surplus21,80,000
(2) Minority Interest31,00,000
(3) Non-Current Liabilities – Long Term Borrowings43,00,000
(4) Current Liabilities – Trade Payables52,00,000
Total13,80,000
II. Assets
(1) Non-Current Assets – Property, Plant & Equipment67,00,000
(2) Current Assets – (a) Inventories73,60,000
   (b) Trade receivables82,20,000
   (c) Cash and Cash Equivalents91,00,000
Total13,80,000

Notes to Accounts: 1. Share capital: 60,000 equity shares of ₹10 each fully paid up = 6,00,000. 2. Reserves and Surplus: General Reserve 1,00,000, add General reserve of Anushka Ltd. (80%) 80,000; Total 1,80,000. 3. Minority interest: 20% share in Anushka Ltd. (WN 3) 1,00,000. 4. Long term borrowings: of Virat 2,00,000 + of Anushka 1,00,000 = 3,00,000. 5. Trade payables: of Virat 1,00,000 + of Anushka 1,00,000 = 2,00,000. 6. Property, Plant and Equipment: of Virat Ltd. 4,00,000 + of Anushka Ltd. 3,00,000 = 7,00,000. 7. Inventories: of Virat Ltd. 1,60,000 + of Anushka Ltd. 2,00,000 = 3,60,000. 8. Trade receivables: of Virat Ltd. 80,000 + of Anushka Ltd. 1,40,000 = 2,20,000. 9. Cash and cash equivalents: of Virat Ltd. 40,000 + of Anushka Ltd. 60,000 = 1,00,000.

Working Notes: 1. Basic Information – Holding Co. = Virat Ltd., Subsidiary = Anushka Ltd.; Acquisition date = Anushka's Incorporation; Consolidation date = 31st March, 2023; Holding Company = 80%, Minority Interest = 20%. 2. Analysis of General Reserves of Anushka Ltd. – since Virat holds shares in Anushka since its incorporation, the entire Reserve balance of ₹1,00,000 will be Revenue (post-acquisition). 3. Consolidation of Balances (Holding 80%, Minority 20%): Equity Capital 4,00,000 → Holding 3,20,000, Minority 80,000. General Reserves 1,00,000 (post-acquisition) → Holding 80,000, Minority 20,000. Total Minority Interest = 80,000+20,000 = 1,00,000. Cost of Investment 3,20,000 less Holding's share of pre-acquisition equity capital 3,20,000 (pre-acquisition reserve is Nil, since held since incorporation) = Goodwill/Capital Reserve NIL. Parent's balance (post-acquisition General Reserve share) 80,000, added to Parent's own 1,00,000 General Reserve = Amount for Consolidated Balance Sheet 1,80,000.

Author’s Note: A common error is splitting Anushka Ltd.'s general reserve into pre- and post-acquisition portions by default, without recognising that since Virat Ltd. held its stake from Anushka's very incorporation, the entire reserve balance is necessarily post-acquisition (revenue) profit, with no capital-profit component.

Question:

Star Ltd. acquires 70% of equity shares of Moon Ltd. as on 31st March, 2024 at a cost of ₹140 lakhs. The following information is available from the balance sheet of Moon Ltd. as on 31st March, 2024 (₹ in lakhs): Property, plant and equipment 240; Investments 110; Current Assets 140; Loans & Advances 30; 15% Debentures 180; Current Liabilities 100. The following revaluations have been agreed upon (not included in the above figures): Property, plant and equipment Up by 20%; Investments Down by 10%. Moon Ltd. declared and paid dividend @ 20% on its equity shares as on 31st March, 2024 (Face value – ₹10 per share). Star Ltd. purchased the shares of Moon Ltd. @ ₹20 per share. Calculate the amount of goodwill/capital reserve on acquisition of shares of Moon Ltd. as on 31st March, 2024.

Answer / Solution:

Revalued net assets of Moon Ltd. as on 31st March, 2024

Particulars₹ in lakhs
Property, plant and equipment [240 × 120%]288.0
Investments [110 × 90%]99.0
Current Assets140.0
Loans and Advances30.0
Total Assets after revaluation557.0
Less: 15% Debentures180.0
Less: Current Liabilities100.0
Equity / Net Worth277.0
Star Ltd.'s share of net assets (70% of 277)193.9
Star Ltd.'s cost of acquisition of shares of Moon Ltd. (₹140 lakhs − ₹14 lakhs*)126.00
Capital reserve67.9

* Total cost of 70% equity of Moon Ltd. ₹140 lakhs; purchase price per share ₹20; number of shares purchased = 140 lakhs / ₹20 = 7 lakhs; dividend @ 20% i.e. ₹2 per share = ₹14 lakhs. Since the dividend received is for the pre-acquisition period, it has been reduced from the cost of investment in the subsidiary company.

Author’s Note: A common error here is computing the parent's share of net assets against the unrevalued figures given in the balance sheet, or forgetting to reduce the cost of investment by the pre-acquisition dividend received before comparing it against the share of net assets.

Question:

Gamma Ltd. acquired 24,000 equity shares of ₹10 each, in Beta Ltd. on October 1, 2023 for ₹4,60,200. The profit and loss account of Beta Ltd. showed a balance of ₹15,000 on April 1, 2023. The plant and machinery of Beta Ltd. which stood in the books at ₹2,25,000 on April 1, 2023 was considered worth ₹2,70,000 on the date of acquisition. The information of the two companies as at 31-3-2024 was as follows: Share capital (fully paid equity shares of ₹10 each): Gamma 7,50,000, Beta 3,00,000. General reserve: Gamma 3,60,000, Beta 1,50,000. Profit and loss account: Gamma 85,800, Beta 1,23,000. Current Liabilities: Gamma 2,54,700, Beta 49,500. Land and building: Gamma 2,70,000, Beta 2,85,000. Plant and machinery: Gamma 3,60,000, Beta 2,02,500. Investments: Gamma 4,60,200. Current assets: Gamma 3,60,300, Beta 1,35,000. You are required to compute impact of revaluation of Plant and Machinery.

Answer / Solution:

Impact of Revaluation of Plant and Machinery:

ParticularsAmount (₹)
Book value of Plant and Machinery as on 01-04-20232,25,000
Depreciation Rate [(2,25,000−2,02,500)/2,25,000 = 22,500/2,25,000×100]10%
Book value of P&M as on 01-10-2023 after 6 months' depreciation @10% (2,25,000−11,250)2,13,750
Revalued at2,70,000
Revaluation profit (2,70,000−2,13,750)56,250
Share of Gamma Ltd. in Revaluation Profit (80%)45,000
Share of Minority in Revaluation profit (20%)11,250
Additional Depreciation on appreciated value to be charged from post-acquisition profits [(10% of 2,25,000 for 6 months) + (10% of 2,70,000 for 6 months) less 22,500 already charged]2,250
Share of Gamma Ltd. in additional depreciation, reducing its 80% share of post-acquisition profit by1,800
Share of Minority Interest in additional depreciation450

Working note — percentage of holding: Holding Co.: 24,000 shares (80%); Minority shareholders: 6,000 shares (20%); Total shares: 30,000 (i.e. Beta Ltd.'s ₹3,00,000 share capital ÷ ₹10 face value).

Author’s Note: A common error here is computing the additional depreciation on the revalued asset for the full year rather than only the post-acquisition 6-month period (1 October 2023 to 31 March 2024), or forgetting to net off the depreciation already charged on the original book value before arriving at the incremental amount.

Total48,00,00024,00,000

On 1 April 2023 Profit & Loss A/c of Q Ltd. showed a credit balance of ₹32,000 and equipment of Q Ltd., was revalued by P Ltd., 20% above its book value of ₹4,00,000 (but no such adjustment effected in the books of Q Ltd.)

Prepare the consolidated balance sheet as at 31st March 2024.

Answer / Solution:

Consolidated Balance Sheet of P Ltd. and its Subsidiary Q Ltd. as on 31.3.2024

Particulars₹
I. Equities & Liabilities
(1)(a) Share Capital16,00,000
(1)(b) Reserve & Surplus (P&L A/c, W.N.5)2,39,600
(1)(c) Minority interest (W.N.4)55,600
(2) Current liability (30,00,000+19,20,000)49,20,000
Total68,15,200
II. Assets
(1)(a) PPE (10,00,000+3,80,000+80,000−4,000)14,56,000
(1)(b) Goodwill (W.N.3)99,200
(2)(a) Other current assets (32,40,000+20,20,000)52,60,000
Total68,15,200

Working Notes:

1. Shareholding: Held by P Ltd. 3,600 shares (90%); Minority interest 400 shares (10%).

2. Analysis of profit (Q Ltd. P&L A/c): Opening balance 32,000; Profit during the year 48,000 (bal. c/d 80,000 − bal. b/d 32,000). Capital profit vs revenue profit split: Opening balance in P&L A/c 32,000 (capital); Profit during the year 48,000 (revenue); Revaluation of equipment (W.N.6) 80,000 (capital); Short depreciation on equipment (4,000) (revenue). Total: Capital profit 1,12,000, Revenue profit 44,000. Q Ltd. (Minority, 10%): capital 11,200, revenue 4,400. P Ltd. (90%): capital 1,00,800, revenue 39,600.

3. Cost of Control: Cost of investment 5,60,000; less dividend out of pre-acquisition profit nil = 5,60,000 (A). Share in net assets of Q Ltd.: share capital (4,00,000×90%) 3,60,000 + capital profit (W.N.2) 1,00,800 = 4,60,800 (B). Goodwill (A−B) = 99,200.

4. Minority Interest: Share capital (4,00,000×10%) 40,000 + capital profit (W.N.2) 11,200 + revenue profit (W.N.2) 4,400 = 55,600.

5. P Ltd.'s Reserve & Surplus: Balance as per balance sheet (P&L) 2,00,000 + share in profit of Q Ltd. 39,600 = 2,39,600.

6. Appreciation on revalued asset: Book value as on 31.3.24 (per B/S) 3,80,000; Book value as on 1.4.23 (given) 4,00,000; depreciation for the year 20,000 (5%). Revaluation of asset (4,00,000+20%) = 4,80,000; Revaluation reserve = 80,000; depreciation on revalued asset (4,80,000×5%) = 24,000; short depreciation = 24,000−20,000 = 4,000.

Author’s Note: A common error is treating the equipment revaluation entirely as a post-acquisition (revenue) item since it was recorded by P Ltd. rather than in Q Ltd.'s own books, missing that the revaluation relates to the asset's value at the 1 April 2023 acquisition date and is therefore a capital profit, while only the resulting short depreciation for the year is a revenue item.

A Ltd. acquired 70% equity shares of B Ltd. @ ₹20 per share (Face value – ₹10) on 31st March, 2024 at a cost of ₹140 lakhs. Calculate the amount of share of A Ltd. and minority interest in the net assets of B Ltd. on this date. Also compute goodwill/capital reserve for A Ltd. on acquisition of shares of B Ltd. from the following information available from the balance sheet of B Ltd. as on 31st March, 2024 (₹ in lakhs): Property, plant and equipment 360; Investments 90; Current Assets 140; Loans & Advances 30; 15% Debentures 180; Current Liabilities 100.

Answer / Solution:

Net assets of B Ltd. as on 31st March, 2024

Particulars₹ in lakhs
Property, plant and equipment360
Investments90
Current Assets140
Loans and Advances30
Total Assets620
Less: 15% Debentures 180 + Current Liabilities 100(280)
Equity / Net Worth340
Share of Minority Interest in net assets (30% of 340)102
A Ltd.'s share in net assets (70% of 340)238
A Ltd.'s cost of acquisition of shares of B Ltd.(140)
Capital reserve98

Since A Ltd.'s cost of acquisition (₹140 lakhs) is less than its 70% share of B Ltd.'s net assets (₹238 lakhs), the difference of ₹98 lakhs is a Capital Reserve, not goodwill.

Author’s Note: A common error is defaulting to labelling the difference "Goodwill" without checking its sign — here the cost of acquisition is lower than the proportionate share of net assets acquired, so the difference is a Capital Reserve, the reverse of the more commonly tested Goodwill case.

MTP May 2025 Set 2 · Q2 · Marks: 14 · Approx Time: 26 minutes (approx.) · Topic 1.11-1.12: Minority Interest reduced to nil by losses exceeding its balance, excess borne by the majority and recouped from Minority's future profit share before normal allocation resumes
Question:

H Ltd. acquire 70% of equity share of S Ltd. as on 1st January, 2021 at a cost of ₹5,00,000 when S Ltd. had an equity share capital of ₹5,00,000 and reserves and surplus of ₹40,000.

Both the companies follow calendar year as the accounting year.

In the four consecutive years, S Ltd. performed badly and suffered losses of ₹1,25,000, ₹2,00,000, ₹2,50,000 and ₹60,000 respectively (2021-2024).

Thereafter in 2025, S Ltd. experienced turnaround and registered an annual profit of ₹25,000. In the next two years i.e. 2026 and 2027, S Ltd. recorded annual profits of ₹50,000 and ₹75,000 respectively.

Show the Minority Interests and Cost of Control at the end of each year for the purpose of consolidation.

Answer / Solution:

Working Note – Minority Interest and Cost of Control at acquisition (1.1.2021):

ParticularsTotal (100%)H Ltd.'s share (70%)Minority Interest (30%)
Share Capital5,00,0003,50,0001,50,000
Reserves40,00028,00012,000
Total5,40,0003,78,0001,62,000
Less: Cost of investment(5,00,000)
Cost of Control (Goodwill)1,22,000

The Cost of Control (Goodwill of ₹1,22,000, since cost exceeds H Ltd.'s share of net assets) is fixed at acquisition and does not change in later years. When the minority's 30% share of a loss exceeds the Minority Interest balance available to absorb it, the excess is charged entirely to H Ltd. (majority) rather than to Minority Interest, and is tracked as a memorandum amount to be recovered from Minority's own future profit share, 100%, before normal 30/70 sharing of profits resumes.

YearS Ltd. Profit/(Loss)Minority's notional 30% shareAmount actually credited/(charged) to Minority InterestAmount credited/(charged) to H Ltd.'s Consolidated P&LMinority Interest balance c/f
1.1.2021 (acquisition)————1,62,000
2021(1,25,000)(37,500)(37,500)(87,500)1,24,500
2022(2,00,000)(60,000)(60,000)(1,40,000)64,500
2023(2,50,000)(75,000)(64,500), reduced to Nil(1,85,500) — 70% share ₹1,75,000 + unabsorbed minority excess ₹10,500Nil (₹10,500 excess memo carried, borne by H Ltd.)
2024(60,000)(18,000)Nil (MI balance already Nil)(60,000) — full loss, since no Minority Interest balance remains to absorb any shareNil (₹28,500 cumulative memo carried: 10,500+18,000)
202525,0007,500Nil — profit share applied first to recoup the memo25,000 — full profit, 70% normal share ₹17,500 + minority's 7,500 redirected to recoup the memoNil (memo reduces from 28,500 to 21,000)
202650,00015,000Nil — still recouping the memo50,000 — full profit, 70% normal share ₹35,000 + minority's 15,000 redirectedNil (memo reduces from 21,000 to 6,000)
202775,00022,50016,500 — ₹6,000 of the 22,500 clears the remaining memo, balance credited to Minority Interest normally58,500 — 70% normal share ₹52,500 + the memo-clearing ₹6,00016,500

Final position after 2027: Minority Interest ₹16,500; Cost of Control (Goodwill) unchanged at ₹1,22,000 throughout.

Author’s Note: A frequent mistake in this kind of multi-year problem is letting the Minority Interest balance go negative when losses exceed it, instead of capping it at nil and tracking the excess as a memorandum recoverable from the minority's own future profits before any new profit share is credited to Minority Interest.

Question:

From the following information of Kedar Ltd. and its subsidiary Vijay Ltd. at 31st March, 2024, prepare a consolidated balance sheet as at that date: (i) Reserves and Profit and Loss Account of Vijay Ltd. stood at ₹62,500 and ₹37,500 respectively on the date of acquisition of its 80% shares by Kedar Ltd. on 1st April, 2023. (ii) Machinery (Book value ₹2,50,000) and Furniture (Book value ₹50,000) of Vijay Ltd. were revalued at ₹3,75,000 and ₹37,500 respectively on 1st April, 2023 for the purpose of fixing the price of its shares [depreciation rates on useful lives: Machinery 10%, Furniture 15%].

ParticularsKedar Ltd. (₹)Vijay Ltd. (₹)
Share Capital: Shares of ₹100 each15,00,0002,50,000
Reserves5,00,0001,87,500
Profit and Loss Account2,50,00062,500
Trade Payables3,75,0001,42,500
Machinery7,50,0002,25,000
Furniture3,75,00042,500
Other non-current assets11,00,0003,75,000
Shares in Vijay Ltd.: 2,000 shares at ₹200 each4,00,000—
Answer / Solution:

Consolidated Balance Sheet of Kedar Ltd. and its Subsidiary Vijay Ltd. as at 31st March, 2024

Share Capital15,00,000
Reserves and Surplus (Note 1)8,61,500
Minority Interest (W.N.5)1,20,375
Trade Payables (Note 2)5,17,500
Total (Equity and Liabilities)29,99,375
Property, plant & Equipment (Note 3)14,94,375
Intangible assets – Goodwill (Note 4)30,000
Other non-current assets (Note 5)14,75,000
Total (Assets)29,99,375

Notes to Accounts: (1) Reserves and Surplus – Reserves 5,00,000 + 4/5 share of Vijay Ltd.'s post-acquisition reserves (W.N.3) 1,00,000 = 6,00,000; Profit & Loss 2,50,000 + 4/5 share of post-acquisition profits (W.N.4) 11,500 = 2,61,500; Total 8,61,500. (2) Trade Payables – Kedar 3,75,000 + Vijay 1,42,500 = 5,17,500. (3) PPE – Machinery: Kedar 7,50,000 + Vijay (2,50,000 + appreciation 1,25,000 = 3,75,000) = 11,25,000, less depreciation (37,500) = 3,37,500 shown net of Kedar's own; combined with Furniture: Kedar 3,75,000 + Vijay (50,000 − decrease 12,500 = 37,500), less depreciation (5,625) = 31,875; PPE total 14,94,375. (4) Goodwill (W.N.6) 30,000. (5) Other non-current assets: Kedar 11,00,000 + Vijay 3,75,000 = 14,75,000.

Working Notes: (1) Pre-acquisition profits/reserves of Vijay Ltd.: Reserves 62,500 + P&L 37,500 = 1,00,000; Kedar's 4/5 share = 80,000; Minority 1/5 = 20,000. (2) Profit on revaluation: Machinery gain (3,75,000−2,50,000)=1,25,000 less Furniture loss (50,000−37,500)=12,500 ⇒ Net profit on revaluation 1,12,500; Kedar's share 90,000; Minority 22,500. (3) Post-acquisition reserves of Vijay Ltd.: (1,87,500−62,500)=1,25,000; Kedar's share 1,00,000; Minority 25,000. (4) Post-acquisition profits of Vijay Ltd.: (62,500−37,500)=25,000, add excess depreciation on furniture @15% on 12,500 = 1,875, less under-depreciation on machinery @10% on 1,25,000 = (12,500); Adjusted post-acquisition profits = 14,375; Kedar's share 11,500; Minority 2,875. (5) Minority Interest: paid-up value of 500 shares (2,500−2,000) held by outsiders = 50,000, + 1/5 share of pre-acquisition profits/reserves 20,000 + 1/5 profit on revaluation 22,500 + 1/5 post-acquisition reserves 25,000 + 1/5 post-acquisition profit 2,875 = 1,20,375. (6) Cost of Control/Goodwill: paid-up value of 2,000 shares held by Kedar = 2,00,000, + 4/5 pre-acquisition profits/reserves 80,000 + 4/5 profit on revaluation 90,000 = Intrinsic value on acquisition date 3,70,000; price paid by Kedar for 2,000 shares 4,00,000, less intrinsic value (3,70,000) = Goodwill 30,000.

Author’s Note: A common error is omitting the depreciation catch-up on the revalued machinery and furniture from the post-acquisition profit split, understating (or overstating) both the parent's share and minority interest's share of post-acquisition profits.

Trade Payables of Star Ltd. include ₹35,000 due to Moon Ltd. for goods supplied since acquisition, charged at 10% above cost. Star Ltd.'s inventories include goods costing ₹55,000 (cost to Star Ltd.) purchased from Moon Ltd. You are required to prepare the Consolidated Balance Sheet of Star Ltd. with its subsidiary as at 31st March, 2024.

Answer / Solution:

Consolidated Balance Sheet of Star Ltd. and its Subsidiary Moon Ltd. as at 31st March, 2024

ParticularsNote₹
I. Equity and Liabilities
(1)(a) Share Capital (1,20,000 equity shares of ₹10 each)12,00,000
(1)(b) Reserves and Surplus18,16,200
(2) Minority Interest (W.N.4)99,300
(3) Current Liabilities – Trade Payables24,10,000
Total25,25,500
II. Assets
(1)(i) Property, plant and equipment313,10,500
(1)(ii) Intangible assets (Goodwill)424,000
(2)(i) Inventories53,25,000
(2)(ii) Trade Receivables66,70,000
(2)(iii) Cash at Bank71,96,000
Total25,25,500

Notes to Accounts: (1) Reserves and Surplus: General Reserve 4,35,000 + 80% share of Moon's post-acquisition reserves 84,000 = 5,19,000; P&L 2,80,000 + 80% share of Moon's post-acquisition profits 21,200 − unrealised gain 4,000 (net 17,200) = 2,97,200; Total 8,16,200. (2) Trade Payables: Star 3,22,000 + Moon 1,23,000 − mutual transaction 35,000 = 4,10,000. (3) PPE: Machinery Star 6,40,000 + Moon (2,00,000+1,00,000 appreciation−30,000 depreciation=2,70,000) = 9,10,000; Furniture Star 3,75,000 + Moon (40,000−10,000 decrease−4,500 depreciation=25,500) = 4,00,500; Total 13,10,500. (4) Intangible assets: Goodwill (W.N.5) 24,000. (5) Inventories: Star 2,68,000 + Moon 62,000 = 3,30,000, less inventory reserve 5,000 = 3,25,000. (6) Trade Receivables: Star 4,70,000 + Moon 2,35,000 = 7,05,000, less mutual transaction 35,000 = 6,70,000. (7) Cash and Bank: Star 1,64,000 + Moon 32,000 = 1,96,000.

Working Notes: (1) Revaluation: Machinery profit on revaluation ₹1,00,000 (3,00,000−2,00,000); Furniture loss on revaluation ₹(10,000) (30,000−40,000). (2) Short/excess depreciation: Machinery (10,000) short, Furniture 1,500 excess. (3) Analysis of Moon's reserves/profits as on 31.3.2024 — pre-acquisition capital profit ₹1,70,000 (50,000 GR + 30,000 P&L + 1,00,000 machinery revaluation − 10,000 furniture revaluation); post-acquisition General Reserve ₹1,05,000; post-acquisition P&L ₹26,500 (35,000−10,000 short machinery depreciation+1,500 excess furniture depreciation). (4) Minority Interest: paid-up value (2,00,000×20%) 40,000 + 20% pre-acquisition profits/reserves 16,000 + 20% profit on revaluation 18,000 + 20% post-acquisition reserves 21,000 + 20% post-acquisition profit 5,300 = 1,00,300, less unrealised profit on inventory (55,000×10/110×20%=1,000) = 99,300. (5) Cost of Control/Goodwill: Cost of investment 3,20,000, less paid-up value of 80% shares 1,60,000, less 80% share of pre-acquisition profits/reserves 1,36,000 = Goodwill 24,000.

Author’s Note: A common error here is forgetting that a downstream unrealised profit (Star Ltd.'s own inventory purchased from Moon, at 10% above Moon's cost) still requires elimination and a proportionate share to be deducted from minority interest, since it originated with the subsidiary supplying to the parent.

CaseSubsidiary Company% of Share OwnedCost (₹) Share Capital 01-01-2024 (₹)Profit and Loss A/c 01-01-2024 (₹) Share Capital 31-12-2024 (₹)Profit and Loss A/c 31-12-2024 (₹)

Case-ivM90%60,00045,00020,00045,00040,000
Case-vN100%85,00025,00025,00025,00050,000
Answer / Solution:

Minority Interest = Equity attributable to minorities. Equity is the residual interest in the assets of an enterprise after deducting all its liabilities, i.e. in this case, it should equal Share Capital + Profit & Loss A/c. Let A = Share capital on 1.1.2024, B = Profit & loss account balance on 1.1.2024, C = Share capital on 31.12.2024, D = Profit & loss account balance on 31.12.2024.

CaseMinority % [E]Minority interest as at date of acquisition [E]×[A+B] (₹) Minority interest as at date of consolidation [E]×[C+D] (₹)
Case-i [100-85]15%29,25030,750
Case-ii [100-70]30%51,00039,000
Case-iii [100-65]35%10,50010,500
Case-iv [100-90]10%6,5008,500
Case-v [100-100]NILNILNIL
Author’s Note: A common error here is computing minority interest only from the closing share capital and reserves figures, without separately building up the acquisition-date minority interest as its own reference point.

Question:

Prepare a consolidated balance sheet of MN Ltd. and its subsidiary RP Ltd. as on 31st March, 2025. Balance Sheets: Share Capital – MN Ltd. ₹7,000 lakh, RP Ltd. ₹4,000 lakh. Reserve and Surplus – MN Ltd. ₹4,000 lakh (General Reserve 2,600 + P&L 1,400), RP Ltd. ₹3,500 lakh (General Reserve 2,000 + P&L 1,500). Long Term Borrowings – MN Ltd. ₹1,800 lakh, RP Ltd. ₹1,400 lakh. Trade Payable – MN Ltd. ₹2,280 lakh, RP Ltd. ₹1,600 lakh. PPE – MN Ltd. ₹6,800 lakh (Land & Building 4,000 + P&M 2,800), RP Ltd. ₹5,500 lakh (Land & Building 3,500 + P&M 2,000). Non-current Investments – MN Ltd. ₹3,280 lakh (Shares in RP Ltd. 3,000 + Debentures in RP Ltd. 280). Inventory – MN Ltd. ₹2,200 lakh, RP Ltd. ₹1,500 lakh. Trade Receivables – MN Ltd. ₹1,800 lakh (Debtors 1,200 + Bills Receivable 600), RP Ltd. ₹1,200 lakh (Debtors 900 + Bills Receivable 300). Cash and Bank – MN Ltd. ₹1,000 lakh, RP Ltd. ₹2,300 lakh.

Additional Information: (1) MN Ltd. acquired 75% shares in RP Ltd. on 1st April, 2024. On acquisition date: General Reserve of RP Ltd. ₹1,600 lakh; P&L Account of RP Ltd. ₹1,200 lakh. (2) On 1st April, 2024, RP Ltd. declared dividend @12% for the year ended 31st March, 2024. MN Ltd. credited the dividend received to its P&L Account. (3) RP Ltd. sold goods worth ₹160 lakh to MN Ltd. during the year, profit ₹40 lakh. MN Ltd.'s inventory includes ₹80 lakh of these goods still unsold as on 31st March, 2025. (4) MN Ltd. holds ₹280 lakh of RP Ltd.'s debentures, included in RP Ltd.'s long-term borrowings. (14 Marks)

Answer / Solution:

Consolidated Balance Sheet of MN Ltd. and its subsidiary RP Ltd. as at 31st March, 2025:

ParticularsNote No.₹ in Lakhs
I. Equity and Liabilities: (1)(a) Share Capital17,000
(b) Reserves and Surplus26,610
(2) Minority Interest (W.N.4)1,870

Notes: 1. Share Capital – 700 Lakh Equity shares of ₹10 each = ₹7,000. 2. Reserves and Surplus – Capital Reserve 2,100 + General Reserve 2,900 + P&L 1,610 = ₹6,610. 3. PPE – Land and Buildings (4,000+3,500) 7,500 + Plant and Machinery (2,800+2,000) 4,800 = ₹12,300. 4. Trade receivables – Debtors (1,200+900) 2,100 + Bills Receivable (600+300) 900 = ₹3,000.

Working Notes:

1. RP Ltd.'s General Reserve: Balance b/d 1,600 + transfer from P&L (balancing) 400 = Balance c/d 2,000.

2. RP Ltd.'s Profit and Loss Account: Balance b/d 1,200 + Net Profit for year (balancing) 1,180 − Transfer to General Reserve 400 − Dividend paid (12% on 4,000) 480 = Balance c/d 1,500.

3. Calculation of Minority Interest: Equity share capital (4,000×25%) 1,000 + Pre-acquisition Profit 580 + Share in Revenue Profit (100+190) 290 = ₹1,870.

4. Analysis of Profit:

ParticularsCapital Profit – Pre-Acq. General ReserveCapital Profit – P&LRevenue Profit
Opening Balance in General Reserve1,600
Add: Transfer from Profit & Loss400

(Total capital profit combining the two capital columns = 2,320; MN Ltd. 75% = 1,740 + 300 = capital, 570 = revenue; Minority 25% = 580 capital + 190 revenue + 100 general-reserve-share, consistent with the Minority Interest working above.)

5. Calculation of Cost of Control: Cost of Investment 3,000; Less: Dividend received out of Pre-acquisition Profit (4,000×12%×75%) (360); Subtotal (A) 2,640. Share in Net Assets of RP Ltd.: Share Capital (4,000×75%) 3,000 + Pre-Acq. Profit (W.N.2) 1,740; Subtotal (B) 4,740. Goodwill/(Capital Reserve) (A−B) = (2,100), i.e. Capital Reserve ₹2,100.

6. Profit & Loss and General Reserve of MN Ltd.: General Reserve – Balance per Balance Sheet 2,600 + Share in Post-Acq. Profit of RP Ltd. 300 = 2,900. Profit & Loss – Balance per Balance Sheet 1,400 + Share in Post-Acq. Profit 570 − Dividend (4,000×12%×75%) (360) = 1,610.

Examiner’s Comment: Several examinees were unable to correctly determine the amounts of capital profits and revenue profits. Errors were also noted in the treatment of unrealised profit in inventory and in the preparation of the consolidated Balance Sheet. Although some examinees attempted the adjustment for dividend paid out of pre-acquisition profits, incorrect treatment of such dividends adversely affected subsequent calculations.

PYQ May 2025 · Q5(a) · Marks: 10 · Approx Time: 18 minutes (approx.) · Topic 1.15-1.16: Preparation of the Consolidated Statement of Profit and Loss, line-by-line addition with elimination of inter-company rent, dividend and expense transactions
Question:

Birds Ltd. and its subsidiary Rooster Ltd provided the following information for the year ended 31/03/2025 (₹): Equity Share Capital – Birds 10,00,000, Rooster 3,00,000. Sales – Birds 28,40,000, Rooster 10,40,000. Purchases (Finished Goods) – Birds 9,15,000, Rooster 1,75,000. Salaries – Birds 7,75,000, Rooster 3,78,000. Rent received – Birds 5,40,000. General and Administration expenses – Birds 2,81,500, Rooster 1,98,000. Selling and Distribution Expenses – Birds 2,21,000, Rooster 90,000. Dividend Income – Birds 1,35,000, Rooster 28,000. Finished Goods Inventory on 01/04/2024 – Birds 3,35,000, Rooster 1,20,000. Finished Goods Inventory on 31/03/2025 – Birds 7,85,000, Rooster 2,90,000. Other Non-operating Income – Birds 2,38,000, Rooster 57,000.

Other Information: On 1st April 2022 Birds Ltd. acquired 2,500 shares of ₹100 each fully paid up in Rooster Ltd. Rooster Ltd. paid a dividend of 12% for the year ended 31/03/2024, correctly accounted for by Birds Ltd. Rooster Ltd. pays ₹11,250 per month to Birds Ltd. towards rent for the portion of premises occupied. Selling and Distribution Expenses of Rooster Ltd. include ₹15,000 received from Birds Ltd.

Prepare Consolidated Profit and Loss Account of Birds Ltd. and its subsidiary Rooster Ltd. for the year ended 31/03/2025. (10 Marks)

Answer / Solution:

Consolidated Statement of Profit and Loss of Birds Ltd. and its subsidiary Rooster Ltd. for the year ended 31st March, 2025:

Revenue from operations (Birds 28,40,000 + Rooster 10,40,000)38,80,000
Other Income (see W.N.)8,33,000
Total revenue47,13,000
Cost of material purchased/consumed (9,15,000+1,75,000)10,90,000
Changes (Increase) in inventories of finished goods (4,50,000+1,70,000)(6,20,000)
Employee benefit expense – Salaries (7,75,000+3,78,000)11,53,000
Other expenses (see W.N.)6,55,500
Total expenses22,78,500
Profit before tax24,34,500

Other Income working: Dividend income – Birds 1,35,000 less dividend received from Rooster (2,500×100×12%=30,000) = 1,05,000; plus Rooster 28,000 = 1,33,000. Other Non-operating Income (2,38,000+57,000)=2,95,000. Rent received – Birds 5,40,000 less rent received from Rooster (11,250×12=1,35,000) = 4,05,000. Total Other Income = 1,33,000+2,95,000+4,05,000 = 8,33,000.

Other expenses working: General & Admin – Birds 2,81,500 + (Rooster 1,98,000 less rent paid to Birds 1,35,000 = 63,000) = 3,44,500. Selling & Distribution – Birds 2,21,000 less paid to Rooster (15,000) = 2,06,000; plus (Rooster 90,000 add received from Birds 15,000 = 1,05,000) = 3,11,000. Total Other expenses = 3,44,500+3,11,000 = 6,55,500.

Note: the ₹15,000 inter-company Selling and Distribution item is a rectification entry – added under Rooster's Selling and Distribution Expenses and deducted from Birds' under the same head, so the inter-company transaction nets to nil on consolidation.

Examiner’s Comment: Most examinees lacked familiarity with the prescribed Schedule III format for the Consolidated Profit and Loss Account under the Companies Act, 2013, and also did not correctly adjust for inter-company transactions.

PYQ May 2025 · Q5(b) · Marks: 4 · Approx Time: 8 minutes (approx.) · Topic 1.11: Calculation of Goodwill/Capital Reserve (cost of control) at acquisition date, with a pre- vs post-acquisition dividend treatment adjusting the cost of investment
Question:

Rubber Ltd. purchased 70% of shares of Tyre Ltd. on 31/03/2024 for ₹4,05,000. The following is the position of Tyre Ltd. as on that date: Issued share capital of Tyre Ltd. on 31/03/2024 ₹5,00,000; Balance in Profit and Loss A/c of Tyre Ltd. on 31/03/2024 ₹70,000; Profit earned during the year 2024-25 ₹45,000; 5% Dividend declared and paid by Tyre Ltd. for 2023-24 ₹25,000.

You are required to calculate the capital reserve / goodwill at the date of acquisition. The calculations are to be made under the following assumptions: Case (i) It is assumed that the dividend is paid out of post-acquisition profits. Case (ii) It is assumed that the dividend is received for pre-acquisition period. (4 Marks)

Answer / Solution:

Case (i) – Dividend assumed paid out of post-acquisition profits: total dividend paid ₹25,000, so the dividend received by Rubber (70%×25,000=₹17,500) is credited to P&L, not netted against cost of investment.

Cost of shares4,05,000
Less: Face value of capital, i.e. 70% of 5,00,000(3,50,000)
Add: Share of capital profits (70,000×70%)49,000
Goodwill6,000

Case (ii) – Dividend assumed received for pre-acquisition period: since the dividend received relates to the pre-acquisition period, it is deducted from the cost of investment in the subsidiary.

Cost of shares4,05,000
Less: dividend received (70%×25,000)(17,500)
Subtotal3,87,500
Less: Face value of capital, i.e. 70% of 5,00,000(3,50,000)
Add: Share of capital profits (70,000×70%)49,000
Capital reserve11,500
Examiner’s Comment: Many examinees were unable to compute Goodwill or Capital Reserve as on the date of acquisition. There was confusion regarding the treatment of dividends – particularly whether dividends were declared from post-acquisition profits or received for the pre-acquisition period. Several examinees incorrectly interchanged assumptions, and many failed to adjust the pre-acquisition dividends from the cost of investment as required.

PYQ September 2025 · Q5 · Marks: 14 · Approx Time: 26 minutes (approx.) · Topic 1.6: Consolidation with a mid-year bonus issue from pre-acquisition reserves and unrealised profit on an upstream (subsidiary-to-parent) inter-company sale
Question:

Seva Limited and subsidiary Meva Limited, Balance Sheets as at 31st March 2025 (₹ Lakh): Seva — Equity Shares of ₹10 6,000, General Reserve 1,500, P&L 2,000, 10% Debentures 1,180, Trade Payable 1,500; Land and Building 4,000, Plant & Machinery 1,460, Investments (Meva shares) 3,000, Inventories 1,400, Trade Receivable 1,420, Cash at Bank 550, Cash in Hand 350. Meva — Equity Shares of ₹10 4,000, General Reserve 1,200, P&L 1,500, 10% Debentures 820, Trade Payable 1,080; Land and Building 4,150, Plant & Machinery 1,650, Inventories 1,100, Trade Receivable 1,000, Cash at Bank 600, Cash in Hand 100. Seva acquired 80% of Meva on 1st April 2024 (Meva's General Reserve ₹2,000 lakh, P&L ₹800 lakh on that date). On 1st November 2024, Meva issued a 1:3 bonus share out of General Reserve (as at 31 March 2024 balance). On 31st March 2025, Seva's inventory includes goods purchased from Meva for ₹125 lakh, on which Meva made a profit of ₹25 lakh. Prepare the Consolidated Balance Sheet as per Schedule III.

Answer / Solution:

W.N.9 Bonus shares: Meva's shares post-bonus 4,000 lakh (at ₹10 face value, i.e. 400 lakh shares) represent 4/3 of pre-bonus holding; pre-bonus = 4,000×3/4=3,000; bonus issued = 4,000−3,000=1,000 (lakh, i.e. ₹1,000 lakh face value), funded from General Reserve.

W.N.1 Meva's General Reserve movement: Opening 2,000 − Bonus 1,000 + transfer from P&L 200 = Closing 1,200.

W.N.2 Meva's P&L movement: Opening 800 − transfer to General Reserve 200 + Net profit for the year (balancing) 900 = Closing 1,500.

W.N.4 Capital profits (pre-acquisition): General Reserve at acquisition, net of the bonus issue (2,000−1,000=1,000) + P&L at acquisition (800) = 1,800. Seva's 80% share = 1,440; Minority's 20% = 360.

W.N.3 Revenue profits (post-acquisition): 900 (from W.N.2); Seva's 80% share: General Reserve 160 (80% of 200) + P&L 560 (80% of 700, i.e. profit after removing the amount already transferred to reserve) = 720; Minority's 20% = 180.

W.N.5 Capital Reserve: Paid-up value of shares held (80% of 4,000) 3,200 + share in capital profits 1,440 = 4,640; less cost of shares 3,000 = Capital Reserve ₹1,640 lakh.

W.N.6 Minority Interest: 20% of share capital (800) + share in revenue profits (180) + share in capital profits (360) = 1,340; less unrealised profit (20% of 25 = 5, Meva's share of the inter-company profit since Meva is the seller) = Minority Interest ₹1,335 lakh.

Consolidated Balance Sheet as at 31st March, 2025 (₹ Lakh): Share Capital 6,000 (Seva's own, unchanged); Reserves and Surplus 5,840 (Capital Reserve 1,640 + General Reserve 1,660 + P&L 2,540); Minority Interest 1,335; Long-term borrowings 2,000 (1,180+820); Trade payables 2,580 (1,500+1,080). Total 17,755. Assets: PPE 11,260 (Land&Building 8,150 [4,000+4,150] + Plant&Machinery 3,110 [1,460+1,650]); Inventories 2,475 (1,400+1,100−25 unrealised profit); Trade receivables 2,420 (1,420+1,000); Cash and cash equivalents 1,600 (Bank 1,150 + Cash in hand 450). Total 17,755.

Examiner’s Comment: Many examinees were unable to prepare the Balance Sheet and Notes to Accounts as per Schedule III. Several examinees failed to give the correct treatment to the issue of bonus shares and the unrealised profit included in closing inventory arising from an upstream transaction. Due to these errors, the computation of capital profits (pre-acquisition) and revenue profits (post-acquisition) was incorrect, which further affected the final answers.

RTP May 2024 · Q17 · Marks: Not stated in source · Approx Time: 10–20 minutes (approx.) · Topic 1.11: Goodwill/Capital Reserve on acquisition = cost of investment (net of pre-acquisition dividend) less parent's share of subsidiary's revalued net assets
Question:

Zoom Ltd. acquired 70% shares of Star Ltd. @ ₹30 per share. Following is the extract of Balance Sheet of Star Ltd.:

₹
15,00,000 Equity Shares of ₹10 each1,50,00,000
15% Debentures15,00,000
Trade Payables82,50,000
Property, Plant and Equipment1,05,00,000
Investments67,50,000
Current Assets1,02,00,000
Loans and Advances33,00,000

On the same day Star Ltd. declared dividend at 20% and as agreed between both the companies Property, Plant and Equipment were to be depreciated @ 10% and investment to be taken at market value of ₹90,00,000. Calculate the Goodwill or Capital Reserve to be recorded in Consolidated Financial Statements.

Answer / Solution:

As per para 13 of AS 21 any excess of the cost to the parent of its investment in a subsidiary over the parent's portion of equity of the subsidiary, at the date on which investment in the subsidiary is made, should be described as goodwill to be recognised as an asset in the consolidated financial statements. When the cost to the parent of its investment in a subsidiary is less than the parent's portion of equity of the subsidiary, at the date on which investment in the subsidiary is made, the difference should be treated as a capital reserve in the consolidated financial statements.

Since dividend is declared by Star Ltd. on the date of acquisition itself, it would be out of the divisible profits of Star Ltd. existing on the date of acquisition i.e., pre-acquisition profits from the perspective of Zoom Ltd. Accordingly, as per para 12 of AS 13, such pre-acquisition dividend would be reduced from the cost of investment, as seen below in the determination of Goodwill on the date of acquisition.

Calculation of Goodwill or Capital Reserve₹₹
Cost of Investment in Star Ltd. (70% stake): 15,00,000 Equity Shares x 70% x ₹30 per share
   Less: Pre-acquisition dividend: 10,50,000 shares x ₹2		3,15,00,000
(21,00,000)		2,94,00,000
Less: Share of Zoom Ltd. in Net Assets of Star Ltd (W.N)(1,55,40,000)
Goodwill on Date of Acquisition1,38,60,000

Working Note: Calculation of net asset

₹₹
Assets
   Property, Plant and Equipment
   Less: Value written off (₹105 lakhs x 10%)		1,05,00,000
(10,50,000)
94,50,000
   Investments at Market Value90,00,000
   Current Assets1,02,00,000
   Loans and Advances33,00,0003,19,50,000
Less: Liabilities
   Trade Payables
   15% Debentures		82,50,000
15,00,000		(97,50,000)
Net Assets of Star Ltd.2,22,00,000
Share of Zoom Ltd. in Net Assets of Star Ltd.: 70%1,55,40,000

Note: In the absence of information about the reserves, it is presumed that the given extract of the Balance Sheet of Star Ltd. is after considering the effects of the dividend declared on the date of acquisition.

Author’s Note: A common error here is treating the dividend declared on the acquisition date as post-acquisition income credited to consolidated reserves, rather than recognising it as a pre-acquisition distribution that reduces the cost of investment used to compute goodwill.
