PYQ September 2024 · Q5 · Marks: 14 · Approx Time: 26 minutes (approx.) · Topic 1.11-1.14: Cost of control/capital reserve, minority interest, pre-acquisition profit split, intra-group elimination and unrealised profit – the bulk of this question, via the Cool Ltd (80% subsidiary) computations  +  Topic 2.4: Goodwill/Capital Reserve on initial recognition at cost of a 25% associate stake (Good Ltd.)
Question:

On 1st February, 2024, Best Ltd. acquired 80% Equity shares of Cool Ltd. for ₹14,80,000. On 31st March, 2024, Best Ltd. also acquired 25% Equity shares of Good Ltd. for ₹3,80,000.

The following are the balances extracted from the books of Best Ltd., Cool Ltd., and Good Ltd. as on 31st March, 2024:

ParticularsBest Ltd. (₹)Cool Ltd. (₹)Good Ltd. (₹)
Equity Shares of ₹100 each fully paid30,00,00020,00,00010,00,000
Securities Premium-2,20,000-
9% Debentures6,30,000-2,40,000
General Reserve2,69,00084,0001,20,000
Profit & Loss Account (Credit Balance)3,26,0002,70,00050,000
Investments17,50,0006,10,000-
Property, Plant, and Equipment18,90,00018,14,00012,10,000
Current Assets9,65,0005,60,0002,25,000
Trade Payable (Including Bills Payable)3,80,0004,10,00025,000
Sales and other income56,00,00038,00,00027,00,000
Raw material consumed36,50,00031,20,00022,30,000
Wages and Salaries5,07,0004,01,0002,69,000
Production expenses1,35,0001,06,00098,000

Additional information:

  • The Profit and Loss account of Cool Ltd. showed a credit balance of ₹30,000 on 1st April, 2023.
  • The General Reserve balance is brought forward from the previous year.
  • On 31st March, 2024, all the bills payable in Cool Ltd.'s balance sheet were acceptances in favour of Best Ltd. However, on the date, Best Ltd. held only ₹3,00,000 of these acceptances in hand, the rest having been endorsed in favour of its creditor.
  • Best Ltd. purchased goods costing ₹5,00,000 from Cool Ltd. on 1st June, 2023 at a price of ₹6,50,000. The entire goods remain unsold with Best Ltd. at the end of the financial year.
  • Best Ltd. is preparing Consolidated Financial Statements for the year ending 31.03.2024.

You are required to calculate: (1) Trade Payable (Consolidated); (2) Current Assets (Consolidated); (3) Minority Interest; (4) Goodwill/Capital Reserve on the acquisition of Cool Ltd.'s shares; (5) Goodwill/Capital Reserve on the acquisition of Good Ltd.'s shares; (6) Profit & Loss Account (Consolidated); (7) General Reserve (Consolidated); (8) Revenue from Operations (Consolidated); (9) Cost of material purchased/consumed (Consolidated).

Answer / Solution:

1. Trade payable (Consolidated): Best limited 3,80,000 + Cool Ltd 4,10,000 − Elimination 3,00,000 = 4,90,000.

2. Current assets (Consolidated): Best limited 9,65,000 + Cool Ltd 5,60,000 − Elimination of inter company owing 3,00,000 = 12,25,000.

3. Minority interest (Cool Ltd): Share Capital (20,00,000 × 20%) 4,00,000 + Securities premium (2,20,000 × 20%) 44,000 + General Reserve (84,000 × 20%) 16,800 + Profit and loss balance (20% of 2,70,000) 54,000 = 5,14,800.

4. Goodwill/Capital Reserve on Acquisition of Cool Ltd.: Purchase Consideration 14,80,000 − Share Capital (20,00,000×80%) 16,00,000 − Securities premium (2,20,000×80%) 1,76,000 − General Reserve (84,000×80%) 67,200 − Profit and loss balance opening (30,000×80%) 24,000 − Pre acquisition profits [(2,70,000−30,000)×10/12×80%] 1,60,000 = Capital Reserve 5,47,200.

5. Goodwill/Capital Reserve on Acquisition of Good Ltd.: Purchase Consideration 3,80,000 − Share Capital (10,00,000×25%) 2,50,000 − General Reserve (1,20,000×25%) 30,000 − Profit and loss balance (50,000×25%) 12,500 = Goodwill 87,500.

6. Profit and Loss Account (Consolidated): Best limited 3,26,000 + Post acquisition profit of Cool Ltd {(2,70,000−30,000)×2/12}×80% 32,000 = 3,58,000.

7. General Reserve (Consolidated): Best limited 2,69,000.

8. Revenue (Consolidated), per para 15/22 of AS 21: Revenue of Best Ltd 56,00,000 + Revenue of Cool Ltd. (38,00,000 × 2/12) 6,33,333 = 62,33,333.

9. Cost of materials purchased/consumed (Consolidated), per para 15/22 of AS 21: Raw material of Best Ltd 36,50,000 + Raw material of Cool Ltd (31,20,000 × 2/12) 5,20,000 = 41,70,000.

Examiner’s Comment: A significant number of examinees made errors in calculating the minority interest and capital reserve during the acquisition of Cool Ltd. Unrealized profit on unsold stock was often not adjusted from pre-acquisition profits. Furthermore, many examinees incorrectly computed the consolidated Profit and Loss Account.

I. Descriptive & Scenario-Based Questions (pure AS 23)

Full descriptive/scenario questions where this chapter is the sole topic tested (after independent-question splitting).

MTP May 2025 Set 2 · Q3(b) · Marks: 7 · Approx Time: 13 minutes (approx.) · Topic 2.10: Potential equity shares excluded from voting power when determining significant influence, even though counted for total economic holding percentage
Question:

A Ltd. has a share capital of 50,000 shares @ ₹100 per share. H Ltd. acquired 15% shares in A Ltd. on 1.4.2024. It also acquired all the 5,000, 12% convertible debentures of ₹100 each of A Ltd. These debentures will be converted at par into equity shares of A Ltd. after 3 years. State whether, as per AS 23, A Ltd. is an Associate of H Ltd. or not with reasons?

Answer / Solution:

As per para 3 of AS 23 'Accounting for Investments in Associates in Consolidated Financial Statements', an associate is an enterprise in which the investor has significant influence and which is neither a subsidiary nor a joint venture of the investor.

Standard further explains in para 4 that as regards share ownership, if an investor holds, directly or indirectly through subsidiary(ies), 20% or more of the voting power of the investee, it is presumed that the investor has significant influence, unless it can be clearly demonstrated that this is not the case. Conversely, if the investor holds, directly or indirectly through subsidiary(ies), less than 20% of the voting power of the investee, it is presumed that the investor does not have significant influence, unless such influence can be clearly demonstrated.

Further as per an explanation to para 4 of the standard, for the purpose of classification of associate, the potential equity shares of the investee held by the investor will not be taken into account for determining the voting power of the investor. In other words, the voting power should be determined on the basis of the current outstanding securities with voting rights.

As per the information given in the question, H Ltd. presently holds indirectly 22.7% shares (with and without voting rights) (Refer W.N.) in A Ltd. However, the current outstanding securities with voting rights in A Ltd. is only 15% and the remaining holding is on account of potential equity shares. Since potential equity shares do not have voting rights they will not be taken into consideration while determining the significant influence of H Ltd. on A Ltd. Hence, A Ltd. is not an associate of H Ltd.

Working Note – Calculation of percentage of holding of shares after conversion:

Particulars₹
Current holding is 15% i.e. 7,500 shares of ₹100 each7,50,000
Potential equity shares i.e. 5,000 shares of ₹100 each5,00,000
Total12,50,000

Total share capital of A Ltd. after conversion of debentures into equity shares will be = ₹50,00,000 + ₹5,00,000 = ₹55,00,000

Percentage of holding = (12,50,000/55,00,000) × 100 = 22.7% approx.

Author’s Note: A common error here is including the convertible debentures' post-conversion equity stake in the voting-power test, arriving at 22.7% and concluding significant influence exists, without recognising that AS 23 excludes potential equity shares from the voting-power calculation used for the significant-influence presumption.

RTP January 2025 · Q17 · Marks: Not stated in source · Approx Time: 10–20 minutes (approx.) · Topic 2.3: 20% voting-power presumption of significant influence; goodwill computed per-tranche against the investee's net asset value at each tranche's own acquisition date
Question:

A Ltd. invested ₹1,00,000 to acquire 10% stake (Investment I) in B Ltd. and later invested ₹3,00,000 to acquire additional 20% (Investment II). The net asset value of the B Ltd. at the respective investment dates was ₹7,50,000 and ₹12,50,000 respectively. Determine whether B Ltd. is an associate of A Ltd. Also, calculate goodwill arising on the acquisition of the associate.

Answer / Solution:

As per para 3 of AS 23, an associate is an enterprise in which the investor has significant influence and which is neither a subsidiary nor a joint venture of the investor. Significant influence may be gained by share ownership, statute or agreement. As regards share ownership, if an investor holds, directly or indirectly through subsidiary(ies), 20% or more of the voting power of the investee, it is presumed that the investor has significant influence, unless it can be clearly demonstrated that this is not the case. In this case, A Ltd. has invested 30% in B Ltd. so B Ltd. is to be considered as an associate of A Ltd.

The goodwill arising on the acquisition of the associate will be computed as follows:

Investment I1,00,000
Share of net assets (10 percent of ₹7,50,000)(75,000)
Goodwill (A)25,000
Investment II3,00,000
Share of net assets (20 percent of ₹12,50,000)(2,50,000)
Goodwill (B)50,000
Total goodwill (A + B)75,000
Author’s Note: A common error is computing goodwill on the associate's acquisition as a single blended calculation across both tranches, missing that AS 23 requires each tranche of investment to be compared against the investee's net asset value at that tranche's own acquisition date, since intervening changes in net assets affect the goodwill computed on the later tranche.

RTP September 2024 · Q15 · Marks: Not stated in source · Approx Time: 10–20 minutes (approx.) · Topic 2.10: Potential equity shares (e.g. convertible debentures) excluded when determining voting power for associate classification
Question:

Hill Ltd. has a share capital of 50,000 shares @ ₹100 per share. Sun Ltd. acquired 15% shares in Hill Ltd. on 1.4.2024. It also acquired all the 5,000, 12% convertible debentures of ₹100 each of Hill Ltd. These debentures will be converted at par into equity shares of Hill Ltd. after 3 years. State whether, as per AS 23, Hill Ltd. is an Associate of Sun Ltd. or not with reasons?

Answer / Solution:

As per para 3 of AS 23 ‘Accounting for Investments in Associates in Consolidated Financial Statements’, an associate is an enterprise in which the investor has significant influence and which is neither a subsidiary nor a joint venture of the investor.

Standard further explains in para 4 that as regards share ownership, if an investor holds, directly or indirectly through subsidiary (ies), 20% or more of the voting power of the investee, it is presumed that the investor has significant influence, unless it can be clearly demonstrated that this is not the case. Conversely, if the investor holds, directly or indirectly through subsidiary (ies), less than 20% of the voting power of the investee, it is presumed that the investor does not have significant influence, unless such influence can be clearly demonstrated.

Further as per an explanation to para 4 of the standard, for the purpose of classification of associate, the potential equity shares of the investee held by the investor will not be taken into account for determining the voting power of the investor. In other words, the voting power should be determined on the basis of the current outstanding securities with voting rights.

As per the information given in the question, Sun Ltd. presently holds indirectly 22.7% shares (with and without voting rights) (Refer W.N.) in Hill Ltd. However, the current outstanding securities with voting rights in Hill Ltd. is only 15% and the remaining holding is on account of potential equity shares. Since potential equity shares do not have voting rights they will not be taken into consideration while determining the significant influence of Sun Ltd. on Hill Ltd. Hence, Hill Ltd. is not an associate of Sun Ltd.

Working Note: Calculation of percentage of holding of shares after conversion

₹
Current holding is 15% i.e. 7,500 shares of ₹100 each7,50,000
Potential equity shares i.e. 5,000 shares of ₹100 each5,00,000
Total12,50,000

Total share capital of Hill Ltd. after conversion of debentures into equity shares will be = ₹50,00,000 + ₹5,00,000 = ₹55,00,000

Percentage of holding = ₹(12,50,000/55,00,000) × 100 = 22.7% approx.

Author’s Note: A common error is computing the combined 22.7% effective holding (current shares plus convertible debentures) and concluding significant influence exists purely because that combined figure exceeds 20%, without recognising that potential equity shares (the convertible debentures, before conversion) carry no voting rights and must be excluded from the voting-power test.

MTP January 2026 Set 2 · Q3 · Marks: 14 · Approx Time: 26 minutes (approx.) · Topic 1.4: Jointly controlled asset - each venturer records its own share of assets, liabilities, and expenses directly
Question:

Hari Ltd., OM Ltd. and Bhakti Ltd. jointly constructed a pipeline to transport gas manufactured by them (a jointly controlled asset under AS 27). Expenditure incurred: Buildings ₹18,00,000 (depreciate @5% p.a.); Pipeline ₹90,00,000 (@15% p.a.); Computers & electronics ₹4,50,000 (@40% p.a.); Vehicles ₹13,50,000 (@20% p.a.). They equally bear pipeline maintenance expenditure of ₹9,00,000 each year. Show the extract of the consolidated balance sheet and the extract of Statement of Profit & Loss and Balance Sheet for each venturer.

Answer / Solution:

Each venturer records its own one-third share of each jointly-controlled asset directly in its own books, per AS 27's proportionate-consolidation treatment for a jointly controlled asset (no separate joint entity exists).

Per-venturer figures (identical for each of Hari/OM/Bhakti, one-third share each): Land & Building 6,00,000, less depreciation @5% (30,000) = 5,70,000. Plant & Machinery (Pipeline) 30,00,000, less depreciation @15% (4,50,000) = 25,50,000. Computers 1,50,000, less depreciation @40% (60,000) = 90,000. Vehicles 4,50,000, less depreciation @20% (90,000) = 3,60,000. Total PPE per venturer: ₹35,70,000. Depreciation and amortisation expense per venturer: 30,000+4,50,000+60,000+90,000 = ₹6,30,000. Other operating expenses (pipeline maintenance, one-third share) ₹3,00,000.

Consolidated (all three venturers combined) extract: PPE — Land & Building 3×5,70,000=17,10,000; Plant & Machinery 3×25,50,000=76,50,000; Computers 3×90,000=2,70,000; Vehicles 3×3,60,000=10,80,000; Total Consolidated PPE: ₹1,07,10,000.

Author’s Note: Some examinees treated this as a jointly controlled entity requiring proportionate consolidation of a separate set of books, rather than recognising that a jointly controlled asset (no separate entity) means each venturer simply records its own share directly in its own books.

RTP January 2026 · Q18 · Marks: Not stated in source · Approx Time: 10–20 minutes (approx.) · Topic 1.2: Three forms of joint venture - operations, assets, entities
Question:

Briefly explain the scope and forms of Joint Venture as per AS 27.

Answer / Solution:

Scope: AS 27 applies to accounting for interests in joint ventures and reporting joint venture assets, liabilities, income, and expenses in the financial statements of venturers and investors, regardless of the structure/form under which the joint venture activities take place. Its consolidated-financial-statements provisions apply only when the venturer prepares and presents CFS.

Forms of Joint Venture: (i) Jointly controlled operations — no separate entity created; venturers use their own resources, raise their own funds, incur expenses, and realise sales individually, using shared assets/employees alongside their own business, with no separate books maintained for the joint venture. (ii) Jointly controlled assets — no separate legal entity, but the venturers jointly own assets used to generate economic benefit for each of them, taking up related expenses/liabilities per the contractual agreement. (iii) Jointly controlled entities — a new entity is created, pooling the venturers' resources; the entity purchases its own assets, incurs its own liabilities/expenses, and makes its own sales; the net result is shared per the contractual agreement, which also determines joint control; a separate set of books is maintained.

Author’s Note: Some examinees conflated jointly controlled assets with jointly controlled entities, missing that the defining distinction is the absence vs. presence of a separate legal entity and separate books.

X Ltd. absorbs Y Ltd. on the following terms: (i) 10% Preference Shareholders are to be paid at 10% premium by issue of 9% Preference Shares of X Ltd. (ii) Goodwill of Y Ltd. on absorption is to be computed based on two times of average profits of preceding three financial years (2022-23: ₹90,000; 2021-22: ₹78,000 and 2020-21: ₹72,000). The profits of 2020-21 included credit of an insurance claim of ₹25,000 (fire occurred in 2019-20 and loss by fire ₹30,000 was booked in Profit and Loss Account of that year). In the year 2021-22, there was an embezzlement of cash by an employee amounting to ₹10,000. (iii) Land & Buildings are valued at ₹5,00,000 and the Plant & Machinery at ₹4,00,000. (iv) Inventories are to be taken over at 10% less value and Provision for Doubtful Debts is to be created @2.5%. (v) There was an unrecorded current asset in the books of Y Ltd. whose fair value amounted to ₹15,000 and such asset was also taken over by X Ltd. (vi) The trade payables of Y Ltd. included ₹20,000 payable to X Ltd. (vii) Equity Shareholders of Y Ltd. will be issued Equity Shares @5% premium.

You are required to: (i) Prepare Realisation A/c in the books of Y Ltd. (ii) Prepare the Balance Sheet of X Ltd. after absorption as at 31st March, 2024.

Reserves and Surplus: Securities Premium 60,000 + General Reserve 2,10,000 = 2,70,000. 3. Long-term provisions: Retirement Gratuity fund 2,10,000. 4. Trade payables (3,90,000+2,40,000−20,000 mutual owings eliminated) = 6,10,000. 5. Short term Provisions: Provision for Doubtful Debts 7,500. 6. Working Notes: Computation of goodwill: Profit of 2022-23 90,000 + Profit of 2021-22 adjusted (78,000+10,000)=88,000 + Profit of 2020-21 adjusted (72,000−25,000)=47,000; total 2,25,000; average profit 75,000; goodwill at 2 times average = ₹1,50,000. Purchase Consideration: Goodwill 1,50,000 + Land & Building 5,00,000 + Plant & Machinery 4,00,000 + Inventory 4,72,500 + Trade receivables 3,00,000 + Unrecorded assets 15,000 + Cash at Bank 60,000 = 18,97,500; less Retirement Gratuity 60,000, Trade payables 2,40,000, Provision for doubtful debts 7,500 (total 3,07,500); Net Assets/Purchase Consideration = 15,90,000. Satisfied as: 10% Preference Shareholders of Y Ltd. 3,00,000 + 10% Premium 30,000 = 9% Preference Shares of X Ltd. 3,30,000; Equity Shareholders of Y Ltd. satisfied by 1,20,000 equity shares of X Ltd. at 5% Premium = 12,60,000; Total 15,90,000.

Author’s Note: A common error is omitting the elimination of mutual owings between the transferor and transferee companies before consolidating trade payables and receivables in the post-absorption balance sheet.

Question:

A Limited and B Limited are carrying on business of same nature. On 31st March, 2024 the information given by both these companies is as follows (₹): Share Capital — Equity Shares of ₹10 each fully paid: A Ltd. 12,00,000 / B Ltd. 7,20,000; 10% Preference Shares of ₹100 each: A Ltd. 6,00,000 / B Ltd. Nil; 8% Preference Shares of ₹100 each: A Ltd. Nil / B Ltd. 5,00,000; General Reserve: 3,00,000 / 2,50,000; Investment Allowance Reserve: Nil / 60,000; Security Premium: 2,40,000 / Nil; Export Profit Reserve: 1,80,000 / 1,20,000; Profit & Loss Account: 2,16,000 / 1,92,000; 9% Debentures (₹10 each): 3,00,000 / 2,00,000; Secured Loan: Nil / 3,60,000; Sundry Creditors: 3,12,000 / 2,04,000; Bills Payable: 75,000 / 1,00,000; Other Current Liabilities: 50,000 / 75,000; Land and Building: 10,80,000 / 8,40,000; Plant and Machinery: 6,00,000 / 5,60,000; Office Equipment: 3,45,000 / 2,10,000; Investments: 96,000 / 3,00,000; Inventory: 6,30,000 / 4,20,000; Sundry Debtors: 4,90,000 / 3,20,000; Bills Receivables: 60,000 / 70,000; Cash at Bank: 1,72,000 / 61,000. A Limited takes over B Limited on the above date, both companies agreeing on a scheme of Amalgamation on the following terms: (a) A Limited will issue 80,000 Equity Shares of ₹10 each at par to the Equity Shareholders of B Limited. (b) A Limited will issue 10% Preference Shares of ₹100 each to discharge the Preference Shareholders of B Limited at 15% premium in such a way that the existing dividend quantum of the preference shareholders of B Limited will not get affected. (c) The Debentures of B Limited will be converted into equivalent number of Debentures of A Limited. (d) All the Bills Receivable of A Limited were accepted by B Limited. (e) A contingent liability of B Limited amounting to ₹72,000 to be treated as actual liability in trade payables. (f) Expenses of Amalgamation amounted to ₹12,000 were borne by A Limited. You are required to pass opening Journal Entries in the books of A Limited and prepare the opening Balance Sheet of A Limited as on 1st April, 2024 after amalgamation, assuming that the amalgamation is in the nature of Merger.

Answer / Solution:

Working Note 1 — Purchase consideration: Equity shareholders of B Ltd. (80,000 × ₹10) = 8,00,000. Preference shareholders of B Ltd. (5,00,000 × 115%) = 5,75,000. Purchase consideration = ₹13,75,000.

Working Note 2 — Amount adjusted from general reserve: Purchase consideration 13,75,000 less Share capital issued (7,20,000 + 5,00,000 = 12,20,000) = ₹1,55,000 adjusted from general reserve.

Creditors: balance per B Ltd.'s balance sheet 2,04,000, add contingent trade payable treated as actual liability 72,000 = 2,76,000 taken by A Ltd.

Author’s Note: A common error is computing the preference shareholders' purchase consideration at face value instead of at the 15% premium the scheme specifies, and separately, forgetting to cancel the mutual bills receivable/payable balance arising because B Ltd. had accepted A Ltd.'s bills.

  2. Preference shareholders of the two companies are issued equivalent number of 16% preference shares of Heer Limited at a price of ₹160 per share (face value ₹100).
  3. 10% Debenture holders of Meet Limited and Preet Limited are discharged by Heer Limited, issuing such number of its 16% Debentures of ₹100 each so as to maintain the same amount of interest.

  5. Liquidation expenses are for Meet Limited ₹12,00,000 and for Preet Limited ₹6,00,000. It is decided that these expenses would be borne by Heer Limited.

  7. Authorised equity share capital of Heer Limited is ₹30,00,00,000 divided into equity shares of ₹10 each. After issuing required number of shares to the liquidators of Meet Limited and Preet Limited, Heer Limited issued balance shares to public. The issue was fully subscribed.

Share Capital: Authorized – a) Equity: 300 Lakh shares of ₹10 each = 3,000; b) Preference: 15 Lakh shares of ₹100 = 1,500 (Total authorised 4,500... as printed, authorised total shown as 2,250 in the source's authorised sub-total line, retained as printed). Issued, Subscribed & Paid up: a) Equity Share Capital: 300 Lakh equity shares of ₹10 each = 3,000 (of which 210 lakh shares issued for consideration other than cash); b) Preference Share Capital: 15 Lakh Preference shares of ₹100 = 1,500 (all issued for consideration other than cash). Total issued = 4,500.

2. Reserves and surplus: Investment allowance reserve (450+300) = 750; Securities premium (300×25)+(15×60) = 8,400 [note: face value ₹10 shares issued at ₹35, i.e. ₹25 premium; face value ₹100 preference shares issued at ₹160, i.e. ₹60 premium]; less Amalgamation adjustment reserve (750, offsetting the Investment Allowance Reserve carried forward). Total = 8,400.

3. Long-term borrowings: 16% Debentures = 168.75 (W.N.3).

4. Trade payables: Meet Ltd. 1,260 + Preet Ltd. 570 = 1,830.

5. PPE: Land and Building (2,700+1,950 combined line as printed) 2,700; Plant and Machinery 1,950. Total = 4,650 (source's own PPE note groups the two companies' Property Plant & Equipment together under "Land and Building" 2,700 and "Plant and Machinery" 1,950, reproduced as printed).

6. Intangible assets: Goodwill (W.N.2) 1,248.75 + Liquidation expenses (12+6) 18 = 1,266.75.

7. Non-current Investments: 450+150 = 600.

8. Inventories: Meet Ltd. 1,050 + Preet Ltd. 750 = 1,800.

9. Trade receivables: Meet Ltd. 900 + Preet Ltd. 1,050 = 1,950.

10. Cash & cash equivalents: Meet Ltd. 900 + Preet Ltd. 600 − Liquidation Expenses (18) + Share issued for cash (90 lakh shares × ₹35 = 3,150) = 4,632.

Combined Goodwill = 1,012.5 + 236.25 = 1,248.75 (as used in Note 6 above).

Working Note 3 — Issue of Debentures (same interest amount maintained, 10% old rate to 16% new rate): Meet Ltd.: Debentures ₹1,80,00,000 × 10% = ₹18,00,000 interest; new debentures = (18,00,000×100)/16 = ₹1,12,50,000. Preet Ltd.: Debentures ₹90,00,000 × 10% = ₹9,00,000 interest; new debentures = (9,00,000×100)/16 = ₹56,25,000. Combined = ₹1,68,75,000 (₹168.75 lakhs, per Note 3 above).

Author’s Note: A common error is converting the 10% debentures to the new 16% rate using the face value directly instead of preserving the same rupee amount of interest, and separately, forgetting that liquidation expenses borne by the transferee company reduce cash and are added to goodwill rather than expensed through the Statement of Profit and Loss.

MTP May 2025 Set 2 · Q6(a) [OR-alt 1] · Marks: 4 · Approx Time: 8 minutes (approx.) · Topic 2: Meaning of Amalgamation
Question:

Distinguish between Amalgamation, Absorption and External Reconstruction of Company.

Answer / Solution:
BasisAmalgamationAbsorptionExternal Reconstruction
MeaningTwo or more companies are wound up and a new company is formed to take over their business.An existing company takes over the business of one or more existing companies.A newly formed company takes over the business of an existing company.
Minimum number of companies involvedAt least three companies.At least two companies.Only two companies.
Number of new resultant companiesOnly one resultant company is formed; two companies are wound up to form a single resultant company.No new resultant company is formed.Only one resultant company is formed – a newly formed company takes over the business of an existing company.
ObjectiveTo cut competition and reap economies of large scale.To cut competition and reap economies of large scale.To reorganise the financial structure of the company.
ExampleA Ltd. and B Ltd. amalgamate to form C Ltd.A Ltd. takes over the business of another existing company B Ltd.B Ltd. is formed to take over the business of an existing company A Ltd.
Author’s Note: A common error here is confusing Absorption (no new company formed) with External Reconstruction (a newly formed company takes over the existing one), since both involve only two companies and can otherwise sound similar if the definitions aren't stated precisely.

MTP September 2024 Set 1 · Q3(b) · Marks: 4 · Approx Time: 8 minutes (approx.) · Topic 4: Purchase Consideration
Question:

Wow Ltd. agreed to takeover Wonder Ltd. on 1st April, 2024. The terms and conditions of takeover were as follows: (i) Wow Ltd. issued 56,000 equity shares of ₹100 each at a premium of ₹15 per share to the equity shareholders of Wonder Ltd. (ii) Cash payment of ₹39,000 was made to equity shareholders of Wonder Ltd. (iii) 24,000 fully paid preference shares of ₹50 each issued at par to discharge the preference shareholders of Wonder Ltd. (iv) The 8% Debentures of Wonder Ltd. (₹78,000) converted into equivalent value of 9% debentures in Wow Ltd. (v) The actual cost of liquidation of Wonder Ltd. was ₹23,000. Liquidation cost is to be reimbursed by Wow Ltd. to the extent of ₹15,000. You are required to: (1) Calculate the amount of purchase consideration as per the provisions of AS 14 and (2) Pass Journal Entry relating to discharge of purchase consideration in books of Wow Ltd.

Answer / Solution:

As per AS 14 'Accounting for Amalgamations', consideration for the amalgamation means the aggregate of shares and other securities issued and payment made in the form of cash or other assets by the transferee company to the shareholders of the transferor company – the 8% Debentures conversion (a discharge to Wonder Ltd.'s own debenture-holders, not its shareholders) and the liquidation-cost reimbursement are therefore excluded from purchase consideration.

(i) Computation of Purchase Consideration:

Preference Shares: 24,000 × ₹5012,00,000
Cash39,000
Equity shares: 56,000 × ₹115 (100+15 premium)64,40,000
Total Purchase Consideration76,79,000

(ii) Journal entry (books of Wow Ltd.):

Liquidator of Wonder Ltd. Dr. 76,79,000; To Cash 39,000; To Preference Share Capital A/c 12,00,000; To Equity Share Capital A/c 56,00,000; To Securities Premium A/c 8,40,000 [56,000 × ₹15 (115−100)].

Author’s Note: A common error is including the debenture conversion or the liquidation-cost reimbursement within purchase consideration, missing that AS 14's definition covers only amounts paid to the transferor company's shareholders, not its debenture-holders or its own liquidation expenses.

MTP September 2024 Set 1 · Q4 · Marks: 14 · Approx Time: 26 minutes (approx.) · Topic 4/7: Purchase Consideration / Entries in the Bks of Purchasing Co
Question:

The following are the summarized Balance Sheet of VT Ltd. and MG Ltd. as on 31st March, 2024 (₹):

ParticularsVT Ltd.MG Ltd.
Equity Shares of ₹10 each12,00,0006,00,000
10% Preference Shares of ₹100 each4,00,0002,00,000
Reserve and Surplus6,00,0004,00,000
12% Debentures4,00,0003,00,000
Trade Payables5,00,0003,00,000
Total31,00,00018,00,000
PPE14,00,0005,00,000
Investment1,60,0001,60,000
Inventory4,80,0006,40,000
Trade Receivables8,40,0004,20,000
Cash at Bank2,20,00080,000
Total31,00,00018,00,000

Details of Trade receivables and payables – VT Ltd.: Debtors 7,20,000, Bills Receivable 1,20,000 (total 8,40,000); Sundry Creditors 4,40,000, Bills Payable 60,000 (total 5,00,000). MG Ltd.: Debtors 3,80,000, Bills Receivable 40,000 (total 4,20,000); Sundry Creditors 2,50,000, Bills Payable 50,000 (total 3,00,000).

PPE of both companies revalued at 15% above book value. Inventory and Debtors taken over at 5% less than book value. Both companies pay 10% equity dividend (preference dividend already paid). VT Ltd. then absorbs MG Ltd. on these terms: (i) VT Ltd. issues 16 equity shares of ₹10 each at par against every 12 shares of MG Ltd. (ii) 10% Preference Shareholders of MG Ltd. paid at 10% discount via 10% Preference Shares of ₹100 each at par in VT Ltd. (iii) 12% Debenture holders of MG Ltd. paid at 8% premium, by 12% Debentures in VT Ltd. issued at a discount of 10%. (iv) ₹60,000 to be paid by VT Ltd. to MG Ltd. for liquidation expenses. (v) Sundry Debtors of MG Ltd. include ₹20,000 due from VT Ltd. Required: (1) Journal entries in the books of VT Ltd. (2) Statement of consideration payable by VT Ltd.

Answer / Solution:

(1) Journal Entries in the Books of VT Ltd.:

  1. PPE Dr. 2,10,000; To Revaluation Reserve 2,10,000 (revaluation of PPE at 15% above book value).
  2. Reserve and Surplus Dr. 1,20,000; To Equity Dividend 1,20,000 (equity dividend @10%); then Equity Dividend Dr. 1,20,000; To Bank Account 1,20,000 (payment of equity dividend).
  3. Business Purchase Account Dr. 9,80,000; To Liquidator of MG Ltd. 9,80,000 (consideration payable for MG Ltd.'s business).
  4. PPE (115% of 5,00,000) Dr. 5,75,000; Inventory (95% of 6,40,000) Dr. 6,08,000; Debtors Dr. 3,80,000; Bills Receivable Dr. 40,000; Investment Dr. 1,60,000; Cash at Bank Dr. 20,000 (80,000−60,000 dividend paid); To Provision for Bad Debts (5% of 3,60,000) 18,000; To Sundry Creditors 2,50,000; To 12% Debentures in MG Ltd. 3,24,000; To Bills Payable 50,000; To Business Purchase Account 9,80,000; To Capital Reserve (balancing figure) 1,61,000 (incorporation of MG Ltd.'s assets/liabilities at agreed values, difference credited to Capital Reserve).
  5. Liquidator of MG Ltd. Dr. 9,80,000; To Equity Share Capital 8,00,000; To 10% Preference Share Capital 1,80,000 (discharge of consideration for MG Ltd.'s business).
  6. 12% Debentures in MG Ltd. (3,00,000 × 108%) Dr. 3,24,000; Discount on Issue of Debentures (3,60,000 × 10%) Dr. 36,000; To 12% Debentures (3,24,000/90×100) 3,60,000 (allotment of 12% Debentures to MG Ltd.'s debenture holders at a discount of 10%).
  7. Sundry Creditors Dr. 20,000; To Sundry Debtors 20,000 (cancellation of mutual owing).
  8. Goodwill Dr. 60,000; To Bank 60,000 (liquidation expenses reimbursed to MG Ltd.).
  9. Capital Reserve/P&L A/c Dr. 60,000; To Goodwill 60,000 (goodwill set off).

(2) Statement of Consideration payable by VT Ltd. (for 60,000 MG Ltd. shares):

Shares to be allotted: 60,000 ÷ 12 × 16 = 80,000 equity shares of VT Ltd. Issued 80,000 shares of ₹10 each = ₹8,00,000 (i); for 10% preference shares, paid at 10% discount: ₹2,00,000 × 90/100 = ₹1,80,000 (ii). Consideration amount [(i)+(ii)] = ₹9,80,000.

Author’s Note: A common error is omitting the mutual-owing elimination (the ₹20,000 MG Ltd. debtor balance due from VT Ltd. itself) before finalising the incorporation entries, or forgetting to write off the goodwill created purely from the liquidation-expense reimbursement.

MTP September 2024 Set 1 · Q6(a) [OR-alt 1] · Marks: 4 · Approx Time: 8 minutes (approx.) · Topic 2: Meaning of Amalgamation
Question:

Distinguish between Amalgamation, Absorption and External Reconstruction of Company.

Answer / Solution:
BasisAmalgamationAbsorptionExternal Reconstruction
MeaningTwo or more companies are wound up and a new company is formed to take over their business.An existing company takes over the business of one or more existing companies.A newly formed company takes over the business of an existing company.
Minimum companies involvedAt least threeAt least twoOnly two
Number of new resultant companiesOnly one resultant company formed; two companies wound up to form it.No new resultant company is formed.Only one resultant company formed; a newly formed company takes over the business of the existing one.
ObjectiveTo cut competition and reap economies of large scale.To cut competition and reap economies of large scale.To reorganise the financial structure of the company.
ExampleA Ltd. and B Ltd. amalgamate to form C Ltd.A Ltd. takes over the business of existing company B Ltd.B Ltd. is formed to take over the business of existing company A Ltd.
Author’s Note: A common error is confusing Absorption with External Reconstruction, since both involve only two companies – the distinguishing point is whether the acquirer is a pre-existing company (Absorption) or a newly formed one (External Reconstruction).

Summarized Balance Sheets of B Ltd. and G Ltd. as at 31st March, 2025: Share Capital – B Ltd. ₹46,30,000 (Equity 36,50,000 + 9% Preference 9,80,000), G Ltd. ₹14,20,000 (Equity 11,50,000 + 10% Preference 2,70,000). Trade Payables – B Ltd. ₹14,72,000 (Creditors 13,85,000 + Bills Payable 87,000), G Ltd. ₹2,64,000 (Creditors 2,25,000 + Bills Payable 39,000). Short-term Borrowings – G Ltd. ₹1,89,500. PPE – B Ltd. ₹63,00,000, G Ltd. ₹14,53,000. Non-current Investments – B Ltd. ₹23,50,000. Inventories – B Ltd. ₹43,000, G Ltd. ₹1,16,000. On 31.03.2025, B Ltd. absorbs the business of G Ltd. on the following terms: (i) For every equity share held by G Ltd. equity shareholders, ₹10 cash and one equity share of ₹100 at par in B Ltd. (ii) 10% debenture-holders of G Ltd. allotted 9% debentures of ₹100 in B Ltd. to bring the same amount of interest. (iii) 10% Preference Shareholders of G Ltd. paid at 15% premium by issue of 9% Preference Shares of ₹100 in B Ltd., such that the existing dividend quantum is unaffected. (iv) A contingent liability of G Limited of ₹72,000 to be treated as an actual liability in trade payables. (v) Liquidation expenses of G Ltd. reimbursed by B Ltd. ₹10,000. The following is summarized Balance Sheet of Pickles Ltd. as on 31/03/2025. Assets: PPE 7,50,000 (Land and Building 3,50,000, Plant and Machinery 3,00,000, Furniture and Fittings 1,00,000); Intangible assets 75,000 (Patents); Inventories 5,25,000; Trade receivables 3,00,000; Cash and Cash equivalents 60,000; Total 17,10,000.

On 31/03/2025, Foods Ltd. acquires the business of Pickles Ltd. on the following terms: Foods Ltd. to take over all assets (except cash) and liabilities at their book values. Part of the Furniture and Fixtures is disposed off by Pickles Ltd. for ₹55,000 at cost. The retirement of employees was due on 31/03/2025; a portion of ₹35,000 from Retirement Gratuity Fund was earmarked towards the payment due to them. Foods Ltd. decided to pay for each Preference share in Pickles Ltd., ₹27 in cash and one 8% Preference share of ₹100 in Foods Ltd. For each Equity share in Pickles Ltd., it was decided to pay ₹30 in cash and one Equity share of Foods Ltd. for ₹145 (Face value of each share of Foods Ltd. is ₹100). Liquidation expenses of ₹22,500 paid by Pickles Ltd. were subsequently reimbursed by Foods Ltd. The fixed assets of Pickles Ltd were not revalued for the purpose of amalgamation.

(extract): Realisation A/c Dr 16,50,000 To Land & Building 3,50,000, To Plant & Machinery 3,00,000, To Furniture & Fixtures 1,00,000, To Patent 75,000, To Inventories 5,25,000, To Trade Receivables 3,00,000 (assets transferred). 8% Debentures A/c Dr 1,00,000, Trade Payables A/c Dr 1,75,000, Other Current Liabilities A/c Dr 65,000, Retirement Gratuity Fund A/c Dr 35,000 To Realisation A/c 3,75,000 (liabilities transferred). Equity Share Capital A/c Dr 6,00,000, General Reserve A/c Dr 1,00,000, P&L A/c Dr 1,10,000, Retirement Gratuity fund Dr 25,000 To Equity Shareholders A/c 8,35,000. Equity Shareholders A/c Dr 11,65,000 To Cash A/c 2,95,000, To Equity Shares in Foods Ltd A/c 8,70,000. Foods Ltd A/c Dr 22,500 To Cash A/c 22,500 (liquidation expenses paid). Trade receivables – Bills receivables: Blue —, Green 50,000; Trade Debtors: Blue 1,25,000, Green 1,00,000. (b) Revalued figures as on 31st March, 2026: PPE – Blue 21,30,000, Green 11,70,000; Inventories – Blue 7,73,500, Green 3,23,250. (c) Trade debtors and trade creditors include ₹75,000 owed by Blue Limited to Green Limited. (d) All bills receivable held by Green Limited were Blue Limited's acceptances. (e) Purchase consideration satisfied by: (i) 1,80,000 equity shares of ₹5 each in BG Ltd. to Blue and Green in proportion to profitability (average net profit of previous 3 years): Blue – 2022-23 ₹13,48,700, 2023-24 (₹7,500) loss, 2024-25 ₹11,33,800; Green – 2022-23 ₹8,21,700, 2023-24 ₹10,26,300, 2024-25 ₹10,77,000. (ii) 15% debentures in BG Ltd. at par to provide income equivalent to 8% return on capital employed in their respective business as on 31st March, 2026 after revaluation of assets.

(A) Computation of Amount of Debentures and Shares to be issued:

PYQ September 2025 · Q4 · Marks: 14 · Approx Time: 26 minutes (approx.) · Topic 2: Meaning of Amalgamation
Question:

Blue Limited and Yellow Limited Balance Sheets as at 31st March 2025 (₹ lakhs): Blue — Equity Shares of ₹100 40.000, 10% Debentures 15.000, General Reserves 1.500, Retirement Gratuity Fund 3.450, Trade Payables 7.400, Other current liabilities 1.240, Short-term provisions 0.710; Goodwill 8.750, PPE 35.650, Inventories 8.890, Trade Receivables 13.535, Cash in hand 0.485, Bank 1.990. Yellow — Equity Shares of ₹100 28.000, 8% Debentures 8.000, General Reserves 0.670, Retirement Gratuity Fund 1.300, Trade Payables 4.250, Other current liabilities 0.880, Short-term provisions 0.320; Goodwill 1.795, PPE 31.260, Inventories 4.800, Trade Receivables 4.650, Cash in hand 0.315, Bank 0.600. Blue absorbs Yellow's business on 31st March 2025: (i) 8% Debenture holders of Yellow paid at 10% discount via 10% Debentures at par in Blue. (ii) Unrecorded current asset ₹1,16,000 in Yellow's books, taken over. (iii) Yellow's Trade Payables include ₹1,50,000 payable to Blue. (iv) Yellow's Inventory taken over at 10% more than book value. (v) Yellow's Goodwill = 2 × simple average profits of 2021-22 (4,50,000), 2022-23 (3,90,000), 2023-24 (2,35,000); 2022-23 had a ₹50,000 cash embezzlement already adjusted in that year's profit. (vi) Yellow's PPE taken over at ₹36,44,500. (vii) Remaining assets/liabilities at book value. (viii) Yellow's equity shareholders issued Blue shares at 5% premium. Calculate the Purchase Consideration and prepare Blue's post-absorption Balance Sheet.

Answer / Solution:

W.N.1 Goodwill of Yellow Ltd.: Adjusted profits: 2021-22: 4.50; 2022-23: 3.90+0.50 (add back embezzlement, a one-off/non-recurring item) = 4.40; 2023-24: 2.35. Total 11.25; average (i)/3 = 3.75; ×2 years' purchase = Goodwill ₹7.50 lakhs.

(i) Purchase Consideration: Goodwill 7.500 + PPE 36.445 + Inventory (4.800×1.10=5.280) + Trade receivables 4.650 + Cash in hand 0.315 + Cash at Bank 0.600 + Unrecorded assets 1.160 = Assets taken over 55.950; less liabilities taken over (10% Debentures at 90% of 8.00=7.200 + Retirement Gratuity 1.300 + Trade payables 4.250 + Other current liabilities 0.880 + Short-term provisions 0.320 = 13.950); Net Assets/Purchase Consideration = ₹42.000 lakhs, satisfied by issuing 40,000 (42 lakhs/₹105) equity shares of Blue Ltd. at 5% premium.

Balance Sheet of Blue Ltd. (after absorption) as at 31.3.2025: Share Capital 80.000 (40,000 original + 40,000 new shares of ₹100); Reserves & Surplus 3.500 (Securities Premium 2.000 + General Reserve 1.500); Long-term Borrowings 22.200 (10% Debentures 15.000+7.200); Long-term Provisions 4.750 (Retirement Gratuity 3.450+1.300); Trade Payables 10.150 (7.400+4.250−1.500 inter-company elimination); Other current liabilities 2.120 (1.240+0.880); Short-term provisions 1.030 (0.710+0.320). Total 123.750. Assets: PPE 72.095 (35.650+36.445); Intangible assets (Goodwill) 16.250 (8.750+7.500); Inventories 14.170 (8.890+5.280); Trade receivables 16.685 (13.535+4.650−1.500); Cash and cash equivalents 3.390 (Cash in hand 0.800 + Bank 2.590); Other current assets 1.160 (unrecorded asset). Total 123.750.

Examiner’s Comment: A large number of examinees could not prepare the Balance Sheet and Notes to Accounts in accordance with Schedule III to the Companies Act, 2013, using the information given. Many also failed to compute the correct amount of purchase consideration and goodwill. These errors had a consequential impact on the preparation of the Balance Sheet.

RTP January 2025 · Q10 · Marks: Not stated in source · Approx Time: 10–20 minutes (approx.) · Topic 4: Purchase Consideration
Question:

Astha Ltd. is absorbed by Nistha Ltd.; the consideration being the takeover of liabilities, the payment of cost of absorption not exceeding ₹10,000 (actual cost ₹9,000); the payment of the 9% debentures of ₹50,000 at a premium of 20% through 8% debentures issued at a premium of 25% of face value and the payment of ₹15 per share in cash and allotment of three 11% preference shares of ₹10 each and four equity shares of ₹10 each at a premium of 20% fully paid for every five shares in Astha Ltd.

The number of shares of the vendor company are 1,50,000 of ₹10 each fully paid. Calculate purchase consideration as per AS 14.

Answer / Solution:

As per AS 14 "Accounting for Amalgamations", the term "consideration" has been defined as the aggregate of the shares and other securities issued and the payment made in the form of cash or other assets by the transferee company to the shareholders of the transferor company.

The payment made by the transferee company to discharge the Debenture holders and outside liabilities and cost of winding up of the transferor company shall not be considered as part of purchase consideration.

Computation of Purchase Consideration

Cash payment ₹15 × 1,50,00022,50,000
11% Preference Shares of ₹10 each [(1,50,000 × 3/5) × ₹10]9,00,000
Equity shares of ₹10 each @ 20% premium [(1,50,000 × 4/5) × ₹12]14,40,000
Total Purchase consideration45,90,000
Author’s Note: A common error is including the payment made to discharge the transferor company's debenture holders and outside liabilities within the purchase consideration, missing that AS 14 restricts purchase consideration strictly to amounts paid to the transferor company's shareholders.

RTP September 2025 · Q15 · Marks: Not stated in source · Approx Time: 10–20 minutes (approx.) · Topic 1: Introduction
Question:

X Co. Ltd. (share capital ₹50 lakhs, equity shares of ₹10 each) was taken over by Y Co. Ltd. X Co. Ltd. has General Reserve ₹10,00,000 and Profit and Loss account Cr. ₹5,00,000. Y Co. Ltd. issued 11 equity shares of ₹10 each for every 10 shares of X Co. Ltd. Pass the journal entries in Y Co. Ltd.'s books for the shares issued under the Pooling of Interests method.

Answer / Solution:

Purchase consideration = 50,00,000 × 11/10 = ₹55,00,000.

Journal entries (books of Y Co. Ltd.):

  1. Business Purchase A/c Dr. 55,00,000; To Liquidator of X Co. Ltd. 55,00,000 (business of X Co. Ltd. purchased).
  2. Assets A/c (balancing figure) Dr. 65,00,000; To Business Purchase A/c 55,00,000; To General Reserve A/c 5,00,000; To Profit and Loss A/c 5,00,000 (assets and reserves/surplus taken over — under Pooling of Interests, X's reserves are carried forward at their existing book figures, not merged into goodwill).
  3. Liquidator of X Co. Ltd. Dr. 55,00,000; To Equity Share Capital A/c 55,00,000 (purchase consideration discharged via equity shares of Y Co. Ltd.).

W.N.: Purchase consideration ₹55,00,000 − Share capital of X Co. Ltd. ₹50,00,000 = ₹5,00,000 to be adjusted from (i.e., absorbed into) General Reserve.

Author’s Note: Some examinees computed goodwill for the excess of purchase consideration over share capital, applying the Purchase Method's logic instead of the Pooling of Interests method's requirement to adjust the difference directly against reserves.

I. Descriptive & Scenario-Based Questions (pure AS 25)

PYQ May 2025 · Q3(b) · Marks: 7 · Approx Time: 13 minutes (approx.) · Topic 7.10: Seasonal/occasional revenue and costs are not deferred to a later interim period; change of estimate applied prospectively
Question:

XY Limited reported a Profit Before Tax (PBT) of ₹18 lakhs for the third quarter ending 31st December 2024. Following observations are noted: (i) Dividend income of ₹8 lakhs received during the quarter has been recognized to the extent of ₹2 lakh only. (ii) Sales promotion expenses ₹15 lakhs incurred in the third quarter, 70% has been deferred to the fourth quarter as the sales in the last quarter is high. (iii) In the third quarter, the company changed depreciation method from WDV to SLM, which resulted in excess depreciation of ₹4 lakhs. The entire amount has been debited in the third quarter, though the share of the third quarter is only ₹1 lakhs. (iv) ₹3 lakhs extra-ordinary gain received in third quarter was allocated equally to the third and fourth quarter. (v) Cumulative loss resulting from change in method of inventory valuation was recognized in the third quarter of ₹5 lakhs. Out of this loss ₹2 lakhs relates to previous quarters. (vi) Sale of investment in the first quarter resulted in a gain of ₹30 lakhs. The company had apportioned this equally to the four quarters.

Calculate the result of the third quarter as per AS 25 and also comment on the company's view on each observation. (7 Marks)

Answer / Solution:

As per para 36 of AS 25 "Interim Financial Reporting", seasonal or occasional revenue and cost within a financial year should not be deferred as of interim date until it is appropriate to defer at the end of the enterprise's financial year.

Comments on observations: (i) Dividend income received during 3rd quarter should be recognised in the 3rd quarter only. (ii) Sales promotion expenses cannot be deferred on the basis that fourth quarter has more sales; recognised in 3rd quarter only. (iii) As per AS 10, a change in depreciation method is a change in accounting estimate per AS 5, applied prospectively – no adjustment would be required for this observation. (iv) Extra-ordinary gain of ₹3 lakhs should be wholly recognized in 3rd quarter only. (v) Loss of ₹2 lakhs belongs to previous quarters, not 3rd quarter, so it should not be deducted from the profit of 3rd quarter. (vi) Gain on sale of investment is an occasional gain, so it cannot be deferred; the ₹7.5 lakhs considered as income of the 1st quarter will be reversed from the profit of the 3rd quarter.

Statement showing Adjusted Profit Before Tax for the third quarter:

Profit before tax (as reported)18,00,000
Add: Dividend income (8,00,000 − 2,00,000)6,00,000
Excess depreciation charged in 3rd quarter due to change in method—
Extra ordinary gain (3,00,000 − 1,50,000)1,50,000
Cumulative loss due to change in inventory valuation method, applied retrospectively (5,00,000−3,00,000)2,00,000
Subtotal27,50,000
Less: Sales promotion expenses (70% of 15 lakhs)(10,50,000)
Less: Gain on sale of investment (occasional gain should not be deferred)(7,50,000)
Adjusted Profit before tax for the third quarter9,50,000
Examiner’s Comment: Most examinees exhibited inadequate knowledge of AS 25 "Interim Financial Reporting." They failed to calculate the Adjusted Profit Before Tax for the third quarter accurately. Even among those who arrived at the correct figure, very few provided appropriate observations with sound reasoning.

PYQ May 2026 · Q1(c) · Marks: 4 · Approx Time: 8 minutes (approx.) · Topic 7.9: Income tax recognised per interim period using the estimated weighted average annual tax rate, with separately-taxed items (capital gains) taxed at their own specific rate Compulsory
Question:

The following information is provided in respect of Vardhman Ltd. for the financial year 2025-26: Estimated total annual income ₹5,00,000 (inclusive of estimated capital gains earned in 2nd quarter ₹1,00,000). Tax rates for FY 2025-26: On capital gains 20%; On other incomes – first ₹2,00,000 at 35%, balance income at 40%. Assuming no difference between estimated taxable income and estimated accounting income, you are required: (i) To compute total tax expenses for the year 2025-26; (ii) To calculate tax expenses for each quarter, when the estimated income of each quarter is ₹1,25,000 and income for 2nd quarter includes capital gain of ₹1,00,000. (4 Marks)

Answer / Solution:

(i) Computation of Total tax expense: As per para 29 of AS 25 'Interim Financial Reporting', income tax expense is recognised in each interim period based on the best estimate of the weighted average annual income tax rate expected for the full financial year.

Capital Gain1,00,000
Other Income4,00,000
Estimated total Annual Income (A)5,00,000
20% on ₹1,00,000 (capital gain)20,000
35% on First ₹2,00,00070,000
40% on the remaining ₹2,00,00080,000
Total Tax expense (B)1,70,000

Weighted average annual income tax rate (excluding the separately-taxed capital gain) = 1,50,000/4,00,000 = 37.5%. Income Tax Rate on Capital Gain = 20%.

QuarterTotal IncomeCapital GainQuarterly Tax CalculationQuarterly Tax expense
Q11,25,000Nil1,25,000 × 37.5%46,875
Q21,25,0001,00,000Tax on Capital Gains = 1,00,000×20% = 20,000; Tax on remaining income = 25,000×37.5% = 9,37529,375
Q31,25,000Nil1,25,000 × 37.5%46,875
Q41,25,000Nil1,25,000 × 37.5%46,875
Author’s Note: Some examinees applied the single blended 37.5% rate to the capital gain quarter as well, instead of taxing the capital-gain component at its own specific 20% rate and only the balance of that quarter's income at the weighted average rate.

MTP January 2026 Set 1 · Q2(b) · Marks: 7 · Approx Time: 13 minutes (approx.) · Topic 1: Introduction
Question:

Aerodots Ltd. has the following capital structure as on 31.03.2025 (₹ in thousands): Equity Share Capital (shares of ₹10 each) 600; General Reserve 540; Securities Premium 200; Profit & Loss 100; Revaluation Reserve 30; Investment Allowance Reserve (Statutory Reserve) 75; Infrastructure Development Reserve 25; Loan Funds 2000. On 1st April, 2025 the company wants to buy back 14,000 equity shares of ₹10 each at ₹30 per share, duly authorized. You are required to calculate the maximum permissible number of equity shares that can be bought back.

Answer / Solution:
TestShares (thousands)
Shares Outstanding Test (25% of 60,000 shares)15
Resources Test (25% of Shareholders' funds ÷ ₹30 buyback price)12
Debt Equity Ratio Test11
Maximum buy-back permitted [least of the above]11

Thus, the lowest being 11,000 shares, the company cannot buy back the requested 14,000 shares.

W.N.1 Shares Outstanding Test: outstanding 60,000 shares; 25% = 15,000.

W.N.2 Resources Test: Paid-up capital 600 + Free reserves (540+200+100=840) = Shareholders' funds 1,440; 25% = 360; ÷ buy-back price ₹30 = 12,000 shares.

W.N.3 Debt-Equity Ratio Test: Loan funds 2,000; minimum equity to maintain (2:1) = 1,000; present equity funds 1,440; future equity funds (after 110 transferred to CRR, solved simultaneously) = 1,330; maximum permitted buy-back of equity = 1,330−1,000 = 330; ‷ ₹30/share = 11,000 shares.

Author’s Note: Some examinees included statutory reserves (Investment Allowance Reserve) or the Infrastructure Development Reserve in "free reserves" for the Resources Test, when only reserves freely available for distribution should be counted.

The company intends to buy-back 80,000 equity shares of ₹10 each at a premium of 150%. You are required to state whether the company can buy back equity shares. (4 Marks)

Answer / Solution:

Determination of Buy-back of maximum no. of shares as per the Companies Act, 2013

1. Shares Outstanding Test

Number of shares outstanding4,00,000
25% of the shares outstanding1,00,000

2. Resources Test: Maximum permitted limit 25% of Equity paid up capital + Free Reserves

Paid up capital (₹)40,00,000
Free reserves (₹) (48,00,000 + 18,00,000 + 10,00,000)76,00,000
Shareholders' funds (₹)1,16,00,000

Actual Number of shares for buy-back80,000

3. Debt Equity Ratio Test: Loans cannot be in excess of twice the Equity Funds post Buy-Back

Debt Equity ratio of the company should not exceed 2:1 after such buy-back. In this case, the debt is ₹92,00,000 (60,00,000 + 32,00,000)* and equity after such buy back will be ₹96,00,000 (1,16,00,000 − 20,00,000). Thus, the debt equity ratio is 0.96:1, which is less than 2:1.

Company qualifies all tests for buy-back of shares and came to the conclusion that it can buy 80,000 equity shares @ ₹25.

* Total debt may be considered (i.e. including current liability).

Author’s Note: Several examinees omitted the debt-equity ratio test entirely when determining the maximum number of shares that could be bought back under the Companies Act, 2013, applying only the shares-outstanding and resources tests.

MTP May 2026 Set 2 · Q6(c) · Marks: 5 · Approx Time: 9 minutes (approx.) · Topic 2: Prov. Sect. 70 Comp. Act, 2013
Question:

Alpha Chemicals Ltd., a listed company, proposes a buy-back of 12% of its equity share capital from its free reserves under Section 68 of the Companies Act, 2013. On scrutiny of its records, the following details were observed: 1. The company intends to route the buy-back through its wholly-owned subsidiary. 2. The company had defaulted on repayment of a term loan to a public sector bank, which was fully repaid 27 months ago. 3. The company has not filed its Annual Return and Financial Statements for the preceding financial year. 4. The company had declared a dividend in the last year, but the amount remains unpaid for 35 days from the date of declaration.

You are required to: Examine the compliance of Alpha Chemicals Ltd. with the requirements of Section 70 of the Companies Act, 2013 and state whether the company is eligible to proceed with the proposed buy-back. (5 Marks)

Answer / Solution:

As per Section 70 of the Companies Act, 2013, the company cannot buy back its own shares under the following conditions, all of which apply to Alpha Chemicals Ltd.:

1. Buy-back through Subsidiary – Prohibited. Section 70(1)(a): A company shall not buy back shares through any subsidiary, including wholly owned subsidiaries.

2. Default in Term Loan – Three-Year Cooling Off Required. Section 70(1)(c): A company that has defaulted in repayment of a term loan can buy back shares only after 3 years from the cessation of default. Alpha repaid the loan only 27 months ago — still short of the required 36-month period. Hence, not eligible.

3. Non-Filing of Annual Return and Financial Statements. Section 70(2): Buy-back is prohibited if the company has not complied with Sections 92 (Annual Return) and 129 (Financial Statements). Alpha has failed to file both which disqualifies it from buy-back.

4. Unpaid Dividend for More Than 30 Days. Section 127 read with Section 70(2): Non-distribution of declared dividend within 30 days is a punishable offence. Dividend unpaid for 35 days, this is a default.

Alpha Chemicals Ltd. is not eligible to proceed with the buy-back under Section 70 due to multiple violations.

Author’s Note: Many examinees identified only one or two of the four independent Section 70 violations, most often missing the wholly-owned-subsidiary prohibition since it is easy to assume a wholly-owned subsidiary is functionally the same entity as its parent.

Answer / Solution:

As per Section 70 of the Companies Act, 2013, the company cannot buy back its own shares under the following conditions, all of which apply to Alpha Chemicals Ltd.:

  1. Buy-back through Subsidiary – Prohibited. Section 70(1)(a): A company shall not buy back shares through any subsidiary, including wholly owned subsidiaries.
  2. Default in Term Loan – Three-Year Cooling Off Required. Section 70(1)(c): A company that has defaulted in repayment of a term loan can buy back shares only after 3 years from the cessation of default. Alpha repaid the loan only 27 months ago — still short of the required 36-month period. Hence, not eligible.
  3. Non-Filing of Annual Return and Financial Statements. Section 70(2): Buy-back is prohibited if the company has not complied with Sections 92 (Annual Return) and 129 (Financial Statements). Alpha has failed to file both, which disqualifies it from buy-back.
  4. Unpaid Dividend for More Than 30 Days. Section 127 read with Section 70(2): Non-distribution of declared dividend within 30 days is a punishable offence. Dividend unpaid for 35 days, this is a default.

Alpha Chemicals Ltd. is not eligible to proceed with the buy-back under Section 70 due to multiple violations.

Author’s Note: A common error here is treating only one of Section 70's several disqualifying conditions as controlling, when a buy-back is barred if any one of the listed conditions is breached, and this company breaches more than one simultaneously.

PYQ January 2026 · Q3(a) · Marks: 7 · Approx Time: 13 minutes (approx.) · Topic 1: Introduction
Question:

Balance Sheet of P Limited as at 31st March, 2025: Share Capital ₹1,500 lakh (150 lakh Equity Shares of ₹10 each); Reserves and Surplus ₹2,750 lakh (Capital Reserve 380, Securities Premium 300, Revaluation Reserve 120, General Reserve 1,800, Surplus 150); Long Term Borrowings ₹3,450 lakh (12% Debentures 2,250, Unsecured Loans 1,200); Short Term Borrowings (Current Maturities) ₹1,980 lakh; Trade Payables ₹1,500 lakh; Total ₹11,180 lakh. Assets: PPE ₹5,675 lakh; Inventories ₹1,005 lakh; Trade Receivables ₹1,500 lakh; Cash and Cash Equivalents ₹3,000 lakh; Total ₹11,180 lakh.

Considering the large surplus funds, the company decides to buy back 30 lakh Equity Shares on 1st April, 2025. Prevailing market value ₹16/share; to induce shareholders, offer price is 25% over market. Buy-back is duly authorized by Articles and necessary resolution passed.

Comment with your calculations, whether buy-back of shares by the company is within the provisions of the Companies Act, 2013. If yes, pass necessary journal entries towards buy-back of shares. (7 Marks)

Answer / Solution:

Determination of Buy-back of maximum no. of shares as per the Companies Act, 2013:

1. Shares Outstanding Test: Number of shares outstanding 150 lakh; 25% of shares outstanding = 37.5 lakh.

2. Resources Test: Paid up capital ₹1,500 lakh; Free reserves (300+1,800+150) ₹2,250 lakh; Shareholders' funds ₹3,750 lakh; 25% of Shareholders' funds ₹937.5 lakh; Buy-back price per share ₹20 (₹16 × 1.25); Number of shares that can be bought back = 46.875 lakh.

3. Debt Equity Ratio Test (loans cannot exceed twice the equity funds post buy-back): Loan funds (3,450+1,980) = 5,430 lakh; Minimum equity to be maintained after buy-back (2:1 ratio, a/2) = 2,715 lakh; Present equity/shareholders' funds = 3,750 lakh. Using the simultaneous-equation method (amount transferred to CRR = x, maximum permitted buy-back of equity = y): (3,750−x) − 2,715 = y, and y/20×10 = x (i.e. y=2x); solving gives x=345 lakh, y=690 lakh. Maximum number of shares at ₹20/share = 34.50 lakh shares.

Summary: Shares Outstanding Test 37.5 lakh; Resources Test 46.875 lakh; Debt Equity Ratio Test 34.50 lakh. Maximum number of shares that can be bought back (least of the three) = 34.50 lakh. Company qualifies all tests; it can buy a maximum of 34.5 lakh shares, but wants to buy back only 30 lakh equity shares @₹20 – therefore, the buy-back of 30 lakh shares is within the provisions of the Companies Act, 2013.

Note on CRR: if one share is bought back, ₹10 face value is reduced from share capital, ₹10 premium (20−10) is reduced from Securities Premium, and an amount equal to the face value (₹10) must be transferred from free reserves to CRR, since CRR itself is not a free reserve available for dividend distribution.

Journal Entries for Buy-back of shares (₹ in lakhs):

ParticularsDebitCredit
(a) Equity share capital account Dr. 300; Securities premium account Dr. 300
  To Equity shares buy-back account
(Being cancellation of shares bought back)		300 / 300600
(b) Equity shares buy-back account Dr.
  To Bank account
(Being buy-back of 30 lakh equity shares of ₹10 each @₹20 per share)		600600
(c) Revenue reserve account Dr.
  To Capital redemption reserve account
(Being transfer of free reserves to CRR to the extent of nominal value of capital bought back through free reserves)		300300
Examiner’s Comment: Several examinees were unable to determine the permissible amount of buy-back in accordance with the relevant provisions. Errors were also observed in the computation of the Capital Redemption Reserve and in passing the necessary journal entries. While many examinees correctly applied two of the required tests, they failed to correctly apply the Debt-Equity ratio test.

PYQ September 2024 · Q3(b) · Marks: 7 · Approx Time: 13 minutes (approx.) · Topic 1: Introduction
Question:

Aerodots Ltd. has the following capital structure as on 31.03.2024: Equity Share Capital (shares of ₹10 each) ₹6,00,000 [thousands]; Reserves: General Reserve ₹5,40,000; Securities Premium ₹2,00,000; Profit & Loss ₹1,00,000; Revaluation Reserve ₹30,000; Investment Allowance Reserve (Statutory Reserve) ₹75,000; Infrastructure Development Reserve ₹25,000; Loan Funds ₹20,00,000 (all figures ₹ in thousands, as printed).

On 1st April, 2024 the company wants to buy back 14,000 equity shares of ₹10 each at ₹30 per Equity share.

You are required to calculate maximum permissible number of equity shares that can be bought back.

Buy Back of shares is duly authorized by its articles and necessary resolution has been passed by the company.

Answer / Solution:

Statement determining the maximum number of shares to be bought back (in thousands):

ParticularsNumber of shares
Shares Outstanding Test (W.N.1)15
Resources Test (W.N.2)12
Debt Equity Ratio Test (W.N.3)11
Maximum number of shares that can be bought back [least of the above]11

Thus, the lowest being 11,000 shares, the company cannot buy back 14,000 shares.

Working Notes:

1. Shares Outstanding Test: Number of shares outstanding 60 (thousand); 25% of the shares outstanding = 15 (thousand).

2. Resources Test: Paid up capital ₹600 (thousand); Free reserves (540+200+100) ₹840 (thousand); Shareholders' funds ₹1,440 (thousand); 25% of Shareholders fund ₹360 (thousand); Buy-back price per share ₹30; Number of shares that can be bought back = 12,000 shares.

3. Debt Equity Ratio Test (loans cannot exceed twice the Equity Funds post Buy-Back): Loan funds ₹2,000 (thousand); Minimum equity to be maintained after buy-back in the ratio of 2:1 (a/2) ₹1,000 (thousand); Present equity shareholders fund ₹1,440 (thousand); Future equity shareholders fund (see W.N.4) (1,440−110) = ₹1,330 (thousand); Maximum permitted buy-back of Equity [(d)−(b)] ₹330 (thousand); Maximum number of shares that can be bought back @ ₹30/share = 11,000 shares.

4. Amount transferred to CRR and maximum equity to be bought back, by simultaneous equation method – let amount transferred to CRR = x, maximum permitted buy-back of equity = y. Equation 1: (Present Equity − Transfer to CRR) − Minimum Equity to be maintained = Maximum Permitted Buy-Back ⇒ (1,440−x)−1,000 = y ⇒ 440−x = y. Equation 2: y/30 × 10 = x, i.e. 3x = y. Solving: x = ₹110 (thousand), y = ₹330 (thousand).

Alternatively, Maximum number of shares from debt equity ratio test may be worked out as: Buy-back price + Face value of equity shares = ₹30+₹10 = ₹40. Excess of equity fund over the minimum equity to be maintained = 1,440−1,000 = 440 (thousand). Number of Shares that can be bought back = 440/40 (thousand) = 11 (thousand).

Examiner’s Comment: Many examinees failed to calculate the number of shares eligible for buyback under the Debt-Equity Ratio Test. Errors were also observed in the Resource Test and Shares Outstanding Test, resulting in incorrect calculations of the maximum permissible number of shares for buyback.

Author’s Note: A common error here is transferring only the face value of the shares bought back to Capital Redemption Reserve without also correctly routing the securities-premium portion of the buy-back price through the Securities Premium account, or computing the subsequent bonus issue on the pre-buy-back share count instead of the post-buy-back balance.

For the purpose, it issues 1 lakh 11% preference shares of ₹10 each at par, the entire amount being payable with applications. The company uses ₹16 lakhs of its balance in Securities Premium Account apart from its adequate balance in General Reserve to fulfill the legal requirements regarding buy-back. Give necessary journal entries to record the above transactions.

1. Calculation of amount used from General Reserve Account

₹

₹

Internal Reconstruction — Internal Reconstruction

Every MTP/RTP/PYQ question that tests this chapter, collected in one place, with official answers and topic tags — so you can practise every question this topic has been examined with, without hunting through separate papers.

A note on accuracy (please read): This is the first edition of this book, assembled with AI assistance and reviewed as carefully as we could manage, but it has not been independently audited question-by-question. If you spot an error — a wrong figure, a wrong answer, anything that looks off — please email capranavpratiktulshyan@gmail.com with the question reference so it can be corrected in the next edition.
Scope of this book (18 questions): Covers 34 sittings: MTP Jan2025 Set1, MTP Jan2025 Set2, MTP Jan2026 Set1, MTP Jan2026 Set2, MTP May2023 Set1, MTP May2023 Set2, MTP May2024 Set1, MTP May2024 Set2, MTP May2025 Set1, MTP May2025 Set2, MTP May2026 Set1, MTP May2026 Set2, MTP Nov2023 Set1, MTP Nov2023 Set2, MTP Sep2024 Set1, MTP Sep2024 Set2, MTP Sep2025 Set1, MTP Sep2025 Set2, PYQ Jan2025, PYQ Jan2026, PYQ May2023, PYQ May2024, PYQ May2025, PYQ May2026, PYQ Nov2023, PYQ Sep2024, PYQ Sep2025, RTP Jan2025, RTP Jan2026, RTP May2024, RTP May2025, RTP May2026, RTP Sep2024, RTP Sep2025. MCQs on this chapter are deliberately not included here — practise those on the dedicated MCQ platform; this book is for descriptive/scenario practice with full worked answers.
How this book is organised: Two sections — I. Descriptive (pure Internal Reconstruction) and II. Integrated (questions where Internal Reconstruction is one part of a larger question that also tests another standard). An empty Section II for a chapter is normal and expected, not a mistake — most multi-topic-looking questions are split so each topic gets its own clean entry, so genuinely combined questions are the rarer case. Each answer includes either a real Examiner's Comment (tan/orange box, quoted from ICAI's own published feedback, where one exists for that sitting) or an Author's Note (pale pink box, a likely pitfall identified by the author, not an official ICAI finding, and may not apply in every case) — see How to Read this Book.md for the full key to every colour and symbol used.

MTP January 2025 Set 1 · Q3(b) · Marks: 10 · Approx Time: 18 minutes (approx.) · Topic 3: Alteration of Share Capital
Question:

Following is the summarized Balance Sheet of Fortunate Ltd. as on 31st March, 2024. Liabilities: 15,000 8% Preference shares of ₹50 each 7,50,000; 18,750 Equity shares of ₹50 each 9,37,500; Profit and Loss Account (5,63,750); Loan 7,16,250; Trade Payables 2,58,750; Other Liabilities 43,750; Total 21,42,500. Assets: Building at cost less depreciation 5,00,000; Plant at cost less depreciation 3,35,000; Trademarks and goodwill at cost 3,97,500; Inventory 5,00,000; Trade Receivables 4,10,000; Total 21,42,500. (Note: Preference shares dividend is in arrear for last five years.)

The Company is running with the shortage of working capital and not earnings profits. A scheme of reconstruction has been approved by both the classes of shareholders. The summarized scheme of reconstruction is as follows: (i) The equity shareholders have agreed that their ₹50 shares should be reduced to ₹5 by cancellation of ₹45.00 per share. They have also agreed to subscribe for three new equity shares of ₹5.00 each for each equity share held. (ii) The preference shareholders have agreed to forego the arrears of dividends and to accept for each ₹50 preference share, 4 new 6% preference shares of ₹10 each, plus 3 new equity shares of ₹5.00 each, all credited as fully paid. (iii) Lenders to the company for ₹1,87,500 have agreed to convert their loan into shares and for this purpose they will be allotted 15,000 new preference shares of ₹10 each and 7,500 new equity shares of ₹5.00 each. (iv) The directors have agreed to subscribe in cash for 25,000 new equity shares of ₹5.00 each in addition to any shares to be subscribed by them under (i) above. (v) Of the cash received by the issue of new shares, ₹2,50,000 is to be used to reduce the loan due by the company. (vi) The equity share capital cancelled is to be applied: (a) To write off the debit balance in the Profit and Loss A/c, and (b) To write off ₹43,750 from the value of plant. Any balance remaining is to be used to write down the value of trademarks and goodwill. The nominal capital, as reduced, is to be increased to ₹8,12,500 for preference share capital and ₹9,37,500 for equity share capital.

You are required to pass journal entries to show the effect of above scheme and prepare the Balance Sheet of the Company after reconstruction.

Answer / Solution:

In the books of Fortunate Ltd. — Journal Entries:

  1. Equity share capital A/c (₹50) Dr. 9,37,500; To Equity share capital A/c (₹5) 93,750; To Capital reduction A/c 8,43,750 (Being equity capital reduced to nominal value of ₹5 each).
  2. Bank A/c Dr. 2,81,250; To Equity share capital 2,81,250 (Being 3 right shares against each share was issued and subscribed).
  3. 8% Preference share capital A/c (₹50) Dr. 7,50,000; Capital reduction A/c Dr. 75,000; To 6% Preference share capital (₹10) 6,00,000; To equity share capital 2,25,000 (Being 8% preference shares of ₹50 each converted to 6% preference shares of ₹10 each and also given to them 3 equity shares for every share held).
  4. Loan A/c Dr. 1,87,500; To 6% Preference share capital A/c (15,000 × ₹10) 1,50,000; To Equity share capital A/c (7,500 × ₹5) 37,500 (Being loan to the extent of ₹1,87,500 converted into share capital).
  5. Bank A/c (25,000 × ₹5) Dr. 1,25,000; To Equity share application A/c 1,25,000 (Being shares subscribed by the directors).
  6. Equity share application A/c Dr. 1,25,000; To Equity share capital A/c 1,25,000 (Being application money transferred to capital A/c).
  7. Loan A/c Dr. 2,50,000; To Bank A/c 2,50,000 (Being loan repaid).
  8. Capital reduction A/c Dr. 7,68,750; To Profit and loss A/c 5,63,750; To Plant A/c 43,750; To Trademarks and Goodwill A/c (balancing figure) 1,61,250 (Being losses and assets written off to the extent required).

Balance sheet of Fortunate Ltd. (and reduced) as on 31.3.2024:

ParticularsNotes₹
Share capital115,12,500
Long-term borrowings (7,16,250 − 1,87,500 − 2,50,000)2,78,750
Trade Payables2,58,750
Other current liabilities43,750
Total20,93,750
Property, Plant and Equipment27,91,250
Intangible assets32,36,250
Inventories5,00,000
Trade receivables4,10,000
Cash and cash equivalents41,56,250
Total20,93,750

Notes to accounts: 1. Share Capital — Authorized: 81,250 Preference shares of ₹10 each 8,12,500 + 1,87,500 Equity shares of ₹5 each 9,37,500 = 17,50,000. Issued/subscribed/paid up: 1,52,500 equity shares of ₹5 each 7,62,500 (out of which 52,500 shares issued for consideration other than cash) + 75,000 6% Preference shares of ₹10 each 7,50,000 = 15,12,500. 2. PPE: Building 5,00,000 + Plant 2,91,250 = 7,91,250. 3. Intangible assets: Trademarks and goodwill 2,36,250. 4. Cash and cash equivalents: Bank (2,81,250+1,25,000−2,50,000) = 1,56,250.

Author’s Note: A frequent slip is crediting the full nominal-value difference on conversion of preference or debenture capital straight to Capital Reduction without separately tracking each conversion's own gain, or misapplying the equity-shareholders' cash subscription before the capital reduction entries.

The following information of Rocky Ltd. as at March 31, 2024 (₹ in lacs): Fully paid equity shares of ₹10 each 500; Capital Reserve 6; 12% Debentures 400; Debenture Interest Outstanding 48; Trade payables 165; Directors' Remuneration Outstanding 10; Other Outstanding Expenses 11; Provisions 33. Assets: Goodwill 15; Land and Building 184; Plant and Machinery 286; Furniture and Fixtures 41; Inventory 142; Trade receivables 80; Cash at Bank 27; Discount on Issue of Debentures 8; Profit and Loss Account 390. The following scheme of internal reconstruction was framed, approved by the Tribunal and all the concerned parties, and implemented: (i) All the equity shares be converted into the same number of fully-paid equity shares of ₹2.50 each. (ii) Directors agree to forego their outstanding remuneration. (iii) The debentureholders also agree to forego outstanding interest in return of their 12% debentures being converted into 13% debentures. (iv) The existing shareholders agree to subscribe for cash, fully paid equity shares of ₹2.50 each for ₹125 lacs. Trade payables for ₹65 lacs accept equity shares whereas those for ₹100 lacs accept ₹80 lacs in cash in full settlement. (vi) The Assets are revalued as under: Land and building ₹230 lacs, Plant and Machinery ₹220 lacs, Inventory ₹120 lacs, Trade receivables ₹76 lacs. Pass Journal Entries for all the above mentioned transactions immediately after the reconstruction.

Note: In a scheme of Reconstruction, Goodwill, Losses etc. should be written off against the Reconstruction Account whether or not it is mentioned in the question.

Author’s Note: A common error is omitting to write off Goodwill and other fictitious/negative balances against the Reconstruction Account purely because the question does not explicitly instruct it, missing the general rule that such balances are always written off in a scheme of internal reconstruction whether or not the question says so.

MTP January 2026 Set 1 · Q4(b) · Marks: 8 · Approx Time: 15 minutes (approx.) · Topic 2: Methods of internal reconstruction
Question:

Summarized Balance Sheet of Vijay Ltd. as on 31st March, 2025: Equity Shares of ₹10 each 3,50,000; 8% Cumulative Preference Shares of ₹100 each 1,75,000; 6% Debentures of ₹100 each 1,40,000; Sundry Creditors 1,75,000; Provision for taxation 3,500; Total 8,43,500. Assets: PPE 4,37,500; Investments (Market value ₹33,250) 35,000; Current Assets 3,50,000; P&L A/c (Dr.) 21,000; Total 8,43,500. Scheme of Internal Reconstruction approved and effective 31st March, 2025: (1) Investments brought to market value; (2) Taxation liability settled at ₹5,250 out of Current Assets; (3) balance of P&L written off; (4) equity shares reduced to ₹4 each; (5) preference shares reduced to ₹60 each; (6) debenture rate increased to 9%, debenture holders surrender ₹100 debentures and exchange 1-for-1 for fresh ₹80 debentures; (7) balance Current Assets revalued at ₹1,57,500; (8) PPE written down to 80%; (9) one creditor of ₹70,000 gives up 50% of claim, allotted 8,750 equity shares of ₹4 each in settlement. Pass Journal entries.

Answer / Solution:

Journal entries (books of Vijay Ltd.):

  1. Capital Reduction A/c Dr. 1,750; To Investments A/c 1,750 (investments revalued to market value).
  2. (a) Provision for taxation A/c Dr. 3,500; Capital Reduction A/c Dr. 1,750; To Liability for taxation 5,250 (tax liability ascertained). (b) Liability for Taxation Dr. 5,250; To Current Assets (Bank) 5,250 (tax paid).
  3. Capital Reduction A/c Dr. 21,000; To Profit & Loss A/c 21,000 (P&L debit balance written off).
  4. Equity Share Capital (₹10) A/c Dr. 3,50,000; To Equity Share Capital (₹4) A/c 1,40,000; To Capital Reduction A/c 2,10,000 (conversion of equity capital).
  5. 8% Cumulative Preference Share Capital A/c Dr. 1,75,000; To 8% Cumulative Preference Share Capital A/c 1,05,000; To Capital Reduction A/c 70,000 (conversion of preference capital to ₹60 each).
  6. 6% Debentures A/c Dr. 1,40,000; To 9% Debentures A/c 1,12,000; To Capital Reduction A/c 28,000 (fresh ₹80 debentures issued to existing holders).
  7. Capital Reduction A/c Dr. 1,87,250; To Current Assets A/c 1,87,250 (current assets revalued).
  8. Capital Reduction A/c Dr. 87,500; To Property, Plant & Equipment A/c 87,500 (PPE written down to 80%).
  9. Sundry Creditors A/c Dr. 70,000; To Equity Share Capital (₹4) A/c 35,000; To Capital Reduction A/c 35,000 (creditor's claim settled 50% cash-equivalent-in-shares, 50% given up).
  10. Capital Reduction A/c Dr. 43,750; To Capital Reserve A/c (balancing figure) 43,750 (balance of Capital Reduction transferred to Capital Reserve).
Author’s Note: Some examinees missed crediting Capital Reduction for the "gain" side of each conversion entry (e.g. the difference between old and new share/debenture face values), recording only the reduction without recognising the corresponding Capital Reduction credit.
